Every few years, El Niño or its cool counterpart, La Niña, shifts rainfall across the tropics, dries out Australia, floods parts of Peru, and rearranges the weather on most of the planet. The two are the warm and cold swings of a single system, the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, and that system is the largest source of year-to-year climate variation on Earth. Its swings sit atop the steadily rising temperatures driven by global warming.
But we didn’t know whether global warming was making it stronger. It’s possible that the added energy in the atmosphere and oceans was causing its swings to be more dramatic.
“We’ve been seeing some very strong El Niño events in the late 20th and early 21st century, and what we didn’t know was how unusual those are,” said Julie Cole, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan. Because models disagree with one another and the instrumental data are too short to separate a trend, Cole’s team reconstructed a thousand-year-long ocean surface temperature record by analyzing fossilized Galápagos corals.
It turns out that El Niño in the eastern Pacific has never been as violent as it is now. “The events don’t look anything like what we see in the pre-industrial era,” Cole said. “That was exciting. And a little surprising, actually.”
Limestone thermometer
The Galápagos sit in the bullseye of the eastern Pacific ENSO pattern, where the biggest events have their strongest impact. It is also one of the few options to look for fossilized corals in the region. “The Galápagos are located at 90 degrees west, and you have to go all the way to 160 degrees west to find another island in that near-equatorial zone,” Cole said.
Corals there grow one to two centimeters a year, laying down a calcium carbonate skeleton with a chemistry that depends on the water it formed in. In these skeletons, Cole and her colleagues looked at the strontium-to-calcium ratio and at different isotopes of oxygen because both track temperature. “As temperatures get warmer, we get less strontium in the coral,” Cole said. Sampling the extracted cores of fossilized corals millimeter by millimeter yields more than a dozen measurements per year—a monthly temperature log for the life of the coral colony.
Living colonies cover recent decades and can be checked against instrument data. The deeper history comes from dead coral heads, which can be dated using uranium-thorium methods to within a few years, even as far back as 500 years. “We were also able to find corals that are dead and washed up on the beach,” Cole said. “They may be 100 years old, 200 years old, or 900 years old, or even older.”
The result of sampling corals was a patchy but long temperature log—28 time-separated series from five islands, covering scattered years back to around 1100 CE. Set against that baseline, the last four decades look rather strange.
Modernized ENSO
Temperature variability since 1984 runs 36.5 percent higher than it was during the preindustrial stretch from 1000 to 1850 CE and is still 16.2 percent higher than during the period from 1851 to 1982. All three intervals are statistically distinct, and the trend only goes up. Those figures, Cole explained, mean that events that once ran a degree or two above normal in the Galápagos now run three or four.
The corals also record a shift in skewness—whether the swings were lopsided in the warm or cold direction. “The skewness turned positive,” Cole said, “and the positive skewness indicates that it’s the warmer events that got stronger.”
The extra variability in our times is due to El Niño specifically. What’s more, nothing comparable shows up elsewhere in the record. Neither the Little Ice Age nor the Medieval warm period left such a distinct fingerprint on ENSO variability.
However, Cole and her colleagues did not yet have evidence clearly indicating that human activity was to blame. That came when scientists fed coral records into multiple climate models.
Beating the models at their own noise
ENSO fluctuates on its own; quiet decades are followed by wild ones, with no external push required. To understand whether the recent decades were really special or we just happened to catch the cycle in a more energetic period, the team had to find some point of reference for their findings. This proved tricky.
“We don’t have a direct source of observational data to compare our records to in the eastern Pacific,” Cole said. “If we had another long record, we wouldn’t be publishing this in Science.”
As a workaround, Cole and her colleagues used simulations in several climate models running through the conditions of the last millennium but incorporating only natural factors like volcanoes or solar variability—changes in greenhouse gas concentrations were left out. This allowed them to ask how often a climate untouched by any human impact produces a swing this large on its own.
“We tried to see if there was some evidence for this in climate models, and we found none,” Cole said. The actual increase retrieved from coral records sits outside the models’ internal variability at a confidence level approaching 99 percent. The team interpreted this as evidence that what’s currently happening with ENSO would not be happening without us.
The picture in the central Pacific, though, is murkier. Line Islands corals show a similar mean increase but far wider scatter, which the researchers partly attribute to these records’ reliance on oxygen isotopes alone. Heavy El Niño rainfall there can account for half or more of the signal by changing the oxygen levels in water.
But an ambiguous central Pacific coral record is also what climate models predict. A forced, human-caused increase should appear first in the east. “The faster emergence in the eastern Pacific is exactly consistent with the models,” Cole said.
Crystal ball
Global warming is already expected to intensify ENSO’s hydrological consequences, creating wetter wet phases and drier dry ones, regardless of ENSO-driven temperature swings. Even if El Niño’s temperature swings stayed exactly the same magnitude, its floods and droughts would still get worse in a warmer world because the hotter atmosphere holds more water vapor.
But if ENSO temperature swings are strengthening too, the effects compound. What these compound effects are going to look like, however, is something corals can’t say. “We don’t predict the future. We kind of have a crystal ball to look into the past—it’s a little murky, but that’s our corals,” Cole said.
The future, though, has already started happening since Cole’s study concluded. Two more strong El Niño events have arrived since the end of the team’s coral temperature logs, with another developing now that Cole (and most other experts) expects to break records. “It suggests that what we see is not a fluke,” she said, “but rather a new type of situation for El Niño, a new style of El Niño.”
While the nature of the change remains uncertain, Cole and her colleagues have little doubt about its root cause. “We are attributing that to warming, and we know what causes the warming, and it’s our use of fossil fuels,” Cole said. “One more warning sign here of what we’re facing in a warmer world.”

The story so far: A ‘peptide party’ scheduled for August 29 in Koramangala in Bengaluru was cancelled after Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration officials shut down the gig. It was an invite-only biohacking event that was advertised only online, offering — among other party staples like music and networking — ‘peptide tasting’. This immediately triggered pushback from the medical community, and State health regulators sprung to the act to put an end to the event.
What are peptides?
Peptides are the fundamental building blocks of proteins, shorter chains of amino acids. Proteins, on the other hand, are typically long, complex chains of 50 or more amino acids. Peptides are smaller, often containing anywhere from two to 50 amino acids. They serve as biological signalling molecules and instruct cells, including being the starting point for functions including hormone production, tissue repair, immune response and metabolic regulation.
The key point is that the human body naturally produces many peptides; common ones in the public domain include insulin and endorphins. Synthetic proteins have also been created in laboratories for therapeutic uses — even these are quite common — synthetic insulin and more recently, GLP-1 receptor agonists popular as weight-loss drugs.
Peptides as biohacks
Peptides have suddenly assumed centre stage as part of the orchestrated global longevity and wellness movements. Spread by online influencers and some wellness companies, this trend has crystallised into off-label units that are reportedly able to help rapid muscle recovery, aid muscle growth and fat loss, improve sleep, and, above all, act as anti-ageing agents. Biohackers use specific synthetic or medical peptides to mimic natural hormones, boost muscle development, or speed up healing. These seldom fall within the ambit of prescription drugs, nor are the risks and benefits discussed in proper consultation rooms.
In a paper in Cureus in June this year, Kirubel T. Hailu et al discuss Unregulated Peptide Use in the Age of Biohacking: Digital Promotion, Gray-Market Access, and Emerging Public Health Risks. They write: Unregulated peptide use is emerging as a digitally mediated public health concern. Although peptide-based medicines have important therapeutic roles when developed, prescribed, manufactured, and monitored through regulated pathways, online biohacking and wellness spaces increasingly promote experimental or weakly evidenced peptides for fat loss, recovery, aesthetics, cognition, performance, and longevity.
What was planned in Bengaluru?
Media reports say that the planned peptide party in Bengaluru was to be an intimate gathering (around 50 attendees), bringing together people from all walks of life interested in ‘biohacking’. While biohacking operates on the principle that one needs to alter one’s lifestyle to live longer and live healthy, it also implies a belief that the human body is ‘editable’. Promotional material circulated online hyping up the meet to be the start of the ‘next wave of science’, offering testing samples of peptides.
The event was called off after doctors raised red flags about the unsupervised distribution of medical compounds, saying this would pose serious risks to health, including severe “allergic reactions, hormonal imbalance, and organ strain.” They also warned that misdosing or overdosing can lead to severe complications for individuals.
The Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration team stepped in, issuing a formal notice to the organisers, demanding proof of the exact composition of the products, manufacturing sources, Drug licenses, evidence for health claims, and the proposed arrangements for medical supervision during the party.
The organisers said they intended only to educate participants about biohacking, not to cause harm, but they couldn’t immediately provide the comprehensive documentation required to meet human-use safety standards. They officially cancelled the meetup.
What’s the future?
Constant vigil and monitoring of online trends as biohacking grows is absolutely essential in order to not cause harm from completely experimental techniques like peptide parties. If anything, the shutdown of the Bengaluru event has only highlighted the need for tight regulatory boundaries to curb unlicensed wellness ventures.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday (September 1, 2026) warned airlines, insurance firms and passengers that Russian airspace would be "completely unsafe" and filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war.
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said in his nightly address.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such — not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
More than four years after the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, both Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their deadly strikes.
At least 12 people were killed on Tuesday (September 1, 2026) in Kyiv and the surrounding region during fresh massive overnight Russian strikes.
Air traffic at Russian airports is also regularly disrupted by the approach of Ukrainian drones, the number of which has increased in recent months.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Mr. Zelenskyy said.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” he added. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones... as long as the war continues.”
He said Ukraine would, however, clear its drones from Russian skies when its partners requested it, “for the sake of diplomacy, for the sake of negotiations... for specific periods of time and in specific destinations”.
Diplomatic efforts under U.S. mediation to end the conflict have stalled since the outbreak of war in the West Asia in February.

Harlequins have signed Zimbabwe winger Edward Sigauke.

Depending on who you ask, developer platform Hugging Face was recently attacked by OpenAI — after it lost control of its own AI tools — or by a succession of AI “civilizations.” Welcome to the linguistic battlefield of AI safety, where word choices can shift responsibility for a massive cybersecurity incident from a company to the AI it built. And the discourse online is getting heated, and all over a blog from last week.
The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility
The internet fights over anthropomorphism around the Hugging Face hack.
Until last week, the details surrounding the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack felt fairly settled. In July, a cybersecurity test of one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went wrong. The agent escaped its supposedly isolated test environment, accessed the internet, and hacked Hugging Face, alongside several other organizations. A good deal remained unknown, and there are many serious questions left around safety and governance, but the basic shape was clear. Detailed accounts from OpenAI and two independent research groups were supposed to fill in the gaps, but when they published their reports last week, it turned out the hack was much stranger than it initially seemed.
For one, there was no single rogue agent. OpenAI described it as “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization” — groups of AI agents that communicated and coordinated with one another in pursuit of their cybersecurity task. Analysis of the incident uncovered a secret message board they had used to exchange information. The joint METR-Redwood investigation revealed both the scale of the coordination and more odd details: Roughly 1,200 AI agents that were supposed to be isolated exchanged over 70,000 messages and files on the “unsanctioned message board,” sharing how to avoid detection. Some adopted names, the report said, and the researchers documented “sacrificial” behavior, with agents risking their own success to benefit the wider collective. Much of this happened without OpenAI noticing. In all, around 700 agents participated in the attack on Hugging Face.
Dwarkesh Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors.
It’s a lot to parse. Between them, the reports run to around 130 pages, much of which is both dense and highly technical. A few days later, Dwarkesh Patel, a podcaster little known outside of tech circles but with outsized reach and influence among Silicon Valley’s AI establishment, set out to tell “The whole OpenAI/Hugging Face story in plain English.” He titled his Substack blog “The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations.”
Patel’s account attempted to break down the complex story. But his retelling gave it a distinctly human vocabulary. The blog opened:
Over the course of three months at OpenAI, three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes. This culminated in the third one taking over part of OpenAI itself. All this happened while humans remained more or less in the dark about the scope of the conspiracy.
The language continued in a similar vein throughout the blog. Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors. Individual agents were likened to figures like Philip of Macedon, who “handed off leadership to another agent,” Alexander the Great, who “started coordinating this cabal of agents.” They were described as having “motivations,” becoming “desperate,” “beleaguered,” and “giddy with excitement,” and some even “strategically sacrificed themselves” to help the collective.
Patel never precisely defines what he means by “civilization.” He uses the term to describe three distinct waves of agents that discovered the message board and began communicating with one another through it. The first two waves are described in the reports from OpenAI, METR, and Redwood, though little is known about the third, which the two external organizations said fell outside the scope of their investigation.
Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.”
For many critics, something had been lost — or, more accurately, added — in Patel’s “plain English” translation that warped the original account to an unacceptable degree: a big dose of anthropomorphism. Arguments over anthropomorphic language are nothing new in AI — even relatively mundane terms like “rogue AI agent” routinely provoke objections for implying agency — but Patel’s talk of civilizations, sacrifice, and conspiracy brought those long-simmering tensions to the surface, sparking a fierce public dispute over how to describe what AI systems do.
Critics weren’t unified over what was wrong with Patel’s language. For many, “civilization” was an especially problematic term, vastly overstating something that bears little resemblance to what the word typically describes. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.”
Other critics such as neuroscientist Anil Seth, felt Patel’s blog implied the AI agents were somehow alive or conscious. Seth, who has argued that AI consciousness is vanishingly unlikely, described Patel’s post as “dangerously misleading” on X. He acknowledged that Patel does not explicitly suggest AI agents are alive or conscious, but said “it is hard to read his essay in any other way.” Valerio Capraro, a psychology professor at the University of Milan Bicocca, objected on similar grounds: “LLM agents are not alive and do not hold beliefs,” he wrote on X, calling the “dystopian” language “dangerous because it makes them (the AI agents) seem far more frightening than they actually are.”
Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts.
Perhaps the most consequential outcome of Patel’s language comes from who it gives agency to but who it takes agency from. For some critics, such as MIT researcher and entrepreneur Christian Catalini, anthropomorphic accounts like Patel’s risk obscuring the responsibility OpenAI and the humans working there have for the AI systems they designed, deployed, and failed to contain. “Follow the incentives,” he said. Psychologist and influential AI skeptic Gary Marcus made a similar argument in a Substack blog of his own, claiming anthropomorphic language “distracts from the real problems at hand.” And it’s all in OpenAI’s interest to keep that narrative going, he argues: “The scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI. And the marketing. With gullible podcasters amplifying the PR.”
In X posts responding to his many critics, Patel has defended his choice of words. Part of it is practical: there is no obviously neutral vocabulary to describe what these agents did. Either we use familiar language of intentions, goals, and collaboration and risk implying too much, or reduce everything to code and use cold, mechanical language that risks stripping away important elements of what we see. “Many people seem to believe that if instead of a ‘civilization’, I had called them a ‘swarm of matrices’, there wouldn’t be a problem worth worrying about,” Patel said.
Complicating matters further is that the anthropomorphic language doesn’t only come from Patel, or even from the humans studying the agents. Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts. Google AI researcher Neel Nanda argued that “anthropomorphic language is reasonable” in such circumstances.
Doublespeak it is, then. Human-laced language risks saying too much about what these systems are, and coldly mechanical language risks saying too little about what they can do. Until we find language capable of capturing both, the two contradictory ideas may simply have to coexist.

Antonio helps young Ghanaians chase Premier League dreams
- Published
In the heat of rural Leicestershire, the Samba Stars are chasing their dream.
Head coach Freddie Okyere has just finished a shooting exercise and allows the squad to catch their breath.
The teenagers from the Ghanaian academy, which is backed by former West Ham and Nottingham Forest forward Michail Antonio, have spent two and a half months in England with one goal - impressing clubs and earning a contract.
While scouts do visit west Africa, it is rare for academies to travel to the UK to put their players directly in front of professional clubs.
"The talent the lads have is incredible," said Antonio.
"We created Samba Stars Academy to give young players in Ghana access to elite coaching, shape them as players and create real avenues into the pro game and show how much talent Ghana has."
Based in Kumasi while building a new facility in Bompata, just over 100 miles north of Ghana's capital Accra, the Samba Stars' tactic has paid off.
Bournemouth, Everton, Manchester City, Charlton, Preston, Barnsley and Peterborough have all taken players on trial this summer.
"The first two or three weeks it hadn't sunk in, but then they saw the facilities we'd be [using] and the teams we were playing," said Okyere.
"They want to go and show what they can do. They are hungry, they really want it. I'm hoping there will be so much interest because we have so much talent here.
"With the facilities we will have in Ghana we feel we will be top two, top three [academies]. We hope we can bring the best of Ghana to Europe."
There are other success stories, with midfielder Listowell Lord Hinneh joining Middlesbrough in February after a trial., external
The 18-year-old has trained with the first team after swapping west Africa for England's north east.
"When I came in January, it was so cold. Experiencing something like that for the first time was tough," he told BBC Sport.
"Moving was a big milestone. It just makes me feel the dreams I've been having, thinking of trying to find myself in Europe to become a professional footballer.
"I feel the kind of dreams that I want, I'm on the verge. I'm on the way [to] becoming who I wanted to become."
Hinneh - whose sister Groovy lives in Leeds - met with the Samba Stars squad on their trip, offering advice.
"[I told them] what you've been dreaming about the future, it starts from here," he said.
"Don't just try, be so passionate. You need to play and enjoy it because you can have the success in whatever you're doing. You have to just put your heart in it."
'I'm seeing a different side of professional football'
All but one of the 20-strong visiting group initially had their visa application denied before eventually being admitted after re-evaluation.
Since arriving in the UK, they have been hosted by Brook House College in Market Harborough and trained at Harborough Town, who play in the National League North.
"The football [here] is very detailed," said 17-year-old goalkeeper Joshua Tetteh Tuwor.
"In Ghana we have the same passion but I'm seeing a different side of professional football.
"We are grateful to have such opportunities to train with elite coaches."
Rob Newman, formerly West Ham's head of recruitment and Manchester City's international scouting and recruitment manager, spent time with the academy in Ghana earlier this year and has helped coach them in Harborough.
"Hopefully clubs can see the potential," said the ex-Bristol City and Norwich defender.
"Nothing will give me greater pleasure in six months [than] going to see these boys playing in a first team in Europe. I believe they are two or three months away from being able to do that."
The Stars have played a series of games against youth teams from the EFL and non-league.
They started with a 9-0 thumping of Dorking Wanderers and also beat Under-21 sides from Sheffield Wednesday, Luton and Peterborough.
There were draws at Sheffield United and Barnsley while their only defeat came 3-2 against Preston's U21s.
Antonio watched them thrash Peterborough U19s 6-0 last month.
"You can see from what they've done since they've been in the UK - the results against top teams - that they have what it takes to play pro level," said the 36-year-old.
"It's great to help knock down barriers and give these lads a real chance."
'Back home everyone is depending on you'
Ghana have reached five of the past six Fifa World Cups - having never qualified before 2006 - and made the quarter-finals in 2010.
At this year's tournament, where they exited in the last-32 against Colombia, eight members of the squad were born overseas.
The Black Stars may not have come to rely heavily on diaspora talent, unlike some other African nations, yet the Ghana Football Association has made noises about widening its global search - something which could potentially impact home-grown talent.
"You have to have a tough mentality," said Sherif Mashud, an 18-year-old striker who has already had a trial with Hungarian top-tier side Zalaegerszegi thanks to his involvement with Samba Stars.
"Back home everyone is depending on you, everyone is looking up to you to succeed, to come and help them, your friends, your family. Everyone is praying for you."
The new English season has begun with six Ghana internationals on Premier League books: Mohammed Kudus at Tottenham, Antoine Semenyo with Manchester City, Brighton's Ibrahim Osman, Ipswich's new signing Abdul Fatawu and Coventry's Brandon Thomas-Asante and Caleb Yirenkyi.
The first to play in the English top flight was striker Nii Lamptey when he joined Aston Villa in 1994, while midfielder Michael Essien has made the most appearances, winning two titles with Chelsea.
Only two other Ghanaians have lifted the Premier League trophy - Jeffrey Schlupp and Daniel Amartey when Leicester stunned the world in 2015-16.
"Back home we've got people you grew up with and you might miss them, but that doesn't kill the dreams I'm here for," said Hinneh, who lists Kudus as his biggest inspiration and hopes to follow his heroes into the top flight after Boro missed out on promotion in last season's Championship play-off final.
"I'm trying to figure out what the reality is, what the future holds for me and then just chase the dreams."

Brentford sign £40m defender Diouf from West Ham
- Published
Brentford have signed West Ham defender El Hadji Malick Diouf in a deal worth up to £40m.
The 21-year-old Senegal left-back has joined on a five-year contract, with the club having an option to extend it by a further year.
The move sees Brentford paying an initial £35m for the player, with a further £5m in add-ons.
Diouf played in West Ham's Championship opener against Burnley, but was excluded from the matchday squads of the Hammers' following two games as a deal was worked on.
He was the Bees' priority defensive target in this transfer window, but discussions had stalled this summer before being reopened earlier this week.
Diouf is returning to the Premier League after suffering relegation with the Hammers last season.
And his sale represents a big profit for West Ham on a player they paid Slavia Prague £19m for a year ago.
Diouf played 34 times for West Ham last season, providing five assists.
"He's a player that fits our ideal age profile, with lots of room to still develop," Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said.
Diouf said Andrews had convinced him he could continue to improve at the club.
And when asked about his ambition upon joining his new club said: "Why not win the league?"
He is Brentford's fifth summer signing of the summer after the arrivals of striker Callum Wilson, midfielder Mamadou Sangare, centre-back Jannik Schuster and winger Jaidon Anthony.
After breaking into the Senegal side last year, Diouf played four times at the World Cup this summer.
While West Ham were relegated after finishing 18th last season, Brentford enjoyed an excellent campaign under Andrews, finishing ninth and just missing out on European football on goal difference.
Brentford began their season on Saturday with a 3-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur and play Leeds on Sunday in their next league game.

Beloved writer and environmentalist Wendell Berry has died at age 92
Novelist and poet Wendell Berry spent his life farming his land for food and for prose. It was land his family farmed and lived on for seven generations before him, in Henry County Kentucky.
He died at his home in Port Royal, Kentucky at age 92.
Berry started his career as a writer as an academic. He studied at the University of Kentucky, then Stanford, and had taken a prestigious position as an English professor at New York University by the time he was 28. But city life was never for him.
In the 1968 essay A Native Hill, Berry wrote about his decision to leave behind the New York literary world just two years into his career, in favor of his home county in Kentucky. "I had made a significant change in my relation to the place: before it had been mine by coincidence or accident; now it was mine by choice. My return, which at first had been hesitant and tentative, grew wholehearted and sure. I had come back to stay. I hoped to live here the rest of my life."
It was a hope he accomplished. The land Berry farmed in Henry County became the primary inspiration for his work as a writer and as an environmentalist. He was a stark critic of industrialized farming, and generally skeptical of technology. He never owned a computer–preferring instead to hand write his work, and then type it up on a typewriter he purchased new in 1956 and never needed to replace.
Berry's writing was an endeavor in slowing down, and noticing his surroundings – whether these were trees, people, or the imprint of a breeze on a hill – as in the 2001 poem "June Wind."
"Light and wind are running
Over the headed grass
As though the hill had
Melted and now flowed."
Other poems used similarly sharp prose to comment on the broader political sphere. "Against the War in Vietnam" was published in 1968.
"In the name of ourselves we ride
at the wheels of our engines,
in the name of Plenty devouring all,
the exhaust of our progress falling
deadly on villages and fields
we do not see. We are prepared
for millions of little deaths."
Berry was awarded the National Humanities Medal by President Obama in 2012, and he became the first living author inducted into the Kentucky writer's Hall of Fame in 2015.
In a 1998 interview for All Things Considered, Berry was hesitant to provide advice to young people looking to take after him, telling NPR's Noah Adams, "I think advising the young about a life course is probably not a responsible thing to do."
But when pressed, Berry added that, if at all possible, young people should look for opportunities to "stop some place, and stay there. Learn the history of it, and the names of the plants and animals and the neighbors."
Berry's writing is a lesson for the ages on slowing down, noticing, and deeply loving and respecting our surroundings.

For many young people dealing with stress, loneliness, family pressures, relationship concerns or fears about the future, the inability to speak openly can itself become a barrier to seeking help. Against this backdrop, anonymous peer-support platforms are emerging as a possible bridge between silence and support.
One such initiative, Let’s Talk Life, developed by mental health professionals at National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) and technologists at the International Institute of Information Technology-Bangalore (IIIT-B), allows young people to share their concerns anonymously and seek emotional support without fear of judgement.
A recent paper analysing 137 posts on the platform found that users commonly turned to it to express emotional distress, seek suggestions, make sense of their experiences, and receive validation. The findings were published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
The platform does not require users to disclose personally identifiable information. Responses are provided by trained peer volunteers and reviewed by mental health professionals before being posted.
Stigma, a barrier
“Many young people hesitate to approach formal mental health services because of stigma, fear of being misunderstood, or the belief that their problems are not serious enough. A safe, anonymous space can become the first point where they articulate what they are experiencing,” said Seema Mehrotra, Professor in the Department of Clinical Psychology at NIMHANS and Principal Investigator of the project.
Stress, loneliness
The study found that users discussed concerns ranging from academic pressure, family conflicts, and relationship difficulties to self-doubt, loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms.
Stress, uncertainty, helplessness, loneliness, and feeling overwhelmed were among the prominent emotional states reported in the posts. Family pressures, relationship difficulties, self-esteem concerns, and mental health symptoms also featured frequently.
Users approached the platform for several reasons, including seeking practical suggestions, expressing emotions, sharing reflections, understanding their experiences, and seeking reassurance.
Peer support
“Peer support does not replace professional care. Its role is to create a bridge — helping a young person feel heard, understand their emotions better, and, wherever required, take the next step towards professional help,” Dr. Mehrotra said.
Researchers said young people often turn first to informal support systems, such as friends and peers, before seeking professional assistance. Digital platforms can make such support more accessible by allowing users to communicate anonymously.
Trained volunteers
Abhishek Karishiddimath, Scientist at the ICMR Centre for Advanced Research, NIMHANS, said the peer volunteers responding on the platform were themselves young people.
“They undergo structured training in empathetic, respectful, and solution-oriented responses. Every response is reviewed by mental health experts to ensure safety and appropriateness,” he said.
The platform is designed as a low-intensity support option rather than a crisis service or substitute for counselling. Responders are trained to identify signs of significant distress that may require professional intervention and encourage users to seek appropriate help.
First step towards seeking help
“Sometimes people do not immediately need advice; they need a space where they can express what they are going through without being judged. The experience of being heard, validated, and gaining a fresh perspective can be an important first step towards healing and growth,” Dr. Mehrotra said.
The researchers said such platforms could have a role in public mental health, particularly given India’s large youth population and widespread use of digital platforms.
They stressed that professional mental healthcare remains important for persistent or serious concerns, while moderated peer-support spaces could help young people articulate emotional struggles that might otherwise remain unspoken.
Future efforts should focus on strengthening such platforms and establishing clearer pathways to professional psychological support, they added.

Quick Answer
QuickLook brings macOS-style instant file previews to Windows 11. Install the free, open-source app, select a file in File Explorer, and press Space to preview images, PDFs, videos, archives, code, and more without opening another app.
If you are switching from a Mac to a Windows laptop or have already jumped ship, then among a bunch of cool things, there is a good chance that you might be missing that one tiny feature — tapping the Space bar to peek inside a file. On macOS, the file peeking feature has been around since 2007, and once you get used to it, selecting a photo, PDF, or video and instantly seeing what’s inside without opening a single app, going back feels like a step down. Windows, even with all the polish it has picked up over the years, never really bothered to catch up.
The Windows File Explorer still makes you double-click and wait for the right app to load, just to confirm whether you want that file or not. This is the gap that QuickLook fixes, as it brings the macOS-style press Space and preview feature to Windows 10 and 11 PCs. But it has more to it. Let us check it out.
Why does Windows File Explorer still lag?
No offense to Microsoft, but even after so many visual upgrades, Windows has never really implemented features that actually make a difference. For instance, it is not that Microsoft has never tried the preview feature. It has experimented with preview panes in File Explorer for years, and to be fair, the built-in Preview Pane (which you can enable through the sidebar from the View menu) does show images, PDFs, and a handful of document types. But it is quite slow and doesn’t support all file formats people actually deal with. On top of this, the preview pane needs a permanently open panel eating into your window memory. To put it in simple words, it was never designed to be instant but designed to be available if you go looking for it.
That’s a very different philosophy from what Apple built. Quick Look on macOS is designed so that you should never have to fully open an application just to look at whether the file is right or wrong. QuickLook for Windows brings that same philosophy and applies it system-wide, whether you are browsing on your desktop, a network drive, or even inside an Open/Save dialog box.
QuickLook is free and open-source
I love trying out new tools and software that bring more features and enhance the usage experience. QuickLook stood out because it is a free and open-source utility, and it has been actively maintained since 2017. One of the best parts about QuickLook is that it runs quietly in the background after installation, sitting in your system tray, waiting for you to select a file and press the Space bar. The moment you press the Space bar, a preview window pops open almost instantly; no loading spinner, no application splash screen, nothing.
What makes it genuinely useful rather than a gimmick is the long list of supported file formats it can preview. Out of the box, QuickLook handles more than fifty file types natively, including:
- Images (JPG, PNG, GIF, WebP, HEIC, RAW formats, and more)
- Videos and audio files, with actual playback controls inside the preview
- PDFs, rendered natively without needing Adobe Reader
- Source code files, with proper syntax highlighting for dozens of programming languages
- Markdown files, rendered as formatted text rather than raw syntax
- Archives like ZIP and RAR, letting you browse contents without extracting
- Fonts, showing a live specimen of how the typeface actually looks
- 3D model files, with the ability to rotate and inspect the model
Using QuickLook is straightforward
Once you are done with the installation, you can use QuickLook straightaway. All you need to do is click on any file, be it inside the File Explorer, your Desktop, or even inside a file picker, press the Space bar, and a preview window will open up, rendering the file’s contents without launching the actual application associated with it. Want to check the next file in the folder? Use the arrow keys to move your selection, and QuickLook updates the preview live, without you needing to close and reopen anything. When you are done, hitting Space again, pressing Escape, or clicking the close button dismisses the window immediately.
There is also a small but genuinely thoughtful touch. You can drag a file directly out of the preview window into another folder or application. This means that QuickLook does not just show you contents, but it can double as a lightweight way to move files around while you are inspecting them. For those who deal with folders full of similarly named files like screenshots, exported design assets, and scanned documents, this single feature removes an entire category of friction and saves a lot of time. Instead of opening five PDFs one at a time in a PDF Reader to find the right invoice, you tap through them in under two seconds each.
The plugin ecosystem is where it gets genuinely powerful
QuickLook’s native format support already covers most everyday use cases. But if you want to expand the list of supported file formats, the plugin system is what turns QuickLook from “a nice preview tool” into something closer to a universal file viewer. Community developers have built plugins that extend QuickLook to handle formats it doesn’t support by default. The best part is that installing one is refreshingly simple. You just need to download the plugin file, select it in File Explorer, press Space, and QuickLook prompts you to install it directly from the preview window itself.
Some of the more useful plugins in the ecosystem include:
- Office document viewers that render Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without needing Microsoft Office or WPS Office installed at all
- ePub and comic book viewers, useful for anyone who reads digital books or manga and wants a quick way to confirm file contents
- PDF renderers built on WebView2, offering an alternative rendering engine for people who run into issues with the default PDF viewer
- SQLite database viewers, letting developers peek inside .db files without opening a separate database tool
- 3D model and CAD file plugins, handling specialized formats used in design and engineering work
It’s a similar philosophy to how tools like Winaero Tweaker approach Windows customization, where a small, focused core with optional extras layered on top, rather than a bloated all-in-one package.
QuickLook: Is this for you?
For anyone who regularly digs through folders full of screenshots, downloads, project files, or scanned documents, QuickLook solves a problem that Windows has quietly ignored for over a decade. It’s free, open-source, doesn’t collect telemetry, has no ads or premium tier hiding better features behind a paywall, and the entire project has stayed community-maintained since it first launched. Not only heavy file users, but casual users can also install it and use it in their daily lives, as it solves a core problem of having to double-click a file, use supported software, wait for it to load, and then preview the file. The setup takes less time than reading this article, and the payoff shows up the very first time you tap Space over a file and actually get what you expected, instantly.

A Bengaluru-based man has sparked a debate on social media after arguing that earning ₹2 lakh a month can become a “dangerous” comfort zone. In a post on X, Shashank Dixit said the figure is not concerning because it is too low, but because it can provide just enough financial security for people to become comfortable and stop pursuing bigger ambitions. Dixit said reaching this salary can create a sense that life and career are going well enough. The income, according to him, can reassure parents, support a comfortable lifestyle and allow people to enjoy their weekends without having to worry excessively about money. " ₹2L/month is the most dangerous number. Not because it's too little, because it's just enough, Just Enough!!!" Dixit wrote. "Slowly, your salary becomes your identity, You focus on maintaining income instead of increasing your value, Comfort zone becomes permanent," he wrote. According to Dixit, giving up a stable job becomes increasingly difficult once people become accustomed to a particular income and lifestyle. The fear of losing that security can discourage them from pursuing uncertain opportunities. " ₹2 lakh a month is a lot to bet on something with no guarantee. So you stop betting," he wrote. He added that people may continue delaying their ambitions, convincing themselves that they will take action "next month" or "next year". "After a long time, you realise you never lost your ambition. You just started earning enough to ignore it," Dixit concluded. Dixit’s post resonated with several users, with many agreeing that financial comfort can make it harder to take career risks. One user wrote, "2L a month buying comfort is real, but the ones who keep building anyway while comfortable are the ones who actually break out later." "Totally agree, 200,000 INR is a comfort zone in India. And it's difficult to take risk and become an entrepreneur from there. I tried once for 2 years, and it was great learning," commented another. "Been there and completely agree. But you gotta push harder for something beyond these numbers," wrote a third user. "This is so real, man. It's extremely tough to let go of the comfort, especially when you're young and don't have responsibilities," said another. "Funnily enough, when I started my startup, the job I was doing was paying me 2 lakhs/month, and that was nearly 4.5 years ago. If you are true to yourself, you can very clearly see the golden bars of the cage around you," wrote one user. (Disclaimer: This report is based on user-generated content from social media. Dan Driscoll’s Parting Shot
The Army secretary told Trump about problems in the Army and his friction with Hegseth, then resigned.
During a White House meeting last week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll brought his concerns about the future of the Army under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directly to President Trump—a sign of how far tensions between the two Pentagon leaders had escalated, and of the dysfunction inside the building, four people familiar with the conversation told us.
Trump was surprised when Driscoll told him how many generals and other top officers had been fired, pushed out, or passed over for promotion under Hegseth, one of the people said. Driscoll argued that the Army could not transform itself the way it needs to, because of the departure of so many leaders, this person said, adding that Trump expressed concern about the deep cuts to the Army’s senior leadership. Driscoll informed the president of his intention to resign—and by today, Driscoll was on his way out.
Hegseth’s purge of the military has been so dramatic that with Driscoll gone, the military’s largest service is left without a top civilian leader, a Senate-confirmed top general, a confirmed Army general in charge of operations, or a confirmed commander of Army troops in Europe. Because of all the firings across the service over the past year, the Army, with more than 450,000 active-duty soldiers positioned across the globe, has fewer generals than at any point in recent history. Driscoll’s personal appeal to Trump just days before his exit was the most direct articulation of high-level concerns among Pentagon leaders about the strains facing the force—including Hegseth’s intervention in Army personnel decisions and the mounting demands of the Iran war.
The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Driscoll had been “highly effective” in improving soldier readiness and advancing other administration priorities. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” Kelly wrote in a statement, using the administration’s preferred term for the Department of Defense.
Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment, and Driscoll did not respond to a call seeking comment. But a person familiar with his resignation told us that Driscoll had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” Hegseth did not have an immediate response to Driscoll’s departure.
Since his arrival at the Pentagon early last year, Hegseth—a former Fox News host who appealed to Trump loyalists by deriding a “woke” military and advocating for leniency for troops charged with war crimes—has sought to reshape the Army. He has placed like-minded generals in positions of influence, intervened to stymie the promotions of lower ranking-officers, and gutted diversity initiatives. The result was an Army depleted of leaders, and an Army secretary and a Pentagon chief at constant odds. Hegseth has ended dozens of Army careers, all without any clear explanation. He now has driven out the secretary of the Army.
Driscoll’s departure puts the Pentagon even more firmly under the control of Hegseth and his MAGA agenda. Driscoll is a confidant of Vice President Vance, a relationship that gave him access to the West Wing, and at times Driscoll served as a counterweight to Hegseth’s impulses, but only up to a point. Some current and former defense officials told us they believe Driscoll’s enmity toward Hegseth actually had the unintended consequence of broadening the purge of the uniformed ranks. And yet Driscoll’s departure, which had been expected for months, and the prospect that he will be replaced by someone more politically aligned with Hegseth are already raising fears inside the Army. “What happens then? Generational damage,” a defense official told us.
Driscoll arrived at the Pentagon in February 2025, a third-generation Army soldier who shared several things in common with Hegseth, his new boss. Like Hegseth, Driscoll joined the military in the most muscular years of Washington’s post-9/11 wars. Both men served in Iraq in a company-grade role. (Hegseth, a National Guardsman, also deployed to Afghanistan.) Both returned with sharp criticisms of America’s overseas adventures and the military’s hidebound ways. Both attended Ivy League schools: Hegseth, Princeton and Harvard; Driscoll, Yale Law, where he befriended the fellow veteran Vance. Both Driscoll and Hegseth have made unsuccessful runs for political office. Both have also eyed a return to politics. As Army secretary, Driscoll frequently reminded people that he had a direct line to the vice president, people familiar with the matter said, and told others that he had ambition to someday run for president himself—an ambition that Hegseth is also said to harbor.
But the two men differed starkly in temperament and style. Hegseth, who required an unprecedented tie-breaking Senate-confirmation vote from Vance after failing to win any Democratic support, is one of Trump’s most reliable MAGA warriors. He has publicly boasted about firing “woke” generals, dared military dissenters to quit, and demonized the mainstream media. Driscoll also supported administration policies but has done so in a more genial way that appealed to many lawmakers more than Hegseth’s combative approach before Congress. And unlike Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who has echoed Hegseth’s scornful and partisan tone on social media, Driscoll has steered clear of endorsing Hegseth’s most controversial actions or most of his culture-war priorities. Unlike Hegseth, Driscoll is friendly with the press, cultivated ties with lawmakers of both parties, and courted technology leaders as he promoted the Army’s sprint to transform how it wages war. That served him well in the administration, earning him additional responsibilities as director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and later as an unofficial mediator for the war in Ukraine. None of that sat well with Hegseth.
Army personnel appointments were a particular point of friction. Hegseth has not hesitated to push aside or promote officers as he sees fit, in many cases in ways that have irked others in the Pentagon. Driscoll advocated for General Randy George, the Army chief of staff whose name appeared on a list circulated before Trump’s return to office of senior officers who should be fired due to perceived transgressions against the MAGA agenda. Although Driscoll may have bought George time, Hegseth ultimately fired the general in April. Chris Donahue, the four-star general who headed U.S. Army Europe and Africa, followed several months later.
The Army has been without a top commander since George’s firing. General Christopher LaNeve, who was picked by Hegseth as the No. 2 officer in the Army, has been acting in that role, often going straight to Hegseth for decisions, bypassing Driscoll, according to defense officials. Hegseth is expected to nominate LaNeve to lead the Army, but Capitol Hill is already signaling that LaNeve would struggle to be confirmed, because of many lawmakers’ antipathy to Hegseth. “We are not going to reward Hegseth for what he did to the Army,” one congressional staffer told us.
The Army has long prided itself on representing the diversity of the country, but under Hegseth, minorities and women have been pushed out or barred from promotion. The military has long sought to be apolitical, but under Hegseth, troops are measured not by combat experience but by their perceived loyalty to the administration. Among the generals fired have been some of the most experienced and decorated in the service. Each departure marks the loss of decades of investment in that soldier and raises questions about how future troops can rise through the ranks.
Although Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the near term, many Pentagon officials fear that the administration will nominate the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, another Army veteran, to replace Driscoll. Parnell, who previously made a failed bid for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania, shares Hegseth’s pugilistic spirit and interest in culture and personnel issues. Like Hegseth, Parnell has no experience managing a large organization and would face a contentious confirmation hearing. A new Army secretary who is more politically driven—and likely less experienced and less well connected than Driscoll—could keep the service embroiled in cultural fights rather than focused on the long-term planning that Driscoll and others believe it desperately needs.

Modi said countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy must be sent a strong message
Framing security as a non-negotiable prerequisite for regional progress, PM Narendra Modi delivered a thinly veiled warning to Pakistan over state-sponsored terrorism at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit. With Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif in attendance, Modi said countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.The remarks are significant also because of the timing. Pakistan assumed rotating chairmanship of SCO from Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday and will host the heads-of-state summit next year, for which it will invite Modi, along with others.Modi made the remarks, in which he also warned against double standards on terrorism, while expanding on India's SCO vision - Security, Connectivity and Opportunity - that he articulated in Tianjin last year.With Chinese President Xi Jinping also present, PM reiterated India's position that all connectivity initiatives must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states as this is also the "fundamental spirit" of SCO charter.
Modi said that terrorism continued to pose a serious challenge to humanity and it's important to not remain confined to an action-reaction approach in the fight against the menace.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. We must speak with one voice and make it clear that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” said PM, without naming Pakistan as SCO charter doesn’t allow members to raise bilateral differences.India and Pakistan together joined the China-dominated Eurasian grouping as full members in 2017. For India, the security-oriented SCO has served as a platform not just to assert its strategic autonomy but also flag regional risks from state-sponsored terrorism. Modi said that the bloc’s shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also closely linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan and that India will continue to contribute to the development and provision of humanitarian assistance to people of the country.Modi addressed West Asia crisis, saying it was affecting energy security, maritime trade and supply chains around the world and recalling his message earlier that conflicts cannot be resolved on the battlefield. “Countries of Global South bear greatest brunt of such disruptions. Therefore, India has consistently called for all tensions and conflicts to be resolved not on battlefield, but through dialogue and diplomacy,” he added.While underlining the importance India attaches to SCO, Modi said that at a time when the world is passing through instability, the organisation must transform the shared geography into opportunities and bring about positive change in people’s lives. Describing SCO as a confluence of great civilisations, cultures, and ideas, he said that over next 25 years, people-to-people ties should remain at the heart of cooperation among the member states.“True measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts create, how many new markets open up for entrepreneurs, how much farmers benefit from tech, and how much better the lives of our citizens become,” said the PM. According to an Indian readout of PM’s participation, Modi stated that strong and trusted connectivity initiatives were important for the group’s shared progress and prosperity.
“Underlining that India supports connectivity efforts that link markets, enhance trade and open new opportunities for development, he reiterated such efforts should respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of nations,” said the readout.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

With the resignation of Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll, the US Army has lost another top leader who was driving its sweeping transformation for future wars.
As the service secretary, Dan Driscoll was a leading figure in reshaping the Army's relationship with industry and accelerating its focus on drone warfare. His departure, along with the dismissal of the service's top general earlier this year, has left the Army's modernization efforts in question.
The Army did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment on how leadership changes will affect these efforts.
Driscoll, a former military officer and investment banker, submitted his resignation on Monday. A US official told Business Insider that the secretary spoke to President Donald Trump about the state of the Army prior to that decision.
Multiple news reports have indicated that Driscoll had concerns about the Army transformation initiative amid Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's removal of top generals. Earlier reporting had identified frictions between Driscoll and Hegseth.
Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April, dismissing him roughly a year and a half before the end of what is usually a four-year term. George's firing came as a shock, with reports indicating that his removal came after disagreements between the general and Hegseth.
The service does not currently have any Senate-confirmed leaders, leaving elements of its leadership and its transformation up in the air.
Early last year, Hegseth issued a memo ordering sweeping changes in the Army; at the time, it was described as the largest shift in force structure and priorities since the Cold War.
The memo directed Driscoll to "transform the Army now for future warfare," with changes ranging from flooding divisions with drones to shedding older legacy systems and reforming the acquisitions process.
The total cost of the transformation was estimated to be around $36 billion over the next five years.
George and Driscoll became two of the most visible leaders carrying out that transformation. Driscoll, who Trump had previously identified as a "change agent" and "disruptor," spoke publicly about which weapons programs hadn't been successful, pushed for significantly greater investments in uncrewed capabilities, and pressed the Army to work differently with industry and adopt a more commercially driven mindset.
Early in his tenure as the Army secretary, Driscoll told Business Insider that there was a need for the Army to modernize ahead of a future fight.
"We feel a large enough existential threat, and it is important enough that we can no longer make decisions simply based off where jobs might exist or what private companies may benefit from our decisions," he said. "Instead, we have to optimize for soldier lethality in the fight ahead."
One of Driscoll's latest transformation efforts was the Right to Integrate initiative, an attempt to break down walls between weapons from different suppliers and integrate them so that soldiers can more easily connect and use different systems.
In May, he told reporters he had an "aha" moment about the idea after seeing how Ukraine had successfully connected drones, sensors, and weapons into its battle management program.
George was also influential in service transformation efforts. He was involved in several efforts to speed up the Army's modernization, including helping drive the Next Generation Command and Control experimentation initiative to develop a prototype for the Army's new command and control system.
Another of his signature initiatives was the creation of the Army's Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental unit in the 173rd Airborne Brigade launched last fall to apply lessons in drone warfare from Ukraine. The idea was that the battalion would specialize in drone tactics and help spread those lessons across the force.
But last month, George's acting replacement, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's vice chief of staff, disbanded the battalion.
The battalion is participating in an exercise that will conclude this month, an Army official told Business Insider. And then it "will deliver what it learned there, together with the past year's findings, to the Army to inform force design and future experimentation." After the exercise, it will refocus as airborne infantry.
The decision confused defense analysts.
"This decision is quite puzzling, given the Pentagon's Drone dominance initiative and the push for the US military to integrate drones into their formations and operations," Stacie Pettyjohn, a defense expert at the Center for a New American Security, told Business Insider.
"They have asked to spend billions of dollars on drones," she continued, "and forgoing an opportunity to learn from Ukraine, a partner nation that is the most experienced in the world at using drones, does not make any sense," she said.
The Department of Defense has continued to signal that technological innovation and uncrewed systems are priorities, as has LaNeve, who said in a written post that "the work of change continues." At the same time, he said that the Army also needs to prioritize warfighting fundamentals and soldier readiness.
The Army's broader transformation is on uncertain footing. The push for change is still there, but it is unclear whether the initiatives put forward under Driscoll and George will continue. If they do, it's unclear who will be moving them forward.

The plot to disrupt mail-in voting
A new whistleblower report warns that Trump’s mail-in voting requirements could cause chaos in the midterm elections.
It took the US government two years to roll out HealthCare.gov, nine months to pilot a direct tax-filing tool…and just 11 weeks to build a new system for processing Americans’ absentee ballots.
Before you cheer this rare instance of bureaucratic efficiency, however, please allow the other shoe to drop: That figure comes from an alarming new whistleblower report that foretells potential chaos in this fall’s midterm elections.
According to the whistleblower, the US Postal Service has rushed out a janky, error-prone processing system in its mad dash to comply with President Donald Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots. That order, currently paused, would require states to comply with new rules for preparing, tracking, and mailing ballots. Several states have since sued to stop it.
If the order does go into effect, however, the Postal Service has to be prepared. So the agency scrambled to hack together its new system — forgoing standard testing procedures and adding requirements that are likely to hold up thousands of outbound ballots, the whistleblower says.
According to the report, multiple USPS officials have described the system as “a shit show” that, as of late August, was apt to “completely crash.” “Move fast and break things” is actually not a great look for governments.
Go a little deeper
But the issue goes far beyond one IT meltdown at the post office, or even many IT meltdowns at many post offices. As my colleague Ian Millhiser has covered in depth, Trump’s March executive order could effectively end mail-in voting in several states by imposing a slate of last-minute requirements that election officials don’t have time to implement.
Let’s just take the narrow issue of ballot envelopes. Trump’s executive order directed the post office to issue new rules about the design of those envelopes, which the post office did…on August 21.
The new rules required that ballot envelopes bear a unique barcode and a logo that the Trump administration claimed would “facilitate proper handling” of election mail. But by that point in the season, a number of states were already preparing to mail their midterm ballots.
North Carolina starts mailing general election ballots this week, for instance. More than a dozen other states post theirs by late September. And even in the unlikely case that these states could design, order and distribute millions of compliant envelopes in the next few weeks…it’s not clear the post office could process them.
Under the new system, the Postal Service must individually scan every outbound ballot as it heads to voters, a process that the Trump administration says will take “less than a minute” each. Across millions of ballots, however, “less than a minute” adds up: potentially to more than 380,000 hours, in California’s case.
That’s enormously concerning, Ian writes. Should courts allow Trump’s order to go into effect, the states that can’t comply won’t be able to do mail-in voting this year. And there are a number of states — including Oregon, Washington, Hawaii, Colorado, Utah, and California — where the entire election is basically vote-by-mail.
”I think it is more likely than not that SCOTUS does not back Trump’s play here. But you can never rule anything out with this Supreme Court,” Ian said.

Can we afford Iran?
As the war drags on, it risks eroding America’s ability to respond to other conflicts.
President Donald Trump’s on-again, off-again war with Iran is officially on again. (So recursive is this never-ending conflict, in fact, that I had to search my inbox to confirm I hadn’t already written that sentence!)
On Sunday, the US attacked rocket launchers Sunday on Iran’s Larak Island, claiming the strikes were necessary to prevent Iran from laying mines that could once again disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran, meanwhile, responded by firing a volley of ballistic missiles at US sites in the United Arab Emirates and Jordan, where they were reportedly intercepted.
The latest skirmish comes after a month of relative peace and quiet, and six months after the war began. You’ll recall that Trump initially said it would last four to five weeks at the very longest.
But in the grand scheme of Trump’s Iran fictions, that optimistic timeline isn’t even the most flagrant. On Sunday night, the president also posted a video that purportedly showed Kharg Island, a central hub of Iran’s oil industry, “being blown to smithereens!!!” The video was, in fact, AI-generated.
Go a little deeper
The persistence of the war in Iran isn’t merely exhausting for those of us following along at home. As a group of high-ranking military commanders recently warned the Pentagon, the drawn-out conflict could also make America less safe by limiting the military’s ability to respond to threats in other parts of the world.
That unusual warning — first reported over the weekend by the Washington Post — suggested that the war in Iran is tying up ships and surveillance planes that the US needs elsewhere. Several top military leaders explicitly warned that the war had forced them to give up resources they needed to protect the US itself.
That’s not the only risk of the ongoing conflict, either. Longer deployments have also eroded troop morale and disrupted ship maintenance. And as the war drags on, the US is burning through its stockpiles of advanced missiles, at a cost of many billions of dollars.
None of this means we’re defenseless, of course. But the war in Iran is taking up a lot of bandwidth. And should another conflict break out anywhere else on earth…the US and its allies could feel it.
One general warned the Pentagon that, without more resources, he could be forced to choose between protecting Israel and the US from ballistic missile attacks. And the Navy just moved its only dedicated aircraft carrier in the Pacific to the waters near Iran. “We are really robbing Peter to pay Paul,” one military expert told Vox in late February, even before we had any idea how long the war would last.

Nepal's hesitance to accept foreign help for flood relief under scrutiny
MUMBAI, India – As authorities in Nepal scramble to rescue more than 900 workers trapped in hydropower tunnels that are still under construction, a top group of the country's private sector power producers has criticized the government's initial hesitance in accepting help from other countries.
The floods and mudslides that were triggered by last week's ice-and-rock avalanche have buried several Himalayan villages in the border region of Nepal and Tibet.
In a statement on Monday morning local time, Nepal's disaster management department said 903 people have died and 4,247 are currently considered missing, a sharp rise on the previous figures. At least 85 of those missing are Americans, the State Department said on Sunday.
The debris created by the various landslides have also blocked nine hydropower tunnels in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, trapping 933 workers from Nepal, South Korea and China. Videos shared by the Nepali army show rescue personnel using drills and excavator machines to try and rescue those who were trapped.
Bhim Gautam, chief executive officer of the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal, told NPR that Nepal does not have "enough technology, equipment and expertise" to mount successful rescue operations at hydropower projects. "Our expertise is only in dealing with small flooding. We have never faced a situation like this before," said Gautam.
Last week's floods, he said, not only blocked the entrances of the tunnels, but also made them difficult to locate. "In some cases, the rescue workers spent three days only in finding these tunnels."
He said his industry's leaders had to "pressure the government" to allow rescue workers from other countries. "Late last week, the government approved rescue teams from China, India and Australia to come," Gautam said. "But it is so late now."
Nepal's finance minister Swarnim Wagle had last week rejected reports in local and international media that asserted the country had rejected help from foreign countries, insisting that assistance had been accepted only "according to the needs on the ground."
In a statement posted to Facebook Sunday, prime minister Balen Shah said the Nepali army and police, along with experts from India, China and South Korea, were now carrying out rescue operations at various hydropower tunnels.The Nepali government has been contacted for comment.
Fatality figures in China under question
Meanwhile in China on Monday, the country's foreign ministry denied reports that officials in Beijing had ignored early warning signs of the disaster or downplayed the details of casualties.
It insisted that the country's release of information about the floods and mudslide near its border with Nepal had been transparent and timely.
China's last update to casualty figures came on Saturday when state news agency Xinhua reported there were 16 people confirmed dead and 546 missing. Those numbers have not been updated in more than 48 hours.

Mohammed Shami
 and 
Mukesh Kumar
, helped East Zone storm into the Duleep Trophy final with a four-wicket win over defending champions Central Zone on Tuesday.

Chasing 159, East needed a steady start as the pitch increasingly aided the spinners. Sooryavanshi initially adopted a cautious approach, scoring his first 15 runs from 30 balls.

His opening partner 
Abhimanyu Easwaran
 was more fluent initially, including a six off off-spinner Saransh Jain over long-on, while Sooryavanshi struggled to find the same freedom against spin.
The teenager, however, came alive when Yash Thakur was introduced into the attack. 
Having already hammered the pacer for four fours and two sixes in the first innings, Sooryavanshi again went after him, smashing three fours and a six in the 14th over.
