Razer just released a cute and teensy mobile game controller
It's called Prio and folds up when not in use, making it pocket-friendly.
Razer just announced the Prio, a compact mobile gaming controller. It attaches via USB-C and works with both iOS and Android. The big hook here is that it folds up when not in use, making it extremely pocket-friendly.
Despite its diminutive size, the Prio actually offers console-grade controls. The gamepad includes a tactile 4-way D-pad, face buttons, bumpers and triggers. It also features capacitive analog thumbsticks that have been "engineered to reduce drift." The company says this should ensure accurate controls, "even on a bumpy commute."
It connects via USB-C, so setup should be fairly seamless. This also means there's no extra battery to charge. The Prio was made to fit most slim-to-medium phone cases and it supports phones up to seven-inches. This includes beefy handsets like the iPhone 17 Pro Max and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.
The Razer Prio integrates with native games on mobile platforms, but also Xbox Cloud Gaming, Steam Link, PS Remote Play and Razer's own PC Remote Play service. This looks like a solid and fairly adorable mobile controller.
It's available to purchase right now and costs $100. The company says this is the first entry in a new line of ultra-portable mobile gaming controllers, so expect more releases down the road.

Not long ago, a diagnosis of advanced cancer left doctors with little more than symptom control and hope. Over the course of a few of decades, however, that picture changed dramatically. Chemotherapy delivered the first meaningful survival gains, though at a steep cost in side effects, a cost later softened by a new generation of supportive drugs that made treatment safer and more tolerable. The mapping of the human genome then opened up an era of precision medicine, as whole-genome sequencing revealed mutations that could be directly targeted. Survival improved again, but a cure remained elusive: tumours kept finding new, resistant mutations to evade each targeted drug. It took a deeper understanding of the immune system to breach the next frontier: immunotherapy taught the body’s own defences to attack cancers once thought untreatable.
Now, a new contender has emerged that could rewrite the story once more: personalized mRNA tumour vaccines. Recent trial results suggest that the next chapter of the cancer treatment story may already be unfolding.
Evolution of treatment
Cancer treatment has advanced in successive waves. In the 1970s and 80s, chemotherapy became the cornerstone of oncology, improving outcomes across the board and curing diseases such as Hodgkin’s lymphoma and testicular cancer. The sequencing of the human genome and subsequent advances in molecular biology then enabled targeted therapies aimed at specific genetic abnormalities — HER2 in breast cancer, EGFR mutations in lung cancer, and many others.
The most dramatic transformation of the past two decades, however, came with immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab (drugs that block certain proteins on T-cells of the immune system, helping to attack cancer cells) changed the outlook for metastatic melanoma, a disease that had previously carried a dismal prognosis. What began in melanoma soon spread to lung, kidney, bladder, liver and head-and-neck cancers, reshaping treatment paradigms worldwide.
Immunotherapy has greatly impacted the management of blood cancers as well. Once primarily managed by chemotherapy, cancers like multiple myeloma and lymphoma, have entered the immunotherapy era through CAR-T cell therapy and bispecific antibodies (lab-made proteins that can attach to two different targets), producing outcomes unimaginable just a decade ago.
Today, personalised mRNA vaccines are poised to build on that foundation.
The melanoma breakthrough
The recent excitement around mRNA vaccines stems from the Phase III INTerpath-001 trial, which evaluated intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157/V940), a personalised mRNA vaccine. The study enrolled roughly 1,100 patients with high-risk melanoma who had undergone complete surgical removal of visible disease. They received either immunotherapy through pembrolizumab alone, or pembrolizumab combined with an individualised vaccine designed, using artificial intelligence, from the genetic profile of each patient’s own tumour. This vaccine essentially trained the patients’ immune systems to recognise and destroy unique mutations (neoantigens) on their tumour cells
The results were striking: the combination significantly improved both recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival compared with pembrolizumab alone. Earlier studies of the same strategy had already shown roughly a 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, and a 59% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis or death, compelling evidence that a personalised vaccine can amplify the effect of existing immunotherapy.
For the first time, a personalised neoantigen-based mRNA therapy has succeeded in a large, randomized Phase III trial, validating a concept researcher have pursued for years.
How does it work?
Unlike traditional vaccines, which prevent infection, these are therapeutic vaccines, developed after a disease has been diagnosed, to help trigger the body’s immune system. Once a tumour is sequenced, sophisticated algorithms pick out the mutations unique to that patient’s cancer (neoantigens), providing the necessary information for production of customised mRNA constructs encoding these tumour-specific neoantigens. When injected, these mRNA constructs train the patient’s immune system, particularly the T cells, to recognise and destroy cancer cells carrying those exact mutations. In effect, every patient receives a vaccine made exclusively for their own cancer.
Cancer is increasingly understood as an ecosystem, shaped by interactions between tumour cells, the immune system and the surrounding microenvironment. Immunotherapy works by altering that ecosystem, changing the ‘immune soil’ in which cancer grows. Personalised mRNA vaccines may be the next step: directing the immune response with even greater precision.
Following on, from immunotherapy
The current moment resembles the early days of immunotherapy. When checkpoint inhibitors first showed unprecedented benefit in melanoma, many assumed the impact would stay confined to a handful of cancers. Instead, immunotherapy became a universal oncology platform, transforming treatment across tumour types.
mRNA vaccines appear to be following a similar trajectory. Melanoma, with its high mutational burden and strong response to immune-based approaches, served as the ideal proving ground. Researchers are now studying personalised vaccine strategies in lung, gastrointestinal, genitourinary and several other cancers.
If these trials succeed, the implications could be enormous. Future treatment may routinely involve genomic sequencing after surgery, followed by the rapid design of a patient-specific vaccine given alongside immunotherapy — aiming to wipe out microscopic residual disease before it can return. This is the essence of personalised cancer treatment.
The path ahead
Further automation of neoantigen discovery through AI and manufacturing techniques refined during the COVID-19 pandemic have demonstrated the capacity to generate sophisticated mRNA therapies at scale. Together, these advances are moving personalised cancer vaccines from concept to clinical reality.
Oncology has moved from supportive care to chemotherapy, from chemotherapy to targeted therapy, and from targeted therapy to immunotherapy. Personalised mRNA vaccines may mark the next great leap.
The battle against cancer is far from over. But history offers an encouraging precedent: melanoma announced the arrival of immunotherapy, and it may now be announcing the arrival of another revolutionary treatment platform. If the promise of mRNA tumour vaccines holds across multiple cancers, future generations may look back on this moment as the beginning of the next major transformation in cancer care.
(Dr. Harish P. is a consultant in medical oncology at Manipal Hospital Yelahanka. harish.p1@manipalhospitals.com)

Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
- Published
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.
Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.
One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.
Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.
The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.
Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.
The motive behind the attack is unclear.
Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."
Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".
Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.
He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.
Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.
He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.
After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.
Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.
According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

Canada’s Liberals sweep special elections as voters back Carney’s crusade against Trump
The most dramatic shift occurred in Quebec, where a Liberal candidate ousted a Conservative for the first time since 2018
Canada’s governing Liberals have secured victories in three special elections on Monday, providing a significant boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney amidst an intensifying trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump.
The Liberal Party claimed victory in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto, and North Vancouver-Capilano in British Columbia.
Carney framed the election results as a clear endorsement of his administration's trajectory.
"At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan," he said in a statement.
The biggest shift occurred in Quebec, where Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil won decisively in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord.
The district had been held by the opposition Conservatives since 2018, but the party fell to third place on Monday. The local economy relies on aluminum production and dairy farming, key sectors affected by the trade conflict.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto, said Carney enjoys higher approval ratings in Quebec than anywhere else in Canada, noting that Trump’s remarks about annexation resonate deeply there.
"Quebecers have the most to lose in an apocalyptic scenario where the U.S. absorbs Canada, and the status of the French language disappears," Wiseman said.
The Liberals maintained control of the other two ridings. In British Columbia, Braeden Caley, Carney’s former deputy chief of staff, took North Vancouver-Capilano.
"The United States is getting a message tonight. Our leader has the support of the Canadian people," Liberal lawmaker Hedy Fry told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. in an interview.
Cross-border trade negotiations broke down on Aug. 21 after negotiators failed to reach a compromise, leading Trump to enact 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion of Canadian exports. Canada countered by announcing intended tariffs on U.S. goods.
Trump has broadened his attacks since the negotiations broke down.
He signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America," while U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remarked Monday that Canada has sparse leverage because the U.S. economy is roughly 13 times larger.
Trump has frequently floated the idea of absorbing Canada as the 51st U.S. state.
Carney has consequently accelerated efforts to build stronger trade partnerships with Europe and other international allies.
The three victories bring the Liberal caucus to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons, solidifying the party's position in Parliament. The special elections were prompted by lawmaker resignations earlier in the year.
Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University, suggested the strong Liberal performance in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord stemmed partly from local backing for Carney’s Aug. 21 choice "to pull the plug on trade negotiations with the White House."
Béland observed that the sharp drop for Conservatives creates trouble for party leader Pierre Poilievre. The Conservatives captured the riding with 34% of the vote last year, but dropped to roughly 13% on Monday. "These numbers do look bad," he said.
Carney won office last year amid widespread public indignation over Trump's annexation rhetoric, promising to lessen Canada's economic reliance on its southern neighbor.

Canada's cadets condemn Hegseth's 'unacceptable' post about program
U.S. Pentagon defends controversial post by war secretary
The Pentagon is standing behind a controversial social media post by U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth about a Canadian cadet program.
Hegseth on Monday posted an image from the Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C., depicting two young women in uniform with the caption "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.
The online response to Hegseth's post was filled with remarks belittling the physical appearance of the people in the photo, but it also triggered massive backlash from Canadians.
Some people posted that it was unfair for Hegseth to target the youth program in an attempt to disparage the Canadian Armed Forces and others criticized him for body-shaming women serving in the cadet program.
Asked about the backlash today, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said "the X post speaks for itself."
Cadets blast Hegseth post
The Army Cadet League of Canada condemned the online harassment and mockery of cadets and their achievements.
"Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable," the league said about Hegseth's remarks in a statement.
It said the league "stands firmly behind cadets, adult staff, volunteers, and officers who dedicate their time to building stronger communities and developing the next generation of Canadian leaders."
- Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
- Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal
The national, community-based cadet program is for youth aged 12 to 18. A federal government website says the program provides "opportunities for youth to gain valuable knowledge and skills that build confidence and help pave the way in a transition to adulthood."
It's not clear how exactly the cadet training program's Instagram account — which had 1,821 followers as of Tuesday morning — came onto Hegseth's radar. Bliss, who works in the office of the assistant to the secretary of war for public affairs, did not respond to questions about how the defence secretary became aware of it.
When asked by reporters in Ottawa today about the post from Hegseth, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the message was "beneath their office."
"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having the discussions, we can have those discussions," he said. "But it's not constructive, but that's their democracy."
B.C. Premier David Eby said Hegseth's post and the Pentagon's defence of it were an embarrassment.
"It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to," Eby said.
He cited an ongoing military conference in Victoria, which includes U.S. representatives, as an example of the importance of co-operation during "unstable times."
Hegseth's post was also condemned by Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, who called the comments "stupid" and "really deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with us."
Comments come amid trade tensions
The post comes as tensions between Canada and the United States increased after trade talks broke down last month.
The Trump administration hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on an array of goods in August, with both countries blaming the other for adding last-minute changes during negotiations.
Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties next week.
Trump has spent the weeks since talks were frozen incessantly targeting Canada in his public remarks and social media posts. Last week, he signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in his latest effort to agitate America's northern neighbour.
Many in Trump's team have turned their insults to Canada's military. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday told CNBC the U.S. isn't at war with Canada.
"What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?" Bessent said.
The week prior, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed on Fox News that Canada "doesn't have a military."
Conservative MP Garnett Genuis responded to Hegseth's post on Monday saying "cadets do great work, and are not members of the military." He added that "158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked."
"Canada and the U.S. have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It's history worth remembering," Genuis said.
Hegseth is facing immense pressure domestically from an unpopular and escalating war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, depleting stockpiles of munitions and the departure of top military figures during his tenure.
In the latest series of shakeups of military leadership, on Monday, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following widely reported tensions with Hegseth.

In March 2026, IIT Kharagpur—the oldest Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) that has been training thousands of minds to design bridges, cars, and computer chips for the last 75 years did something unprecedented. It formally applied to the National Medical Commission (NMC) to offer a postgraduate medical degree, the Doctor of Medicine (MD).
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
It was not an isolated move. In August 2026, an alumnus of IIT-Kanpur pledged a massive ₹400 crore boost —building on a landmark ₹100 crore donation in 2022 — to expand its medical school and 450-bed super-specialty hospital to offer postgraduate programs in super-specialty medicine.
Within days, IIT-Madras stepped up to announce an even bolder vision: offering not just an MD, but an MBBS and a Ph.D. in medicine through its School of Medical Sciences, started in 2023.
A century-old assumption — that engineering colleges build engineers and medical colleges make doctors — is falling apart.
The quiet convergence
For over six decades, the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have served as India’s temples of engineering excellence. So why are they suddenly stepping into healthcare and running hospitals?
The short answer is: modern healthcare is no longer just about stethoscopes and prescriptions. It is driven by algorithms, microfluidics, robotic surgery, and biocompatible materials. Walk into a high-tech operating theatre today, and you will find as much engineering as medicine: robotic arms, real-time imaging, AI-assisted diagnostics, and 3D-printed implants.
Medicine is not the only sector witnessing this shift. Nursing and allied health are also transitioning. IIT Guwahati’s School of Health Sciences and Technology already trains students jointly with AIIMS Guwahati and the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER). Meanwhile, IIT Kharagpur’s hospital project includes explicit plans for a nursing college and a paramedical training school alongside its medical courses.
India’s premier technology institutes have realised that the major challenges of this century — climate change, cancer, cognition, and clean energy — cannot be solved from inside a single-discipline silo. Engineering schools that just focus on engineering risk becoming mere component suppliers to the institutions that have a massive impact on solving these problems.
Research and pharma co-innovation
While the IITs made headlines with plans for traditional medical degrees, the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, has pursued a distinctly different, research-first pathway into medical education.
Now established as the Tata IISc Medical School following a partnership with the Tata Group, the campus is executing an ambitious clinical and research infrastructure rollout.
The foundation stone for the 832-bed non-profit multi-specialty hospital — supported by a landmark ₹425 crore donation — was laid by the Prime Minister way back in June 2022 and was originally scheduled to be functional by December 2024. Now it is slated to become fully operational by late 2026 and admit the first batch of students in its flagship integrated dual-degree MD-Ph.D. program in July 2027.
What sets IISc apart from traditional medical colleges — and even peer technical institutes — is its structural integration with the global and domestic pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries. Instead of treating industry interactions as post hoc research grants, IISc embeds pharmaceutical co-innovation directly into its medical school ecosystem.
Specialised research hubs on campus — such as the Cipla Foundation Centre for Pulmonary Medicine — are integrated into the curriculum to deliver advanced respiratory care, targeted clinical trials, and drug development training alongside specialised units like the Centre for Brain Research (CBR).
The bigger opportunity
Hidden beneath the admissions headlines is an even bigger opportunity. Cross-disciplinary campuses are where medical devices, diagnostics, and therapeutics actually get invented.
This is because the clinicians who understand the patient’s pain points and the engineers who can build the solutions are finally standing in the same hallway.
For a country that imports the vast majority of its high-end medical devices, the economic and social benefits of getting this right are immense: indigenous implants, affordable diagnostics, and AI tools designed for Indian disease burdens and price points. This vision aligns with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which actively pushes higher education institutions to break down rigid disciplinary walls and evolve into Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities (MERUs).
Top-tier medical institutions like AIIMS, CMC Vellore, and JIPMER built their reputations on a time-tested formula: elite NEET-UG entry, massive patient volumes, and clinical research deeply embedded in bedside patient care.
What the IITs and IISc are betting on is a completely different edge: training doctors and physician-scientists who are fluent in engineering and computational tools—like signal processing, AI/ML, medical robotics, genetics, and device design—from day one, inside the very institute building those tools.
However, a technical institute’s medical degree will only be distinct if its curriculum, admissions, and thesis requirements are deliberately built around that engineering core. Otherwise, it risks simply becoming a smaller, newer, and less clinically proven version of a standard MBBS.
The private university precedent
The IITs and IISc may be among the top public institutions attempting this, but private universities have been testing the waters for decades.
Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE) started India’s first self-financing private medical college in 1953, later building the Manipal Institute of Technology and expanding into an Institution of Eminence. Decades of shared governance birthed a robust biomedical engineering department, a bio-incubator spinning out medical-device startups, and an ICMR-MAHE Centre for Advanced Research explicitly bridging clinical and engineering expertise.
Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham co-located its medical and engineering schools under one university umbrella, running a dedicated M.Tech in Biomedical Engineering with research spanning biosensors, prosthetics, and drug-delivery systems.
The lesson for public tech campuses is double-edged. While shared governance and funding work over the long haul, interdisciplinary outputs tend to be concentrated in dedicated programs rather than completely reshaping what every single graduate becomes.
As institutes weigh how to execute this cross-disciplinary vision, they generally find themselves standing at crossroads between two distinct administrative approaches.
On one side lies the research partnership model, best exemplified by long-standing collaborations like AIIMS Delhi working alongside IIT Delhi. Under this framework, institutions enjoy low capital expenditure and virtually zero regulatory risk, as degree-granting authority remains cleanly divided between the parent specialised units. However, these initiatives rely heavily on inter-faculty MoUs and individual relationships, which can fade as leadership changes.
On the other side lies the integrated campus model, pursued by pioneers such as the IITs at Kanpur, Kharagpur and Madras, and IISc Bengaluru. Here, a single institution builds or manages its own hospital and native “Physician-Scientist” track. While this guarantees complete curriculum control and seamless continuity, it comes with a steep price tag: massive upfront infrastructure costs, heavy operational risk, and the administrative burden of running a 24x7 clinical facility.
Challenges ahead
As the IITs step into clinical medicine, they face a reality check: setting up and running a world-class hospital is fundamentally different from commissioning a quantum computing lab.
The journey of IIT Kharagpur’s hospital project reads like a case study in institutional perseverance. It all began in 2007 when late President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam laid the foundation stone for the B.C. Roy Institute of Medical Science and Research. By 2012, the Centre sanctioned an initial grant of roughly ₹230 crore, with officials ambitiously promising an MBBS-ready medical college by 2018.
However, constructing and commissioning a high-capacity teaching hospital from scratch proved far more complex than anticipated, leading to repeated deadline slippages between 2018 and 2021. When the pandemic hit between 2020 and 2022, the facility was repurposed to serve as a COVID-19 quarantine center, eventually expanding to about 160 general beds and 90 ICU beds—still well short of its original 400-to-750 bed vision.
By early 2026, despite a fresh ₹300 crore investment and Board of Governors clearance, the undergraduate MBBS remained on hold. Adapting to these realities, the hospital performed its historic first surgery in 2025 and pivoted toward a pragmatic 20-seat postgraduate MD program, submitting its formal application to the NMC by March 2026.
Even the IISc has seen a delay of about two years in commissioning its hospital.
.
Housing engineering, medicine, and nursing on one campus has challenges in execution:
Faculty recruitment and pay clashes: Engineering professors can join straight out of Ph.D. programs, whereas clinical faculty require years of hospital practice after an MD. Standard academic pay scales are rarely competitive enough to attract top neurosurgeons or cardiologists from private practice. As a result, tech institutes end up hiring practicing doctors on hospital-linked appointments, creating a two-tier faculty dynamic that must be carefully managed.
24x7 operational risk: A failed lab experiment wastes mere time and effort; a hospital failure involves a human life. Hospitals require continuous staffing, blood bank licenses, patient-safety audits, bio-waste management, and medico-legal liability coverage—a rhythm entirely alien to an academic calendar.
Capital intensity: A major super-specialty facility requires hundreds of crores of investment before a single student walks in. Unlike engineering labs funded by grants, hospitals require continuous subsidies in operations, insurance link-ups, and government health-scheme empanelment to attract patients and stay afloat.
Multiple regulators: An integrated technical campus is simultaneously answerable to the Ministry of Education, the National Medical Commission (for medical degrees), the Indian Nursing Council (for nursing), and the Pharmacy Council of India. Each body has its own inspection schedules and minimum norms, and none are obliged to coordinate with the others. Crucially, the draft HECI regulations do not close this inter-regulatory gap.
Collaborative integration
The classic example is the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology (HST), running since 1970. The regulatory and degree-granting authority remains clearly separated—degrees are awarded by the respective parent unit—while teaching and research are integrated across campuses.
Several benchmark partnerships across India prove that deep collaborative integration works without single-institute degree ownership. Since 1971, the joint Biomedical Engineering Centre between AIIMS Delhi and IIT Delhi has accumulated five decades of shared device, implant, and imaging research without either campus altering its core degree authority.
Similarly, the three-way pipeline between CMC Vellore, IIT Madras, and SCTIMST requires students to physically rotate across all three campuses every semester, combining clinical exposure with engineering rigor. Even IIT Kharagpur itself maintains an inter-institutional MoU with AIIMS Kalyani for joint research and clinical training, proving that collaborative pipelines can operate alongside internal hospital ambitions.
The IIT leaders point out that full degree ownership allows an institute to train “physician-scientists” from year one rather than relying on post hoc MoUs, while ensuring institutional continuity without depending on leadership changes.
Restructing courses
The traffic is starting to flow in reverse direction, too. Medical institutions are embedding engineering capabilities right inside their campuses.
However, duplicate infrastructure is expensive. A medical college’s advantage is patient access and clinical data; an engineering college’s edge is computational power and specialized labs. Rather than building engineering departments from scratch, medical colleges benefit far more by establishing joint-degree pipelines with established technical institutes—much like the CMC Vellore-IIT Madras model.
The underlying drive pushing IITs and IISc into medicine applies to India’s broader engineering ecosystem. They can achieve meaningful cross-disciplinary integration with life sciences without building multi-crore hospitals. This can be done by: Integrating curriculum by offering biotechnology and bio-engineering as cross-listed electives or minors. Partnering with local hospitals for joint student capstone projects and co-supervised dissertations. Establishing joint research initiatives with medical colleges via simple MoUs.
For premier institutes and policymakers, a pragmatic roadmap includes: focusing initially on PG, PhD, and M. Tech-PhD programs in partnership with existing medical schools before taking on massive capital investments and the intense regulatory burden of undergraduate MBBS programs. Establishing distinct, clinically competitive contracts for hospital faculty right from the start. Pushing for a formal inter-regulator coordination mechanism across HECI- the NMC, the pharmaceutical council, and the Nursing Council to streamline multidisciplinary campus reviews.
The way forward
Beyond educating full-time medical students, the IITs are uniquely positioned to address an urgent challenge in modern healthcare: upskilling the existing workforce of practicing clinicians who graduated before AI, computer vision, and health informatics became mainstream. They can design targeted, short-term executive programs tailored for senior physicians and surgeons, in areas such as interpreting AI-assisted radiology scans, evaluating diagnostic algorithm accuracy, and understanding predictive analytics for patient outcomes.
The foray of the IITs and IISc into medical education is a necessary natural evolution. In an era where AI diagnoses disease, surgical humanoid robots assist in operating theatres, and bio-printers fabricate body tissue, keeping India’s best doctors and engineers in separate silos is not a prudent strategy.
While regulatory gaps and operational hurdles remain real, starting with postgraduate programs and research in partnership with medical schools and industry offers a pragmatic path forward. With smart policy reforms and flexible operating models, the marriage between the stethoscope and the algorithm could fundamentally redefine the future of Indian healthcare—ensuring quality, access, and inclusivity.
(Professor O.R.S. Rao is the Chancellor of the ICFAI University, Sikkim. Views are personal)

Meta Platforms agreed to pay a maximum $16.68 billion as part of a settlement to resolve claims brought by states across the country that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children, misled consumers about their safety, and improperly collected personal data of children who used its platforms, court papers show.
The settlement was reached during a California federal trial over claims brought by 29 states, averting one of the highest-profile tests yet of allegations that social media companies harmed young users.
Meta also agreed to make changes for teenage users of Facebook and Instagram nationwide, including daily usage limits and nighttime blocks, court papers show. The Menlo Park, California-based company denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle. Shares of Meta rose 4.4% in pre-market trading.
The claims were part of a broader wave of litigation brought by states, local governments, school districts and individuals alleging Meta and other social media companies fueled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.
The federal trial covered claims from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that Meta violated their state laws protecting consumers. It also covered claims from 29 states that Meta violated the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal data from users it knew were children without parental notification or consent, and using the data to train machine learning and generative AI models.
Meta has denied the allegations, saying it has worked hard to protect children on its platforms. The company had argued it could not have misled consumers about whether its services were addictive because “social media addiction” is not a recognised psychiatric condition.
In a filing before the trial, Meta said California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were seeking up to $1.4 trillion in penalties. The states suggested before the trial began that the figure would be closer to $200 billion. The states were also seeking additional monetary damages, plus an order directing Meta to make major changes to its platforms and to bar children from creating accounts.
A mental health crisis
Meta, Snapchat and its parent Snap, YouTube and its parent Alphabet, and TikTok and its parent ByteDance still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims they knowingly designed their platforms to have features that are addictive to children and teens, fuelling a mental health crisis.
The federal cases were consolidated before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, and include lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and state governments.
Thousands more cases against the companies are pending in state courts. A judge in Los Angeles is overseeing thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals who say they or their loved ones were harmed by the platforms’ designs.
Around 30 states have filed lawsuits against the companies in state courts, court records show. A trial has been ongoing in Nashville since July over claims brought by the state against Meta. The settlement comes after Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico.
A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms. On August 6, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and implement youth-safety measures. Also in March, the first trial over an individual’s claims against Meta and Google ended with a verdict in the plaintiff’s favor. A Los Angeles jury found the companies liable for plaintiff Kaley G.M.’s depression and anxiety and ordered them to pay a combined $6 million in damages.
The companies have said they will appeal those verdicts. All four companies settled the first case set for trial in federal court, where a Kentucky school district alleged they were liable for harm to students. Breathitt County School District was set to receive a combined $27 million, public records showed.

A group of saffron-clad men painted the walls of the Anandabazar Patrika (ABP) office in Kolkata saffron on September 1, days after West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had demanded an apology from the daily for describing the recent violence at Jadavpur University as “gerua gundami” — or “saffron hooliganism”.
Videos show two men painting two pillars at the main entrance of the office while several police personnel stand by. Some of the police officials can also be seen recording the incident on their cellphones.
Several other saffron-clad men had gathered at the spot, raising slogans including “Bhagwa ka apmaan nahi sahega” (“We will not tolerate the insult of Bhagwa”) and “Anandabazar Patrika haye haye”. An ABP editor told Alt News that the demonstration began around 1:30 pm on Tuesday and continued for nearly an hour.
In another video, the group can be seen addressing a motley crowd and saying, “This land belongs to Shyama Prasad Mukherjee. This land belongs to Swami Vivekananda. This land is Saffron”.
Alt News procured more footage from the incident where the saffron-clad men could be seen sloganeering near the main gate in Hindi and Bengali before being escorted away by the police.
Anandabazar had carried the headline “Saffron Hooliganism: Logo broken during raid on JU campus” on its front page on August 21. Following this, Adhikari launched a sharp attack on the media outlet while maintaining that his demand for an apology did not amount to a threat to the media.
Meanwhile, Kolkata Police lodged an FIR at Bowbazar police station against editor Ishani Dutta Roy, chief reporter Soma Mukherjee and “others from its editorial team” following a complaint by Sanjay Shastri Maharaj. He alleged that the headline that Anandabazar Patrika had used implied an intention to “hurt Hindu sentiments and disturb public peace”. He stated that the phrasing was “highly objectionable, derogatory, misleading and offensive”.
“It is necessary to ascertain through investigation who proposed the expression, who approved it, who was involved in editing the report and determining the headline…” the complaint said.
“…An apology will have to be made. Otherwise thousands of sadhus in saffron robes are getting ready. They only want my consent…”, Adhikari declared during his rally in Jadavpur on August 28.
Anandabazar, however, did not issue apologise or retract its reports. In fact, they carried a follow-up story containing the chief minister’s statements.
Alt News spoke to a senior editor at Anandabazar Patrika, who said additional security had been deployed at the newspaper’s office near Chandni Chowk since Saturday, following Adhikari’s statements.
“We had a hunch something like this might happen. We were told not to go to office today. Police officials had come with them and left with them as well,” the editor said. Asked whether the men were affiliated with any organisation, the editor said, “They were not carrying any banners. But I do know that most of them were non-Bengalis.”
Alt News contacted Bowbazar police station, which said that no FIR had been lodged yet. Police also confirmed that the officials present at the scene were from Bowbazar PS, before ending the call.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Surviving summer | What is it like to endure extreme heat in a city pushed beyond its capacity to cope? In a dispatch from Mumbai’s sweltering summer in Equator magazine, Aruna Chandrasekhar provides a dystopian glimpse of a climate-stressed future.
Cost of reporting | Uttar Pradesh journalist Abhishek Upadhyay, among the first to report on the theft of donations at Ayodhya’s Ram Mandir Temple, has alleged police harassment and retaliation over his reporting.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Diet Sabya (@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Rs 8,452 crore
The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.
Vibe check
For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek. Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation.

Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.
Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.
One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.
“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”
In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.
In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.
“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.
“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods hit parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). Against this background, a video showing several houses being swept away by floodwaters is being shared on social media, claiming that the visuals are from the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa area (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing the floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa area.
Fact: These visuals are not from Nepal’s Rasuwa area. They show the flooding in NEEPCO Colony in Posa, Kei Panyor district, Arunachal Pradesh, on 24 June 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
We conducted a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video and found a longer version posted by an X account on 24 June 2026, with the caption stating that the video showed the flash floods and devastation caused by them in the NEEPCO Colony in Posa, Kei Panyor district, Arunachal Pradesh, on 24 June 2026.
Based on this, we performed a relevant keyword search and found videos of the flooding in the NEEPCO Colony posted by several social media accounts in Arunachal Pradesh on 24 June 2026 (here, here). These posts featured scenes matching those seen in the viral video.
Further, we found several media reports covering the incident from Arunachal Pradesh on 24 June 2026, which also featured the same visuals seen in the viral video (here, here, here).
To sum up, old flood visuals from Arunachal Pradesh’s Kei Panyor district were shared as recent visuals from Nepal’s Rasuwa area.

Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
The Venezuela operation is the purest distillation of his amoral foreign policy.
“We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.
Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post, Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present.
Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor.
Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form.
The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers.
Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years.
The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting.
When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post’s (headline: “Justice in Venezuela.”)
Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr. Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.”
It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price.
Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests. But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny. Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal. The Journal’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties. Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering. Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes.
They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners. The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies). He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit). Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump.
Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil. Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years. Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016.
Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest. In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. The Best MagSafe Phone Grips
Featured in this article
The best MagSafe phone grips are basically necessities at this point. Once you start using a grip, it's hard to go back. They just offer such security, especially in this world of phones growing ever larger and sleeker. They can help prevent you from dropping your fancy glass screen on the ground (or worse, on your face), and they also add some visual flair to a device that might otherwise look exactly the same as all the others. The grips often double as kickstands, too—all the better to prop up your phone while you watch YouTube over dinner.
The grips in this guide are designed to be used with Apple's MagSafe technology (or compatible cases, including those for Android). They're easy to take on and off, with a secure hold that stays until you dictate otherwise. We've tested these grips in our day-to-day lives and are always checking out more.
Read our MagSafe guides for additional recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Wallets, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best 3-in-1 Apple Chargers, and Best iPhone 17 Cases.
Updated August 2026: We've reformatted portions of this guide, checked for accuracy throughout, and added some grips to our new “avoid” section.
What Is MagSafe?
MagSafe is Apple's magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 lineups, as well as the iPhone Air (the iPhone SE and iPhone 16e are excluded). It consists of a ring of magnets on the back of the phone designed for a faster, more precise wireless charging system. But these magnets also opened up the ability to attach different kinds of accessories, like wallets and power banks. It even makes docking an iPhone to a car mount easier.
If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it comes with MagSafe support (you'll see a ring of magnets on the inside). That way, the MagSafe accessories will have a proper connection. Otherwise, if you use a non-MagSafe case, the accessories will likely slide off due to a weak connection.
If you need a recommendation for a great MagSafe case, we have plenty in our guides:
If you want a magnetic grip, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2, or at least mentions magnets on the product page. All the recommendations here are MagSafe grips.
Can Android Phones Use MagSafe Grips?
Most Android phones are incompatible with MagSafe grips. But there are magnetic cases available for top Android phone models enabling MagSafe-like functionality. You can find WIRED-tested magnetic cases for select Android phones here.
Over the coming years, thanks to the new Qi2 wireless charging standard that incorporates the Magnetic Power Profile, you'll start seeing more high-end Android phones embed magnets inside the device. Google already has Qi2 devices with the Pixel 10 range. That will allow greater compatibility with MagSafe accessories with or without a magnetic case. The road is bumpy, though. Samsung's latest Galaxy S26 range, for example, are “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can only access Qi2 charging speeds and features with a magnet case. Hopefully, manufacturers will add native magnet support soon.
The Different Types of Phone Grips
MagSafe grips are hardly the only type of phone grips available. There are four main other types of grips you can buy.
Cases with attached grips. These are cases with a grip attached to the back. You get a strong and durable grip that will never fall off, but the trade-off is a thicker phone, and these cases typically are incompatible with wireless charging and may not work with other MagSafe accessories.
Clamp-style grips. Also called universal phone grips, these clamp to a phone so you can easily take them on and off, and they're not limited to a particular kind of phone. The downside is they're not the fastest to take on and off, and they can sometimes slide up and down the phone.
Adhesive grips. You can stick a phone grip to the back of your phone or case, and while this will typically give you a well-attached grip that likely won't fall off your phone, the downsides are similar to cases with attached grips. It may block features like wireless charging and restrict you from using other accessories. These grips can also be difficult to remove when you're ready—some have swappable tops, but they don't necessarily allow for easy mixing and matching with different phone cases.
MagSafe grips. These grips are all about convenience. You can easily take them on and off, but they only work with devices or cases with built-in magnets. While you can dangle a phone from a MagSafe grip without issue, additional force could cause the magnets to separate and fling your phone to the ground.
How We Test MagSafe Grips
Each MagSafe grip in this guide is one we used as a primary phone grip for weeks or months at a time. We make sure they snap securely to an iPhone or MagSafe case, and we also ensure they provide a comfortable hold for long periods and are durable enough to withstand drops and heavy use. We use the phone as we normally would—scrolling through social media, FaceTiming with friends, and sending texts and emails—and evaluate the grip to see if it gets in the way or makes life easier.
Other MagSafe Grips We’ve Tested
Spigen OM104 MagSafe Phone Grip: The OM104 is a phone/grip combo accessory for MagSafe and Qi2 devices that comes with a flexible nylon strap to slide your finger through while holding your phone. Dual magnets and a robust metal construction make the OM104 feel like money well spent, and even after hours of sliding my finger in and out of the strap, it still feels soft, flexible, and most importantly, comfortable. It has one annoying design oversight. As you slide your phone in and out of your pocket, the nylon strap will start to droop down. The strap is longer than the grip itself, so when you close the kickstand, it’ll get pinched inside and won’t allow the stand to fully close. It’s comfortable to use, but that quibble knocks it down.
Casely MagRing: Unlike other metal grips we've tested, Casely's MagRing is made of soft silicone. We find it more comfortable on the fingers. It also has a 360-degree swivel, so you can position the grip at virtually any angle. This is strictly a grip, so you can't use it as a kickstand. Since the grip doesn't fold in, your phone won't lie fully flat on a surface. We also tested the MagRing+, which comes with a ring clip for attaching your keys. That comes in handy for quick trips to the grocery store or when you go to the gym and need a place to put your car keys and key fob. But Jacob prefers the standard MagRing, since he typically carries his keys in his pocket or bag. Casely has a few variations of the MagRing and MagRing+ in stock, but it appears to be on its last legs.
Smartish Wallflower: It isn’t perfect, but we still love it. The Smartish Wallflower comes with seven small suction cups that look like a flower, allowing you to attach your phone to a wall (or any other surface) and leave it be. It mostly works, but it largely depends on how heavy your phone is and what surface you’re attaching it to. We didn’t have issues with an iPhone 17 and drywall, but the iPhone 15 Pro Max attached to a particleboard cabinet was too heavy for the grip to manage.
Avoid These MagSafe Grips
OhSnap! Snap Grip: I like that this grip allows you to use other MagSafe accessories, but the point of a MagSafe grip (to me) is that you can remove it easily enough that it doesn't hinder accessories in the first place. So it seems like sort of a needless feature. More importantly, this grip doesn't feel secure to me. I have a harder time keeping a good handle on my phone when I use it, which negates the purpose. The lack of bulk is nice, but a phone ring can provide essentially the same thing with a bit more security. And this grip has a tendency to stick to your accessories rather than your phone when you remove it.
PopSockets Low-Pro Grip and Stand: All phone grip analyses are going to be subjective, but I'm not a fan of how flimsy this new PopSocket feels. It's quite floppy, so I feel like my hand has to do more work to compensate for holding my phone, in which case I'd rather not use a grip in the first place. It's also very difficult to open with one hand. I'm of the mind that accessories shouldn't require more work than you'd need to put in without them. This PopSocket fails that test. Finally, like the OhSnap grip, this sticks to accessories too well. It regularly pulls off or sticks to the car mounts I'm testing rather than sticking to my phone.

Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial
- Published
A 23-year-old Utah man has pleaded not guilty to the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk – as a judge ruled prosecutors can seek the death penalty at trial.
Tyler Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in Utah, and six other charges in connection with the shooting of Kirk at a campus event on 10 September 2025.
Defence lawyers had tried to have the death penalty taken off the table, but prosecutors argued that aggravating factors, such as firing into a crowd in the presence of children, warranted a capital trial.
Turning Point USA co-founder Kirk, 31, was shot in the neck while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem.
The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday.
Kirk's widow, Erika, the mother of their two children, and his parents, Robert and Kathryn, were also at the hearing.
In a statement shared afterwards, the Kirk family said the judge's decision "marks an important step" in their "pursuit of justice".
"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," the statement added.
Closing arguments followed a five-day preliminary hearing in July, during which prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.
That included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.
"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court on Tuesday, outlining video that he said showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting.
"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.
Prosecutors said the accused, a former apprentice electrician, was in a relationship with his roommate and regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant" - which they argued was the motive.
On Tuesday, prosecutors also outlined "aggravating" factors - accusing the defendant of "gambling with the lives of others" when he allegedly fired towards Kirk, who was surrounded by other people.
"He was playing, in effect, a game of ballistic roulette," prosecutor Chad Grunander said.
"It's been 356 days since Tyler Robinson assassinated Charlie Kirk," Grunander added. "It's time for him, the defendant, to be bound over for trial and arraigned. Today."
Defence lawyers attempted to sow doubt about the prosecution's evidence.
During July's hearing, they raised questions about procedure and the credentials of experts who testified. Robinson's lawyers have repeatedly objected to cameras livestreaming court proceedings.
Judge Tony Graf again listened to arguments on the issue during a sealed hearing on Tuesday morning before closing arguments began - but he ruled in favour of transparency in a case that has sparked conspiracy theories.
On Tuesday, the defence sought to downplay the aggravating factors outlined by prosecutors - arguing that no bullets hit anyone in the crowd apart from Kirk.
The court heard and saw during July's hearing how the accused allegedly scouted the campus repeatedly on the day Kirk was shot - interacting with TPUSA members and eating Chick-fil-A before returning in different clothes.
The new outfit included "long pants to obscure the rifle he had concealed down his pants", McBride said on Tuesday.
According to prosecutors' evidence presented during the July hearing, Robinson's DNA was found on his grandfather's rifle stashed in a wooden area near campus after the shooting, as well as on a towel it was wrapped in and a screwdriver recovered at the scene.
McBride also told the court on Tuesday that engravings found on casings from the shooting allegedly matched a Dremel tool recovered at the home the defendant shared with his roommate.
Twiggs' videotaped interview with prosecutors was played in July during the hearing. Robinson's roommate testified that the defendant had confessed to the shooting, cried and said he wished he hadn't done it.
Robinson, in the company of his family and a neighbour, turned himself in the day after the murder.
He is next due in court on 23 October, when a trial date is expected to be set.

"Gavin is so great at what he does, I felt a lot of pressure to kind of prove that. It didn't really show within the first two weeks, which is normal."
That was then. Now Gauff possesses a serve which is a serious weapon - even though she still leaks some double faults.
Showing greater consistency on the toss, not throwing the ball too far in front and keeping her wrist straighter have been MacMillan's pointers for a more reliable serve.
It was a key factor in her charge to the Cincinnati Open title earlier this month.
Analysis from that tournament showed how Gauff is hitting closer to the line but still maintaining her serve speed - underlining a significant improvement in her accuracy.
Gauff now has full confidence her serve can be too hot for opponents to handle - and it showed immediately against Sonmez.
The opening game saw Gauff thump a 112mph ace down the middle, followed by an unreturned first serve and another ace, on her way to holding serve in less than 90 seconds.
Sonmez struggled to get balls into play whenever Gauff landed a first serve in the first set, with the world number four winning 93% of those points.
Gauff broke again for a 1-0 lead in the second set, but her serve was not as effective as Sonmez levelled at 2-2 and held three more break points for a 4-2 lead.
But a precise ace out wide and a 115mph unreturned first serve enabled Gauff to cling on in a game which you felt she would have lost a year ago.
The gutsy hold laid the platform for Gauff to immediately break for 4-3 before securing victory with another service game which displayed her belief.
Gauff hit a trio of unreturned first serves - all just under the 120mph mark, teeing up three match points as Sonmez buckled on the first after a short rally.
"Psychologically, I'm now going to go for the ace, or I know I can hit the serve and the return is probably not going to come back," said Gauff, who will play Spain's Paula Badosa or Australia's Daria Kastakina in the second round.
"Last year I literally was like I hope I make it in. It's such a big difference knowing almost every serve I'm trying to basically hit 110, 115, 120mph if I can."
