It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

In August 2026, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed in an X post that the vaccine used to prevent measles, mumps and rubella contained "fetal tissue."
Kennedy was responding to Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, who accused him of peddling conspiracy theories about vaccines. In his X post on Aug. 25, Kennedy defended his claim (archived). He said, in part:
The rubella virus used in MMR-II is grown on the cultured cell line composed of lung tissue from an aborted three-month-old female embryo and listed as "WI-38 human diploid lung fibroblasts" in the ingredients of MMR-II as portions of these cells end up in each vial of MMR II.
This was not the first time Kennedy made this claim. On April 30, 2025, he claimed during a NewsNation townhall with television presenter Chris Cuomo that the MMR vaccine "contains a lot of aborted fetus debris" (starting at the 1:08 mark).
However, the health secretary's claim that the vaccine contains fetal material from abortions was incorrect. Therefore, we have rated the claim false.
The 2025 measles outbreak
It is true that, in 2025 and 2026, the U.S. was seeing its worst outbreak of measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with 2,777 cases from the beginning of 2026 to Aug. 20, 7% of which required hospitalization. As of this writing, the CDC has also reported three deaths in 2025 and none in 2026.
(Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
(CDC)
Measles is a highly contagious disease that requires 95% of the population to be immunized to prevent its spread, according to Harvard Medical School. For years, the country was able to prevent new cases by keeping the vaccination rates at or above 95%. However, in more recent years, the vaccination rate began to fall. It was at 92% in 2023 and at 82% in the area where the 2025 outbreak started in West Texas, also according to Harvard Medical School. Experts have long identified disinformation and misinformation as key forces causing fears about the safety of the MMR vaccine and others, and, as Snopes reported in February 2024 and in May 2017, Kennedy has been a prominent voice in promulgating false claims about vaccines.
For full immunization, the schedule calls for two doses of the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC. Most people who were infected in the 2025 and 2026 measles outbreak were either unvaccinated, had an unknown vaccination status or had received only one of the two doses, according to Harvard Medical School.
False claims about the MMR vaccine
The MMR vaccine has long been the target of false claims. For example, a now-debunked article, reported on by Snopes in January 2019, succeeded in convincing many concerned parents that a mercury-based preservative known as thimerosal, which some vaccines and other injections used to contain, was responsible for an increase in autism rates. While it is true that autism diagnoses have continued to increase in the U.S., it is not for this reason. In fact, childhood vaccines no longer contain thimerosal.
The combined MMR jab contains three live attenuated viruses. These versions of the viruses are too weak to cause an infection but are strong enough to provoke an immune reaction in which the body produces specific antibodies to fight the viruses if the person is exposed to them later.
The claim that the MMR vaccine contains fetal material stems from a misunderstanding of how the rubella attenuated virus is produced. According to an article that appeared in the Jan. 29, 2020, issue of the medical journal Vaccine, the most common rubella strain used in vaccines is attenuated in a cell culture that uses the specific cell line WI-38:
The most commonly used vaccine strain for the rubella virus is attenuated strain RA27/3, which was extracted using explant liver culture and attenuated by passaging in human diploid fibroblasts (WI-38), at temperatures of 30 °C and 35 °C.
The cell line WI-38 was isolated "from the lung tissue of a 3-month-old, female, embryo," according to the description of a website that commercializes the cells for use in vaccine development. eonard Hayflick, a U.S. scientist, isolated the cells from the embryo of a legal abortion in Sweden in the early 1960s. The cell line is credited with preserving countless lives, according to a 2024 obituary for Hayflick in the journal NPJ Aging (emphasis ours):
The 'Hayflick cells', WI-38, have been the basis for producing vaccines for poliomyelitis, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, adenovirus, rabies, and hepatitis A. Over the last 50 years, the number of people benefiting from these vaccines has been estimated to be several billion worldwide.
However, vaccine development has not needed to take new cells from more recent abortions. Further, while vaccine developers do attenuate the virus in the cells, they later extract it and purify it, removing all trace of WI-38 cells. In sum, no trace of the cells appears in the vaccine.

North Carolina Rep. Chuck Edwards is formally censured over harassment allegations
The Republican-led House has voted to censure outgoing Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., after a months-long investigation by the ethics committee into allegations he sexually harassed two young female staff members.
The vote on Tuesday was 413 to 2. A censure, which is tantamount to public shaming on the House floor, is the strongest punishment the House can adopt against a member short of expulsion.
Edwards has denied the allegations, but ended his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee posted their investigative findings last month.
Speaking from the House floor ahead of the censure vote, Edwards pleaded with his colleagues to "judge me on the facts, not on the inference, insinuation or headlines."
He apologized to the two staffers at the center of the investigation, saying, "I recognize now that my understanding of those relationships may not have always matched yours." He insisted, however, that "regret is not an admission of sexual harassment."
The House Ethics panel recommended the censure as part of an Aug. 3 report on their investigation — a report that determined he "engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers."
The committee found he created a hostile work environment, citing "substantial evidence" he "violated the spirit of the House's prohibition on sexual harassment and unwanted advances."
The committee said Edwards gave the staffers gifts that included jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, a KitchenAid mixer, vacations and one-on-one-dinners.
"A Member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person's appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers," the report said. "That Representative Edwards did all these things to two young staffers, repeatedly over a sustained period, was beyond inappropriate."
Edwards addressed the spending in his remarks Tuesday, saying "generosity is not sexual harassment."
The bipartisan committee said it did not find evidence Edwards propositioned his staffers or engaged in sexual activity with them. However, the committee said Edwards appeared to not understand this didn't insulate him from sexual harassment claims.
House censures are rare. Before Tuesday's vote, the punishment has been doled out just 28 other times. The last, in 2025, was to Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, for interrupting a joint address to Congress by President Trump.
Multiple investigations
The investigation into Edwards was one of several for the ethics committee this Congress involving allegations of sexual misconduct, assault or other improprieties.
Last month, the committee announced it was investigating allegations of sexual misconduct against Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif. That included "inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer." Gomez has denied the allegations, but has acknowledged "personal mistakes" outside his marriage, which he described as "consensual in nature."
In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat and ended a gubernatorial bid amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct that he too denied. Texas Republican Tony Gonzales also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member who later died by suicide.
Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida have also faced House Ethics investigations tied to domestic violence allegations. Both have denied the claims.
Miller, who is facing a difficult re-election fight, said he requested the probe in the midst of a child custody fight with his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. Mills lost his bid for another term when he was defeated last month by a GOP primary challenger.

Odisha FC owner Rohan Sharma has admitted that he has been “particularly depressed” about the state of Indian football and acknowledged his own mistakes in the club’s recent struggles, while expressing renewed optimism ahead of the new season.
In a lengthy statement issued on the eve of the transfer deadline, Rohan said he believed Indian football was in a worse position than it was when his family took over an ISL club in 2016.
“It’s been 10 years since my family took over an ISL club, and it saddens me that Indian Football is in a worse place than where it was in 2016,” Rohan said. He also accepted responsibility for some of the problems, saying owners, including himself, had played a part in Indian football’s “slow spiral downwards”.
‘Ego took over the club’
Rohan identified the 2024-25 season as a turning point for Odisha FC. The club had enjoyed what he described as the best season in its history, topping its AFC Cup group and winning the Indian Women’s League for the first time. However, Sharma said expectations of further progress were followed by internal problems.
“I wrongly gave carte blanche to the wrong people within the organisation to push our club to the next level. In-fighting and greed took over, and in the end the club started crumbling from within,” he said. Rohan took personal responsibility for the situation, saying he should not have allowed individuals to put themselves ahead of the club “no matter the resume and stature of the profile”.
READ: India beats Syria in AFC U-20 Asian Cup 2027 Qualifiers
The uncertainty surrounding Indian football intensified after the 15-year Master Rights Agreement between the AIFF and Reliance-backed FSDL officially expired in December 2025. Rohan said the development forced him to reassess Odisha FC’s future, particularly given the scale of investment made in the club.
“Having Reliance involved meant a certain degree of professionalism and revenue growth. We had no idea what to expect in the future, and everything was up in the air,” he said.
With the league effectively in limbo, Odisha paused operations, prompting speculation that the club could shut down. “From an owners' perspective, we just lost a crucial element of why we invested in the league in the first place,” he said.
The intervention of the Government of India eventually provided a pathway for the league to continue, although Rohan remained sceptical about the viability of a shortened season with limited revenues and sponsorship opportunities. After discussions with his father, however, the family decided to keep the club alive on a “shoestring budget”.
Rohan takes greater control of recruitment
With Indian football appearing to regain momentum after the league’s ownership transition, Rohan said he has also taken a more hands-on approach to rebuilding Odisha FC. He revealed that he had created a ‘think tank’ comprising people he trusts, with the group collectively involved in recruitment and player signings.
“I’m proud of all the players we brought this window and I stand by the recruitments we’ve made this year – 100 per cent... I feel today that this is a squad of hungry men, hungry coaches, hungry players wanting to make a difference,” he said.

What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
- Published
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.
Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.
Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.
That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.
With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.
The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.
It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.
However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.
More involved, more shots - but a smaller sample
On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.
The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.
Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.
His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.
That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.
Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.
During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.
Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).
Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.
There is, however, an important caveat.
Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.
Are Villa getting a different type of striker?
Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.
Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.
Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.
The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.
He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:
- 1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8
- 1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82
- 2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.
Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.
Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.
Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.
Greater intensity without the ball
There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.
Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.
His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.
The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.
Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.
Why Emery believes he can unlock Jackson
Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.
Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.
"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,
Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.
Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.
Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.
Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.
Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.
His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.
Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.
Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.
A replacement - but not necessarily a replica
Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.
Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.
There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.
But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.
If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.
They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Iron deficiency can develop gradually, with the body’s stored iron being depleted before there is a measurable fall in haemoglobin. So, a normal haemoglobin level does not always mean that the body has adequate iron stores.
Steve Thomas A., consultant haemato-oncologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, explains that haemoglobin and ferritin measure different things. Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, while ferritin reflects the body’s iron reserves. The body can maintain haemoglobin for some time by drawing on these reserves. As a result, iron deficiency may be present even when a routine blood test shows normal haemoglobin.
Ferritin is one of the key markers used to assess these iron stores. Gopinathan M., consultant, haemato-oncology (BMT), MGM Cancer Institute, compares ferritin to a warehouse where iron is stored for use whenever the body needs it. Iron is stored mainly in tissues such as the liver and spleen and within cells called macrophages. It is subsequently mobilised for erythropoiesis, the process through which red blood cells and haemoglobin are produced.
Iron deficiency without anaemia, therefore, can be missed if testing is limited to just haemoglobin measurement.
In India, the latest available NFHS-5 data showed that 57% of women aged 15-49 years live with anaemia.
Ferritin levels
Ferritin is an important marker of iron stores, but there is no single number that can be interpreted in isolation for everyone. Dr. Gopinathan says, along with ferritin, serum iron and total iron-binding capacity are assessed to calculate transferrin saturation. A transferrin saturation below 20% can support a diagnosis of iron deficiency, particularly when ferritin is difficult to interpret.
Dr. Thomas, however, cautions against treating ferritin cut-offs as universal rules. Age, sex, pregnancy, menstruation and a person’s clinical history can influence how the result should be interpreted.
Inflammation is particularly important. Ferritin is also an acute-phase reactant, meaning its level can rise during infection or inflammation. This can make iron stores appear better than they actually are. The World Health Organization recommends taking inflammation into account when interpreting ferritin and, where appropriate, using markers such as C-reactive protein alongside it.
This is why a ferritin value that appears to be within a laboratory’s reference range does not necessarily rule out iron deficiency in a person who has inflammation or chronic illness.
Who is affected?
Iron stores can gradually decline when iron loss continues or the body’s requirements increase. Women who have heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding are particularly vulnerable. Pregnancy also increases iron requirements. Frequent blood donors can lose significant amounts of iron through repeated donations. People who follow vegetarian diets may also be at risk because the iron in plant foods is generally less readily absorbed than haem iron from animal foods.
Chronic, unnoticed blood loss is another important cause. Experts point to conditions such as ulcers and bleeding piles as examples, while gastrointestinal blood loss can continue without obvious visible bleeding.
In such situations, ferritin may fall while haemoglobin remains normal for months. This makes a low ferritin an important finding.
What can tiredness say
Iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia can produce symptoms that are often vague and overlap with many other conditions. Headache, body and muscle aches, itching, episodes of blackout, ringing in the ears and breathlessness are among symptoms that may occur. Persistent tiredness, weakness, hair loss and poor concentration should prompt evaluation when they do not improve with adequate rest, particularly in people who have risk factors for iron deficiency.
However, these symptoms are not specific to iron deficiency. This is why symptoms alone should not be used to decide whether iron supplements are needed. A complete blood count is generally an important starting point. Ferritin and other iron parameters can then help determine whether depleted iron stores are contributing to the problem.
Causes of low ferritin
Finding a low ferritin is only part of the evaluation. The more important question is why the iron stores have fallen.
“Iron deficiency is a symptom of something else, not a disease on its own,” Dr. Thomas says. Treating the deficiency without addressing its cause can allow the problem to recur.
Experts caution against starting iron tablets simply because a report shows a low ferritin. Treatment commonly continues for several months, including after haemoglobin improves, to replenish iron stores, but the dose and duration depend on the cause and severity of the deficiency.
Seeking diagnosis
The widespread availability of iron supplements can make self-treatment tempting, particularly when symptoms such as fatigue or hair loss are attributed to low iron.
But unnecessary supplementation can cause nausea, constipation and abdominal discomfort. More importantly, it can delay the diagnosis of the underlying reason for iron loss. Excessive iron accumulation can also be harmful, particularly in people with disorders that cause increased iron absorption.
The message, experts say, is not to panic over an isolated ferritin value, but neither should a low ferritin be ignored simply because the haemoglobin is normal. Dr. Thomas says medical advice is therefore important to determine whether iron deficiency is actually present, identify its cause and decide on the appropriate treatment and duration.

Video of Hochul in the mosque authentically shows her wearing a headscarf, with some of her hair visible.
Hochul was not wearing a traditional hijab, which is a way of life that involves practicing modesty, covering the head and all the hair.
In late August 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul was criticized after she purportedly wore a head covering to a mosque.
Videos (archived) on Instagram, Facebook, and X (archived) claimed to show Hochul wearing a black head scarf or hijab while speaking at a mosque, which conservative critics claimed was disrespectful so close to the anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. Snopes readers asked us to confirm whether Hochul was wearing a hijab — a covering for the head, hair and neck that is typically worn by some Muslim women.
The above video is authentic. On Aug. 28, 2026, Hochul visited the Islamic Cultural Center of New York and covered her head as a gesture of respect as she was speaking in the prayer hall. Hochul has worn a head covering at events with Muslims before and has even spoken out in favor of Muslim women choosing to wear the hijab. She was not, however, wearing a traditional hijab. As such, we rate this claim as a mixture of true and false information.
Social media posts and media coverage often erroneously simplify the meaning of "hijab" and claim it is just a headscarf. The term "hijab" has many interpretations but broadly refers to a veil or barrier and is a practice involving modesty for both men and women. Wearing hijab involves modest clothing in an Islamic context, including a head covering. It is worn in many styles but for Muslim women today, the hijab colloquially refers to the covering that typically conceals the head, all the hair and neck while leaving the face uncovered.
In available photographs of Hochul covering her head, her hair is visible. She is wearing a headscarf, and not participating in the practice of wearing hijab, as is typically done by Muslim women.
Hochul was visiting the Islamic Cultural Center in New York City during Friday prayers. The above video shows her standing before the front wall of the mosque with the decorative glass niche behind her (visible in these videos of the Islamic Cultural Center at 0:23 and 3:29).
The official Instagram account for the Islamic Cultural Center School — which is affiliated with the Islamic Cultural Center— posted about Hochul's visit and noted that the governor joined for Friday prayers:
 
Governor Hochul joined our community at ICCNY for Friday Jumaa, where she addressed the congregation, before visiting the Islamic Cultural Center School of New York. She toured the school, stepped into our classrooms and learned more about the community we are so proud to serve.
Hochul is wearing the same outfit in the above Instagram post and in the videos being shared on social media. However, during her visit to the Islamic Cultural Center School, Hochul's head was uncovered. She covered only it when speaking at the gathering at the prayer hall.
All Muslim women cover their heads when praying or when inside the prayer hall of a mosque, with some — but not all — in hijab. Given that Hochul was in attendance for Friday prayers at the mosque, covering her head can be seen as a sign of respect.
This was not the first time Hochul covered her head at a religious gathering for Muslims. In July 2025, she covered her head when speaking at the funeral of a slain Muslim police officer. In 2020, she covered her head when speaking at the Jamaica Muslim Center.
In February 2024, Hochul posted (archived) on X in support of World Hijab Day, writing: "we stand in solidarity with our Muslim sisters who choose to wear the hijab. New York's diversity has always been its strength, and together, we will always promote respect, inclusion, and religious freedom in the face of hate."
The post also showed Hochul shaking hands with a Muslim hijabi woman while wearing a head covering. Another Muslim woman in the photograph is wearing a head covering similar to Hochul's:
Hochul has not publicly addressed the criticism as of this writing.
Snopes has previously covered examples of other leaders wearing head coverings as a sign of respect among Muslim communities, including former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.

What is the ‘Cat in the Hat’ viral trend that is landing teens in trouble with the law?
Authorities in Kentucky and Colorado have cracked down on the trend over concerns about students’ safety
A viral social media trend has landed teens in trouble with police in at least two states as authorities warn students about threats to school safety.
The so-called Cat in the Hat trend has spread across the country as young people share AI-generated content of someone wearing a costume of the famous Dr. Seuss character and appearing to be coming after people at their schools or homes.
Authorities in Kentucky and Colorado are among those to have cracked down on the trend.
The Allen County-Scottsville Crime Task Force in Kentucky opened an investigation last Thursday after it said multiple local students reported receiving threatening messages through Snapchat and other social media platforms from someone who identified themselves as the “Cat in the Hat.”
The task force said in a Facebook post Saturday that it had identified the minor behind a TikTok account involved in the investigation and that “the matter is being handled accordingly.”
A minor linked to the “Cat in the Hat” videos targeting Allen County turned themselves in to police Saturday, WKRN reported.
The Allen County-Scottsville task force told the news outlet that the minor faces criminal charges, but avoided harsher penalties. It’s unclear whether this is the same minor that the task force referred to on Facebook.
“The ‘Cat in the Hat’ accounts are part of a viral social media trend that has spread well beyond Allen County.
“Young people have been creating accounts and using AI-generated images and videos to make it appear that the character is coming to their town, school, neighborhood, or even after specific people,” the task force explained in a statement shared by WKRN.
“What may start as an internet trend or prank can quickly cross the line when it causes students to genuinely fear for their safety.”
A 14-year-old student from Grand Junction High School in Colorado was arrested Monday in connection with the viral trend.
Last Friday, local police were made aware of a social media post referencing the “Cat in the Hat” trend on TikTok and suggesting someone may appear at a local middle school and at random houses.
“The posts are intended to cause alarm and fear in individuals,” Grand Junction Police said in a Facebook post.
The 14-year-old was charged with Interference with Staff, Faculty, or Students of Educational Institutions and Harassment and released to his parents.
“GJPD takes reports involving school safety seriously and will continue working closely with our community partners to prioritize the safety and security of our students, staff, and schools,” the Facebook post read.

6 more byelections on horizon will test Liberal momentum, pressure other parties
Carney being 'very strategic in grouping the byelections,' says political scientist
The Liberals are taking a victory lap after scoring a hat trick of byelection wins on Monday night — but there are still a batch of seats that need to be filled and will serve as another temperature check of the electorate in the months to come.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's party garnered over 50 per cent of the vote in each riding that was up for grabs on Monday, picking up seats in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec.
"The message from Canadians I think is clear. They've given their support … to the government's plan and I think that's because Canadians are united," Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.
Lori Turnbull, a political science professor at Dalhousie University, said the Liberal wins in North Vancouver-Capilano and Beaches-East York aren't surprising given that they're considered safe Liberal seats. But she said she thinks Daniel Gobeil's win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord was a vote of confidence in how Carney is handling the trade war with the U.S.
- Liberals sweep 3 federal byelections in Ontario, Quebec and B.C.
- Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal
Turnbull said the Liberals picking Gobeil was a sign the Carney government wanted to make the byelection about the trade war.
"The fact that he chose a dairy farmer as a candidate, [signalled] a clear commitment to supply management," she said.
Three MPs resigned in the past week, which makes for five official vacancies at the moment. With Ontario Conservative Larry Brock set to step down later this month, that means six byelections will need to be held.
Conservative Cathay Wagantall officially resigned her Saskatchewan seat on Monday. Her resignation was preceded by former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault — who officially resigned on Friday after giving notice that he was leaving back in May — and former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice who stepped down last Tuesday to run in Quebec's provincial election.
The Bloc Québécois' Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, also to run provincially. Liberal Shaun Chen resigned in mid-August.
Éric Grenier, author and analyst with The Writ, told CBC's Power & Politics that as things currently stand in the polls it's likely that the Liberals will keep the ridings they previously held and possibly pick up a few more.
"Still going to have lots of intrigue and interest in that next set of byelections and the Liberals will be looking to expand their majority," he told guest host John Paul Tasker.
Grenier said although Brock's riding of Brantford-Brant South-Six Nations has previously been considered a reliable Conservative seat, it will be one to watch when the campaign kicks off.
Brock won re-election in 2025 with just over 50 per cent of the vote, but the Liberals pulled in about 40 per cent. The Liberals picked up around 30 per cent in previous iterations of that riding.
"That will be a lot of pressure for [Conservative Leader] Pierre Poilievre," Grenier said.
Turnbull expects the Liberals will make a push for Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, Boulerice's former riding. The former NDP MP was the last ripple of the 2011 Orange Wave — the only New Democrat who remained in Quebec. Like in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Turnbull said the trade war might become a key issue in the Montreal riding.
"The Bloc and the NDP are in a really tough spot because if the question is, 'who do you want to run the country' — they are not in a position to form government," she said.
When Carney set Monday's three byelections in motion, he opted not to include Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton.
That riding, east of Montreal, has been largely Bloc territory since the early 1990s. Turnbull said Carney avoiding that byelection in this round of votes "was no accident."
All parties have caps on how much they can spend promoting candidates during byelections. But the cap for a party increases if they're running candidates in multiple byelections and it's up to the party to decide how they want to distribute campaign funding amongst those ridings.
By calling two byelections in safe seats and one in a competitive Quebec riding, the Liberals had a spending advantage over the Bloc who only run candidates in that province. If Carney had included Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, it would have given the Bloc wiggle room to direct more campaign funding to Chicoutimi-Le Fjord.
"Clearly Carney has been very strategic in grouping the byelections in ways that will make sense for him," Turnbull said.
"I think that there will be machinations for sure to try to maintain a Liberal advantage in those [upcoming byelections], both financially and also in terms of just the overall ground game."
Grenier added that the Bloc might have concerns about how safe Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton is after Monday.
"The Bloc is going to have to defend their seat … which, after the results in Chicoutimi, might make them sweat a bit," he said.
Of the six byelections coming, three will be in Quebec, two in Ontario (including in a safe Liberal Toronto seat, Scarborough North) and one in Saskatchewan.
In addition to the Bloc stronghold riding, Turnbull said she expects Carney will aim to use the timing of byelections to give his party some sort of advantage over the Conservatives in Brock's Ontario riding.
Once an MP officially resigns, the Speaker has to inform the chief electoral officer of the vacancy, at which point election rules state the prime minister has 11 to 180 days to call a byelection.
Because Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, the last day that Carney can legally call the next byelection is Dec. 19.

- Fortnite update 42.10 will release on September 3, 2026, at 6 AM ET.
- The new Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 update will bring new Sprites, Match Overrides, and more.
- A brand new Fortnite OG Season and LEGO Fortnite Batman update are also coming this week.
Early patch notes for Fortnite update 42.10 are finally out, and there is quite a bit to go over. Three new Sprites are being added alongside new Match Overrides, Loot Hacks, and let’s not forget Fortnite OG Season X. That said, here’s what you need to know about the Fortnite update 42.10 early patch notes for Chapter 7 Season 4.
Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 Update 42.10 Downtime Details
Fortnite downtime for Chapter 7 Season 4 update 42.10 will begin at 4 AM ET on September 3, 2026, and is expected to last until 6 AM ET.
You can expect matchmaking to be taken offline 30 minutes before downtime begins. Once the downtime is over, you’ll be able to drop back in.
Fortnite September 3 Update Early Patch Notes
New Match Overrides
As per the early patch notes for Fortnite update 42.10, two new Match Overrides will be introduced. They are: Big Heads and Prop Hunt. Big Heads was part of the April Fool’s celebration this year and gave everyone a giant head. Players were also given the ability to Shoulder Ride in Fortnite. The mechanic could make a return this week.
As for the Prop Hunt Match Override, it should turn players into props when activated. This should make finding opponents harder during a Fortnite Battle Royale match, but there is an element of fun to it. If you manage to obtain the 1-Up Token in Fortnite, even if you’re discovered, things should pan out in your favor.
New Sprites and Sprite Garden
It’s not just the overrides that are being added to Fortnite this week; three new Sprites are being introduced as well. They are: X-Ray Sprite, Onigiri Sprite, and Unknown Sprite. The first two are the winners from the “Design a Sprite” Fortnite contest that was held earlier this year, while the last is an original design by Epic Games. Here’s what each Sprite can do:
- X-Ray Sprite: Reveals players through walls and other objects for a short duration of time.
- Onigiri Sprite: Consumables give extra health. (Note: We don’t know why the Bullet Sprite was swapped for the Onigiri Sprite).
- Unknown Sprite: TBA
With the Sprite Garden in Fortnite now live, you can visit it to see all your Sprites collected since Chapter 7 Season 3. Epic Games is actively improving the experience by adding more features and QoL improvements.
New Loot Hacks
Six new Loot Hacks will be introduced in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 this week. You can use them to augment your personal Fortnite loot pool during the course of a Battle Royale match. They are not to be confused with Fortnite Lobby Hacks (Admin Panel) Codes, which are limited to the main lobby.
If you’re wondering which weapons and items are being added as Loot Hacks in Fortnite update 42.10, here’s the full list:
- Rocket Ram
- Golden Banana
- Tracking Visor
- Holo Twister Assault Rifle
- Deadeye Assault Rifle
- Wrecker Revolver

Fortnite OG Season X Update

Following the Fortnite OG Final Showdown Live Event, the island has undergone several changes, and there’s a lot of new content coming, including a new Battle Pass. Map Changes
New POIs are coming to the island in Fortnite OG Season X. They are: Tilted Town, Starry Suburbs, and The Meteor. As always, expect Tilted Town to be a hot-drop location in most matches, whereas The Meteor is going to be a great place to hang out with friends.

New Loot Pool
Like every seasonal update, the Fortnite OG loot pool is going to be modified a bit in Season X. Epic Games will add new content to the mix; this includes weapons and items. Here is the full list of all the loot pool changes coming to Fortnite OG:
- Junk Rift
- Automatic Sniper Rifle
- Glitched Forageable
- B.R.U.T.E.
- SR Tactical Submachine Gun
- Shield Bubble
- Zapper Trap
- Spicy Taco Forageable

New OG Pass

Cellulitis is a common bacterial infection that can be treated with a course of antibiotics. This skin infection is caused by a bacteria entering the system through broken skin, a wound or contracted by those with weak immune systems. The infection can affect the subcutaneous tissues, and is commonly found to affect the legs, feet and toes but could occur on the face, arms, hands and fingers as well. If left untreated the infection could spread to the lymph nodes and the blood stream, requiring hospitalisation.
What is cellulitis?
Cellulitis is a common skin infection caused mostly by streptococcus and staphylococcus bacteria. It can affect the tissues beneath the skin. Though it can affect any part of the body such as the face, arms, hands and fingers it usually affects the legs, feet and toes. Cellulitis can also affect just one side of the body. Anyone can contract cellulitis, but persons with skin wounds, or compromised immune systems, which allows the bacteria to enter easily, are at higher risk. Poor skin hygiene may also be a contributing factor. Cellulitis is not contagious but if untreated or if severe, it can spread to tissue under the skin, the lymph nodes and the bloodstream.
Symptoms and treatment
Infected skin may appear slightly discoloured, and warm to touch. As the infection spreads, the discolouration darkens and the skin swells and becomes tender. Apart from swelling and warmth, the infection could be painful. Affected persons could have fever, feel fatigued, experience chills, develop spots on the skin, blisters filled with fluid and dimpling of the skin.
Treatment usually consists of a course of oral antibiotics. Severe cases may need hospitalisation and IV antibiotics.
Preventing relapses
Good skin hygiene can help prevent a relapse. It is necessary to wash hands regularly with soap and warm water. Cleaning and trimming finger and toenails and thoroughly drying the skin after a shower, wearing clean clothes and keeping small wounds clean can prevent the infection.
Cellulitis in India
An observational study by Tripta S. Bhagat, Luv Kumar, et al published in the The International Journal of Lower Extremity Wounds in March 2023 found that cellulitis was commonly seen in men, in the working age group. The mean age of those affected in the study was around 36 years. The affected were in field jobs, and among them 50% of the time, the risk factor for the condition was trauma. Other factors included diabetes mellitus and smoking. The commonest complication was abscess. While over half the persons required only conservative management the rest needed surgical intervention, requiring hospitalisation for five or more days.
What research has found
A 2023 multi-centre clinical study on 247 individuals,The natural history of antibiotic-treated lower limb cellulitis: analysis of data extracted from a multicenter clinical trial, by three O. Martin Williams, Fergus Hamilton and Richard Brindle, has thrown more light on how the bacterial infection is resolved.
The study found that while swelling reduced by half within 10 days of administering antibiotics and the size of the affected area also shrank to half its original size and a blood marker of the inflammation reached near-normal levels in all the participants, more than half the participants reported discomfort in the affected leg and around 14% of the participants said the pain was severe, ranking it 5 or greater on a scale of 1 to 10.
Residual symptoms can persist in some cases even after the course of antibiotics has been completed.
Home treatments include warm compresses to reduce swelling, elevating the leg to improve blood flow, compression socks and walking to reduce discomfort. Rest and refraining from touching the affected areas can also help.
It is, however, important to consult a doctor to have cellulitis treated and essential to complete the entire course of treatment as prescribed, in order prevent progression and complications.

Kennedy did not explicitly that hospice patients cost taxpayers too much money because they received treatment for too long. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud in California.
In late August 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said people in hospice care weren't dying fast enough and were costing taxpayers too much money.
For example, independent journalist Aaron Rupar shared a clip of Kennedy speaking on X and wrote, "RFK Jr complains that people in hospice aren't dying quick enough and therefore cost too much money."
Similar claims about Kennedy's alleged comments on people receiving hospice care also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Though Kennedy did speak about hospice care during an appearance on the Fox News program "Saturday in America" on Aug. 29, summaries such as Rupar's on X did not accurately reflect his words.
Kennedy did not explicitly say that hospice patients cost taxpayers money because they received treatment for too long. Rather, he said hospices in California had fraudulently received federal funds, pointing to billing for patients over multiple years instead of the typical several months as one example.
In August 2026, The Associated Press reported on one incident of fraud where a California hospice billed Medicare for a healthy 71-year-old woman.
In a recording of the "Saturday in America" town hall featuring Kennedy, he said (at 52:52):
We closed down thousands of hospices in California, they didn't have patients, they were just billing us. And the way we found them is because the patients would never die. And so, we could see, we've been paying for this guy for five years — usually, if you go to a hospice, it means you've got three months left to live — these people were never dying, they just had the patient numbers and we were being charged $6,000 a month and just paying, I think 8,000 of them, of these hospices. We're talking about tens of billions of dollars stolen every year.
Given the above, we find claims that Kennedy said hospice patients weren't dying fast enough and costing taxpayers money false. Instead, he was specifically referring to instances of suspected hospice fraud.
We contacted the Department of Health and Human Services to ask when it closed the 8,000 hospices Kennedy mentioned and how much money the department estimated hospice fraudsters had received and await a reply.
Medicare, the U.S. federal health insurance program for people 65 and older, covers hospice care for eligible patients. According to Medicare's website, a patient is eligible if one or more doctors certify they are terminally ill, with a life expectancy of six months or less — not three, as Kennedy said. The insurance program covers hospice care for two initial 90-day periods and successive unlimited 60-day periods.
The Associated Press reported in August 2026 that fraudsters opened fake hospices and tricked real patients into enrolling, or stole people's identities to bill Medicare for hospice services they did not receive.
In May 2026, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced six-month moratoriums on Medicare enrollment for hospices and home health agencies. The centers said they had worked with Vance's anti-fraud task force to suspend federal payments to 800 hospices and home health agencies suspected of fraud in Los Angeles. The suspected fraudulent companies received $1.4 billion in Medicare payments in 2025, according to the news release.
The release noted that hospice fraud was especially prevalent in Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
California's Department of Justice described hospice fraud as "an epidemic" in the state. The department said it carried out its own investigations into hospice fraud within Medi-Cal, California's state-level health insurance program and that it had secured 51 "hospice related convictions" since 2021.

On the job review platform Glassdoor, one faction hates artificial intelligence more than any other.
“Pushing AI to the point that you are asking humans not to use their thoughts and brains is such a turn off,” reads one representative review. “Stop forcing AI onto everyone,” reads another. And then there’s this one: “The AI apps this company uses are all trash.”
The reviews in question all come not from journalists or teachers, but from insurance claims adjusters. In fact, recent research from Glassdoor found that claims adjusters who mention AI in their posts are critical a whopping 98 percent of the time—enough to win them the mantle of the biggest AI haters in the American workforce.
Typically, insurance adjusters complain about “AI-obsessed leaders forcing error-prone AI on them and their clients,” according to the research. When AI falls short in this job, adjusters say, they have to clean up a very human mess.
Take Ahmad Jackson. About a year ago, he was working in the claims department for a major insurance company. His employer decided to use AI for initial loss reporting, which involves setting up claims and gathering information when someone first discloses an incident. It was supposed to be a boon for employees and policyholders alike, streamlining simple claims while transferring more complex situations to actual people.
Instead, Jackson says, he and other adjusters faced a sudden influx of misclassified claims that required rerouting to the correct department. He encountered AI-driven hallucinations while reading claims summaries; when he inadvertently relayed those errors to claimants or their attorneys, he bore the brunt of their fury.
He quit the company not long after, switching to a different insurance carrier. AI is “getting things wrong,” Jackson tells WIRED. “And it's implementing more work onto the adjusters.”
“There's an AI fatigue,” says Geoffrey Conrad, a claims executive in Mobile, Alabama. “We're pretty much exhausted as far as the amount of AI being shoved down our throats.”
Glassdoor senior economist Chris Martin didn’t expect claims adjusters to hate AI quite this much. When he saw the results, he tells WIRED, he did a double take—then started digging. Martin’s conclusion: The profession is in the midst of a reckoning.
In 2024, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that it expected the number of claims adjusters in the United States to fall by 18,900, or 5 percent, in the coming decade. Between May 2025 and May 2026, employment in the sector dropped a staggering 21 percent, according to BLS data. For early-career adjusters, the decline was even sharper: Entry-level postings have fallen 50 percent since 2025, according to Glassdoor.
The BLS cited technology as a major force behind the decline. In the last few years, AI startups like Liberate and Pace have raised millions of dollars based on promises to “reinvent” insurance, while insurers have scaled their use of AI to handle more and more claims.
In practice, this could look like talking to a chatbot instead of a person to file a claim. Instead of sending people to inspect a damaged home, AI tools might analyze photos or videos to provide estimates for payouts. Hundreds of pages of medical records could be summarized by AI to pull out crucial details. Or an insurer’s AI tool could process a policyholder’s uploaded information—photos, videos, documentation, receipts—then send a payout, all within seconds.
That’s the goal of Lemonade. Since its founding in 2015, the insurance company has promised to replace bureaucracy with “bots and machine learning.” By the end of last year, its proprietary chatbot, AI Jim, handled initial reports 96 percent of the time, with automation handling roughly 55 percent of all claims. While more traditional insurance companies like State Farm emphasize that claims require a mix of human and digital expertise, some claim adjusters still worry they’re training their replacements.
“AI is going to impact many jobs and threaten many incumbents in insurance and the economy,” a Lemonade spokesperson, Paul Staats, tells WIRED, adding that automating allows employees to focus their “empathy, care, and expertise on the most complex claims.”
Glassdoor’s report “should be taken seriously across the industry,” Staats adds.
“There's no jobs, there's no good job prospects,” Martin says. When workers sense layoffs looming, Glassdoor data indicates that their reviews become increasingly anti-AI. Martin says that reviewers also express skepticism about AI when they feel a subpar product is being forced upon them—or upon clients.
Conrad, the Alabama claims adjuster, says people in his profession do feel like they’re being replaced by AI models. “AI is just a tool,” he says. “It should never be given the keys.”
There are instances where AI can make claims adjusters’ lives easier; Jackson says it’s helpful for administrative tasks. He uses it for what he considers “nuisance calls,” like extending someone’s rental car booking by a few days. Justin Tomczak, a representative for State Farm, tells WIRED that the company aims to “give State Farm agents and employees better tools so they can spend more time doing what matters most: helping customers.
But claims adjusters don’t have “a lot of faith in the output,” says Sandy Avina, a claims adjuster turned insurance industry consultant. A smudge in a document from an attorney can result in a hallucination, which leads to an incorrect payout. A missing point in an AI summary of a medical report can do the same. Customers often don’t realize when AI is the root cause of confusion or misinformation, and they assume the adjuster is the one who made the mistake.
Conrad understands that many people see claims adjusters as soulless vultures circling after a catastrophe. But he insists that a good claims adjuster is one who is both empathetic and determined to get the policyholder as much money as possible. He knows, he says, because he’s been there.
Twenty-five years ago, before Conrad started working in the insurance industry, his house burned down. It was a total loss. “If you would have told me that someone was just gonna come take photographs, and an estimate would be generated [by AI] off of photographs, I probably would have lost my mind,” Conrad says.
“I needed somebody to make sure that I'm OK, my family's OK, that we're safe,” Conrad says. AI can be helpful, but not when it’s used as a replacement for humanity. “I think that's a dangerous strategy,” he says.

World No. 24 Hariharan Amsakarunan and M.R. Arjun retired at the first-game interval of their China Masters opening-round match against China’s World No. 10 pair Chen Bo Yang and Liu Yi on Tuesday.
The Indian duo made a slow start as Chen and Liu raced to a 5-1 lead and then stretched their advantage to 7-3. Hariharan and Arjun, however, fought their way back into the contest, levelling the score at 7-7.
The Chinese pair managed to regain the lead and went into the first break with an 11-8 advantage. Hariharan and Arjun then retired at the interval, handing Chen and Liu victory and sending the Chinese duo into the next round. The reason for the Indian pair’s retirement was not immediately ascertained.
Chen and Liu will next face the winners of the match between Japan’s Hiroki Okamura and Kyohei Yamashita and Malaysia’s Aaron Chia and Soh Wooi Yik.
Hariharan and Arjun had entered the China Masters after being knocked out in the Round of 32 at the BWF World Championships in New Delhi. The Indian pair lost 21-17, 21-14 to South Korea’s Kang Min Hyuk and Ki Dong Ju.
The Indian duo will now travel to Japan for the Asian Games, which get underway later this month. Arjun was part of the Indian men’s team that won silver at the 2023 Asian Games.

The lack of proper roads and bridges continues to severely disrupt daily life for the Muthuvan tribal community in Edamalakkudy, Keralam’s first tribal panchayat near Munnar.
Transporting critically ill patients on makeshift bamboo stretchers across rugged forest terrain has become an alarming routine.
On Monday (August 31, 2026), a 40-year-old woman suffering from high fever had to be carried over seven kilometres through dense forests to access medical care. The woman, identified as Sumathi from the Parappayarkudy settlement, was eventually admitted to the Munnar General Hospital. This marks the fourth such incident reported in the panchayat in under a month.
‘No other option’
Edamalakkudy panchayat president Binu M. stated that Sumathi developed a severe fever, leaving villagers with no option but to transport her on a bamboo stretcher.
“There is no road between Parappayarkudy and Vellavarakkudy. The residents carried the woman from Parappayarkudy to Keppakkad near Pettimudy—the entry point to the Edamalakkudy panchayat—from where she was shifted by vehicle to the Munnar Tata Hospital. Carrying a patient through more than seven kilometres of dense forest is an arduous task,” Mr. Binu said.
Mr. Binu emphasised that these recurring emergencies reflect the dire conditions in the panchayat.
“Without roads and bridges connecting our tribal hamlets, we cannot resolve this pathetic situation. The community urgently demands proper road connectivity to ensure timely emergency medical care,” he added.
Recent incidents
According to the panchayat president, four patients have had to be carried on bamboo stretchers over the past month alone. On August 22, Rajathi, 33, a resident of the Keezhvalayamparakudy settlement who suffered from severe fever and chest pain, was carried on a bamboo stretcher for over five kilometres—crossing the Manaliyar river—to reach the primary health centre (PHC) at Edamalakkudy.
On August 14, Poomani, 50, from Meenkuthikudy, suffered from high fever for several days; when her condition worsened, villagers carried her on foot to the primary health facility at Societykudy, the panchayat’s base camp.
On August 12, Malayappan, 75, from Koodallarkudy, had to be carried nearly 10 kilometres through dense forest to Mankulam before being transferred to the Adimaly Taluk Hospital.
Similar incidents were reported last year as well. On August 21, 2025, a five-year-old boy, Karthik, developed a severe fever, forcing his family to trek through the forest with him on a stretcher towards Mankulam hospital; the child died during the journey. The next day, his family had to carry his coffin on foot back to their settlement.
In September 2025, Karthik’s grandmother, Rajakanni, also fell ill with high fever and had to be carried to Mankulam on a bamboo stretcher, surviving the trek.
