Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say
- Published
Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave at the end of July.
That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.
She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents.
Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.
Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.
Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.
Rojas said many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta".
The Spanish Society of Epidemiology has warned that violence against women "cannot be considered an isolated event".
Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.
The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.
The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".
Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave.
"We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."
The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave.
Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.
In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007.
He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold.
Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.
- Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues 
  - Published3 days ago
Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.
Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe".
He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".
Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.
A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.
Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.
The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.
Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

How different would Lindsay Clancy's murder trial look if it happened in Canada?
Unlike the U.S., Canada has an infanticide provision in the Criminal Code
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children, infanticide and suicide.
As jurors deliberate whether or not Massachusetts mom Lindsay Clancy is criminally responsible for killing her three children, some observers have questioned whether the trial that has gripped the public for the past five weeks could have played out differently had it happened somewhere else.
That's because, unlike Canada, the U.K., and parts of Australia and Europe, the U.S. doesn't have infanticide provisions in its criminal code.
In Canada's Criminal Code, infanticide applies exclusively to mothers who kill their newly born children — defined as a person under the age of one year — while suffering from a "disturbed" mind as a consequence of birth and lactation.
It's a criminal offence, but carries a lesser sentence than murder or manslaughter, so legal experts say it is sometimes argued as a partial defence to the latter two charges.
The major difference is the sentence, with infanticide punishable by a maximum of five years, said Isabel Grant, a University Killam Professor in the Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia who specializes in criminal law.
"Women who kill as a result of not recovering from childbirth should not face life imprisonment — that doesn't really serve anyone's interests if there was truly a postpartum illness at play," Grant, who has published extensively in the area of homicide, including infanticide, told CBC News.
"The United States has taken a much harsher approach to these cases than in Canada, with young women being sentenced to extraordinarily long periods of incarceration in some of these cases."
Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Over the past five weeks, jurors at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., have heard that she strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
- Why Lindsay Clancy, on trial for the deaths of her 3 children, has so many supporters
- What is postpartum psychosis, the illness at the centre of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial?
She then attempted to take her own life by jumping out of a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed.
Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.
Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.
Jurors could find Clancy guilty of murder or manslaughter or acquit her if they find that she wasn't criminally responsible due to psychiatric illness. Clancy’s sentence could be as severe as life in prison, or, if acquitted, she could remain confined in a mental health facility or be released.
Could Clancy have used infanticide defence?
Arguing for the lesser charge of infanticide in cases of this nature isn't a perfect solution, but is, on the whole, "far more just and merciful than the life sentences so common in the United States," Michelle Oberman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law and author of When Mothers Kill, recently wrote in the New York Times.
However, even if the U.S. had similar provisions to Canada, it may not have changed much for Clancy's case because of the ages of her older children, experts agree.
To qualify for the reduced sentence, the accused must meet all the criteria of the legal definition of infanticide, said criminologist Kirsten Kramar, author of Unwilling Mothers, Unwanted Babies: Infanticide in Canada.
The accused must be the woman who gave birth to the child killed, the child must be less than one year old at the time of the act or omission and the mother must be suffering from a disturbed mind as a consequence of birth and lactation, Kramar told CBC News.
Technically, in Canada, Clancy could have raised infanticide as a defence for the murder of Callan, who was eight months old, said Grant, the criminal law professor at UBC. But the killing of Clancy's older children could not be defended as infanticide even if she hadn't recovered from the birth of the youngest child when she killed them, she added.
"That is a shortcoming in the Canadian law."
Given what Grant called the extensive evidence of Clancy's serious mental health problems, "it is possible she would have been charged with manslaughter for the older children and infanticide for the infant but that would be a significant determination," she said.
Jurors have heard that Clancy was prescribed 13 psychiatric medications across different providers, and her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help, including going to the emergency room, calling a suicide hotline and checking herself into a psychiatric hospital.
Whether or not the charges might have changed, Grant says she suspects that, in Canada, "we would probably have less information about the case before it gets to trial, the trial would not be televised and she would have the option of being tried by a jury or judge alone."
That sentiment was echoed by Oberman, in the New York Times, who wrote these "tragedies can avoid becoming true-crime dramas" because they typically avoid going to public trial.
"Ms. Clancy’s trial, with its high-stakes drama and surrounding media frenzy, does little to honour her children," she added.
The judge in Clancy's trial told jurors to keep deliberating Tuesday after they said they could not reach a unanimous decision.
About Canada's infanticide legislation
Canada's infanticide legislation was passed in 1948, amended in 1955 and upheld in a few recent landmark cases. It's both an offence and a partial defence. Researchers have called its use "rare and complex."
Its purpose was to address situations where women — usually young, unwed women — felt compelled to kill their babies due to societal pressures, such as the stigma attached to unwed motherhood or the fate of the baby, said Kramar.

- Infanticide convictions upheld for Meredith Borowiec, who dropped 3 babies in dumpster
"These were considered altruistic killings that did not merit the death penalty," Kramar said.
In Canada, capital punishment was abolished from the Criminal Code in 1976.
"It provides for mitigation of punishment that recognizes the social conditions of motherhood and that the killing is not done out of malice towards the baby," Kramar said.
Lawyers have previously noted the wording is intentionally vague so it can be handled case by case.
In 2011, the law was upheld by Ontario's top court in the case of a Guelph woman convicted of infanticide after smothering two of her children. In 2016, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the infanticide convictions for a Calgary woman who left three babies in a dumpster.
Most recently, in January, a Charlottetown woman who inflicted life-ending injuries on her three-month old daughter was sentenced to one year in jail after pleading guilty to infanticide.
Cassie Acorn was originally charged with first-degree murder, but a psychiatric evaluation determined she had a “disturbance of the mind” — namely postpartum depression — at the time of the crime.
During sentencing, provincial court Judge Jeff Lantz spoke about how many cases of infanticide involve mothers who did not want to be pregnant, gave birth in secret and then either killed or abandoned the infants to their death.
Acorn wanted the child to be born, Lantz said, but also recognized she was an abuse survivor with a cognitive disability who found herself overwhelmed with postpartum depression.

Flagging the exclusion of 2.06 crore names in Maharashtra’s draft electoral rolls after the special intensive revision (SIR), the Congress on Tuesday (September 1, 2026) said votes were being added and deleted to ensure that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) wins elections.
The deletions in Maharashtra, where draft rolls were published on Monday (August 31), are the largest in absolute numbers for any State in the ongoing Phase 3 of the SIR.
Following the 2024 Maharashtra elections, the Congress had formally submitted representations to the Election Commission alleging large-scale voter roll manipulation, including unusual voter spikes in several constituencies. It had alleged that forged documentation, such as fake Aadhaar cards with mismatched names and photos, were used to add fictitious voters without physical verification of addresses.
On Tuesday (September 1, 2026), Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said “the BJP and the ‘vote theft commission’ keep changing their tactics, and they will continue to do so; the goal remains just one: BJP’s victory at any cost, and the end of India’s democracy”.
In a post on X, he said: “Maharashtra 2024 - Suddenly, 3.9 million new voters were added between the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections. I said it then, and I say it today: This was vote theft.”
“And now in Maharashtra, 2.07 crore voters have been removed from the draft list — that’s every fifth voter. Lok Sabha 2024: 9.29 crore, Vidhan Sabha 2024: 9.7 crore, SIR 2026: 7.78 crore. Which list was correct,” Mr. Gandhi asked.
“For a government built on vote theft, the people are not important—that’s why this BJP neither listens to the people nor obeys their command,” he added.
Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge said votes are added when it suits the BJP. “Where it doesn’t, votes are split to perpetrate vote theft,” he said.
“The BJP’s conspiracy to hollow out Indian democracy by stealing votes is coming out into the open. Instead of acting as the guardian of fair elections, the Election Commission is functioning like the “Save BJP’s Chair Commission,” he wrote on X.
Both leaders said that in West Bengal, 91% of the voter names struck off in the SIR had to be reinstated after appeals. “That means 9 out of every 10 names were wrongly deleted, and added back only after the election. I said it then, and I say it today: This was vote theft”, Mr. Gandhi said.
Mr. Kharge said that the “same game” was being repeated in Delhi. “Voters were increased before the Assembly elections, then names of 4.756 million voters vanished from the draft list, and preparations are underway to issue notices to 3.3 million other voters,” he said.
He said that in Telangana and Karnataka, Congress workers faced similar manipulations every day. “The country is now uniting against vote theft. The nation has understood the BJP’s conspiracy, the thief has been caught. Punishment will surely be meted out for holding democracy captive,” he added.
The Election Commission, meanwhile, has shared figures showing that 3,35,910 booth-level agents appointed by different recognised political parties were engaged in preparing the draft electoral roll for Maharashtra, and another 33,226 for Delhi.

Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but judge asks them to keep trying
- Published
Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.
Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.
Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong.
The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them.
The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses.
On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked.
Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer.
- Not just guilty or not - The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial 
  - Published9 hours ago
It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations.
A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC.
"If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said.
But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.
Criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC she was not surprised to hear that the jury was deadlocked, as people had strong opinions on the case.
"The facts are difficult and a lot of the evidence is graphic so they have a lot weighing on them," she said.
The judge can declare a mistrial if the jury is not able to agree on a verdict.
Clancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home in January 2023.
The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth, and that she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings.
If found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.
She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars.
If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed. She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life.

How catastrophic flash flood unfolded at remote Nepal-China border point
- Published
The video lasts only seconds.
A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time.
What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.
Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August.
Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated.
"This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist.
The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.
On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.
Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.
Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.
The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.
Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.
Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.
Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day.
But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.
The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.
The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.
When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area.
"Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC.
Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration.
Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.
That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.
At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.
China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.
People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.
And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.
It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day.
"My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said.
Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.
The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.
For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.
Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done.
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.
Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.
When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Reuters: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."
The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.
Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.
Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.
Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.
Posh Kumar Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.
Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.
Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports.
The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network.
"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says.
"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."
Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.
The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck.
"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

Apple is joining Google in taking the plunge into controversial waters.
On Tuesday, Apple Maps changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move follows President Donald Trump's recent executive order, which he issued amid a trade war with Canada. Earlier Tuesday afternoon, the lake was still labeled Lake Ontario on the map itself, but some American users could only see "Lake America" as an option when searching for the body of water.
Google Maps, Apple Maps' main rival, announced on August 29 that it had renamed one of the five Great Lakes in its system to "Lake America." Google's change, which largely affects US-based users, has sparked a backlash online.
MapQuest has experienced renewed interest in defying the Trump administration's wishes, going so far as to create a template that lets users call the body of water whatever they wish.
Google has said that its naming reflects "name changes in official government sources." On Google Maps, US-based users see Lake America. In Canada, users see Lake Ontario. And in the rest of the world, users see Lake Ontario with Lake America in parentheses.
Both Google and Apple previously renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" after Trump ordered the change in January 2025.
Following Trump's executive order, the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) formally changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
Name calling
Trump's order only applies to the federal government. Private companies, including Apple and Google, individual states, and other countries are free to choose their own course.
When Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico, governors leading the states that border the Gulf, all of which are Republicans, followed suit. This time, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, has said her state will continue to refer to the body of water as Lake Ontario.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney scoffed at the notion that the US could rename the lake.
"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms," Carney wrote on X. "Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always."
The US Geological Survey, part of the Interior Department, maintains the information system on behalf of the US Board of Geographic Names, a federal body whose roots date to the 1890s and is responsible for ensuring the uniform use of names for geographic features across the federal government.
The use of the name "Lake Ontario" dates back over 300 years. According to the City of Toronto, the largest city perched on the lake, the name comes from either the Wendat (Huron) word Ontarí:io, meaning "great lake," or the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) word Skanadario, meaning "beautiful water."
In the US, it was referenced by the Second Continental Congress in 1776, a week after the colonies formally declared their independence. Lake Ontario is also mentioned by name in the Treaty of Paris of 1783, which ended the war, in which King George III's representatives formally recognized the newly independent United States.

Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Joshua Wong has pleaded guilty to collusion with foreign entities, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison under Beijing's sweeping National Security Law (NSL).

Wong has continued seeking out new interests while in prison, including learning how to play the guitar and working out.
"I hope everyone can learn from him," Lee says.

Scientists at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) have developed a low-cost, user-friendly point-of-care diagnostic system for the detection of Alzheimer’s.
The system uses a smartphone-enabled platform employing a fluorescence-responsive tiny molecule to help in the detection of the Alzheimer’s biomarker amyloid-β (Aβ).
Alzheimer’s is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioural impairment.
Central to its pathology is the misfolding and aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ), which self-assembles into fibrils and deposits as extracellular plaques that trigger neurotoxic cascades leading to synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration.
The National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association framework identifies Aβ, tau, and neurodegeneration as core biomarkers for definitive Alzheimer’s diagnosis across the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, and blood.
Early bio marker
According to the Department of Science and Technology, Aβ pathology is an early Alzheimer’s disease-specific biomarker, making Aβ a more reliable diagnostic indicator.
“Although positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging provide valuable diagnostic information, their high cost, need for specialised infrastructure, technical expertise, and limited accessibility restrict widespread use. Blood-based assays targeting Aβ and tau have emerged as promising alternatives, but are expensive and complex. These limitations highlight the need for simple, sensitive, and scalable diagnostic platforms capable of the early and accurate detection of Aβ for diagnosis,” it said.
The scientists have developed a smart fluorescence lifetime-responsive probe that enables highly selective, sensitive, and differential detection of Aβ fibrils (Aβf) through turn-on fluorescence and distinct lifetime signatures.
“Upon interaction with Aβ, the tiny molecule called TZ-48 undergoes changes in fluorescence intensity, which are captured and quantified using a dedicated smartphone application. This enables rapid and user-friendly detection, with potential applications in the screening and staging of the disease,” the department said.
Robust detection
Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy has emerged as a powerful sensing modality because fluorescence lifetime is largely independent of probe concentration and photobleaching, enabling the robust detection of biomarkers and enhancing diagnostic precision.
A team of scientists comprising Krithi K. Bhagavath, Madhu Ramesh, Yogendra Kumar, Sabyasachi Mandal, Hiriyakkanavar Ila, and Thimmaiah Govindaraju developed ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform that leverages the fluorescence response of TZ-48 for rapid, unbiased quantification of serum Aβ load.
The system combines dual-mode brain imaging, biofluid detection, and smartphone-based quantification of Aβ in biofluids, establishing it, along with ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform, as a foundation for next-generation smart diagnostics for Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases.

Are all TVs at risk from burn-in? Here's how to avoid the problem altogether
OLED screens run the biggest risk, but with a little common sense you can mitigate the issue.
If you're shopping for a new TV or monitor, you may have heard that OLED offers some of the best picture quality available today. While OLED TVs often cost a premium compared to budget and even mid-range LCDs, you get excellent contrast, vivid colors and deep blacks in return. However, there can be one major caveat to the display technology: the possibility of permanent image retention or burn-in.
While the term burn-in may sound alarming, especially if you're on the verge of spending hundreds or thousands of dollars, it's not something you need to worry about immediately. And even though it's inevitable, burn-in remains unnoticeable in many cases and takes years to appear even if it does. Better yet, you can take some simple precautions to significantly reduce the risk and extend the lifespan of an OLED display to keep burn-in at bay until it's time to upgrade.
So, what exactly is burn-in, what causes it on modern TVs and how can you minimize the risk? Here's a quick rundown.
What is burn-in and what causes it?
An OLED display is made up of millions of tiny organic light-emitting diodes — hence the name OLED. This is unlike an LCD, which relies on a backlight to illuminate its pixels. This means that each pixel in an OLED generates its own light and can be dimmed or turned off independently. But while this granular control provides excellent contrast and deep blacks, it also means that individual pixels can wear out independently of each other.
Each time you use an OLED display, these individual pixels undergo some infinitesimal amount of degradation. In the real-world, this wear translates to a dimmer light output. To further complicate matters, each pixel is actually made up of several smaller sub-pixels that produce different colors, typically red, green and blue. These sub-pixels don't necessarily age at the same rate, either.
Practically speaking, the OLED display is continuously varying the brightness of each pixel and sub-pixel to reproduce the colors you see on the screen. Over time, though, this can cause some pixels can experience more wear than others and become dimmer. Eventually, the difference in brightness can become noticeable enough to our eyes.
Put simply, burn-in occurs when some pixels appear brighter than those that have experienced greater wear, creating a persistent outline or ghosting of previously displayed content.
Static elements like channel logos have a higher potential to cause OLED burn-in, since the sub-pixels in that region wear out unevenly. This is why OLED displays aren't the best choice if you exclusively watch news or sports channels for several hours each day. Playing the same game for hundreds of hours can also have the same effect, as on-screen text and other fixed elements can accelerate burn-in in certain localized spots.
Is burn-in still a risk for modern OLED TVs?
If you end up buying an OLED TV, you can still take several steps to prevent rapid burn-in. Besides turning off the display when you're not actively watching content, one of the most consequential accelerators for burn-in is brightness. High brightness levels place greater strain on the LEDs that make up the display, which can cause premature wear. The organic material used in an OLED panel also degrades faster when exposed to heat, with higher brightness levels exacerbating this effect. This is one reason OLED manufacturers have historically been more conservative with sustained brightness, although newer generations have pushed the envelope in this area.
Still, running an OLED display at maximum brightness for extended periods of time can result in noticeable burn-in. The solution is simple: head into the TV or monitor's settings menu and lower the brightness setting. This will lengthen the lifespan of each pixel, which should keep burn-in at bay for a long time.
Having said that, I wouldn't worry about image retention if you only use your OLED display for a few hours each day, especially if it's mostly to watch varied content with no static elements like channel logos. Modern OLED displays have plenty of burn-in mitigation features, ranging from pixel shifting and refreshing to automatic dimming in bright scenes. I've owned the same OLED TV for five years and haven't noticed any burn-in even though I frequently watch HDR or high-brightness content.
Do LCD TVs suffer from burn-in?
If you'd like to avoid the risk of permanent burn-in altogether, a modern LCD TV can be a great alternative to OLED. Since LCD panels don't use self-emissive pixels, they don't suffer from OLED-style burn-in caused by uneven pixel degradation. While LCD backlights can and do sometimes fail with age, you can watch content with static elements like news channels without worrying about wearing out specific areas of the display.
Having said that, LCD panels can also exhibit temporary image retention after displaying static content for long periods of time. This is less of a concern for LCD than OLED, as the image retention typically recedes on its own as you switch over to more varied content.
Modern LCD TVs with Mini LED backlighting technology can offer excellent black levels and contrast, although they cannot match OLED's perfect pixel-level control. High-end models can also get significantly brighter than OLED since they don't rely on organic light-emitting material. This makes high-end LCD TVs a perfect choice for bright, sun-filled rooms or if you don't want to think about the risk of image retention at all.

Sonam Wangchuk explains why he softened Dharmendra Pradhan resignation demand
“By 22 I didn't see resignation as the first priority,” Sonam Wangchuk said, adding that he was also considering the damage the continued demand was causing.
Activist Sonam Wangchuk has revealed that he softened his demand for Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation during negotiations with the government, making protection from legal harassment of protesting students his “non-negotiable” condition for ending his hunger strike.
Wangchuk, speaking to Prakhar Gupta on the PGX podcast, said that by July 22 he no longer considered Pradhan's resignation his top priority as he became increasingly concerned about the possibility of violence spreading to other cities.
“By 22 I didn't see resignation as the first priority,” Sonam Wangchuk said, adding that he was also considering the damage the continued demand for resignation was causing.
He said he began to believe that Pradhan's resignation could happen later and that other people were also demanding it.
“So I started thinking that this resignation will probably happen because they should have done much earlier,” Wangchuk said. “Maybe they didn't have resignation in mind. If it doesn't happen, it will happen in two-four days, and there are others also demanding it.”
'Non-negotiable' was no legal harassment
Wangchuk said his focus during the negotiations shifted to ensuring that students who had participated in the protest would not face criminal cases or other forms of legal harassment.
“But my main point was that there should be no legal harassment,” he said. “So I softened the resignation demand a little and said — you can consider accountability through resignation, but the non-negotiable is that you will not do legal harassment.”
The demand assumed greater importance for Wangchuk because of his experience following the September 2025 violence in Ladakh. He said more than 80 cases were still pending a year later and that people who had been trying to prevent violence had themselves been jailed.
Wangchuk said he feared a similar situation could develop around the Delhi protest.
Wangchuk insisted on written assurance
According to Wangchuk, government interlocutors initially told him that they could provide only a verbal assurance that protesters would not face legal harassment.
He rejected that proposal.
“I said, ‘If it happens, it will be written. Later, there is no honour in anything,’” Wangchuk recalled. “I want a written signature that no FIR, no legal harassment will be on any students who are exercising their fundamental right.”

He said he was eventually informed around 11.30pm on July 23 that the government was willing to provide the assurance in writing.
The negotiations followed meetings with Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, who Wangchuk said first met him at the hospital on the night of July 21 and asked him to end his hunger strike.
At that stage, Wangchuk said his demands included accountability through resignation, compensation and a parliamentary discussion aimed at finding long-term solutions. He later added the demand that peaceful protesters not face FIRs or harassment.
Why Wangchuk feared continuing the protest
Wangchuk said his decision to prioritise the legal-protection demand was also influenced by the violence he believed could erupt if the agitation continued.
He recalled seeing reports of a “violent buildup” in Connaught Place on the night of July 23, including preparations around metro stations and the deployment of police and paramilitary forces.
“If two-three lakh people in Ladakh had so many people killed, what could happen in Delhi?” Wangchuk said, adding that if the unrest spread to Mumbai, Lucknow and other cities, it could become a “civil war situation”.
He said he therefore wanted to make an appeal that the hunger strike and the confrontation should end once adequate assurances were secured.
CJP continued to seek Pradhan’s resignation
Wangchuk’s decision to soften the resignation demand during negotiations did not end the issue for the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
After Wangchuk’s hunger strike was broken, CJP leaders decided to continue the protest and demand Pradhan’s resignation.
Wangchuk said he supported that decision, arguing that resignation represented accountability for what had happened during the protest, even if a change of minister did not necessarily lead to major improvements in education.
“An accountability and some responsiveness” had been achieved, he said, but he did not see a major transformation in the education system following Pradhan’s departure.

The Women Obsessed With Lindsay Clancy
Horrific crimes have always attracted attention, but the women who have filled the courtroom are seeking something beyond spectacle.
Updated at 7:35 p.m. ET on August 31, 2026
On one of the final days of the trial, dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, filling two long rows of wooden benches. They stood and watched the judge and jury take their seats. Then they strained for a view as a nurse wheeled in the defendant, Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her three young children to death in her suburban Boston home in January 2023, before swallowing prescription pills, slashing her wrists and neck, and throwing herself out of a bedroom window headfirst.
Seeing her there in a wheelchair, one woman crossed herself and whispered, “Please, God.” As an officer gaveled the court into session, others pulled out notebooks, folders, and scraps of paper. “WHY,” Marta Quijano wrote as a prosecutor called a psychiatrist to the stand. “Motivation,” she added, starring the word as the doctor began explaining his opinion that Clancy was not in the throes of psychosis on the night of the killings, as her defense has argued, but deeply suicidal and still capable of knowing right from wrong. In the back row, a woman who had flown in from Cleveland shook her head. She had a true-crime novel in her lap and turned to a blank page at the end. “Stupid experts,” she wrote.
Americans have long been obsessed with murder trials, especially those involving the primal nightmare of mothers who kill their children. The public loves to watch mothers on trial and partake in their judgment. There was Susan Smith, who had drowned her three children in a South Carolina lake and was found guilty of murder in 1995, despite having a history of trauma and sexual abuse. And there was Andrea Yates, who had drowned her five children in a bathtub and was convicted of capital murder in 2002 and then retried in 2006, when she was found not guilty by reason of insanity after witnesses testified that Yates had experienced severe postpartum psychosis and schizophrenia.
The Clancy trial is now part of this sadistic American tradition, but it has also become something else for the women who have been showing up in person. It was not enough for them to watch the proceedings on television, or listen to some lawyer on YouTube, or even stand outside the courthouse wearing pink and waving signs in support of Clancy, as hundreds of women did one day earlier this month. They did not want to be outside rendering judgment; they wanted to be inside, on the third floor, sitting on the wooden benches, as close as possible, in case they could notice some detail, some gesture, some pause or expression or word that might reveal a truth they could recognize from their own experience. Each was there for their own reasons.
A jury of nine women and three men will decide in the coming days whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor-and-delivery nurse, is criminally responsible for killing her children or not guilty by reason of insanity. The two prosecutors have argued that the killings were the premeditated decision of an entitled and controlling woman who had been frustrated that she could not master her worsening depression and sought a way out of a life that she no longer wanted. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has cast her as a loving mother failed by a fragmented mental-health system even as she repeatedly sought help for intensifying depression, anxiety, and insomnia after giving birth to her third child.
Clancy saw her psychiatrist 14 times, tried 13 different medications, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room, tried to enroll in an inpatient program, and confided to her husband that she’d had thoughts of harming her children. Defense experts testified that doctors had missed an underlying bipolar disorder and prescribed pills that made Clancy’s symptoms worse, starting a downward spiral that culminated in a rare condition called postpartum psychosis that can cause hallucinations. Clancy has said that she heard a male voice telling her to kill her children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, on January 24, 2023.
After being resuscitated following her suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed from the waist down, Clancy was handcuffed, placed under armed guard, and arraigned from her hospital bed. A judge allowed the moment to be livestreamed from the courtroom; a video screen showed her unblinking eyes above a white surgical mask. The trial itself has also been livestreamed, fueling conspiracy theories that have tended to blame the killings on Clancy’s husband or an intruder, attempting to find clarity where there is little, as many women at the trial already understood. At first, only a few showed up. By last Monday, they were waiting in an hour-long line to get into the courthouse, and another that stretched down a bright hallway to the courtroom doors.
“I can’t imagine what’s going through her head,” one woman was saying to her friend.
“It’s not just cold-blooded murder,” the friend said.
“I had suicidal thoughts, clear as a bell,” a retired teacher named Dottie Kiley told another woman in line, explaining her experience with antidepressants. “So bad I called the police and told them, and they had a cop come down and sit with me. It was a small town, and they had time to do that.”
The woman behind her nodded. “She could be any one of us,” she said as the courtroom doors opened.
Inside, the women listened to Avram Mack, a psychiatrist and prosecution witness, explain his clinical opinion that Clancy, having made up her mind to kill herself, then made the decision to kill her children to prevent their suffering a life without her—a theory called “altruistic filicide.” Quijano leaned over to the woman sitting next to her.
“What is the validity of this three years later?” she whispered, shaking her head.
After the morning break, she stood in line again for the afternoon session.
“With my first daughter, because it was so difficult breastfeeding, I had insomnia and anxiety—I was worried the baby is hungry,” Quijano told a woman she had just met. “I remember one time—she was a cranky baby—and I remember not so much shaking her but going like this,” she said, demonstrating how she squeezed her daughter’s shoulders and screamed. “They are called intrusive thoughts because your brain says something, and you don’t recognize it.”
Ashlyn Rizzo, who’d been attending the trial for two weeks straight, nodded.
“I had been planning to run away,” Rizzo said, referring to a moment after her first child was born. “I liquidated all my 401(k) and squirreled the money away. I was going to go without the baby. I figured everyone was better off without me. I had delusions. I couldn’t tell wake from sleep. I didn’t confide to anyone. I wrote a note.”
“My cousin had a plan,” Quijano said, not needing to finish.
“I was just going to start driving,” Rizzo continued. “Stay in hotels.”
As it happened, Rizzo said, she had called her psychiatrist, who that very day got her into the same specialized program in Rhode Island that had rejected Clancy one month before she killed her children. “Saved my life,” Rizzo said.
On Tuesday, the line was longer.
“I wonder, what does justice look like in this case?” a retired teacher named Lisa was saying. She had been keeping the livestream of the trial on in the background of her daily life all month, until she decided to come to see it for herself. She had driven up from Virginia.
“My daughter had a moment,” Lisa, who didn’t give her last name, told the woman standing behind her, referring to postpartum depression. “I’ve been there, trying to get psychiatric appointments.”
“I had a miscarriage in the second trimester and drifted into depression,” Sheila Sullivan replied, explaining that she’d wound up committed to a psychiatric facility in the 1970s. “They gave me shock treatment. Back then, they didn’t know.”
“I’m sorry,” Lisa said, hugging her.
“Thank you,” Sullivan said.
“They don’t do any research on how hormones affect mental health,” Lisa said.
“She didn’t have any symptoms until they put her on the drugs,” Sullivan said.
“It’s all interconnected,” Lisa said as the courtroom doors opened and the women filled the back benches.
“Can you tell us what peritraumatic disassociation is?” a prosecutor asked an FBI forensic psychiatrist, Gregory Saathoff.
“It’s when you feel things are unreal, not you—like you’re watching yourself,” Saathoff began.
A woman wrote down, “Witness staring at jury,” and whispered, “I think that’s weird.”
Sullivan took out her notebook.
“Moral judgement??” she wrote.
She listened as Reddington, the defense attorney, questioned Saathoff, going through his 75-page résumé and pointing out that he had treated only two women with postpartum depression, and that that had been decades ago. Reddington went over the times that Clancy had described feeling “like a zombie” and had been in a “disassociated state,” and asked why health-care providers had not asked more questions when Clancy indicated that she was suicidal.
“She was trying hard to get help,” the doctor acknowledged.
“I can relate to all of this,” Jodi Fournier said as she stood in line later that afternoon. “Not at the extreme, but I can understand.”
For several days, she had been driving to court with two friends from a town 30 minutes away.
“The other thing is, when you work in health care, you learn not to trust the doctors,” her friend Susan Hatfield said. “She was questioning her doctors. She didn’t trust them, and neither did I.”
“See that woman over there?” Fournier said, noticing a blond woman standing by herself and praying at a window outside the courtroom.
“She’s does it every day,” Hatfield said.
Sullivan joined the line behind them.
“I had a miscarriage, then depression, then thoughts of suicide,” she began, retelling her story, and soon they went inside.
Every day, the court officer gaveled in the session, a call to order that ended with the phrase “You will be heard.” Every day, a nurse wheeled in Lindsay Clancy.
“That’s her,” Fournier whispered.
On Tuesday afternoon, Reddington continued questioning Saathoff. “Do you remember Linsday talking about how she can’t feel love? She can’t feel fear?” Then he quoted from Clancy’s journal: “It takes all the effort in the world just to breathe,” she had written, as well as “I want help” and “I want to be well.”
In the back benches, the women leaned forward so they could hear. They pulled out notebooks.
“WTF,” one woman wrote as Reddington went over Clancy’s medication list.
“I am afraid,” another woman wrote down on Wednesday, quoting something Clancy had said.
Rebecca Olszewski, a pharmacist and mother of three, had flown in from Cleveland to attend the trial. She told me that she was recovering from anorexia, bulimia, and generalized anxiety disorder, all of which she said she had learned to mask, as Clancy had apparently done at times. Prosecutors submitted into evidence photos of her smiling with her kids. “There would be outings, and my mom would be like, ‘You seem in good spirits,’” Olszewski said. “And I’d say, ‘Mom, I’m just here going through motions.’”
She wrote down a list of questions: Why hadn’t the people who’d answered the suicide hotline asked Clancy more questions about her suicidal thoughts—not simply whether she had a plan at that moment, but whether she’d ever had a plan? Why hadn’t doctors placed her in an inpatient program? Why hadn’t they paid closer attention?
Now Olszewski sat on the wooden bench, studying the jury to see whether they were paying attention. Then she watched the judge, noticing how he looked at Clancy and the witnesses.
On Thursday, the day of closing arguments, the line was longer than it had been all week. Not everyone could get into the main courtroom, so another one was made available, and women filled more wooden benches, including Joni Villemez-Comeaux, a mental-health counselor there from Texas.
“This is shining a very poor light on our field, and it needs to,” she was saying, and now several women began asking her about how she would have handled Clancy—which sorts of details mattered, and which didn’t. “Every fucking thing matters,” Villemez-Comeaux said, and soon the courtroom was quiet.
In closing, Reddington once again went over all the ways that Clancy had sought help. The medications. The psychiatrist visits. The journal in which she’d chronicled her worsening symptoms until her handwriting had turned into what he described as “chicken scratch.”
“My God, what does she have to do?” Reddington said, and when he finished, women clapped and cheered, and then listened as the prosecutor for the Commonwealth, Jennifer Sprague, delivered her closing argument.
“This case is not about the mental-health system,” she began.
On the wooden benches, a woman quietly said to herself, “Yes, it is.”
After that, Sprague continued for nearly an hour. She talked about how depressed and suicidal Clancy had been but emphasized how much support she’d had. Her parents, a nanny, health insurance. “She had more access to care and treatment and support than most people do.” She once again painted Clancy as an entitled woman who’d known that what she was doing was wrong, who’d decided to strangle her children anyway, leaving them “discarded on the basement floor like broken toys because she was done playing the game.”
By the time she spoke those words, though, many of the women who’d stood in line and listened to days of testimony had already left the courtroom. They had heard enough.
This article originally misidentified Kevin Reddington as Patrick Reddington.

Industrialist Harsh Goenka has joined the debate over a viral video showing a group of Indian tourists singing and clapping loudly inside a crowded public bus in Germany. Reacting to the clip on X, Goenka acknowledged the group’s enthusiasm but said Indians travelling abroad also have a responsibility to respect the norms of the country they are visiting. “Again, a group of Gujaratis singing loudly on a public bus in Germany has sparked a debate. I love the Gujarati joie de vivre, but abroad we are ambassadors of India. We must respect local etiquette and fellow passengers or risk making Indian tourists unwelcome.” The video shows several Indian tourists standing in the aisle of a crowded vehicle and turning part of the journey into an impromptu singing session. The group can be seen singing or chanting loudly while clapping, raising their arms and gesturing enthusiastically. Some of them appear to be recording the moment on their phones, while others smile and move along to the song. Their performance continues as other passengers remain seated around them. The surrounding commuters appear noticeably quieter, with several watching the group as the singing and clapping continues. Some passengers appear disappointed, while others simply observe the tourists without participating in the celebration. The video subsequently sparked discussion online, with users questioning whether such behaviour is appropriate on public transport and how much travellers should adapt to local customs while abroad. Goenka’s comments added another dimension to the discussion, particularly around the idea that tourists can influence how fellow travellers perceive Indians overseas. The industrialist has previously used social media to comment on public behaviour and the experience of travellers in India. About a week ago, another video circulating on X caught his attention. It showed the duty-free area at Delhi Airport, which international passengers pass through after completing immigration. The duty-free section features products including spirits, cosmetics, luxury fragrances, chocolates and snacks from international brands, which are sold without certain local import duties, sales taxes or value-added tax (VAT). The video featured a flyer expressing dissatisfaction with the experience of passing through the shopping area upon arriving in India. Sharing it on X, Goenka criticised what he described as aggressive sales tactics at airports. He said, "At most of our airports, as you clear immigration and walk through the duty-free area, salespeople swarm around passengers, aggressively pushing products. Surely we can do better. Let's give passengers a dignified, hassle-free entry into our country @RamMNK." CM Vijay gifts his Dior sunglasses to elderly woman, sweet gesture goes viral: ‘Looked just like in movies’
The old woman, overwhelmed with joy following Vijay's gesture, said that he looked “just like he does in his movies”.
Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay may have quit acting and his on-screen life, but his stardom and connect with people still remain a key highlight of his new political career, a glimpse of which was on display when he made an impromptu stop during his official duties and made the day of an old woman with his sweet gesture — gifting her his sunglasses.
Vijay was in Salem on Tuesday, where he conducted inspection of the Mettur hydroelectric power station and opened the sluice gates of the Stanley Reservoir at Mettur to facilitate agricultural activities.
Later on his way to the airport, he made a stop which was not part of his schedule — a roadside farm house.
He stepped down and walked towards a group a elderly women working in a field there to greet them, one of whom was Chellam.
As Vijay's convoy attracted crowd, Chellam also moved towards him to get a better view of who he was. Once she realised, she held Vijay's hand. Together, both of them took a walk around the garden area as Vijay asked her name and checked on her well-being.
Then, in a real-life hero-like fashion, he reached for his Christian Dior sunglasses and placed them on her eyes, even as he hesitated. With little persuading, she let him. The moment, according to Chellam, was like winning a "crore of rupees."
Vijay then went to a cattle shed owned by local farmer Palanisamy and interacted with people there during his short 15-minute stop.
‘Looked just like he does in his movies’
Chellam, overwhelmed with joy following Vijay's gesture, said that he looked “just like he does in his movies”.

“I was so happy I told him I would defend him if anyone ever tried to harm him,” she said, as quoted by news agency PTI.
Chellam recalled that Vijay asked her if she had eaten. “I told him I hadn't, because I was waiting to see him first”.
"He told me he had already eaten and insisted that I go and eat," she added.
“I was so surprised that he suddenly came here. I used to hate when someone would beat him in movies,” Chellam said.
During Vijay's visit, in which he also distributed gifts such as dhotis and sarees to the host family, he also discussed agricultural matters with them.
However, overwhelmed with joy of meeting Vijay and his gesture for her, Chellam forgot to mention the hardships she is facing, including losing her ration card, inability to do physical labour due to old age and dependency on a modest monthly allowance just to buy food, the report said.
But the gesture deeply moved Chellam and became a memory that she said will never forget.

UPI operator NPCI is reportedly looking to launch a framework which would see AI agents execute small-ticket digital payments without requiring explicit user authorisation for every transaction. The NPCI is likely to unveil the ‘Unified Agent Protocol’ next week at the 2026 edition of the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai, as per a report by Reuters. The protocol aims to leverage existing UPI mechanisms, including UPI Circle and Reserve Pay, to allow users to delegate payment authority to AI agents within a pre-set limit. For context, the UPI Circle feature enables a primary user to authorise family members and other trusted individuals to make payments on their behalf, while Reserve Pay allows users to block funds at one time for multiple future payments. NPCI declined to comment when Inc42 reached out for their inputs. The initial rollout of the agentic AI framework will target low-value, high-frequency transactions such as grocery orders and routine digital purchases. Over time, NPCI expects AI agents to handle more sophisticated use cases like placing orders automatically based on sales or discounts, as per sources close to the publication. The payments body plans to provide merchants with infrastructure to directly integrate with the protocol. It will also enable customers to set rules for AI agents on when and how much to pay. The NPCI began piloting an agentic AI framework for UPI last year, marking the next phase of what it calls “intelligent commerce”. The payments body had showcased a live demo of the offering at the Global Fintech Fest 2025. Besides the agentic AI framework, the NPCI is also likely to announce a few other updates for UPI at the GFF 2026. It is also reported to be announcing interoperability for UPI AutoPay, allowing users to port their existing mandates across UPI apps and merchants to move mandates from one payment provider to another. However, AI integration within UPI has been in the works for some time now. In the last edition of GFF, NPCI partnered with Razorpay and OpenAI to launch agentic payments on ChatGPT and explore AI-driven commerce at a national scale. Powered by Razorpay’s banking partners, Axis Bank and Airtel Payments Bank, and built on UPI innovations such as UPI Circle and UPI Reserve Pay, the initiative allows UPI transactions for AI-native shopping. As agentic AI becomes more advanced, payments are naturally coming to the forefront as a prime use case. Global credit card networks Visa and MasterCard are already experimenting with frameworks to allow consumers’ AI agents to execute transactions on their behalf. Fintech startups have also been working on enabling agentic payments in the domestic private sector. Pine Labs rolled out its own agentic payments protocol, P3P, earlier this year. Razorpay has been experimenting with agentic commerce by helping merchants build storefronts that can be integrated into AI platforms like ChatGPT, while Cashfree is focusing on products that enable merchants to enable in-chat transactions on the same.

Premier League breaks transfer record for second straight summer
- Published
Premier League clubs have broken their all-time summer transfer record after spending reached £3.198bn.
English top flight clubs had already pushed well beyond the £3bn barrier when Iliman Ndiaye's move from Everton to Manchester City on deadline day for an initial £60m took the amount spent past the previous mark of £3.14bn from 12 months ago.
The amount dwarfs the £1.13bn spent by clubs just five years ago and underlines the power top English clubs have to attract talent, according to figures provided to BBC Sport by Paul Macdonald, founder of FootballTransfers.com.
English clubs splashing the cash
Four of the 11 most expensive signings in the history of football have happened this summer – with three of them being Premier League signings.
Chelsea's £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa and Manchester City's £116m spend on Nottingham Forest midfielder Elliot Anderson are the two most expensive British players ever.
And Liverpool paid an initial £106m, which could rise to £123m, for Paris St-Germain and France forward Bradley Barcola.
Yan Diomande's move to Real Madrid and Anthony Gordon's switch from Newcastle to Barcelona are the only deals completed so far this summer by clubs outside the Premier League to involve fees in excess of £60m.
Tottenham's acquisition of Sandro Tonali was a club-record fee which could reach £100m, while the north London club have also spent heavily on Mateus Fernandes (£85m) from West Ham and Savio from Manchester City (£75m potentially rising to £85m).
Other transfers around this range include the £85.6m deal that City struck to bring in Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, Bruno Guimaraes' arrival at Arsenal for £75m from Newcastle, and Manchester United landing Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton for £70m.
So maybe it is not surprising then that in the compilation of the 20 most expensive transfers completed that only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.
Indeed, newly-promoted Ipswich Town have spent more on new signings than the likes of Barcelona, AC Milan, Juventus and reigning European champions PSG.
Premier League keeping its deals in house
This summer, 38% of deals involving a transfer fee have been from one Premier League club to another, which is an increase from last year, when the figure was 30%.
That then increases to 48% in instances where Premier League clubs have bought players from lower down the English football pyramid.
On top of that, the Premier League net spend remains over £1bn for this window - by far the most in Europe - despite many of the biggest sales this summer coming from the English league too. Bundesliga and Ligue 1 clubs have received more in transfer fees than they have spent.
Aside from French-based duo Barcola and Bouaddi, the majority of major signings made by Premier League clubs this month have been from rival clubs in the same division.
They include England team-mates Rogers and Anderson, while Newcastle sold Tonali to Spurs and Guimaraes to Arsenal.
Manchester United snapped up Baleba from Brighton after a 12-month chase to aid their midfield revamp, while Tottenham's recruitment of Fernandes and Savio is in the same category.
But why are English clubs buying each other's players more than ever this summer instead of shopping abroad for the biggest deals?
One reason could be the temptation for players who are proven in the Premier League.
Many of last season's big-money signings - with a good chunk of them coming from the Bundesliga - failed to meet expectations or justify their transfer fee.
There have also been deals this summer involving the same clubs, possibly with accounting in mind, with Chelsea and Villa selling players to each other.
And there is also a feeling that teams abroad increase the transfer fees they are asking for when English teams - with all their TV riches - show interest in their players.

Lost island in northern B.C. lake located, says B.C. Hydro
Newly formed island found along shore of Williston Reservoir after drifting for 30 kilometres
A newly formed island in B.C.'s largest lake has been located.
B.C. Hydro said Monday that the forested land mass, bigger than a Canadian football field, landed ashore after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location in the middle of Williston Reservoir.
The island's curious appearance, and seemingly sudden disappearance in the massive man-made lake in northern B.C., has captured international attention and intrigue since boaters first made the discovery in August.
B.C. Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said satellite imagery dated Aug. 15 shows the island resting in the north entrance of the Ospika Arm, where the Ospika River flows into the reservoir.
He said the island appears to be intact, and that it has moved even further away from the W.A.C. Bennett Dam connected to the reservoir.
"For it to disappear and now to reappear, that just creates a lot of excitement," Gammer said.
"It's great to know that we found it and it's not causing any trouble right now and hopefully that's the way it stays."
The island's origin still hasn't been confirmed though B.C. Hydro believes record high water levels likely caused it to break off somewhere along the reservoir's sprawling shoreline.
Gammer said strong winds would have moved it through the open waters over the last month.
"It's certainly not current. The water does very slowly move to the east to the [dam]," Gammer said. "The wind is really what's going to drive things."
The Williston reservoir was created in 1968 and is the seventh-largest in the world.
John Clague, an earth sciences professor at Simon Fraser University, said decades of erosion have left the banks of the reservoir vulnerable to landslides.
He said the reservoir is "notorious" for having strong winds that can create waves and currents that undermine shallow rooted trees along the shoreline.
B.C. Hydro estimates the island to be around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.
"This has to be a world's record in terms of size for floating wood mats with trees that were quite healthy and growing nicely and now are part of an island," said Clague.
B.C. Hydro will want to get a better understanding of where it came from and how it formed, Clague said.
"There should be a big scar along the shoreline."
Clague said he's surprised how far the island has travelled, and B.C. Hydro will want to investigate to understand where it came from and how it formed.
That's quite a distance for it to travel and not essentially fall apart," he said. "It's a big piece of real estate, but it's thin. It's not like an iceberg that extends further beneath the water in an ocean."
The island's whereabouts have been a curiosity for residents in northern B.C. as well as interested observers from around the world.
Video of the island bobbing in the middle of the reservoir first went viral in local Facebook groups in early August.
After a decade spent running fishing charters on Williston Lake, Marianne Anderson said she has never seen anything like it.
She said a local fishing guide showed her the video of what looked like a giant carpet of trees, bobbing in the middle of the lake.
The next time fishing guides were in the area, the island was gone.
"It looked unreal," she said.
Finlay Farquhar, a radio engineering assistant based in the United Kingdom, said he was able to track the island's new location using open-source satellite websites after reading about it on social media.
He also found it nestled on the shoreline in the Ospika Arm.
"Quite curious, and it was really quite surprising that there'd been a floating island," Farquhar said. "I was quite surprised by how far it moved."
Gammer said B.C. Hydro was able to locate the island after independently confirming new reports of its location.
Gammer said it's possible the island might move again if strong winds break it free from shore.
"It's nothing that's going to require us to take some serious action," he said.
"We will monitor this just to see what happens, whether it breaks apart and if we then have a debris field instead of one big chunk, that may cause us to take some other action."
He said the island is unstable and boaters should be cautious.
"Go ahead, boat up to it, get near it, take your own pictures, get your drone out, whatever you'd like to do to image it," he said. "But we really warn people about trying to climb on it, as tempting as it may be."

బుర్ఖా ధరించిన ఒక మహిళ కాషాయ రంగు బైక్ను ధ్వంసం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఈ ఘటన నిజమైనదని, బైక్ రంగు నచ్చకే ఆ ముస్లిం మహిళా ఇలా చేసిందని వైరల్ పోస్టులో పేర్కొన్నారు. దీనిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బుర్ఖా ధరించిన ముస్లిం మహిళ కాషాయ రంగు బైక్ని ధ్వంసం చేయడాన్ని చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో, నిజమైన ఘటన కాదు. వినోదం కోసం ఇటువంటి వీడియోలను చిత్రీకరిస్తుంటామని, ఈ వీడియోలో నటించిన శివాన్ష్ యాదవ్ తన ఫేస్బుక్ బయోలో పేర్కొన్నారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) ‘shivanshyadav_prank‘ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ పేజీని పరిశీలించగా, ఈ వీడియోలోని వ్యక్తి బుర్ఖా ధరించిన మహిళతో ఉన్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) చిత్రీకరించినట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, ఈ పేజీలో వివిధ మహిళలతో చిత్రీకరించిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు, ప్రాంక్ వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా ఉన్నట్లు చూడవచ్చు.
ఈ పేజీకి సంబంధించిన ఫేస్బుక్ ఖాతాను పరిశీలించగా, తాను ఒక ఆర్టిస్ట్నని, వినోదం కోసం కామెడీ వీడియోలు చిత్రీకరిస్తుంటానని వైరల్ వీడియో నటించిన శివాన్ష్ యాదవ్ తన ఫేస్బుక్ బయోలో పేర్కొన్నారు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, అదొక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
చివరిగా, కాషాయ రంగు నచ్చక ముస్లిం మహిళ బైక్ను ధ్వంసం చేసిందంటూ ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోని నిజమైన ఘటనగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

The story so far: On August 26, Meta reached a landmark settlement of up to $17.1 billion with 29 U.S. States, including California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, ending a lawsuit which the States had brought against the tech giant, accusing it of hiding harms caused by its platforms to children and deliberately using tactics to keep teens engaged or ‘addicted’ to its platforms. The settlement also came with certain conditions on how Meta should change its safety features on Instagram and Facebook.
The 233-page lawsuit, first filed against Meta in 2023, alleged that the company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental consent thus breaking various State and federal privacy laws. It also alleged that the company deliberately designed platforms to be addictive in order to keep teens engaged, leading to mental health disorders such as depression, anxiety etc. The suit accused Meta of refusing to “abandon its use of known harmful features” and instead, focusing solely on profits and financial gain over the safety of children.
