The standard explanation for why rain causes corrosion is that water carries dissolved salts and acids to a surface, constant drumming of raindrops abrades whatever protective coating is on it, and oxygen does the rest. Nearly all our tools to prevent this—paints, polymer films, or oxide layers—are built around this idea. But we’ve apparently been missing something important about the rain.
A new study led by Zhongyuan Ni, Rüdiger Berger, and Hans-Jürgen Butt at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Mainz, Germany, has shown that water drops routinely arrive at a surface carrying an electrical charge large enough to punch through an insulating coating. Not scratch it. Not slowly dissolve it. Electrically blow a hole in it, the way a spark jumps a gap.
Charged rain
The starting point of the study is a phenomenon called “slide electrification,” which has only been properly quantified in the past few years. When a water drop slides across an insulating surface like a leaf, a painted wall, a windowpane, or a plastic panel, it strips charge from that surface and leaves an opposing charge behind. The voltages involved are not trivial. Drops charged this way have been measured at up to 9,000 volts.
The question Ni, Berger, Butt, and their colleagues asked was what this charge does to the surface that the drop lands on next. To find out, the team released 35-microliter water drops, about the size of a large raindrop, containing a pinch of salt to mimic rainwater, onto a surface tilted at 50 degrees. The drops slid about four centimeters, picked up a charge, rolled off the edge, and then fell five millimeters onto a copper plate coated with a 60-nanometer film of Teflon, which is one of the most chemically resistant coatings on the market today.
The tilted surfaces were mostly chosen to mimic raindrops in the real world. One was a leaf from a Tradescantia spathacea plant growing in one of the researchers’ offices. Another was a PVC foam board from a hardware store. The third one was a sheet of transparent polystyrene sold as window glazing. Only the fourth one, the fluorinated coating on quartz, was more of a lab creation than something people usually see everywhere around them. The charges the drops picked up ranged from 0.2 nanocoulombs off the leaf to two nanocoulombs off the fluorinated quartz. A nanocoulomb in something the size of a raindrop works out to be a few thousand volts.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher EU rules such as removing illegal content or face potential fines, the European Commission said on Monday, as Brussels grapples with how its existing digital regulation applies to rapidly evolving AI services.
The Commission said the chatbot, social media forum Reddit, and gaming platform Roblox would be classified as so-called very large online platforms under the EU Digital Services Act, its landmark online safety regime.
The designation means all three services will face additional obligations such as removing illegal content and protecting the privacy and security of minors and could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.
The decision marks a further expansion of the DSA into generative AI, with X’s AI chatbot Grok already facing an investigation under the law.
“ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the European Union, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” said the EU’s tech chief Henna Virkkunen.
The move comes after all three services surpassed 45 million monthly users in the EU, the threshold for enhanced scrutiny under the DSA. They now have until the end of December to comply with the additional obligations.

A rumor that the CEO of a popular chain of convenience stores in the southern United States said the the company would no longer pursue locations in so-called "blue states" circulated online in August 2026.
Users on Facebook and a popular thread on Reddit suggested Buc-ee's CEO Arch "Beaver" Aplin III said the company was focused on building in "conservative, business-friendly states."
The quote was correctly attributed to Aplin.
The Buc-ee's CEO said it during public remarks on Aug. 17, celebrating the opening of a Buc-ees location in Benton, Arkansas, after being introduced by Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Aplin's full remarks are viewable on YouTube.
The quote in question began at the 2:11 mark, when Aplin revealed Sanders had asked him to build a Buc-ee's in Arkansas. He said:
We're building in a lot of places but when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference. And I'm starting to realize life's too short to try and build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing. Versus a place like this, where people do appreciate what you're building.
So that leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept, works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the very top at the governor's office.
A Buc-ee's news release said the Benton location was the company's 58th store and would create more than 200 jobs for the community. Buc-ee's was founded in 1982 and operates primarily in the South.
Local media covered the store opening, including NBC affiliate KARK, CBS affiliate KTHV and the Arkansas Democrat Gazette. The local reports didn't mention Aplin's specific comments nor did they report anything about the chain avoiding blue states.
On Aug. 18, Sanders posted a clip of Aplin's remarks to her Facebook page and wrote, "That's why red states like Arkansas are surging and people and businesses are fleeing blue states."
Later reporting from The Comeback and Fox Business homed in on Aplin's comments, as well as Sanders' takeaway that the chain intended to stop pursuing locations in so-called blue states. It was these reports that started circulating wider online and got increased media pickup, resulting in the claim gaining popularity.
While we found this to be a reasonable interpretation of Aplin's comments, it's crucial to note that Aplin himself didn't explicitly say the company would be "avoiding blue states" during his remarks on Aug. 17. We reached out to Buc-ee's for clarification on the company's plan's for development in red vs. blue states and will update this article if we hear back.

Syria was building nuclear reactor in Deir el-Zour under Assad, UN report finds
Under the ex-president, Syria was believed to have operated an undeclared nuclear programme that included a reactor built by North Korea
Inspectors with the UN nuclear watchdog visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work, according to a confidential report circulated to member states and seen Tuesday by Associated Press.
Based on this visit, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported that it is “able to establish that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities as required under the NPT Safeguards Agreement”.
This information included a nuclear reactor under construction in Deir el-Zour, a fuel fabrication plant and another site used for fuel storage during the rule of former president Bashar al-Assad.
Under Assad, Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear programme that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province.
The site in Deir el-Zour became public knowledge only after Israel launched air strikes in 2007 that destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it.
The IAEA took samples at the site in 2024 and reported last year that they contained uranium particles.

President Trump yesterday demanded that the Federal Communications Commission punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements. In the latest example of how Trump is using the FCC to harass reporters and news organizations that he dislikes, he said Meet the Press host Kristen Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” for what he claimed was a “purposeful inaccuracy.”
“Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm. How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
A separate post from Trump yesterday said, “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” Trump also posted a rant on Friday about New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her “an unattractive person both inside and out” who “should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.” Trump referred to Haberman throughout his post as “Maggot Haberman.”
Trump’s post about Welker included an image purporting to show he has near-perfect results in his endorsements this year. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.
Perhaps indicating that he will refer additional journalists for FCC punishment, Trump wrote that Welker “is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”
Trump’s FCC chair has eagerly obeyed orders
The idea of the FCC punishing reporters for basic analysis of election results would have seemed far-fetched in previous administrations. The FCC website says the commission “cannot prevent the broadcast of any particular point of view,” and that it “generally will not intervene” in complaints about “one-sided news reports” because “it would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.”
Even during Trump’s first term, then-FCC Chairman Ajit Pai said that under the First Amendment, “the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast.” Pai made the comment less than a week after Trump called on the FCC to revoke broadcast licenses from NBC and other networks for “fake news.”
An FCC investigation of Welker over an ordinary statement about election results seems much less far-fetched under Carr, who has embraced his role as Trump’s chief censor. Carr has made it clear he takes orders from Trump, abandoning his previous position—which he held under Democratic presidents—that the FCC must operate independently of White House interference.
Welker said in an appearance on NBC 4 Washington that Trump “has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries” and that “he’s had some mixed results but most recently his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course the sister of the late Senator Lindsay Graham, was successful in her primary battle.” Trump’s post attacking Welker claimed that “the story of [Graham’s] Victory was hardly covered by anybody,” despite Welker mentioning it in the very statement that triggered Trump’s wrath.
Poynter Senior Media Writer Tom Jones writes, “What Welker said about Trump’s endorsements having mixed results was true. Trump just didn’t like it.” While Trump praised himself for his successful endorsements, he didn’t mention primary losses by Republican gubernatorial candidates Burt Jones in Georgia and Randy Feenstra in Iowa and the failed re-election bid by Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida).
Carr uses news-distortion policy to threaten networks
An NBC News spokesperson told several media outlets that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.” We contacted NBC News and will update this article if it has any further comment.
Welker is hardly the first TV journalist to discuss Trump’s mixed endorsement results. “Already, just this month alone, six of the president’s endorsed candidates have lost their races, and so there are questions about the power of his endorsements,” CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene said on Inside Politics.
In June, Trump abruptly ended an interview with Welker after she challenged his claims of election rigging in California. Trump stated that “all I have to do is look” when Welker asked him for evidence of cheating. “That’s not evidence,” Welker responded.
If Carr does investigate Welker, he could do so under the FCC’s news distortion policy. Carr has repeatedly invoked the rarely enforced news distortion policy and a rule against broadcast hoaxes in various threats to Trump’s perceived enemies in the media. We asked the FCC chairman’s office today if the commission will investigate Welker and will update this article if we get a response.
Previous FCC leaders set such a high bar for proving news distortion that the policy was all but abandoned until Carr made it a focal point of his attempts to punish broadcasters. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for news distortion if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel’s show.
Trump and FCC try to reshape the media
While Carr can cause trouble for licensed broadcasters and networks simply by issuing threats, he went far beyond mere threats in the case of ABC. The Carr FCC ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates and justified the proceeding by accusing ABC of violating anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices.
ABC owner Disney is fighting back with a lawsuit against Carr and the FCC, saying it has faced a campaign of censorship in retaliation for the protected speech of its journalists and network programs. Both conservative and liberal groups have urged the FCC to back off.
The Trump administration has also sought to reshape the media through merger approvals. Paramount won FCC approval to buy Skydance after agreeing to install what Carr called a “bias monitor” at CBS. Paramount later won Justice Department approval to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, months after CEO David Ellison reportedly told Trump administration officials that he would make big changes at the Warner-owned CNN.
In March, Trump and Carr demanded more positive media coverage of the Iran war, with Carr claiming without evidence that broadcasters aired “hoaxes and news distortions.” Last year, Carr accused Comcast of news distortion when its subsidiary NBC refused to adopt the Trump administration narrative on the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, responded to Trump’s latest threat yesterday. “As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote. “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

Body odour is a normal part of life. Contrary to popular belief, sweat in itself does not usually smell. The familiar odour develops when bacteria and fungi that live on the skin break down substances in sweat, particularly secretions from glands in the armpits and groin. In most cases, body odour is harmless and may vary depending on factors such as heat, physical activity, diet and hygiene.
However, a new or persistent change in body odour should not always be dismissed as a hygiene issue, doctors say. In some cases, an unusual odour may be linked to an underlying health condition and may need medical evaluation.
Heat, food and hormones
Several everyday factors can alter body odour. Hot weather and physical activity increase sweating, while tight or synthetic clothing can trap moisture. Garlic, onions, spicy foods, alcohol and certain medicines can also affect body odour.
Hemanath M. J., consultant, internal and family medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, says the apocrine glands in the armpits, groin and scalp contribute more to odour than the eccrine glands, which cover most of the body. Stress can stimulate the apocrine glands and intensify odour.
Hormonal changes can also play a role. Puberty, menstruation and menopause may temporarily alter sweating and body odour. Puberty is one common situations in which changes in body odour are routinely seen. An overactive thyroid, which can cause excessive sweating, may also make odour more noticeable.
A change is more likely to be temporary when there is a clear trigger and the odour settles after the trigger passes. “If somebody develops an odour after eating a particular food, drinking a particular drink, starting a medication or strenuous exercise, or during a period of hormonal change, and it returns to normal after some time, the context helps explain the change,” says Narayanan A., consultant, dermatology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai..
Body odour as a health clue
A persistent or unexplained change can sometimes be associated with a skin condition or an underlying medical problem. Skin infections in the armpits, groin or other moist areas can alter odour. These may be accompanied by redness, soreness, itching, peeling or discharge.
“An infection in the groin or axilla (armpit) or excessive growth of bacteria or fungi can alter the odour,” says Dr. Narayanan.
Dr. Hemanath says conditions such as erythrasma and fungal infections can produce a distinct smell, particularly in warm, moist areas. Excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, does not itself cause odour but can provide more moisture for bacteria to act on.
Certain metabolic conditions have also been associated with distinctive smells. Uncontrolled diabetes can produce fruity or sweet-smelling breath because of ketone build-up. A rare condition called trimethylaminuria can cause a fish-like odour because the body is unable to break down certain compounds properly.
Odour changes have also been described in advanced kidney and liver disease. But doctors caution against treating these smells as diagnostic tests.
“Some distinctive smells have been described with complications of diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease, but these are clues rather than reliable diagnostic tests,” says Dr. Narayanan. The overall clinical picture, including symptoms, examination and biochemical investigations, is what guides diagnosis.
Need for evaluation
The first step when there is a change in body odour is to look for an obvious trigger. Regular washing, changing sweaty clothes, washing clothes properly and using an antiperspirant can help determine whether the problem responds to routine measures.
But a sudden change in body odour without a clear cause is reason to consult a doctor.The physician would first consider what changed at the same time as the odour. If there is no obvious trigger and the change persists or keeps recurring, a deeper evaluation may be required.
A sudden unexplained increase in sweating, night sweats without an obvious reason, or sweating that interferes with daily activities should also prompt medical attention. Experts list other warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, excessive thirst or urination, fatigue, swelling, fever, night sweats or skin changes. A fruity odour with excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting or confusion requires urgent assessment.
Depending on the symptoms, a doctor may conduct a physical and skin examination and consider tests such as blood glucose and HbA1c, kidney and liver function tests and a thyroid profile. Skin scraping or culture may be considered if an infection is suspected.
Doctors say, body odour should not be used to self-diagnose a disease. Most changes have an everyday explanation, but a smell that is new, persistent, unexplained or accompanied by other symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor

Former Republican congressman George Santos has received a first-of-its-kind lifetime ban from the prediction market platform Kalshi, which has also fined him $71,356 for violating its rules around insider trading and market manipulation.
According to the notice of disciplinary action Kalshi posted today, the former politician placed trades in markets related to whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February 2026. He then “began making a series of public statements regarding his attendance at the event in an attempt to influence the price” of certain contracts, some of which were “false or misleading,” per the notice.
The day before the address, Santos posted, “I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys” on X. During the speech, he sent a follow-up noting that he was actually at an airport watching the address on television. “FML,” he wrote.
Kalshi’s enforcement team flagged the trades, froze Santos’ account, and referred the case to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets. This summer, he settled with the CFTC for $35,000 over these suspicious trades; a little over $17,500 was returning the profit he made, with an additional $17,500 fine. At the time, his lawyer issued a statement stressing that Santos settled to “put this matter behind him” and that he had done so “without admitting the Commission’s allegations, findings or conclusions.”
Through his legal representative, Santos declined to comment to WIRED. However, on social media, he already weighed in, sarcastically thanking Kalshi “for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform,” adding, “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for 💋,” a nod to the prediction market’s ongoing battles with state authorities over how it is regulated.
Once upon a time, Santos had a rosier relationship with the industry; he was once paid for promoting Kalshi’s rival Polymarket, but Polymarket severed ties with him once federal regulators began looking into his behavior around February’s State of the Union.
This is far from Santos’ first brush with the law. He was expelled from Congress following an ethics investigation in 2023, and eventually pleaded guilty and served time in federal prison for embezzling from campaign donors, lying to Congress, and defrauding campaign contributors. He was released from prison in 2025 after President Trump commuted his sentence.
According to today’s notice, the prediction market found that Santos successfully influenced the pricing of several markets. Kalshi also issued four additional notices of enforcement actions today, but Santos was the only person penalized who did not settle with the company.
“He wouldn’t talk to us, and actively dodged us,” Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana tells WIRED.
In the past year, Kalshi has issued a number of other enforcement actions against politicians who it found had broken its rules. In this most recent round of enforcement actions, it fined North Carolina Congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout, California gubernatorial candidate Stephen Kloobeck, and Maine gubernatorial candidate Ben Midgley for attempting to trade on contracts related to their races; they are all temporarily suspended.
“I bet on myself. Literally. It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right. Safe to say my career as a Kalshi trader was short-lived,” Buckhout, a retired military officer, told WIRED in an email. Kloobeck and Midgley did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Previously, it fined US Senate candidate Mark Moran for insider trading; at the time, Moran told WIRED that he “did it on purpose” and did not intend to cooperate with Kalshi.
Kalshi’s Diana says that Santos can expect “legal action” if he does not pay.

A common way to deal with emotions is through food, says Lakshmi Venkatraman, consultant psychiatrist and assistant director of Psychosocial Rehabilitation Services at SCARF (Schizophrenia Research Foundation). Dieting and restrictions on food are also culprits. The vicious circle begins when people tend to eat more, end up feeling guilty at their act, reduce their self-esteem, because of which they binge eat and feel more guilty.
Simple measures such as eating regular meals with all foods, including favourites in moderation, helps. “When we realise emotions are pushing us (to eat), finding ways to tackle the emotions will help,” Dr. Lakshmi explains. “Be mindful while eating, focus on what we are eating, take it quite slow while eating which helps to prevent binge eating,” she points out.
R.M. Anjana, managing director of Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, cites the various studies done by the Foundation at various intervals of time, to explain the importance of regulating “what we put into our mouth”. When a person finds that they binge once a week and this persists for three months then it should trigger an alarm, she says. “Diet and physical activity alone can prevent 50% of diabetes,” she said and cited studies that state that binge eating contributes to about 15 to 20% of type 2 diabetes.
A bariatric surgeon aims to moderate the gut hormones, says P. Praveen Raj, consultant and head of the Department of Minimal Access Bariatric and Robotic Surgery in the Department of Surgical Gastroenterology, GEM Hospital and Research Centre, Coimbatore.
The first step is to take a thorough history of the person’s issues. There are various hormones in the gut that regulate satiety, trigger appetite and aid digestion. An imbalance in any one of them could be the cause for obesity. The aim is to treat the cause, he explains. “You rule out the psychological reasons, and the pathological abnormality. Once this is understood we can start to treat it (the condition),” he adds.
The specialists were panelists at a webinar on “The Binge: Learning to handle addictive behaviours,” organised on Sunday by The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cl4wxf7_HRI

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

Farrell had less-than-lethal options on his utility belt that he did not employ, including a taser.”

On June 5, at the American Diabetes Association’s Scientific Sessions in New Orleans, several attendees were removed after repeated disruptions. I apologized soon after — to the individuals directly involved and to the broader diabetes community — for the distress that day caused, and I meant it.
I also promised a full accounting by independent reviewers of what happened. That review, conducted by five independent volunteer investigators, is now complete. I believe its findings deserve to be heard directly, rather than filtered through three months of competing narratives.
Two claims have driven much of the public anger, and the review examined both directly.
The first is that ADA suppressed a viewpoint — that attendees were removed for distributing an editorial critical of federal research cuts. The review found no merit to that claim. That editorial was published in our own journal, Diabetes Care. We were not censoring content we ourselves had put into print. What led to people being asked to leave was conduct during the session — repeated disruptions, continuing after multiple requests to stop — that runs counter to our conference code of conduct, not the substance of what anyone was handing out.
The second claim is that ADA called in police to intervene against our own members. The review found that did not happen. Security personnel were on-site, as at any conference of our size, and some of them were off-duty police officers, acting in their capacity as event security, not as law enforcement. The review found no evidence that a call was placed to the New Orleans Police Department by anyone from the ADA.
I share these findings not to declare what happened June 5 a nonissue, or to suggest ADA staff and security got everything right. Let me be clear: We didn’t. The review makes clear there were missed opportunities for better communication — from our staff and from security — in the moments before and during the disruption, and we take that seriously.
But I do think it matters that established facts, once they exist, replace assumptions — including ones I did not correct quickly enough myself.
The ADA’s long-held commitment to open debate isn’t just words. Diabetes Care has published critical viewpoints of federal research policy — including the very editorial at the center of this controversy. The ADA has also made numerous public statements calling out the current and former administrations for cutting diabetes prevention programs, reducing research support, and decreasing health care coverage. We intend to keep making those comments when federal actions undercut the diabetes community.
We will also keep making room for others’ points of dissent, in our journals and in other fora. A scientific community that only tolerates agreement isn’t a healthy one. What we ask is that disagreement be expressed in ways that don’t come at the expense of everyone else’s ability to participate in the same room.
There’s another lesson from these events that I think matters more, and it’s one about us, not about that day.
This is a period of deep anxiety across the medical research community about the future of federal funding, and that anxiety is not misplaced — significant cuts to diabetes research funding have been proposed in recent budget cycles. What often goes untold is that most proposed cuts to diabetes research have thus far not materialized. Diabetes research funding has been kept largely whole against those proposals, because our community fought for it — including ADA’s role this year in the ongoing pushback against a White House Office of Management and Budget proposal that would have let political appointees, rather than career grantmaking processes, decide which research got funded. That advocacy has had impact: The Senate recently added language to the pending continuing resolution that would block the OMB rule from taking effect, and we are pressing to get the same language into House legislation.
This is the kind of work ADA does every day on behalf of this field, often without notice. But we have not always told that story well to the people most affected by it: the researchers and clinicians who show up to our meetings wondering whether anyone with influence is in their corner. That gap is at least part of why frustration that belonged elsewhere landed on us in New Orleans. We intend to close it.
Here is what I know independent of any review: This is not a moment our community can afford to spend fighting itself. Every hour spent contesting the story of one difficult day is one not spent on the fight that will determine what the next decade of diabetes research looks like. That fight has one opponent: policy that harms the health and research interests of the diabetes community.
I am not pretending that June 5 didn’t happen, and I will hold our organization accountable for where we came up short. Accountability, including the kind this review represents, is part of how trust gets rebuilt.
What I ask is that we hold two things at once: a clear-eyed accounting of what occurred, and a shared recognition that researchers, clinicians, and advocates in our community remain each other’s strongest allies against a far larger threat to work we’ve all given our careers to.
We have weathered funding fights and internal disagreements before, and come through them by choosing, eventually, to face outward together. I know we can do that again.
Charles “Chuck” Henderson is the CEO of the American Diabetes Association.

United Nations, Sep 02: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will participate in the 18th BRICS Summit later this month in New Delhi.
As the chair this year, India will be hosting the 18th BRICS Summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. The summit will bring together leaders of BRICS member and partner countries as well as outreach invitees, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.
Stéphane Dujarric, spokesman for Guterres, said at the press briefing here Tuesday, "… we have yet to officially announce that the secretary-general will participate in the BRICS meeting in New Delhi in about 10 days' time."
He was responding to a question on possible meetings between Guterres and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit hosted in Kyrgyzstan on August 31-September 1.
The theme for India’s BRICS chairship is ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’.
Over 350 meetings and high-level engagements have been held in over 25 cities across India to further strengthen the BRICS strategic partnership across three fundamental pillars: political and security, economic and financial, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Through these engagements, and business-to-business and people-to-people initiatives, India's BRICS chairship has contributed to advancing BRICS cooperation through practical and development-oriented outcomes, the MEA has said.
India, a founding member of BRICS, has previously held its chairship in 2012, 2016 and 2021. India assumed its fourth BRICS chairship on January 1, 2026. BRICS is celebrating its 20th anniversary this year.
Guterres, whose second five-year tenure as head of the United Nations ends in December 2026, had travelled to India in February this year to attend the India-AI Impact Summit 2026 in New Delhi.
The summit was the first-ever global AI summit hosted in the Global South.
In Bishkek, Guterres met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the margins of the SCO Summit.
The secretary-general expressed his concern regarding the devastating humanitarian and economic consequences of the conflict in Iran, in the region and beyond. He stressed the urgent need to resolve the conflict through dialogue and negotiations, with full respect for international law, including international navigational rights and freedoms in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Guterres also reaffirmed the commitment of the UN to support all diplomatic efforts aimed at a comprehensive and durable solution, his spokesperson said.
Putin and Pezeshkian are among the world leaders who will arrive in New Delhi for the BRICS summit. Xi is also widely expected to attend the BRICS summit before visiting the US for a summit meeting with President Donald Trump later this month.

Goa passes bill to drop ‘leprosy’ references from child law to eliminate social stigma
The amendment has been brought to remove social stigma and discrimination against persons affected by leprosy.
The state assembly has passed the Goa Children's (Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeking to remove references to "leprosy" from the state's child protection legislation to eliminate social stigma and discrimination against people affected by the disease.
State Women and Child Development Minister Vishwajit Rane introduced the bill, seeking to amend the Goa Children's Act, 2003, in the assembly on Tuesday. It was later passed in the House by voice vote.
The amendment has been brought to remove social stigma and discrimination against persons affected by leprosy and bring the state law in line with a Supreme Court order dated May 7, 2025, as per the statement of objects and reasons.
The bill sought to omit the word "leprosy" from two provisions of the principal Act.
Under Section 2 dealing with definitions, the amendment removes "leprosy" from a provision that earlier referred to it along with HIV as an illness carrying social stigma.
It also removes the reference to leprosy from Section 5 relating to health and nutrition. The provision prohibits healthcare facilities and hospitals from denying treatment or admission to children or pregnant mothers suffering from conditions associated with social stigma.
The amendment will have no financial implications and does not involve any delegated legislation. It will come into force immediately after receiving the governor's assent, according to the legislation.

A Greenlandic commission is to present a highly anticipated report Friday to determine whether Denmark's forced contraception of thousands of the Arctic island's indigenous Inuit constituted a "genocide".
The forced contraception campaign between the 1960s and 1990 is one of the darkest chapters in Greenland's history with its former colonial master, Denmark.
Once the conclusions are presented, Greenland's government will decide how to move forward.
"For us, it's about trying to understand our history," Naaja Nathanielsen, a member of parliament representing Greenland in Denmark's parliament, told AFP.
"Others may feel that we should simply keep quiet about this and try to be conciliatory, because of the United States' aggressiveness toward Greenland."
Nathanielsen announced the creation of the commission, tasked with shedding light on the legal implications of the campaign, in August 2024 when she was Greenland's minister of justice and gender equality.
During the 1960s to 1990, more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were forced to wear a contraceptive coil -- or intrauterine device (IUD) -- in the vast majority of cases without their consent or that of their parents if they were minors.
Greenland, a Danish colony for three centuries and now an autonomous territory, still has a complicated relationship with Copenhagen.
Despite many thorny issues between them, both Copenhagen and Nuuk have presented a united front rejecting US President Donald Trump's threats to take over Greenland.
He has repeatedly accused Denmark of treating Greenland badly.
"Everything that is happening between Denmark and Greenland now is scrutinised," said historian Astrid Andersen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).
"There's this pressure on the relationship so of course, when we start talking about genocide, that increases the pressure.
"But everyone in Greenland has been very clear that this tragic case should not be used to legitimise other political purposes internationally."
The commission's four appointed experts were unable to agree on which approach to take and ended up writing two reports, submitted nearly six months behind schedule.
Not just about history
One of the victims, Henriette Berthelsen, told AFP the conclusions, regardless of what is decided, were skewed from the start since no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life, and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
The campaign affected girls as young as 12, some of whom were never able to have children afterwards.
Nuuk and Copenhagen are also shedding light on several other painful chapters from the past, including children adopted without parental consent or torn from their families.
On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation from Copenhagen, an initiative pushed by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen who presented Denmark's official apology last year.
Beyond imagination
Media coverage of the case has revived trauma that had been buried for decades.
"I realised everything it had cost me -- all those hospitalisations, those surgeries, the schooling I missed and, above all, those pains I had never associated with that damn IUD," said Kirstine Najarak Berthelsen.
"It was buried so deeply in my subconscious... Everything that happened to people is beyond imagination if you haven't experienced it yourself," she added.
By the late 1970s, one in two Greenlandic women of childbearing age -- at least 4,070 women -- had been fitted with an IUD, according to an investigation presented in September 2025.
The scandal came to light when one of the victims spoke out in the media about the trauma she experienced.
A podcast series in 2022 then revealed the full extent of the campaign.
Henriette Berthelsen has called for a "Truth and Reconciliation" commission to be established. The Danish government is considering the idea.
According to the 68-year-old psychologist, that would make it possible to "acknowledge what happened".
"I believe that only then will we be able to begin to heal and move forward -- not as adversaries, but as human beings and as peoples equal in dignity."

South African airline defends low-altitude aerial stunt over packed stadium
- Published
The South African airline behind a dramatic stunt that saw two of its aircraft in close formation fly reportedly within feet of the top of a stadium has defended itself in the face of some criticism.
The jets roared over Cape Town's DHL stadium as flares shot up before the start of a rugby match featuring fierce rivals South Africa and New Zealand.
Some labelled the manoeuvre reckless, while others have praised the precision and expertise required to pull it off.
In response, Airlink said it was carefully planned with the support of the aviation authorities.
"Planning. Precision. Performance," was the airline's message in social media posts, external accompanied by the footage.
In a statement reproduced on a government news site, external, Airlink went into more detail.
"The two aircraft were flown by highly experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer," the airline said.
It added that the flights were performed with the "approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast".
The flight tracking website Flightradar24, external said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet (15 metres) above the top of the stadium".
Questions have been raised over the risk and potential for disaster involving two planes and a packed stadium, but many South Africans have responded with expressions of national pride that its country's pilots could pull this off.
The low-altitude flyby has become a feature of the build-up to some big matches.
The most notable was when a South African Airways jet flew over a Johannesburg stadium before the start of the 1995 rugby World Cup final which saw South Africa beat New Zealand.
The match, immortalised in the Hollywood film Invictus, was highly symbolic as the country's first black president, Nelson Mandela, donned the jersey of the national side, which had been closely associated with the apartheid government and previously excluded players who were not white.

Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.

In August 2026, a claim circulated online that tech giant Amazon was acquiring large quantities of books, some of them rare, and cutting off the spines to more efficiently scan the pages for artificial intelligence training data — destroying the books in the process.
The rumor emerged amid news that AI companies such as Anthropic were scanning — and destroying — millions of books to train their AI models.
Social media users across multiple platforms claimed Amazon was similarly destroying books, and dozens of Snopes readers contacted us seeking answers.
"Amazon is buying massive quantities of books, scanning them for AI training data, and destroying them in the process," one Instagram user posted (archived) on Aug. 18, gaining more than 2.2 million views, as of this writing.
(Instagram user @aaronparnas)
The rumor stemmed from an Aug. 17, 2026, story by digital investigative outlet 404 Media. Reporter Emanuel Maiberg collaborated with a bookseller who suspected a large order of books was linked to Amazon's book scanning project, planting an Apple AirTag in the shipment that eventually appeared at an Amazon facility in Las Vegas called LAS8.
Maiberg pointed to posts from booksellers raising concerns about unusually large shipments as well as online forum posts by people claiming to be Amazon employees writing in about the work at VGT3, the name for the operation, which Snopes tracked down and verified below.
In a follow-up story Aug. 26, Maiberg reportedly spoke with an employee who worked at Amazon's VGT3 warehouse. The employee, who was quoted anonymously, reportedly described how machines cut the spines off books before 20 to 25 scanners flipped through the loose pages "like machines that count cash."
Asked for a response to 404 Media's reporting, an Amazon spokesperson wrote in an email to Snopes: "Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use."
We also reached out to Maiberg regarding whether Amazon specifically sought "rare" books and whether he came across any evidence that Amazon was scanning books for e-books, but did not immediately hear back. We will update this story if we do.
Although we verified the location of the VGT3 operation and identified the online messages referred to in 404 Media's reporting, and Amazon confirmed it purchases books for the purposes of developing its products, we left this claim unrated because it remains undetermined whether Amazon specifically seeks out "rare" books and whether it uses the books exclusively for AI training data, as well as whether the online posts truly came from Amazon employees who worked at the Las Vegas facility.
Evidence of Amazon's book-scanning operation
In July 2026, a bookseller reportedly told Maiberg they received an order of around 1,000 books on Biblio, an online bookselling marketplace. In cooperation with 404 Media they placed an AirTag in the shipment, which eventually turned up at an Amazon warehouse at 5801 Nicco Way, Las Vegas.
(Google Maps)
The entrance to the facility, where a window bears a large illustration of a dinosaur with its jaws bared holding an open book, is currently publicly viewable on Google Maps. A reporter for a local Las Vegas news outlet also captured another angle of the facility's entrance.
Google Street View imagery from February 2026 shows the same building entrance — though it did not have the dinosaur emblem at that time.
We asked Amazon whether there were similar operations in other cities or countries, which the spokesperson did not address in their response.
The Wall Street Journal also reportedly spoke with a bookseller in the Pacific Northwest who similarly followed a shipment using location trackers inside the book covers. Reporter Melissa Korn wrote:
The other book went first to a warehouse in Kenosha, Wis., then to a spot in northern Las Vegas at an intersection with at least two Amazon facilities. It eventually moved to a position in Mexicali, Mexico. While the seller couldn't determine the exact address, a Google map of the location shows a sprawling recycled-paper manufacturing facility.
404 Media also pointed to messages in Amazon support channels in which booksellers raised concerns about large orders. "This is the first order I've seen like this in over 10 years of selling here," one bookseller wrote in September 2024, reporting that the buyer's address matched an "Amazon Fulfillment Center" in Las Vegas.
An Amazon support representative responded that they were investigating the concerns, before eventually confirming the orders were legitimate.
What have purported Amazon employees said?
Both The Wall Street Journal and 404 Media referenced posts on online forums by purported Amazon employees from more than a year prior to the 2026 stories in which they described work at the Las Vegas facility, reportedly involving cutting and scanning books for up to 12 hours at a time.
"Some are assigned to cut books, and others go to receive where they get books and scan the bar codes," one comment reportedly read.
Snopes verified that this post was real (archived), as were other posts dating back to at least July 2025 (archived, archived), although we were unable to verify they were truly made by Amazon employees.

It's a machine people operate. Each of these machines is just like a little workstation, and there'll be one person at each of these stations. Because we do not rely on anonymous sources for our fact-checking, we do not consider this account to be primary evidence.
How did 404 Media define 'rare' books?
According to 404 Media, the books in the shipment it tracked were rare, meaning "there are not many copies of them in circulation." Though many people online appeared to believe Amazon and other AI companies were specifically seeking out rare books, perhaps with the intention of gatekeeping or monetizing their contents by converting them into exclusive digital copies, we did not find evidence of this, as of this writing. Maiberg wrote:
That employees are scanning the barcodes or ISBNs on books — a unique serial number given to every published book — before scanning their content gives further credence to another theory put forth by booksellers: AI companies are trying to methodically scan every printed book in the world by working through the list of ISBNs. One bookseller told me they suspected this was the case because the very large orders they were getting never included very rare books that do not have ISBNs.
In other words, Amazon may be indiscriminately acquiring printed books, which may include some that have few copies in circulation.
This would align with the internal Anthropic documents we previously reported on, which stated that the goal of its book-scanning project, "Project Panama," was to "scan and destroy 'all the books in the world.'" In an email to a bookseller, project director Tom Turvey said "less common books are a great place to start." It's unclear whether "less common" refers to a book's actual market rarity or the number of circulating copies.
It's unclear, as of this writing, whether Amazon was specifically seeking out rare or collectable books in any capacity. We reached out to Maiberg seeking clarification. We also asked the Amazon spokesperson about how it chooses the books the company purchases, and they did not address this question in their response.
The anonymous employee who reportedly spoke with 404 Media said the shipments contained "all kinds of books":

There was even like, I don't know what you would call them, but it was like kind of stapled together papers that said that they were presented to Parliament on the behalf of Her Royal Majesty the Queen. So they were like government documents. I don't know if they're public. Probably they're public, but it was just interesting that we found all that in there.
According to The Wall Street Journal, several "rare-book sellers" reported receiving these mass orders, with one seller reportedly claiming his sales more than doubled in one year. It's unclear what percentage of the total amount of books Amazon has acquired has come from rare-book sellers as opposed to standard book marketplaces.
Unclear whether Amazon uses books for AI training
Amazon did not respond to our question regarding whether the book scans were used to train AI, converting the physical books into e-books or some other purpose.
"They didn't tell us it was for AI, I personally thought we were scanning them to make them into e-books, that was depressing to realize," a Reddit user who claimed to have once worked at VGT3 posted in August 2026.
As we previously reported, AI companies such as Anthropic have sought to train their models on books as high-quality data to prevent "model collapse," which happens when AI trains on its own content. This feedback loop degrades the quality of AI output and results in AI slop.

Hegseth’s Pentagon Lurches off the Rails
The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is the latest sign of severe dysfunction in the Defense Department.
Making Pete Hegseth the secretary of defense was always a huge gamble. A television host with little background in national-security or defense affairs, who topped out as a major in the National Guard, he was nominated based on the same qualification shared by most of Donald Trump’s other appointees: loyalty. And now the price of that gamble is evident. The Pentagon is careening offtrack under a secretary of defense who is firing or forcing the resignations of officers and civilian officials, not because they are unqualified but because he believes they are insufficiently loyal to him, personally.
The latest casualty of Hegseth’s ongoing purge is Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned today after repeatedly clashing with the secretary of defense. As my colleagues Nancy Youssef, Missy Ryan, and Michael Scherer report, a person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation said that he had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” In the careful circumlocutions of Washington-speak, that means that Driscoll went to the White House to complain about Hegseth, and the president sided with Hegseth.
But more issues were in play than “Army transformation.” Hegseth’s tenure has been disastrous on multiple scores. Instead of giving sound advice to the commander in chief and ensuring that America remains secure while the president fights a deeply unwise war of choice, he has instead been pursuing his political grievances about DEI and other pet peeves against the U.S. military. Hegseth seems to have a special animus toward the Army, an institution he claims “spit me out.” He fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, and he has pushed out other senior Army officers; at this point, the Army has no Senate-confirmed chief of staff or secretary. (George’s replacement, General Christopher LaNeve, so far does not have the necessary votes to be confirmed.)
Even in less dangerous times, Hegseth’s irresponsible behavior would be a hazard to American national security. The Defense Department is a huge bureaucracy; it requires a leader who understands more than the mechanics of teaching trainees how to do push-ups or how to handle a weapon. Secretaries of defense must grasp the economics of the defense industry, the nature of alliances, congressional politics, the policy process, and dozens of other issues for which Hegseth seems to care little and about which he knows even less.
In a time of war, however, Hegseth’s shortcomings may prove deadly. Leave aside his early stumbles, including the mishandling of sensitive information. Leave aside, even, that Hegseth dissembled about the severity of Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf that had succeeded in disrupting the logistical support for American forces in the theater and led to the kind of deprivations that were suffered by the crew of the aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln. Hegseth’s incompetence, and his commitment to staying in Trump’s good graces, helped launch the war itself in the first place.
Hegseth was reportedly virtually alone among senior officials in supporting Trump’s decision to attack Iran—when he should have been the one person in the room who knew better. The secretary of state and CIA director were against the idea. According to the The Wall Street Journal, and even then–Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, another of Trump’s unqualified-but-sycophantic appointees, mustered the courage to give the president bad news, telling Trump that killing the reigning ayatollah and striking Iran would “likely usher in a more hard-line regime open to acquiring nuclear weapons”; that the Iranians “would rush to close the Strait of Hormuz, destabilizing the global energy market”; and that Iran “would strike U.S. forces and partners in the Middle East,” all of which happened almost immediately after Trump gave the order to go to war.
Hegseth, however, supported Trump’s fantasies of a quick victory. A man of principle would have warned his president even at the risk of his job, but Pete Hegseth is not that man.
And now Hegseth has banished another enemy, Driscoll, from the Pentagon. But as the saying goes: play stupid games, win stupid prizes. Hegseth, more than ever, now owns every aspect of the Pentagon’s dysfunction. Yesterday, The Washington Post reported that multiple senior military leaders of the military—those still left, that is—have warned Hegseth that the United States cannot indefinitely extend military operations against Iran. Even the Chief of Naval Operations, Admiral Darryl Caudle (who campaigned for the job by signaling his agreement with the secretary’s culture-war obsessions) told Hegseth that the Navy cannot “sustain its current level of support for the Iran conflict because there is no anticipated end date.”
Hegseth’s response to this story was to send his spokespeople out to castigate the press for revealing classified information. In an amateurish bungle, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said that the reports were “inaccurate” but also a “betrayal of the force”—leading sensible people to ask how the stories could be false and dangerous at the same time. And these were just the responses from people who are officially authorized to speak for the Pentagon; another bombshell report over the weekend revealed that the department has recruited online influencers into paid roles, but without either the influencers or the Pentagon telling anyone about their cozy arrangement with the government.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has dutifully overseen the raiding of assets from other theaters to support Trump’s war with Iran, leaving the U.S. and its allies exposed to potential threats from China and Russia. When Trump returned to office, Hegseth and others supported a reorientation away from the Middle East and Europe. Now the secretary and the other supposed China hawks have discarded those positions, and dumped everything into a war that still has no clear strategy and no clear goal beyond stopping Iran from attaining a nuclear weapon it didn’t have in the first place.
Fortunately, even under the strain of a petty and incompetent secretary, and a president mired in his delusions, senior military officers are still speaking up and telling their boss the truth about America’s parlous defense situation. One of the advantages of a large bureaucracy staffed with professionals is that much of it can run and function, at least for a while, under even the most inept leaders.
But Hegseth is apparently close to getting the Pentagon he wants: Much like his boss at the White House, Hegseth seems to desire a building full of loyalists who put the boss’s personal fortunes over the national interest. Some reports indicate, for example, that Hegseth wants to replace Driscoll with Parnell—who has no significant qualifications for the post beyond his time fighting with the press on the secretary’s behalf.
The result of all this is that the United States is losing a war to a third-rate power in the Middle East. The Russians, meanwhile, are continuing their rampage in Europe, and apparently considering things so perilous that the CIA director had to fly to Moscow just to warn the Kremlin off of whatever it was thinking of doing. The Chinese are watching as Trump and Hegseth have stripped the Pacific theater of its only American aircraft carrier. In the midst of this chaos, Hegseth does chin-ups while he ponders calling all of America’s admirals and generals back to another mass meeting so he can again carp at them about fat soldiers and bearded sailors.
Pete Hegseth has failed in every mission except one: keeping his job. But firing or forcing out everyone else in the Pentagon will not make Pete Hegseth into the secretary of defense America and its men and women in uniform need. With each dismissal, he only exposes his own insecurities, even as he manages to stay employed—but the people and the armed forces of the United States are paying the inevitable price of his incompetence.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
- Published
The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest of the 17 the country has faced as it continues to spread. United Nations experts have described it as the fastest growing outbreak on record in terms of new infections.
Getting the spread of the deadly virus under control is challenging because it involves a rare species of Ebola for which there is no vaccine - though some are being tested - and the epicentre is in an area affected by conflict.
What is Ebola and what are the symptoms?
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus.
Ebola viruses normally infect animals, typically fruit bats, but outbreaks among humans can sometimes start when people eat or handle infected animals.
It takes two to 21 days for symptoms to appear. They come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Ebola outbreaks used to be small and contained to remote rural areas. However, urbanisation is pushing larger populations closer to these natural reservoirs of Ebola and increasing the risk of transmission.
Why is this Ebola outbreak different and is there a vaccine?
This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which had not been seen for over a decade.
Named after a district in Uganda where it was first detected, Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012.
One study showed that it killed about a third, external of those infected, far less than the more common Zaire (66.6%) and Sudan (48.5%) species. About 48% of those known to have been infected in the current outbreak have died.
Initial blood tests for Ebola in the affected areas were negative as they were designed to identify the more common form of the disease.
In July, the UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, said it had given permission for the first human trials of a vaccine for Bundibugyo to go ahead.
It was created by a team from the University of Oxford based on the same technology used in the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.
It took scientists just eight weeks to develop the new jab after plugging in genetic code from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.
The vaccine is being tested on 50 volunteers from Oxford aged 18 to 55 to see whether it triggers the correct antibody response without causing significant side effects.
Three other groups are also developing different vaccines for Bundibugyo although they have not yet entered clinical trials.
While treatments are available for other species of the Ebola virus, no drugs have been specifically approved to treat those infected with Bundibugyo.
DR Congo is currently preparing to roll out the Ervebo vaccine - which helps protect against the Zaïre species of Ebola - as part of a trial to see if it is effective against the Bundibugyo species.
The World Health Organization (WHO) is also sponsoring a separate clinical trial in the country to see whether two existing antiviral therapies can improve survival rates.
The two drugs selected as the most promising are an experimental monoclonal antibody called MBP134 and remdesivir, an injection into a vein, which is also used to treat Covid.
A further complication is that the outbreak is taking place in a conflict zone, with a quarter of million people displaced from their homes and people moving across porous borders into neighbouring countries.
How did the current Ebola outbreak start?
The first known case was a nurse who developed symptoms on 24 April, which means the virus had been spreading undetected for weeks.
The nurse died in Bunia, the capital of eastern DR Congo's Ituri province, according to Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba.
The victim's body was repatriated to Mongbwalu.
Kamba said one of the reasons the virus spread so quickly was the number of people exposed to the body during the funeral ceremony.
But researchers believe that it may have been spreading since February but it was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.
How many Ebola cases have been reported and where are they?
On 23 August, officials said there had been 5,514 confirmed cases and 2,642 confirmed deaths from the virus in DR Congo.
There have also been 1,200 recoveries from Ebola so far, including four nurses whose discharge from hospital was celebrated at a special ceremony.
Ituri province is the epicentre of this outbreak and accounts for the vast majority of confirmed infections.
Cases have also been confirmed in North Kivu (714) and South Kivu (3), provinces partly controlled by the rebel AFC-M23 alliance. These discoveries signalled the outbreak's spread from its epicentre.
The last patient being treated for Ebola in neighbouring Uganda was discharged from hospital on 16 July. Up to that point, the country had recorded 20 confirmed cases - with most having travelled from DR Congo - and two deaths.
Uganda has since announced it is Ebola-free, going against the protocol of waiting 42 days - until 27 August - from when the last patient recovers to declare an outbreak over.
What is being done in DR Congo to tackle the current Ebola outbreak?
Mass gatherings have been banned in the six provinces with confirmed cases - Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele.
The capital city, Kinshasa - which has no confirmed cases and is located some 1,800 km (1,100) miles from the outbreak - has also been ordered to ban mass gatherings.
The government has now established four laboratories in Ituri - in Bunia, Mongbwalu, Beni and Aru - which can test blood samples for Bundibugyo and deliver results within 24 hours, removing earlier delays.
Surveillance systems, contact tracing and the treatment infrastructure, with dedicated centres in several affected towns, have also been expanded, according to the health minister.
The WHO has dedicated $3.9m (£2.9m) to tackling the outbreak, while Africa CDC has announced a $319m budget.
A toll-free number, 151, has been provided for reporting symptoms and people are being reminded to:
- avoid contact with bodies of people who died with symptoms, or with dead animals
- not eat raw meat, as undercooked food may transmit the virus
- practise social distancing.
How have the rebels responded to the latest Ebola outbreak?
The AFC-M23 group has created an Ebola response team in an effort to prevent transmissions in the areas it controls.
In late June, the rebel authorities had declared their zones Ebola-free, but introduced new restrictions in August, following two travellers testing positive in North Kivu.
Shared taxis and passenger boats between government-held and rebel-held areas of the province, have been suspended, highlighting the hostilities between the two sides.
The region's Ebola response co-ordinator Dr Freddy Kaniki, told the BBC in July that while UN agencies such as the WHO and Unicef - for children - had been helping, there has been no co-ordination with the Congolese government.

What are Rwanda and other countries doing about the Ebola outbreak?
Rwanda closed its borders with DR Congo earlier on in the outbreak. According to Congolese media, authorities began to reopen parts of the border late in June following a lull in local infections.
Uganda has temporarily suspended flights, buses and all other public transport crossing the border with DR Congo.
Several other African countries have tightened border screenings and bolstered health facilities.
The US has extended travel restrictions on its citizens who have been to DR Congo. Anyone who wants to return home must spend 21 days in a third country before being allowed into America.

EXCLUSIVE: After Only Murders In the Building‘s sleuthing trio of Charles (Steve Martin), Oliver (Martin Short) and Mabel (Selena Gomez) trekked to London for the upcoming Season 6, the writers room of the Hulu mystery comedy series is on the move too.
Based in Los Angeles for the first six seasons, the room will relocate to New York for Season 7, Deadline has learned. OMITB has not been renewed for a seventh season yet but that is expected given its status as a signature Hulu series that continues to do well, recently garnering five more Emmy nominations.
The writing team for the likely new installment has not been set yet, but some writers are expected to stay on, moving to New York for an in-person room led by co-creator, executive producer and showrunner John Hoffman, sources said.
Watch on Deadline
A rep for 20th Television, which produces Only Murders In the Building, declined comment.
It is standard practice among streamers to commission writers rooms ahead of formal greenlights for subsequent installments as a way to shorten gaps between seasons. In the case of Only Murders In the Building, the goal from the start had been to keep the series on a yearly cadence, something it has been able to maintain so far, with Season 6 slated for Dec. 8 release. (The 15-month gap between Seasons 5 and 6 is the longest so far in the series’ run; the wait had been typically around 12 months.)
Up until now, OMITB would finish writing a season in Los Angeles before Hoffman would go to New York for the filming. With the complex logistics of the Season 6 shoot in London, which only wrapped last week, that would not have been possible for Season 7, which is expected to bring back the action to New York.
In order to get the new season ready for 2027 (or the start of 2028), writing and filming would have to overlap, which led to the decision to move the writers room to New York, allowing Hoffman to juggle writing and production.
	Only Murders in the Building was created by Martin and Hoffman. The duo executive produces Season 6 alongside Short, Gomez, Dan Fogelman, Jess Rosenthal, Ben Smith, Jennifer Crittenden & Gabrielle Allan.

The military has said such operations are intended to prevent attacks by Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups. It says four Israeli soldiers have been killed in militant attacks since the ceasefire began.
In a statement posted to Telegram, Hamas called Tuesday's attack a "serious crime" that constitutes a "deliberate disregard for civilian lives." They also said this was an "extension of the brutal genocide" against Palestinians that has continued despite the ceasefire.
The statement continued, saying that the attack reflected a "policy of defiance and arrogance" on Netanyahu's part. Finally, they called on mediators and the international community to stop Israel's ongoing violations of the agreement.
