In the United States, building a data center now polls roughly as well as abolishing the police. If current trends continue, server warehouses may soon be less popular with Americans than pizza topped with pineapple and shattered glass.
The data centers are winning
Why the AI buildout (probably) can’t be stopped.
In an August survey from Heatmap Pro and Embold Research, just 15 percent of Americans said they would support a data center being built in their area, while 75 percent expressed opposition. One year earlier, 43 percent of respondents in the same poll had approved of nearby data center development, while just 42 percent opposed it.
Key takeaways
- Data center projects are increasingly unpopular and vulnerable to local opposition.
- Nevertheless, the AI infrastructure buildout remains massive.
- The economic forces driving the data center boom are extremely strong.
- Since AI data centers can be located almost anywhere, it’s difficult to stop them from being built somewhere.
This soaring backlash is visible in other surveys — and in the actions of elected officials. In recent weeks, Wisconsin’s gubernatorial candidates sparred over who hates data centers more, Pennsylvania’s center-left Gov. Josh Shapiro enacted new restrictions on AI infrastructure projects (after previously championing such investment), and even Texas’s staunchly pro-business Republican government announced a temporary moratorium on new approvals.
Meanwhile, data center projects are being canceled at a record rate, as local opposition mounts.
This has led some in the pro-tech minority to worry that the data center buildout is about to collapse — and take the US economy down with it. Anti-AI commentators, for their part, are cheering the industry’s impending crisis.
But such panic and celebration are both premature.
In truth, despite exploding opposition, the data center boom is still going strong. Interviews with industry experts and recent construction data suggest that the economic forces driving the buildout remain more powerful than the political winds blowing against it. And unless Congress enacts a national moratorium, AI companies will almost certainly be able to continue finding jurisdictions willing to tolerate hyperscale campuses, in exchange for sufficient revenue and incentives.
America’s data center boom can be slowed and geographically shifted. But it probably can’t be killed, absent a collapse in demand for computing power or a much bigger revolution in American politics.
The boom is bigger than the backlash
There are two fundamental facts about today’s data center boom: 1) The backlash against it is huge, and 2) the buildout is even bigger.
The climate news outlet Heatmap has kept a tracker of new data center restrictions and cancellations. As of late July, it found that more than 500 jurisdictions had enacted severe constraints or bans on data center construction. The vast majority of these measures had been enacted since the beginning of this year.
The publication also found that contested data center projects face a skyrocketing cancellation rate. In late 2024, 20 percent of disputed developments were canceled; in the first half of 2026, that figure was closer to 50 percent. By Heatmap’s tally, more than 100 data center projects have been nixed this year in the face of local opposition, while more than 200 are currently being fought.
This surge of mass resistance is remarkable. And yet, it is also nowhere near sufficient to end the AI buildout.
Although the number of places with severe restrictions (or outright bans) on server farms is rapidly rising, more than 90 percent of US counties had no significant constraints on data center development at July’s end.
What’s more, many of the most eye-catching recent policy changes are less significant than they appear. For example, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pause does not actually halt data center construction in the Lone Star State. Rather, it essentially establishes a more thorough screening process, when server farms apply for electricity from the state’s grid. Projects that supply all of their own power through on-site natural gas — as a rising share of new data centers do — are exempt.
Pennsylvania and New York’s recently enacted restrictions on data center development are more substantial. Yet neither of those states are particularly important to the AI buildout. Taken together, New York and Pennsylvania host only about 6.5 percent of America’s data centers, according to Data Center Map.
And their share of all pending developments is even more negligible, as the trade publication Construction Connect has illustrated:
Meanwhile, although half of contested data center projects are now failing, many still go undisputed. In the aggregate, cancellations have not kept pace with construction or new development. In the first quarter of this year, at least 3.5 gigawatts of data center capacity were canceled amid local opposition, in Heatmap’s tally. During the same three months, at least 36 GW of capacity were added to the US pipeline of proposed and active projects, according to the analytics firm Wood Mackenzie. As of April 1, that pipeline contained a total of 106 GW worth of developments that had already survived the permitting gauntlet.
To be sure, cancellations have risen sharply since March. By Heatmap’s count, at least 13 gigawatts of capacity have been nixed so far this year. But the capacity of permitted projects has also grown since April 1. And the ratio between blocked and active developments has not radically changed, according to industry analysts.
“At this point, we do not think the recent wave of opposition and policy intervention has materially changed our national capacity growth trajectory,” Maya Barkin, an analyst at the AI industry research firm SemiAnalysis, told me.
Indeed, monthly construction spending on data centers in the US hit a record high this June.
In short, data centers are marching forward despite taking heavy fire, like a pack of gut-shot zombies.
The secrets of the AI buildout’s success
Why has the AI buildout proven so resilient? There are at least two reasons.
First, and most importantly, demand for computing power remains astronomical. As frontier AI companies have built out larger models — and consumers and companies have increased their use of artificial intelligence and digital services — our economy’s appetite for computation has far outstripped supply. According to a recent report from the commercial real estate firm JLL, 99 percent of North America’s data centers are occupied. What’s more, of the 66 GW of data center capacity currently being constructed in JLL’s count, 95 percent has already been reserved.
Second, data center projects are unusually location-flexible. If a housing developer gets chased out of San Francisco’s suburbs by zoning rules and local opposition, it can’t relocate its condo tower to a mostly uninhabited stretch of Nevada desert. By contrast, data centers can — and do — operate in the middle of nowhere.
For certain purposes, these facilities need some proximity to the users they serve; you can’t adequately support online gaming in New York City with data centers on the West Coast. But even in such cases, servers merely need to be in the same broad region. The hyperscale facilities used to train AI models, meanwhile, can be located virtually anywhere with land, fiber optic cables, a modicum of labor, and electricity (and now that many data centers are powering themselves through on-site natural gas plants, even the latter is potentially expendable).
Taken together, these two realities make data center construction extremely difficult to choke off. Sky-high demand for compute means that hyperscalers can afford to throw a lot of money at localities, in order to secure a project’s approval. And location flexibility makes it very difficult for data center developers to run out of host jurisdictions, particularly when so many rural counties throughout the United States are starving for revenue and investment. Thus, unless Congress imposes a national moratorium, development deals will almost certainly keep getting struck.
“I think companies will need to open up their wallets and make sure that communities receive clear benefits,” John Arnold, a billionaire investor and philanthropist who sits on Meta’s board (and whose foundation has given funding to Vox), told me. “There will be places that raise their hands and say, ‘For X amount of benefit, we will welcome you into the community.’”
Just this week, West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey signaled that he was moving forward with plans to encourage data center development and use the consequent revenue to slash the state’s income tax.
Municipal permitting won’t preempt the robot apocalypse
On one level, all this may seem to validate anti-data center activism: If there are countless potential locations for these facilities, then why should any community host one it doesn’t want?
This said, many oppose new data centers out of concern for their aggregate impacts, rather than their local ones. Climate activists fear that the AI buildout will generate perilous increases in carbon emissions. Populists on the right and left, meanwhile, want to slow the progress of artificial intelligence, so as to prevent the technology from causing mass unemployment — and/or human extinction.
For these factions, the buildout’s resilience has more complicated implications. If state and local bans are unlikely to end the boom, then green groups might be unwise to push for such measures in relatively climate-conscious areas. After all, doing so could shift development toward jurisdictions with less renewable energy, and/or fewer restrictions on carbon pollution. Given that risk, blue-state environmentalists may do more to mitigate AI’s climate impacts by regulating data center development than by banning it. Specifically, climate groups could demand that hyperscalers help bankroll the vast expansions of clean energy and transmission infrastructure that the green transition has always required.
For AI doomers, on the other hand, local bans may have some instrumental value. Moratoria and other restrictions are surely slowing the data center buildout at the margin. Still, as long as hyperscale facilities remain location-flexible — and tech companies stay well-capitalized — AI infrastructure will get built somewhere. A national moratorium could buy significant time. But ultimately, humanity’s security from the risks of AI hinges less on whether data centers get built than on what companies are allowed to do with them — and how the wealth they generate is distributed.
The data center rebellion is among the most remarkable popular movements in recent memory. But it is arrayed against one of the largest investment frenzies in human history. Unless or until the AI industry’s alleged “bubble” bursts, its buildout will be exceptionally difficult to stop. Yet where that buildout happens, how it’s powered — and what communities extract from it — are all up for grabs (and, increasingly, being grabbed).

- The claim that the Trump administration uses a legal loophole to sell protected wild horses to slaughterhouses is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from reporting by The New York Times in August 2026 and was backed by research by animal rights groups that suggested buyers of wild horses sold through the Bureau of Land Management's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter.
- According to its website, it is BLM policy "not to sell or send any wild horses or burros to slaughter," and buyers from the sale program sign a bill of sale saying they will not slaughter or sell for slaughter the animals they buy.
- The Times' reporting brought to light a long-standing issue within the BLM about what to do with excess wild horses and burros. The bureau is bound by law to regulate populations but has historically avoided euthanizing healthy animals due to concerns about public perception.
- Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses.
- Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that more recent buyers have purchased horses from the BLM and sold them for slaughter, the article did not include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administration. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- We contacted the Times journalist who wrote the article to ask for additional evidence and await a reply.
In August 2026, The New York Times published an investigation into the Bureau of Land Management's sale of wild horses, titled "Under Trump, Protected Wild Horses Are Going to Slaughter."
Synopses of the Times' findings circulated widely online. For example, one Facebook page wrote (archived):
A heartbreaking investigation revealed that Trump's Bureau of Land Management is systematically rounding up thousands of America's wild horses, then quietly selling them off to buyers who are shipping them to slaughterhouses abroad. Before, the U.S. government rarely sold wild horses. But since Trump took office, government sales have more than doubled.
Versions of the claim also circulated on Threads (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to learn more about it. One reader wrote, "Is Trump really rounding up horses to sell to slaughterhouses?"
The Times article reported how the U.S. government, faced with the ballooning costs of taking care of more than 50,000 wild horses it has rounded up to control herd sizes, sold thousands every year to buyers who purchased the animals for as little as $25 to sell at auction to other buyers that shipped them to slaughterhouses. This was allowed to happen, the Times reported, because selling a wild horse removes its statutory protection from "capture, branding, harassment, or death."
Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers of wild horses sold through the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter, the article didn't include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administrations.
Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses after being sold to private buyers before the start of the Trump administrations.
Snopes contacted Skydog Ranch and Sanctuary, an animal rescue organization. That nonprofit underwent an investigation into the BLM's sales program that formed the basis of the Times article.
Skydog publicly shared copies of complaints it submitted to the BLM about buyers for the agency allegedly buying wild horses and then taking them to "kill pens," as described in the Times article. The animal rescue organization accused the BLM of failing to stop the buyers despite the complaints.
We also contacted Dave Phillips, who wrote the Times article, to ask what primary evidence he used for his reporting. We await a reply to our queries.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A BLM spokesperson said in an emailed statement on Aug. 24, 2026:
The Bureau of Land Management does not sell or send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and allegations that individuals are violating federal law or the terms governing the sale of these animals are taken seriously.
The Times article suggested the BLM had found a way to offload its large off-range holding population of wild horses and burros that was effectively sending the animals to slaughter without incriminating the bureau.
The Wild Horse and Burro Program allows the BLM to sell animals that are more than 10 years old or that it has unsuccessfully listed for adoption at least three times. However, the Times reported, "Livestock inspection records show mustangs sold by the government soon ended up on trucks bound for slaughter plants in Canada."
The article focused on one reported buyer from Ohio, who the Times said had bought 500 horses from the BLM in a matter of years. Some of those horses, the article said, later showed up for sale at "an auction in Tennessee frequented by slaughter buyers."
The article also alleged that a week after the Ohio buyer received a shipment of 97 formerly wild mares, an Ohio exporter of animals for slaughter shipped two trucks of horses across the Canadian border. The Times said that, according to one image its reporter had viewed, at least one of those horses had a BLM freeze mark.
The Ohio buyer reportedly spoke to the Times reporter for two hours but "refused to say specifically what had happened to the horses he purchased from the government, other than to insist that none had gone to slaughter." He declined having worked with the Ohio exporter that shipped the two trucks across the Canadian border. The exporter would not comment to the Times on whether he had purchased horses from the buyer.
Without primary evidence — meaning sales documents tracking individual animals from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the auction in Tennessee or from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the Ohio exporter to a slaughterhouse — it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify the claims in the Times article.
Holding costs tie up BLM program budget
The Times article highlighted an issue that the BLM has grappled with for years: how to legally, effectively and tastefully control wild horse populations. According to the bureau's data, wild horse and burro populations exceed the BLM's Appropriate Management Level, meaning the number of animals that can thrive in balance with other public land resources and uses, in nearly all the states where the bureau tracks populations.
The BLM is required by The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 — the same act that protects wild horses and burros from "capture, branding, harassment, or death" — to uphold the AML for the populations it tracks (Sec. 1333b1). Under the Act, the BLM is allowed to euthanize excess animals "in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible" (Sec. 1333b2C). However, a 2008 report by the Government Accountability Office on the BLM's management of "unadoptable" horses found that the bureau hesitated to do this because it was thought to be "unacceptable to the public" (Page 56).
The BLM estimates that wild horse and burro populations, if left unregulated, would double every four years. Therefore, the bureau rounds up and removes thousands of animals from the wild to control populations. Those animals end up in the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program's off-range corrals and pastures. By May 2026, the program reported that it held 58,025 formerly wild horses and burros and that its total capacity for off-range holding was 78,751 animals. According to the program's figures it spent $101 million — 66% of its budget — on off-range holding costs in fiscal year 2024.
A long-standing problem
According to the 2008 GAO report, the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program faced the same challenges then that the Times article highlighted 18 years later. The report said the cost of caring for off-range animals was already overwhelming the program in 2008, and that the program had "limited" options for "dealing with" animals it could not adopt out because it feared the public would not support humanely euthanizing healthy animals (Page 9).
The program had reportedly sold animals since 2005, though at that point also faced issues with animals ending up at slaughterhouses after the sale (Page 43). As a result, the bureau implemented a mandatory "statement of intent" at purchase, which required the buyer to say that they did not intend to sell the animals they bought for slaughter. BLM bills of sale for wild horses and burros still included such a clause in 2026.
The effectiveness of the clause was unclear because the BLM also said on its website about its sales program that it did not track animals after it sold them. The 2008 report noted that the introduction of a "statement of intent" was part of the reason the BLM sold fewer horses than before.
The existence of the "statement of intent" did not deter one buyer, who admitted in a 2015 investigation carried out by the Office of the Inspector General that "most of" the 1,700 wild horses he bought through the BLM between 2008 and 2012 had gone to slaughter.
The GAO and OIG reports suggest that the issue of wild horses and burros ending up at slaughterhouses after BLM sales is documented and predates the Trump administration.
Aside from adoption, sale or euthanasia, the BLM has been pursuing fertility treatment as a way to control populations since 1992 (Page 69). However, the BLM itself and peer-reviewed research have found it comes with its own challenges around finding and accessing animals and keeping up with treatment. According to the BLM, it delivered 921 fertility treatments to wild horses and burros in fiscal year 2025. That same year, it removed 7,853 horses and burros from the wild.
The Times report said that although government experts did recommend wider use of fertility treatment to control populations the recommendation was hard for the BLM to act on because its funds were largely tied up in the removal, holding and care of excess animals.
In sum, while it was not possible to verify the exact elements of the Times' reporting, the article brought to light a complicated issue for the BLM that predated both Trump administrations but nonetheless had lethal consequences for the horses and burros the U.S. government is bound to protect.

Battery swapping platform Yuma Energy has raised $35 Mn (₹333 Cr) in its Series A funding round from existing backer and Canada-based automotive giant Magna International. The startup plans to use the fresh proceeds to expand its battery swapping network across India, broaden its customer base and strengthen its tech platform. As part of the deal, Yuma Energy and Magna will also work together to scale the former’s presence in the electric two- and three-wheeler ecosystem. "... Crossing 6 Cr swaps was a defining moment for us, and with Magna's support, we're accelerating our infrastructure rollout and deepening our partnerships with fleets and OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) to make swapping the default choice for every electric two and three-wheeler on Indian roads." said Yuma managing director Muthu Subramanian. Founded in 2023 as a joint venture (JV) between Magna and electric mobility platform Yulu Energy, Yuma Energy offers battery swapping infrastructure and services for electric vehicles (EVs). While Yulu then contributed certain assets and intellectual property for a 49% stake, Magna infused $52 Mn in the startup for a controlling 51% stake in the JV. Yuma Energy operates more than 2,500 charging stations across 18 Indian cities. It also claims to have accumulated 1 Lakh batteries and delivered more than 6 Cr battery swaps so far. Going forward, the startup said that it plans to broaden its customer base to serve a wider mix of EV users, fleet operators and OEMs. It is also eyeing EBITDA-profitability by FY27. Yuma operates in the growing Indian battery swapping market, which is being driven by novel products, need for convenience and substantial capital subsidies from the government. However, despite rising EV registrations, the lack of adequate charging infrastructure across the country remains a major hurdle. To fill this gap, EV charging and infrastructure ventures continue to attract healthy interest from investors. In July, EV charging startup Statiq raised $18 Mn, via a mix of equity and debt, in a round led by Tenacity Ventures. Prior to this in June, EV charging startup Exponent Energy also bagged ₹200 Cr in a round co-led by 360 ONE Asset and TDK Ventures. Earlier last month, reports also surfaced that battery swapping startup Battery Smart was looking to list on the bourses, with plans to file the DRHP by October. At the heart of all this is the Indian EV market, which is projected to become a $132 Bn opportunity by 2030.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction as rivers including the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli overflowed and swept away homes, roads, bridges, and other infrastructure. Experts said the disaster was likely triggered by the collapse of a glacier and a massive ice-and-rock avalanche in the Himalayas, which sent huge amounts of debris and water into the river systems. As of 28 August 2026, the death toll in Nepal had risen to 469, according to Nepal Police, while nearly 1,000 people remained missing as search and rescue operations continued (here, here, and here).
Amid the disaster, multiple visuals are being shared on social media with the claim that they show visuals of the August 2026 Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind these visuals in this article.
Claim: The visuals show the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: None of the videos are related to the Nepal floods in August 2026. They are either old videos from other locations or AI-generated videos that are being shared as visuals of the disaster. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
This video is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows a Chinese helicopter reaching the site where a glacier had broken, causing a massive amount of water to be released and resulting in widespread destruction in Nepal.
In our investigation, we found that the video was originally uploaded (archived) on the Instagram account of Leigh Coates, an American commercial helicopter pilot based in Valdez, Alaska. She posted the video on 22 August 2026 and specifically identified the location as Columbia Glacier in Alaska. She explained that a Jökulhlaup, also known as a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), occurs when water trapped by glacier ice suddenly finds a way out, causing the water to drain rapidly beneath the glacier and rush downhill with immense force. She further stated that such events have been occurring annually at Columbia Glacier since 2014, although they are rarely captured because they generally occur in remote areas.
Video 2
The video is being shared on social media with claims that it shows the largest lake in the mountains whose embankment breached, causing the massive Nepal-Tibet floods.
We found that the video was uploaded by Leigh Coates on her official YouTube channel on 16 August 2026, before the Nepal floods. The video is titled “Before and After a Jökulhlaup Glacial Outburst Flood” and shows an example of the glacial outburst flood that occurred in Juneau, Alaska. This confirms that the video is unrelated to the August 2026 Nepal-Tibet floods.
Video 3
The video (here, here, and here) is being shared with claims on social media that it shows vehicles and buildings being swept away by flash floods in Nepal.
However, we found (archived) that this video has been available on the internet since 04 August 2026, at least 22 days before the Nepal floods. Moreover, upon examining the video, we noticed that the movement of the water and vehicles appeared unnatural.
We also analysed the video using AI detection tools such as Hive, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Video 4
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows vehicles being swept away by heavy floods during the August 2026 Nepal disaster.
We found that this video is related to the flash floods that occurred in the Chamoli region of Uttarakhand on 10 August 2026. Media reports (here, here) from the time also carried the same visuals and reported that vehicles were swept away after a bridge collapsed amid the flooding.
Video 5
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a mudslide rapidly turning into a torrent of muddy floodwater during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found that the video is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. The video was actually recorded in Hpakant, Myanmar, in January 2024 (here, here).
Video 6
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows water and debris rushing down from a mountainous area and sweeping away homes during the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
We found (here, here, and here) that this video is from Dharali village in Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand, and dates back to August 2025. It shows flash floods that occurred following a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga River. The resulting floodwaters, debris and silt surged through Dharali, washing away houses and other structures. At least four people were confirmed dead, while more than 50 others were reported missing.
Video 7
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a massive landslide occurring during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found (here, here) that this video has been available on the internet since at least 11 August 2026, predating the recent Nepal floods. Several users have claimed that the landslide was triggered by an earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August 2026.
Video 8
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a power plant being devastated amid the August 2026 Nepal floods. News outlets like NDTV, Dainik Bhaskar, and Divya Bhaskar also shared the video, claiming it was from Nepal.
We found (here, here, and here) that this video has been available online since at least 2022 and is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Video 9
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows people in Nepal running ahead of fast-moving floodwaters during the severe floods on 26 August 2026. Dainik Bhaskar, Punjab Kesari TV, and News18 Tamil Nadu also shared the video in the context of the Nepal floods.
We found that the video was available online as early as 04 August 2026, well before the 26 August 2026 Nepal floods, and therefore predates the disaster. The original post stated that the video showed rainfall in Yafa, a mountainous region of Yemen (here, here).
Video 10
The video (here, here) shows an elephant rescuing a man during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found that the video shows an elephant rescuing a man in Assam, India. The video was filmed several weeks before the August 2026 Nepal floods and is therefore unrelated to the disaster.
To sum up, none of these visuals are related to the Nepal floods in August 2026.

Lionel Messi says he's retiring from playing internationally for Argentina
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday after two decades representing Argentina.
"It was a decision that hurt — and still hurts deeply — but I understand that the time has come," the 39-year-old Messi said on his Instagram account.
"I swear to you that I always gave it my all — not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football."
Messi played in a record-tying six World Cups, won it in 2022 in Qatar and led Argentina to this year's final, losing to Spain in extra time in New Jersey.
In the World Cup hosted in the U.S., Mexico and Canada, Messi played all eight matches and scored eight goals. He finished just one goal behind France's Kylian Mbappé, the tournament's top scorer. He concluded his international career as Argentina's all-time leading scorer with 125 goals, 21 of which were scored in World Cups.
He explained he wrote his retirement letter on July 21 — two days after the World Cup final — but waited to publish it because his father was facing health issues that eventually claimed his life.
Jorge Messi died on Aug. 8 in his native Rosario.
Messi will continue to play for Inter Miami. Over the weekend he scored four times in a 7-1 win over CF Montreal.
He made his Argentina debut in 2006 but his journey was fraught with frustration until he finally lifted the World Cup in 2022.
"Thank you for all the love these past 20 years," he said. "I'm going to miss hearing you all from the inside so much. Now I'm going to be one of you, cheering and supporting you from the outside (through thick and thin, even more so)."
In the letter, the Inter Miami captain did not say how long he intends to continue playing.
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — along with my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of. Experiencing this with you was incredible. I love you all," he added.
The second retirement
Messi's stellar recent success with Argentina nearly didn't happen.
A decade ago, before the World Cup triumph and Copa América titles in 2021 and 2024, he retired from the national team. The decision followed Argentina's defeat in the 2016 Copa América final to Chile on penalty kicks, one of which he missed.
But Messi shook off the notion of not being able to win the big match. He continued starring for Barcelona, then Paris Saint-Germain, then Inter Miami.
He's the two-time defending Most Valuable Player in Major League Soccer, the star of the league reigning champion, someone who still creates goals in the biggest moments.
"He is pure history," Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said during the recent World Cup. "History. A legend."

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.
Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.
Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians.
The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.
The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”
The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.
Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.
Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.
“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”
Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.
Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”
Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”
Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

For the past five years, security researcher Matt Burch has immersed himself in the esoteric and high-stakes world of ATM security, in which small software flaws can sometimes expose cold, hard cash. As Burch has bored deeper into the computers powering these digital lock boxes—and continued to find vulnerabilities in key digital security systems—he has started working to raise the alarm, not just about overlooked ATM flaws, but about how that same software used in other industries can introduce weaknesses in an array of critical systems.
At the Black Hat and Defcon security conferences in Las Vegas this month, Burch presented findings about nine vulnerabilities that have been fixed in disk encryption and pre-boot authentication software called CryptoPro Secure Disk. The flaws could have been exploited to bypass CryptoPro's integrity checks and gain full access to encrypted devices.
Made by the German software firm CryptWare, CryptoPro is marketed to ATM makers and is used in some ATMs, including as part of Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Suite. But CryptoPro is also sold as a security solution for other embedded-device makers, as well as big organizations using Microsoft Windows, underscoring the supply chain challenge of addressing bugs when software is widely implemented in numerous industries.
“ATMs are what brought me down this path, but I think there may be an even higher impact of these findings beyond that,” Burch says. “From the perspective of ATMs and the financial network, there are a lot of layers, and I think as a result of that, things just get implemented a certain way and then there’s limited technical insight—bugs can get overlooked or they don’t get addressed.”
CryptWare managing director Uwe Saame tells WIRED that the company patched the nine bugs in two phases with CryptoPro version 7.7.2 in early November and 7.7.3 in early December. Burch says the company was prompt and collaborative throughout his disclosure process and he validated that the patches actually fix the vulnerabilities he found. While CryptoPro does not seem to publicly release update notes, Burch says he believes that the company distributed information about the patches to its customers.
Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson Michael Jacobsen tells WIRED in a statement that only two of the nine vulnerabilities are relevant to Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Hard Disk Encryption, the system where the ATM maker uses CryptoPro software. Jacobsen says that Diebold Nixdorf issued fixes related to those two bugs in December, but that they could not have been exploited on their own to compromise a Diebold Nixdorf ATM.
In ATMs, embedded devices, and enterprise security more broadly, the challenge of the software supply chain comes from all of the steps to actually apply fixes in the world. As in this case, a developer has to release a patch, then companies that implement the product in their own software need to develop a tailored fix, and then customers need to actually hear about and install that patch—which can be difficult for systems that are running in the field or can't easily be paused and updated.
Speaking generally about this challenge, Jacobsen, the Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson, says that “when a security issue is identified, Diebold Nixdorf assesses the impact, identifies affected products and configurations, and develops any needed updates through our product security and engineering processes. We then notify impacted customers and provide updates through standard software distribution channels, including the Global Security Portal where applicable. For deployed ATMs, updates are coordinated with each customer based on their operating model, service agreements, and change-management processes.”
Security researchers have warned for decades about the danger of relying on “security through obscurity” by trying to hide software from view or keep it locked away. And, as a result of this work, internet-of-things manufacturers and those in critical industries like the financial sector and medical device manufacturing have made some progress on transparency and promoting patch adoption. But Burch points out that as AI systems make it easier to evaluate software and find vulnerabilities—even for researchers or attackers who don't have granular expertise in a given area—it is more pressing than ever to shed light on niche security products.
“AI really blows away the obscurity model,” Burch says. “You don’t need to fully understand how something works anymore to move forward and potentially have a big impact.”

The past 10 months have brought several milestones for our family.
My wife, Barb, and I both turned 50. Our oldest daughter finished her graduate coursework and started fieldwork, and our youngest son graduated from high school this spring.
For the first time, all four of our kids, ages 18 to 23, were either in college or preparing to start. Barb and I thought we had reached the point when we could exhale and look back on years of school, activities, and raising four kids into young adults.
We assumed our noisy, crowded house would soon become much quieter. Instead, a series of decisions and circumstances have kept three of our kids home, with our oldest son planning to return after graduation.
The empty nest we expected at 50 suddenly looks much further away.
All 4 of our kids have different reasons for living at home
Our youngest son was accepted to several colleges, but he chose the closest school and decided to commute. His dream career path requires a doctorate, so living at home will help him save money early in his education.
Meanwhile, our 21-year-old daughter is close to earning an associate degree from a local community college. She may eventually pursue a bachelor's degree. Physical limitations prevent her from driving, so living at home currently works best for school and work.
Then there's our 23-year-old daughter, who's an occupational-therapy student. When the program switched to a hybrid format last year, she moved home and shared an Airbnb during the three weeks of in-person classes each semester.
Completing her required fieldwork here in Cleveland has given her access to its world-class hospitals and healthcare systems. Once she finishes, she may continue living at home while working and paying down her student loans.
Our oldest son is the only one who doesn't live at home right now. He attends school out of state and will graduate with a bachelor's degree in psychology this winter. Because he plans to pursue counseling, he'll need an advanced degree and expects to move home for graduate school, either locally or online.
If he does, all six of us will live under the same roof for the first time in several years, with our kids back in their childhood bedrooms.
Our own long-term plans are still up in the air
Over the last few years, Barb and I have talked about retirement, downsizing, and increasing our investments. We've discussed whether to stay in Cleveland or move somewhere warmer.
Those conversations started before several of our kids made plans to live at home longer.
We still haven't made firm plans because so much has depended on what our kids decide to do. When several planned to live at home longer than we expected, our own timeline adjusted.
We don't blame them for changing that timeline. We've always wanted our kids to know they can live at home until they're ready to move out, and we'd rather they make that decision when it makes sense than rush into it because of an arbitrary timeline.
We've decided to stop waiting for an empty nest to travel and try new things
When it became clear that our nest would remain pretty full for the time being, we realized we needed to separate the plans that require an empty house from those that don't.
We love to travel, and our kids are mature enough to handle the house, care for our dog, and help each other while we're away.
Because Barb teaches full time, we're starting with weekend getaways during the school year and discussing longer trips for when her schedule allows.
Moving is still on the table, most likely after our youngest earns his bachelor's degree and no longer needs to qualify for in-state tuition. I've started researching cities with warmer climates, lower costs of living, and access to a midsize or major airport.
I'm also exploring additional income streams that could give us more flexibility to retire early or relocate.
Although having adult kids at home has complicated some plans, it's also been great. We actually have more family dinners now than when we did before they left for college.
Our kids have also become more open with us. Our oldest daughter recently leaned on us for support during a difficult time, something she may not have done a few years ago. We've learned to give them more space, trust their decisions, and treat them more like adults.
At first, we assumed that our kids would need to move out before we gained more freedom. Instead, we're discovering that there's so much we can enjoy while they're still living at home.

River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
- Published
Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week.
It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining.
The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away.
"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it."
Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing.
A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation.
"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency.
"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease."
Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill.
"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly."
His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted.
Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project.
The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid.
There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out.
But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation.
"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone."
Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit.
Only his wife, son and one nephew survived.
"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says.
"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer."
Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die."
The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived.
Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive."
Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them.
He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him.
He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place.
This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives.
Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.
These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable.
The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say.
But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives.
Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites.
"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says.
"I know many people who are still trapped there."
Additional reporting by Justin Rowlatt, climate editor

- Social media posts allege U.S. President Donald Trump's mother, Mary Anne MacLeod Trump, once called him "an idiot with zero common sense" and predicted he would be a "disaster" if he ever entered politics. The rumor is unfounded.
- The alleged quote has circulated since at least 2019. On multiple occasions, Snopes has attempted to find evidence of Trump's mother making the statement without success.
- Some posts spreading the alleged quote included images that resembled newspaper clippings. We have found no evidence of any real newspapers attributing the quote to Mary MacLeod Trump.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
An alleged quote by Mary Anne MacLeod Trump, the mother of U.S. President Donald Trump, expressing doubt about her son's intelligence and ability to succeed in politics has circulated for years.
A meme with the quote that spread on Facebook in August 2026 read:
Trump's mom knew best!
"Yes, he's an idiot with zero common sense, and no social skills, but he is my son. I just hope he never gets into politics. He'd be a disaster."
Mary Anne Trump: Telling the truth before it was trending.
(Facebook user JOE BIDEN 2024)
Snopes readers wrote in to ask us whether the quote was real.
Versions of the alleged quote have circulated for years, usually with the part reading "I sincerely just hope he never gets into:" ending with the word "politics." We've hunted for evidence the quote was real since 2019 and have found no proof that Trump's mother ever said these words. Other publications, such as PolitiFact and Reuters, also fact-checked the quote and found no indication it was real.
Because digital archives of newspapers, books and magazines grow and change over time — meaning it is always possible for new evidence for historical claims to become available — we took another look at the quote after it began circulating again in 2026, during Trump's second term as president.
In short, just as in 2019, there was no compelling evidence supporting the claim that the quote is authentic, as of this writing.
Searches for the full alleged comments — as well as the distinctive clauses "he's an idiot with no common sense" and "I just hope he never goes into politics" — on Newspapers.com and Gale OneFile, both of which are large databases of periodicals, uncovered no evidence supporting the quote's authenticity. Searches on Google Books and the Internet Archive likewise returned no evidence that the quote ever appeared with secure attribution in any legitimate publication.
A Google search found no instances of the alleged remark at all before 2019, nearly two decades after Mary MacLeod Trump's August 2000 death. The absence of any evidence of a quote dating within the alleged originator's lifetime is a common red flag for fake or misattributed quotes.
One development since 2019 was the emergence of the supposed newspaper clipping featuring the in-question comment underneath a photo of Trump and his mother, which appeared (archived) to have first circulated (archived) online in June 2020. Examples of the clipping, which did not include the name of the paper in which it was allegedly published or a date, appeared (archived) in numerous (archived) posts on X (archived).
(X user @RobertCStern)
It has not been possible to find proof that the clipping is genuine. Although it included a genuine photo of Trump and his mother that was prominently featured in a 2016 New Yorker article titled "Donald Trump's Immigrant Mother," searches uncovered no instances of the picture paired with the quote in any real newspaper or magazine.
It remains possible that a primary source proving the quote's authenticity exists somewhere — for example, in a newspaper archive that has not been digitized as of this writing — and for that reason we've refrained from issuing a definitive rating.
Previously, we looked into the claim that Trump's mother was an immigrant in the country illegally.

Teen girl charged with murder over recording of San Diego mosque attack
- Published
A 17-year-old girl has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting after prosecutors say she recorded a livestream of an attack on a San Diego mosque that left three people dead.
Prosecutors say the girl also published a manifesto from two teenage gunmen who carried out the attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May.
The teenager, from North Carolina, was arrested last week and indicted by a grand jury on Monday, according to Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill.
Speaking at a news conference, O'Neill said: "The thought of her going back to school, with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of."
The teenager now faces three murder charges and one count of conspiracy. O'Neill explained that under North Carolina law, a person accused of aiding and abetting a crime can be held criminally responsible in the same way as the person who carried it out.
Authorities say the attack was carried out by two males - aged 17 and 18 - who opened fire at the mosque, before taking their own lives.
O'Neill said the pair had two aims that day: "Number one, to kill as many people as possible on that day. Secondly, they wanted this carnage and destruction recorded ... livestreamed."
A security guard at the mosque, Amin Abdullah, exchanged gunfire with the attackers and initiated a lockdown, helping protect around 140 children who were inside the building.
Abdullah and two worshippers - Mansour Kaziha and Nader Awad, who drew the attentions of the shooters in a parking lot - were fatally shot.
San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl previously described Abdullah's actions as "heroic", saying they had "undoubtedly" saved lives.
According to investigators, the shooters recorded the attack using cameras mounted on GoPro-style helmets. O'Neill said the pair had also planned further attacks "at a local Jewish temple and finally at a predominantly African American high school".
Authorities said the teenagers had an arsenal of around 30 guns and a crossbow, which investigators say were taken from one of the shooter's parents.
The attackers also left behind writings containing racist and antisemitic views, as well as references to white supremacist ideologies.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on August 17 announced a new national social media team, replacing Amit Malviya with Deepak Mhaskey as its IT cell in-charge. The party also named four new social media co-convenors — Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav.
Alt News had earlier reported that within minutes of BJP’s announcement, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible. However, screenshots and archived versions of their past tweets, often containing personal and contentious opinions, are available, raising concern over the sudden disappearance of their accounts. Yadav, for instance, deleted more than 60,000 posts before making her X handle accessible again. Mhaskey deleted at least 1,342.
Gandhi’s X account, which has over 500,000 followers, remains ‘protected’ or hidden from public view at the time of this article being published. A notice from the platform states “Only approved followers can see @MrsGandhi’s posts”.
An earlier screenshot of her profile captured by us shows her following 2,015 handles, which has now gone down to 1,875. In other words, she has recently unfollowed 140 X users.
Alt News spoke to Gandhi, and asked her why she had hidden her X posts, but she refused to comment. Her Facebook profile bio describes her as ‘IT & Social Media National In-charge for all 7 BJP Morchas’ and ‘Official Spokesperson, Maharashtra BJP’.
Recently, in November 2025, Gandhi courted controversy after targeting Indian cricketer Jemimah Rodrigues over her expression of faith during a post-match interview. In her older tweets dating back to 2012-13, she expressed disdain for her surname, saying she would rather have ‘Modi’ or ‘Godse’ as a surname. She has repeatedly praised Nathuram Godse, the assassin of Mahatma Gandhi, in her tweets.
Declaring herself as a “huge fan and follower” of Godse, she has multiple tweets announcing that she “misses him” and that there is a need for “1000 more Godse’s” and that “India misses him.” Much of that record, however, is no longer readily accessible, but screenshots of her past tweets are shown below:
Long-time BJP Supporter
Her association with BJP, however, predates her formal organisational role. Gandhi has been a pro-BJP voice since around 2012. Initially, her X (then Twitter) handle was @pritirules. Aafter her anti-Congress posts were being shared by prominent BJP leaders, she changed her handle to @MrsGandhi. “I realised this name has a lot of potential, as there would be one Gandhi questioning the other. So I changed my handle,” she explained to the Telegraph.
In 2012, Modi started following Priti Gandhi on Twitter. According to her, she put forward her opinions aggressively — which caught Modi’s attention. Gandhi was even invited to Gandhinagar to meet Modi. “He [Modi] liked that I, as an independent person, defend him on social media”, Gandhi told The Telegraph.
In January 2014, Gandhi had falsely claimed that Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, had stated that “Modi is incorruptible”. Gandhi allegedly amplified a fake endorsement of Modi by Assange, featuring a poster of Assange alongside a quote that read, “America fears Modi because they know he is incorruptible.”
