History Of Misinformation
Gandhi’s rise within the BJP’s digital ecosystem closely coincided with a long record of disseminating and amplifying misinformation. Alt News has fact-checked her claims repeatedly over the years.
For instance, in 2019, Gandhi circulated an edited video suggesting that Rahul Gandhi wanted to leave India and settle abroad. In 2020, Gandhi revived the ‘potato-gold’ remark, a claim that stemmed from a clipped video with distorted context, to mock Rahul Gandhi and mislead people.
In 2021, during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, Gandhi also shared a misleading video purportedly showing an absence of crowds in Haridwar during the Kumbh Mela. The post appeared amid intense scrutiny of the religious gathering, where millions of pilgrims had assembled, and thousands of COVID-19 cases were subsequently reported among attendees and seers.
The video, however, did not depict the principal pilgrimage area around Har Ki Pauri. It was reportedly shot at Govind Ghat, several kilometres away, and at a time when the location did not see large crowds. The video was therefore misleadingly presented as evidence that Haridwar was not crowded during the Kumbh Mela.
During the 2021 West Bengal post-poll violence, Alt News had fact-checked a doctored video shared by Gandhi showing men wielding swords while dancing to the TMC election song, ‘Khela Hobe’.
In another instance, Gandhi shared a misleading video claiming that “Modi Modi” slogans were being raised inside Pakistan’s Parliament. Alt News found that the chants were actually “Voting Voting”.
More from the Archives: Propaganda & Disinformation
A recurring feature of Gandhi’s social media activity over the years has also been the amplification of communal or polarising misinformation.
In 2020, she shared an image of Priyanka Gandhi embracing the mother of the Hathras rape victim and described the woman as “fake Naxal-bhabi”. She falsely accused both Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi of consoling the “Naxal operative who had infiltrated the family’s home and was posing as the victim’s sister-in-law”.
The same year, she also circulated a clipped video of journalist Arfa Khanum Sherwani speaking about the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), using the edited clip to distort the context and present the speech in a communal light.
A Newslaundry article cites a 2021 Centre of the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) paper, which identified Gandhi among BJP figures who amplified the ‘Love Jihad’ narrative in the aftermath of the killing of Nikita Tomar – a student who was shot outside her college in Ballabhgarh by a Muslim youth.
According to a 2020 report by Lokmat, Gandhi said in a tweet on October 27, 2020, “Those in denial of the existence of Love Jihad are only closing their eyes to reality, maybe even purposely. Unless we don’t accept the problem, finding a solution is impossible. Today it is Nikita, tomorrow it could be you!”
It is important to note that the chargesheet of the Nikita Tomar case had no sections of the IPC related to forced conversions and other associated crimes, as per a Times of India report.
In 2019, both Gandhi and Bengal BJP shared a clipped video to falsely claim a communal bias in a speech by then Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee. They shared a 12-second excerpt of her speech clipping out the part where Banerjee had recited Hindu scriptures. Alt News had fact-checked this.
In 2021, Gandhi shared a video of a man apparently blowing on food, suggesting that he was spitting on it, giving the footage an explicitly communal framing. In 2022, she claimed that participants at a Popular Front of India (PFI) protest in Pune had raised “Pakistan Zindabad” slogans. Fact-checkers found that the slogan was in actuality “Popular Front Zindabad”.
Again, in 2022, while sharing a photo of Rahul Gandhi with a girl, Gandhi falsely claimed that she was Amulya Leona, who raised ‘Pakistan Zindabad’ slogans during the anti-CAA protest in Bangalore in 2020. In reality, the girl with Rahul was Miva Jolly, an activist associated with the Kerala Students Union, the student wing of the Congress party.
During the 2024 farmers’ protest, Gandhi shared an image claiming a farmer was seen sitting on a Mercedes car worth Rs 3 crore, thereby portraying that the protesters were ‘rich’ and thus the movement was not legitimate. It was found in an investigation by Alt News that the car was actually an SUV Gurkha by Force Motors whicbh had been modified to look like a Mercedes vehicle. We spoke to the owner of the car as well.
In January 2022, Gandhi falsely claimed that Uttar Pradesh BJP MLA Vinay Shakya had been kidnapped after he had been pressured by Samajwadi Party to join them. Local police replied to her tweet clarifying that the abduction claim was entirely false. Gandhi, then, deleted her tweet.
Target of Misinformation Herself
Priti Gandhi herself became a target of misinformation when a viral thread in 2021 shared three genuine screenshots of her old posts alongside a fabricated tweet claiming that her husband had escaped the Capitol Hill riots. The thread, which gained over 10,000 likes and was amplified by several journalists and Congress members, falsely portrayed the manufactured tweet as part of a pattern in which Gandhi’s husband had narrowly escaped multiple major incidents. While three screenshots were genuine and referred to same incident (the 26/11 Mumbai attack), the Capitol Hill tweet was fake.

Since we were unable to identify the video's original source, we could not definitively confirm its authenticity. However, the clip predated the August 2026 flooding in Nepal and displayed visual inconsistencies that pointed to AI generation.
As Nepal suffered from catastrophic flooding that left more than 900 people dead and thousands of others missing in late August 2026, a video appearing to show an elephant wading into floodwaters to rescue a man and carrying him to shore circulated online.
The video spread on multiple platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Reddit and YouTube, garnering millions of views. Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether it was real.
"In Nepal Elephants were saving people," one X post caption read (archived). "What an amazing world we live in."
(X user @TonyGunk123.)
The earliest version of the video that we could find was posted to YouTube on Aug. 5, 2026 (archived).
The video contained multiple anomalies commonly found in AI-generated media. Our analysis of screenshots revealed a lack of detail, harsh or unnatural shadows, inconsistent skin color and texture, degraded quaity, object bleeding and misshapen extremities.
(Snopes Illustration.)
Although the Aug. 5 video featured a song as the audio, in other iterations of the post, people spoke in the background and yelled as the man appeared to climb onto the elephant.
The text over one such video was in Hindi (archived), reading "Watch Nature's Display/View" and "How the elephant saved a human" (translation via native speaker). However, the audio was in Thai — further evidence it was not captured during the August 2026 flooding in Nepal. One man can be heard saying "flood" while another woman says, "It's an elephant" before asking, "What is it going to do?" (translation via native speaker).
Several commenters on Reddit and Facebook claimed the video depicted a real incident in which an elephant rescued her caretaker as a stunt at an elephant park in Thailand.
"The story originates from a genuine, widely celebrated 2016 video filmed at the Elephant Nature Park in Chiang Mai, Thailand," one Facebook user wrote. "The clip captures a real moment where a young elephant named Kham Lha rushed into a fast-flowing river to 'rescue' her favorite human caretaker, Darrick, whom she believed was drowning."
Although that story was authentic and KhamLa is a real elephant at Elephant Nature Park in Thailand, the widely shared video of the 2016 incident is not the same video that spread in August 2026.
Another article claimed the video was authentic and depicted a real 2017 incident in which elephants helped rescue hundreds of people from a flooded Nepali safari park. We found no proof the video was connected the the 2017 flooding. The image attached to the article was also AI-generated, as evidenced by the man's disfigured fingers and the merging of his arm and shirt sleeve (archived).
Unlike the 2016 video of KhamLa swimming to her caretaker or the 2017 news reports regarding elephants helping to rescue people, no reputable news outlets reported on the August 2026 video or confirmed it was authentic.
In sum, the video appearing to show an elephant rescuing a man from floodwaters is not from the August 2026 Nepal floods. The clip also displayed visual inconsistencies that pointed to AI generation, such as unnatural lighting, texture movement and shapes.
For further reading, we confirmed that CCTV footage authentically showed floodwaters destroying the Gyirong Port, a Nepal-China border crossing.

Following the attacks on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) workers in Rajasthan, several social media users claimed that CJP convenor Ashutosh Ranka was accompanied by a man who had earlier been found calling for demolishing the Parliament and provoking Nepal-like violence during the July 20 protest in Delhi.
As part of its ‘School Thik Karo’ initiative, a CJP team visited a government school operating from a buffalo shed at Rampura in Kanwarpura area of Jaipur district in Rajasthan when they were allegedly attacked. They reported being beaten with sticks and pelted with stones. CJP later accused the attackers of being affiliated with the BJP.
On August 21, X user Office of Vijay Patel (@VijayGajeraO) claimed that Ranka had arrived with “goons” who wanted to attack Parliament and trigger Nepal-style mass violence in India. The post featured a collage comparing a man accompanying Ranka with another man seen in a viral video from the CJP protest. The latter had allegedly said that Parliament would be attacked and a Nepal-like situation created if Dharmendra Pradhan did not resign. (Archive)
Ashutosh Ranka came with the goons who wanted to attack the parliament and wanted to cause Nepal-style mass violence in India. pic.twitter.com/yoKV2KnetZ
— Office Of Vijay Patel (@VijayGajeraO) August 21, 2026
The handle is run by Right-wing influencer Vijay Patel who claims to be an investigative journalist. The post has garnered over 850,000 views.
Abhijit Iyer Mitra (@Iyervval), another Right-wing influencer, shared and amplified the claim. (Archive)
The most important part of this video isn’t what happened today. It’s the fact that this video captured a stated intent to commit violence on 20th July outside parliament. Also that far from being “outsiders”, the rioters were in fact core CJP members. https://t.co/r0VbwXGEfU
— Abhijit Iyer-Mitra (@Iyervval) August 21, 2026
The post amassed over 150,000 views.
Another pro-BJP handle user, Raushan Sinha (@Mrsinha), also shared a similar comparison, claiming that the man who once threatened to turn India into a Nepal-like situation during the protest is now a CJP volunteer. His post read, “From threatening Parliament to becoming a ‘volunteer’ for CJP, quite a journey for the champions of democracy.”
The post gained around 100,000 views, and thereafter it was deleted.
This is not the first time that such comparisons have been made. Immediately after the July 20 protest, it was claimed that the man who called for Nepal-like violence had been seen sitting with Abhijeet Dipke, and was a CJP core member.
Fact Check
A closer examination of the two visuals — the Rajasthan video and the Jantar Mantar footage — reveals that the comparison is flawed, as they are two different people.
The man seen with Ashutosh Ranka and the CJP team is Vijay Sherawat, who hails from Jaipur, Rajasthan.
Alt News found a video that Sherawat had shared in response to the older claim, in which he defends himself against false accusations. He clarifies that he was not the same person who remarked that a Nepal-like situation would be created in India and the Parliament would be set afire if Pradhan did not resign.
In the video uploaded on July 31, Sherawat stated, “It is the IT cell people who are engaging in this low-level politics to defame the CJP team. I am not that person.” He also strongly condemned the remarks made by the other individual during the protest and called for appropriate punishment for those comments.
अंधभक्तों से सावधान🚨#cockroachjantaparty #abhijeetdipke pic.twitter.com/rYrYDxhjKA
— Vijay Sherawat🇮🇳 (@vijaysherawat5) July 31, 2026
The individual whose video went viral during the ‘Chalo Sansad’ march has also been identified as Saurav Singh, who claims to be a physiotherapist by profession.

Below is a comparison between the a screengrab from the viral threat video and a close-up shot of Singh from a reel he shared on Instagram:
To sum up, the individual who provoked violence and threatened to set the Parliament ablaze is not the same one as the one seen with Ashutosh Ranka during the CJP team’s visit to Rajasthan or with Abhijeet Dipke in an older video. The individual seen with the CJP leaders is Vijay Sherawat. The man who issued threats at Jantar Mantar is Saurav Singh.

Goa assembly toughens prison rules, makes phone possession punishable with 3 years in jail
Panaji, The Goa assembly has passed a bill making possession of mobile phones and other prohibited electronic gadgets inside prisons a non-bailable offence, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of ₹25,000.
The sentence for the offence will commence after the prisoner completes the term already being served, as per the Goa Prisons and Correctional Services Bill, 2026, tabled in the assembly on Tuesday.
Personnel deployed in sensitive barracks and cells would also be periodically rotated to prevent the development of "inmate-staff nexuses" and complacency, according to the proposed legislation.
It also provides for reporting the release of high-risk, hardened or habitual offenders after completion of their sentences, undertrials released on bail and inmates temporarily released on parole or furlough to the district Superintendent of Police concerned for monitoring.
Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant tabled the bill in the assembly, proposing a comprehensive law to replace the existing prison legislation and introducing tougher provisions against contraband, mobile phone use and organised criminal activities from within jails.
The House later passed it by voice vote in the evening.
Goa has one central prison located at Colvale village in North Goa district.
No prisoner, visitor or prison official would be permitted to possess or use prohibited communication devices, introduce or remove prohibited articles, supply them to inmates or facilitate unauthorised communication.
Prison officials who knowingly allow such activities would also face punishment, as per the bill.
The new legislation makes possession or use of mobile phones and other prohibited electronic communication devices inside prisons a cognisable and non-bailable offence, punishable with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine of up to ₹25,000.
It also proposes a minimum two-year jail term, extendable to three years, for possessing, operating or using electronic or wireless communication devices, their components or accessories inside prison premises.
Any sentence imposed on a prisoner under these provisions would run after completion of the sentence already being served, according to the bill.
The provisions would also apply to those who assist, abet or instigate the supply of such devices, as well as persons involved in manipulating, damaging or destroying prison equipment.
The proposed law also provides for enhanced intelligence gathering and surveillance of high-risk, hardened and habitual offenders to prevent gang activities, organised crime, witness intimidation and criminal operations from inside prisons.
Prison authorities would gather intelligence, monitor inmates and analyse information in coordination with the State Police Intelligence Wing.
High-risk barracks and cells would be subjected to periodic searches for contraband and mobile phones, besides surprise checks and the use of advanced jamming solutions, as per the bill.
It also empowers the government to establish open and semi-open correctional institutions aimed at rehabilitating prisoners and facilitating their reintegration into society.
The proposed legislation covers prison management, prisoner discipline and security, contraband control, rehabilitation, skill development, vocational training, human rights and correctional services.
The officer-in-charge of every prison would be responsible for maintaining discipline, while prisoners would be required to obey lawful orders and comply with the provisions of the Act and rules framed under it.
The bill draws from the Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023, circulated by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, and seeks to consolidate prison-related laws while introducing reformatory measures and protecting prisoners' basic human rights.

Victor Miller, the screenwriter behind Friday the 13th, has died. He was 86.
Miller’s son Ian confirmed his father had died on Monday, August 30, but didn’t reveal the cause of death.
“Yesterday my father, Victor Miller, went to his final reward,” read the Instagram post in honor of the screenwriter. “He was almost always the smartest, funniest person in whatever room he was in. He inspired in me, and many others, a love of photography, music, and storytelling.”
The post continued, “He is survived by his wife, two sons, and his grandson. He had a helluva run and will be missed dearly.”
Ian said that a celebration of Miller’s life will be held in November, “on Friday the 13th, of course.”
Watch on Deadline
Miller wrote the screenplay for the 1980 film directed by Sean S. Cunningham that would go on to spawn multiple sequels. Before the horror film, Miller co-wrote the family comedy Manny’s Orphans (1978) with Steve Miner, which Cunningham also directed. In 1978, worked with Cunningham, writing the sports comedy Here Come the Tigers under the pseudonym Arch McCoy.
The screenwriter would work with Cunningham once again after Friday the 13th on the thriller A Stranger Is Watching (1982). Other film credits include Getting In (1994), Jury Duty (1995), Rock, Paper, Scissors (2017), The Once and Future Smash (2022), and the short film Sweet Revenge (2025), among others.
Miller also wrote for television, becoming an Associate Head Writer on the daytime drama One Life to Live from 1982 to 1984. In 1984, he joined All My Children in the same role and later did the same with Guiding Light, Another World, and General Hospital. He won several Daytime Emmys for his work on All My Children in 1985, 1988, and 1998.
Miller’s legacy will live on in Crystal Lake, which is the A24 series based on the Friday the 13th franchise and a prequel to the film Miller wrote. The series will premiere on Peacock on October 15.

USPS could throw out millions of mail-in ballots under ‘s*** show’ Trump changes, whistleblower warns
Postal Service illegally defied court orders with ‘secretive’ and ‘rushed’ process to implement new rules, anonymous official says
An anonymous federal official has warned members of Congress that Donald Trump’s “secretive, rushed” and “chaotic” plans for the U.S. Postal Service to implement new rules for mail-in ballots could disenfranchise millions of voters this fall.
Tuesday’s whistleblower report outlines “potentially catastrophic problems” with the administration’s brand-new system, including a “zero-percent failure policy” that could reject tens of thousands of ballots at a time if any single mistakes are made, including misread barcodes or inadvertent errors from postal workers.
Postal officials and IT specialists called it a “mess” and a “s*** show” that illegally defied court orders against putting the new ballot-tracking system in place ahead of crucial midterm elections, according to the report.
“We are crossing the Rubicon of American elections,” said Libby Liu, CEO of WhistleblowerAid.org, which is representing the anonymous official who submitted the complaints.
“This dangerously defective mail-in ballot process could disenfranchise millions of voters, ensnaring ballots in red tape under the guise of solving a non-existent problem,” she added. “People in states that rely heavily on vote-by-mail will have a more difficult time making their voices heard in our challenged democracy this November. The whistleblower’s service to our nation is warning the public that their ability to vote is in serious jeopardy.”
Federal courts have repeatedly blocked the Postal Service from implementing Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots, which called for the creation of a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot.
On August 21, the USPS published its new certification requirements, changes that could not go into effect until federal courts lifted an injunction against them. The Supreme Court allowed Trump’s executive order to stand, for now, leaving the door open for lawsuits to proceed against the new USPS rules themselves.
Three days after the Supreme Court’s decision, District Judge Indira Talwani issued a temporary restraining order that blocks the changes, but the administration is continuing to fight the case in court to overhaul mail-in voting rules just weeks before Election Day.
Dozens of election officials from across the country have repeatedly warned that a last-minute scramble to upload lists of voters into an online portal designed by USPS would amount to an unconstitutional attack on election administration that would only sow more confusion and introduce potentially catastrophic errors.
If the plans are allowed to go into effect, USPS workers would be required to scan barcodes on a sample of envelopes to ensure the voters appear on the state’s list, according to the whistleblower report. If there is even one mismatch, that whole batch of ballots — which could be in the thousands at a time — could be rejected, the whistleblower said.
“As designed, the process is entirely unforgiving,” according to the report. “It could delay ballots by the thousands in repeated verification cycles — and thus prevent states from mailing enormous numbers of ballots.”
States are constantly updating their voter rolls, the lists sent to USPS could be out of date shortly after voters re-register with new personal information or addresses, or if new voters sign up but aren’t reflected in the already-approved list designed by the administration.
USPS and the Department of Justice have repeatedly defended the program, though election officials fear the government’s list could be dangerously too slow to reflect changes from the states.
“Their system is set up to fail — and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail,” according to Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, whose office received the whistleblower report.
“Given this new information, such sloppiness and haste seems clearly part of a purposeful attempt to create chaos and prevent people from voting,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “I am demanding answers and accountability.”
Voting rights groups fear the president’s efforts to centralize control over election administration, which is left to the states under the Constitution, is an attempt to boost Republican candidates and suppress Democratic turnout during an election that is likely to determine the balance of power in Congress — and the fate of Trump’s remaining years in office.
Trump spent years baselessly insisting that voting by mail is ripe for fraud, and that manipulated ballots were “rigged” against him in elections he lost. He complained throughout 2020 elections that Republicans would “never” win without changing rules for voting by mail, which he has called “inherently corrupt” and “cheating” despite routinely casting his own ballots by mail.
The administration is pushing for mail-in ballot changes in court while the president simultaneously demands Senate passage his SAVE America Act, which would also severely restrict mail-in voting and impose nationwide voter ID rules, among other changes.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune has repeatedly expressed doubts about sacrificing the filibuster to pass Trump’s bill. Still, Trump has tried to argue for its passage in increasingly desperate terms, including not ruling out the possibility of a national emergency to put the rules in place.
“The crown jewel of American democracy, our historic record of free and fair elections, deserves so much better than this slipshod effort,” WhistleblowerAid.org senior vice president and special counsel David Kligerman, who is representing the whistleblower, said in a statement.
States are scrambling to prepare for midterm elections, with impending deadlines for voters to receive ballots that can be filled out and returned in time to count by November.
Officials in North Carolina have already started preparing ballots under a new state law requiring voters to start receiving them 60 days before an election. More states are set to start mailing out ballots in the coming days and weeks.
But the “slapdash rollout” of Trump’s new system “could prove a major threat to voting rights in upcoming midterm elections,” Kligerman said. “We hope that the courts across the country looking at this issue are able to take note of these fundamentally troubling revelations.”
Members of the House Oversight Committee are also sounding alarms.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the committee’s top Democrat, joined all Democrats on the committee in a letter to the Postmaster General, warning that the administration’s“reckless actions undermine the foundation of our nation’s democracy and violate the basic principle that all citizens have the right to have their vote counted.”
“We demand that you immediately cease implementation of this irresponsible and illegal scheme to implement the Trump Administration’s plan to control our federal elections,” they wrote.
In a statement, Garcia blasted the USPS measure as a “power grab.”
“The Trump administration’s illegal effort to interfere with our elections must be stopped immediately and we are fighting this attack on our voting system in the courts,” he said.

England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

Aaron Renn was in a good mood. And that was fair: It’s not every day that you get labeled the No. 1 “intellectual super influencer” for a major swath of the Trump-era right.
Meet the “intellectual super influencers” of the new right
A new top 20 ranking of influences on the “national populist” right is at once surprising and revealing.
“It’s always good to have some independent validation of your work,” he told me.
A former partner at the consulting firm Accenture, he’s now best known for his writing on urban policy and the role of evangelical Christians (like himself) in American culture. His concept of the “negative world” — the idea that contemporary mainstream culture is inherently hostile to anyone taking evangelical principles seriously — has become influential enough to receive feature treatment in the New York Times.
Yet for anyone familiar with American politics, the idea that someone like Aaron Renn is in any way the No. 1 “super influencer” on the right might seem implausible. He’s not a social media warrior with the White House’s ear, like Laura Loomer or Chris Rufo. He’s not a household name like Tucker Carlson. He doesn’t run a big media outfit like Ben Shapiro. So where does Renn’s achievement come from, and what does it mean?
The source is a new report from the boutique risk analysis firm Baron Public Affairs LLC. Baron makes its money, in part, by advising corporate clients on how best to navigate the DC political environment to advance their interests. Its new report is an attempt to guide them through a specific subset of the right: the national-populist corner of the right-wing policy world that’s achieved greater prominence since 2016.
Baron’s report paints a fascinating picture of today’s conservatism, shining a light on some of its most thoughtful, relevant, and interesting quarters. Yet in doing so, the report also skates over divisions inside the group under consideration — splits that matter immensely for the American right’s future.
The “super influencers,” explained
In its report, Baron compiled papers published by six right-wing think tanks and one right-leaning intellectual journal. They then used a proprietary research platform to comb through 29,181 citations to individual people in those papers, and assembled a list of the top 20 most cited names in their sample. These, in Baron’s estimation, are the “super influencers” who “most inform the policy leaders of the nationalist-populist movement,” the conservatives building intellectual scaffolding to support the GOP’s turn toward both economic and political nationalism.
Baron did not publish the full list of 20 names (and did not respond to my repeated requests for comment). But alongside Renn, the most cited name in its sample, it revealed two other “super influencers” in an accompanying podcast: Brad Wilcox and Michael Lind. Both are revealing.
Wilcox is a sociologist at the University of Virginia and a senior fellow at the Institute for Family Studies, a think tank known for taking an unusually empirical approach to social conservatism. If you’ve followed Wilcox, whose work has often been relevant to our coverage at Vox, you’ve probably seen him offering charts, graphs, and regression analyses to defend his view that marriage is one of society’s most important and valuable institutions. His most recent book is titled, simply enough, Get Married.
Lind, by contrast, arguably isn’t a conservative at all. A longtime commentator on American politics, he began his career as a kind of left labor populist — hostile to mass immigration due to the same (empirically doubtful) fears about the harmful effects on native-born workers that once shaped Bernie Sanders’ views on the issue.
Long critical of the cultural elitism of American liberals, Lind has drifted more and more toward writing for conservative outlets: becoming in effect, if not in self-identification, a real influence on the populist right. (He is not the only liberal on the list, which per Baron includes “two Biden-era White House officials and a writer who leads one of the more prominent tribes of the Left.”)
These three men — Renn, Wilcox, and Lind — reflect what Baron sees as the defining preoccupations of the “super influencers” more broadly.
Unlike previous generations of conservatives, the right’s new intellectuals aren’t especially interested in maximizing economic growth or projecting American power abroad (in fact, none of Baron’s top 20 were foreign policy experts at all). Instead, they’re overwhelmingly focused on different questions: how to reverse declining fertility rates, or the effect of trade competition with China on American cities and families.
Unlike previous generations of conservatives, the right’s new intellectuals aren’t especially interested in maximizing economic growth or projecting American power abroad.
In our conversation, Renn suggested a uniting concept for the issues these writers cared about: “the social health of the nation.” By this, he meant things that couldn’t be fully captured by traditional economic metrics: whether Americans feel happy, whether they feel like they live meaningful lives, whether they feel like their families and communities are secure and stable.
“There are these trends that don’t seem super healthy even if the GDP line continues to go up,” Renn says. “Those have been issues that weren’t part of Donald Trump’s initial set of issues, but are ones that have become widely talked about — even on the left.”
Though the preoccupations of the right’s new social thinkers may have arisen alongside Trump to challenge Reagan-era free-market conservatives, they themselves are not necessarily Trumpy. Befitting the fact that many have backgrounds in quantitative social science, and that some see themselves as liberals, they tend to be looking for answers beyond MAGA demagoguery. That’s true even though their research topics have some obvious appeal within MAGA spaces.
Super influencers against themselves
Baron’s report paints an appealing portrait of the modern right. Renn’s oeuvre is indeed fascinating, and Wilcox’s empiricism fosters a more serious conversation around social policy than the traditional culture war hysterics. More broadly, I think Baron is right that the sorts of issues that preoccupy these thinkers will indeed remain important for the right for quite some time.
But I think there’s a danger in treating this group as homogenous, or as representative of the right as a whole.
To see why, it’s helpful to go back to the report’s basic methodology — tracking citations in right-wing publications. Those publications were drawn from the following seven sources:
- American Affairs
- American Compass
- The Foundation for American Innovation (FAI)
- The Claremont Institute
- The America First Policy Institute (AFPI)
- The Center for Renewing America (CRA)
- The Heritage Foundation
These are extremely different outfits. Three of them — American Affairs, American Compass, and FAI — indeed overlap with the kinds of questions that Baron’s “super influencers” are interested in. The other four, by contrast, are MAGA more than anything else: Their mission, at least as currently constituted, is to mount an intellectual defense of the president’s worldview and/or develop policy ideas that might flesh out Trump’s inchoate impulses.
This isn’t necessarily relevant for Baron’s mission in advising clients on which influential voices deserve their attention. But for those of us interested in mapping the intellectual right, these distinctions are vital.
Indeed, by Baron’s own estimation, there is a significant difference between the kinds of people cited in reports by these two sub-groupings in its sample. The first grouping, Baron found, will regularly cite “heterodox liberals” like Lind who share some of their priorities; the second did not cite a single such liberal in any of the reports it surveyed.
Thus, there actually isn’t one unified cadre of intellectual “super influencers” shaping the national-populist right. There are two distinctive groupings: one which influences the sorts of New Right outfits committed to their own ideological project, the other which influences reports released by MAGA appendages. While there is some overlap between those two groups, Baron’s own analysis suggests they are meaningfully distinct blocs.
This matters for the right’s future. In fact, it matters a lot.
Publications from the first three of Baron’s sources tend to be less hard-edged about partisan conflict; they engage with liberals quite a bit because they prioritize their long-term policy goals and are looking for coalition members who can help advance them. In their work, you can see some of the virtues the Baron report documents amongst the cited “super influencers” — empiricism, “genteel temperament,” a focus on distinctively 21st century social problems.
Work by the other four, by contrast, tends to paint American political divisions in apocalyptic terms. Claremont writers, for example, have famously described the 2016 election as “Flight 93” and declared that “most people living in the United States today — certainly more than half — are not Americans in any meaningful sense of the term.” They do not cite liberals approvingly because they see them as worse than political rivals: as villains, the authors of America’s ills, whose power must be crushed for the country to survive.
“We are in the process of the second American Revolution, which will remain bloodless if the left allows it to be,” as Heritage president Kevin Roberts put it in an interview on Steve Bannon’s podcast.
One of the principal questions of the right’s looming post-Trump era will be whether it can move past this kind of zero-sum partisanship. The Baron report might lead one to be optimistic on that front: if Aaron Renn truly is the leading influence among the American right’s national-populist intellectuals, that portends a future where America’s warring political tribes can finally start to find common ground.
But I wouldn’t bet on it, at least not for some time now.
There are deep reasons why Trump, a human embodiment of rage and division, leads the Republican Party — and why some of the right’s top thought leaders are so loyal to him. So long as those reasons persist, the influence of more thoughtful “super influencers” on practical politics may be more limited than one might hope.

- The claim that the Trump administration uses a legal loophole to sell protected wild horses to slaughterhouses is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from reporting by The New York Times in August 2026 and was backed by research by animal rights groups that suggested buyers of wild horses sold through the Bureau of Land Management's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter.
- According to its website, it is BLM policy "not to sell or send any wild horses or burros to slaughter," and buyers from the sale program sign a bill of sale saying they will not slaughter or sell for slaughter the animals they buy.
- The Times' reporting brought to light a long-standing issue within the BLM about what to do with excess wild horses and burros. The bureau is bound by law to regulate populations but has historically avoided euthanizing healthy animals due to concerns about public perception.
- Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses.
- Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers did purchase horses from the BLM and sell them for slaughter, the article did not include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- We contacted the Times journalist who wrote the article to ask for additional evidence and await a reply.
For example, one Instagram user wrote:
America's wild horses are supposed to be protected—not sold into a system that is funneling them to slaughter. Records show the Trump Administration's Bureau of Land Management's wild horse sales more than doubled in 2025, with some horses sold for as little as $25. A New York Times investigation shows that some buyers are taking advantage of a legal loophole, using middlemen to unconscionably sell these beautiful sentient beings to slaughter.
Similarly worded posts circulated on X (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim and searched our site for more information. One popular search term was, "Is Trump killing horses?"
The story originated from reporting in the New York Times about the Bureau of Land Management's sale of wild horses, titled "Under Trump, Protected Wild Horses Are Going to Slaughter."
The Times article reported how the U.S. government, faced with the ballooning costs of taking care of more than 50,000 wild horses it has rounded up to control herd sizes, sold thousands every year to buyers who purchased the animals for as little as $25 to sell at auction to other buyers that shipped them to slaughterhouses. This was allowed to happen, the Times reported, because selling a wild horse removes its statutory protection from "capture, branding, harassment, or death."
Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers of wild horses sold through the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter, the article didn't include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers.
Snopes contacted Skydog Ranch and Sanctuary, an animal rescue organization. That nonprofit underwent an investigation into the BLM's sales program that formed the basis of the Times article.
Skydog publicly shared copies of complaints it submitted to the BLM about buyers for the agency allegedly buying wild horses and then taking them to "kill pens," as described in the Times article. The animal rescue organization accused the BLM of failing to stop the buyers despite the complaints.
We also contacted Dave Phillips, who wrote the Times article, to ask what primary evidence he used for his reporting. We await a reply to our queries.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A BLM spokesperson said in an emailed statement on Aug. 24, 2026:
The Bureau of Land Management does not sell or send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and allegations that individuals are violating federal law or the terms governing the sale of these animals are taken seriously.
Times tracked horses sold to Ohio buyer to slaughter auctions
The Times article suggested the BLM had found a way to offload its large off-range holding population of wild horses and burros that was effectively sending the animals to slaughter without incriminating the bureau.
The Wild Horse and Burro Program allows the BLM to sell animals that are more than 10 years old or that it has unsuccessfully listed for adoption at least three times. However, the Times reported, "Livestock inspection records show mustangs sold by the government soon ended up on trucks bound for slaughter plants in Canada."
The article focused on one reported buyer from Ohio, who the Times said had bought 500 horses from the BLM in a matter of years. Some of those horses, the article said, later showed up for sale at "an auction in Tennessee frequented by slaughter buyers."
The article also alleged that a week after the Ohio buyer received a shipment of 97 formerly wild mares, an Ohio exporter of animals for slaughter shipped two trucks of horses across the Canadian border. The Times said that, according to one image its reporter had viewed, at least one of those horses had a BLM freeze mark.
The Ohio buyer reportedly spoke to the Times reporter for two hours but "refused to say specifically what had happened to the horses he purchased from the government, other than to insist that none had gone to slaughter." He declined having worked with the Ohio exporter that shipped the two trucks across the Canadian border. The exporter would not comment to the Times on whether he had purchased horses from the buyer.
Without primary evidence — meaning sales documents tracking individual animals from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the auction in Tennessee or from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the Ohio exporter to a slaughterhouse — it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify the claims in the Times article.
Holding costs tie up BLM program budget
The Times article highlighted an issue that the BLM has grappled with for years: how to legally, effectively and tastefully control wild horse populations. According to the bureau's data, wild horse and burro populations exceed the BLM's Appropriate Management Level, meaning the number of animals that can thrive in balance with other public land resources and uses, in nearly all the states where the bureau tracks populations.
The BLM is required by The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 — the same act that protects wild horses and burros from "capture, branding, harassment, or death" — to uphold the AML for the populations it tracks (Sec. 1333b1). Under the Act, the BLM is allowed to euthanize excess animals "in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible" (Sec. 1333b2C). However, a 2008 report by the Government Accountability Office on the BLM's management of "unadoptable" horses found that the bureau hesitated to do this because it was thought to be "unacceptable to the public" (Page 56).
The BLM estimates that wild horse and burro populations, if left unregulated, would double every four years. Therefore, the bureau rounds up and removes thousands of animals from the wild to control populations. Those animals end up in the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program's off-range corrals and pastures. By May 2026, the program reported that it held 58,025 formerly wild horses and burros and that its total capacity for off-range holding was 78,751 animals. According to the program's figures it spent $101 million — 66% of its budget — on off-range holding costs in fiscal year 2024.
A long-standing problem
According to the 2008 GAO report, the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program faced the same challenges then that the Times article highlighted 18 years later. The report said the cost of caring for off-range animals was already overwhelming the program in 2008, and that the program had "limited" options for "dealing with" animals it could not adopt out because it feared the public would not support humanely euthanizing healthy animals (Page 9).
The program had reportedly sold animals since 2005, though at that point also faced issues with animals ending up at slaughterhouses after the sale (Page 43). As a result, the bureau implemented a mandatory "statement of intent" at purchase, which required the buyer to say that they did not intend to sell the animals they bought for slaughter. BLM bills of sale for wild horses and burros still included such a clause in 2026.
The effectiveness of the clause was unclear because the BLM also said on its website about its sales program that it did not track animals after it sold them. The 2008 report noted that the introduction of a "statement of intent" was part of the reason the BLM sold fewer horses than before.
The existence of the "statement of intent" did not deter one buyer, who admitted in a 2015 investigation carried out by the Office of the Inspector General that "most of" the 1,700 wild horses he bought through the BLM between 2008 and 2012 had gone to slaughter.
The GAO and OIG reports suggest that the issue of wild horses and burros ending up at slaughterhouses after BLM sales is documented and predates the Trump administration.
Aside from adoption, sale or euthanasia, the BLM has been pursuing fertility treatment as a way to control populations since 1992 (Page 69). However, the BLM itself and peer-reviewed research have found it comes with its own challenges around finding and accessing animals and keeping up with treatment. According to the BLM, it delivered 921 fertility treatments to wild horses and burros in fiscal year 2025. That same year, it removed 7,853 horses and burros from the wild.
The Times report said that although government experts did recommend wider use of fertility treatment to control populations the recommendation was hard for the BLM to act on because its funds were largely tied up in the removal, holding and care of excess animals.
In sum, while it was not possible to verify the exact elements of the Times' reporting, the article brought to light a complicated issue for the BLM that predated both Trump administrations but nonetheless had lethal consequences for the horses and burros the U.S. government is bound to protect.

Top strategist warns Trump and MAGA face ‘historic losses’ in the midterms
With just two months until the midterm elections, Republicans are down in crucial battleground Senate races, according to new aggregate polling data
Republicans are looking at “historic losses” in the upcoming midterm elections, with new polling showing the GOP lagging in eight battleground Senate races, a top strategist has warned.
Historically, the party of the president has almost always lost House seats in the midterm elections, but the Senate polling has GOP operatives especially worried. Republicans currently hold slim majorities in both the House and the Senate.
With just two months until the elections, Republicans are down 8 points in North Carolina, 7.5 points in Georgia, 2.6 points in Ohio, 2.3 points in Maine, 1.9 points in Texas, and 2 points in Alaska and New Hampshire, according to the latest RealClearPolitics polling aggregate data for the upcoming Senate races.
“It points out the obvious that Republicans are in pretty bad shape going into the midterms and that they’re looking at historic losses,” GOP strategist Terry Holt told The New York Post.
“The question is whether some of these races can be saved with some miraculous turnout that apparently is going to be very expensive or whether or not the mood in this country can be changed fundamentally,” Holt added.
The bleak polling comes as President Donald Trump has resumed strikes against Iran, and the cost of living remains the most pressing issue for voters.
“National Republicans have been sounding the alarm that midterms are hard since last year, and we’ve been firm that not a single race should be taken for granted,” another Republican strategist involved in Senate races told the Post.
Not everyone is convinced by the polling. Veteran GOP pollster Jim McLaughlin told the outlet that “Republicans are in much better shape than what a lot of these media polls are showing,” referring to private polling.
“Look, we still got a long way to go between now and Election Day,” he added.
While the president isn’t on the ballot, Republican candidates and political operatives in battleground states are hopeful that Trump will throw his political weight behind them, as he has done in South Carolina for Darline Graham Nordone, the sister of the late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.
Trump’s affiliated MAGA Inc. super PAC dropped more than $800,000 in ad spending and organizing costs to secure Graham the GOP Senate nomination.
A strategist involved in several key battleground races told Politico that it was time to “put up or shut up” for the president and his allies.
“You’ve got September and October to really move the needle here, and it just doesn’t seem like there’s any sense of urgency, or like we understand that we are down big in some of these states,” they said.
Fox News personality Laura Ingraham last week urged Republicans to “get their act together” ahead of the midterms, while conservative activist Ned Ryun, the CEO of America Majority, warned that the GOP risks losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened
- Published
"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give."
Lionel Messi retired from international football on Monday as Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player. He captained them to World Cup glory at Qatar 2022 and to Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.
But the world was almost denied his most successful period in the famous blue and white shirt.
On Sunday, 26 June 2016, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Messi broke the hearts of a nation.
Just two days after his 29th birthday and soon after missing a penalty in Argentina's Copa America final loss to Chile in a shootout, Messi decided he had seen enough.
After 113 appearances, he was adamant. In his mind, he would never pull on an Argentina shirt again.
"For me, the national team is over. I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion," he said.
The pain was understandable. Argentina had lost in the 2014 World Cup final, plus Copa America finals in 2007, 2015 and now 2016. The player many classed as the world's greatest had failed when it mattered most for him.
"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over," Messi said, fighting back tears after another trophy chance slipped away. "I think this is best for everyone."
Fortunately for Argentina, Messi would have second thoughts.
Over the subsequent 10 years, he completed one of football's greatest ever stories. But it was a decade of dominance that almost never happened.
Since that retirement U-turn, Messi has played a further 94 times and scored another 70 goals for Argentina. He has lifted four major trophies.
The six-week period between his June 2016 retirement declaration and the 12 August announcement he would play on for the "love of the country" could be considered the most significant in Argentine football history - even in world football.
- Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give' 
  - Published3 hours ago

  - Published1 hour ago
'He lacks the character to be a leader'
As Messi departs the international stage, words of criticism 10 years ago from the country's other legendary number 10 seem almost laughable.
"He's a really good person, but he has no personality," Diego Maradona said just weeks before Messi's first retirement. "He lacks the character to be a leader."
Back then it was the comparison with Maradona that was held against him. Yet Messi had already won eight La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues with Barcelona and was a five-time Ballon d'Or winner, and not yet 30.
Maradona's club career hadn't come close, but Messi's only major international honour had been Olympic gold at the 2008 Games. Maradona had almost single-handedly won the 1986 World Cup for Argentina.
It's hard to imagine it now, with Messi shirts dominating the last two World Cups, the Argentina team being built completely around him and the nation's fans worshipping him to an almost religious extent – but, back then, there was a lot of criticism.
"He's not as good as Diego", "he goes missing on the big occasion", "he is part of the country's failure". All accusations that were thrown in his direction.
This wasn't the first time Messi had considered walking away either.
Spanish football expert – and Messi biographer – Guillem Balague said: "Leo goes really down when he loses. He felt the pressure of being the captain of Argentina and the Maradona thing.
"Pecho Frio, people in Argentina called him, which means cold chest. It was an insult to say he had milk in his veins. So when he failed in 2016 at the Copa America, that was the third time – the first time in public – he had decided to leave the national side.
"The two previous ones was a matter of letting him lick his wounds, but this one he came out and said I've had enough. He sometimes cannot help himself as he says what he thinks."
The Maradona versus Messi debate is now surely over. Messi is Argentina's greatest, by most judgements. There are many who will say he is challenging Pele for the title of football's greatest ever.
A campaign, a statue and many apologies
Even people who criticised Messi eventually said sorry.
From the moment Messi quit his country, shockwaves reverberated around Argentina.
Yes, he had lost in four successive finals. But he was also the country's record goalscorer and the world's best player.
The 'Get Messi back' campaign started immediately as team-mates called for him to change his mind just minutes after his announcement.
"I can't imagine a national team without Messi," said goalkeeper Sergio Romero.
The social hashtag #NoTeVayasMessi (Don't go Messi) was used more than 20,000 times within 24 hours.
By that time, Argentina's President Mauricio Macri had already spoken with Messi over the phone to try to convince the Barcelona star to reconsider.
"I told him not to pay any attention to the comments being made because, in truth, we are very happy" with the job he has done," Macri told journalists at the time.
Less than a day later, the mayor of Buenos Aires, Horacio Rodriguez Larreta, had unveiled a statue in Messi's honour and called on the public to show him their love.
"As a football fan, Leo, I am asking you to please reconsider your decision," the mayor said.
Thousands of fans gathered in central Buenos Aires, while street signs throughout the capital displayed implored Messi to play on for Argentina.
Maradona stated Messi had to stay to take the team to the 2018 World Cup.
'It reminded us how much we loved him'

What’s Behind the Sudden Anger at Flock
The sudden, intense pushback against these cameras seems to reflect more than just wariness about the surveillance system.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
As corporate names go, Flock is cleverly flexible. It evokes the many cameras that compose the company’s surveillance system and also a group of sheep, protected by a watchful shepherd. The recent backlash against the company, however, more closely resembles a flight of starlings, seeming to erupt out of nowhere and move as one unified body.
Flock Safety’s cameras are a network of automated license-plate readers (ALPRs), which snap images of passing cars and feed them into an AI-powered-data system. The company has contracts with police departments and government agencies as well as with some private companies. The crime-fighting power of such a tool isn’t hard to grasp: It allows law enforcement to track vehicles’ movements over any area where the readers exist. The privacy concerns about such a dragnet are just as easy to fathom.
The company has existed for nearly a decade and has been growing steadily in recent years. But something has turned in the past couple of months. People are pushing cities to cancel contracts and in some cases have taken matters into their own hands. Individuals have clandestinely sawed down the poles that hold cameras or splashed paint over them. In one notable example, a Florida man obstructed the devices simply by holding up cardboard placards, a low-tech solution to a high-tech challenge. The pushback against Flock, like the pushback against data centers, does not have a clear partisan bent. Critics include some of the most obnoxious voices on both the right and the left (Tucker Carlson, Hasan Piker), and defenders include technocratic wonks of different political persuasions.
Politicians are catching up. Yesterday, the Florida Department of Transportation announced that it was revoking permits for ALPRs on all state roads. (This means that cameras on locally maintained thoroughfares are still allowed.) On Thursday, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, halted state funding for Flock. An anti-surveillance advocacy group has tallied 169 canceled contracts with Flock so far this year—90 of them last month alone.
Labeling the anger at Flock as a reaction to ever-present surveillance in contemporary society seems accurate, but this doesn’t explain why it’s happening right now. Not only has Flock been around for some time, but ALPRs are even older. My colleague Conor Friedersdorf was sounding the alarm a decade ago. “Your diminished privacy is their product. And the police are their customers,” he wrote in January 2016.
Some anger focuses on governments that spend huge amounts (including money obtained through opioid settlements whose funds were earmarked for community aid) on technology during a moment of economic worry. More damaging to Flock’s reputation has been a series of cases of police officers allegedly abusing their access to the system to stalk people, typically current or former love interests. (Flock says that such uses are “unacceptable” and has created some guardrails around data access.) Writing in The Atlantic last month, Charles Fain Lehman argued that Flock can be a valuable tool and merely needs better regulation to address bad behavior and maximize privacy: “In our surveillance-saturated society, police cameras can help make the criminal-justice system both fairer and less punitive—if we let them.”
That seems to beg the question. Flock is useful because it is ubiquitous. Reforms such as strict data-retention limits would only marginally answer privacy concerns, and anything more drastic would undermine the system’s efficacy. As National Review’s Charles C. W. Cooke noted, no one doubts that Flock works. “Lots of things would reduce crime if implemented,” he wrote. “That doesn’t mean that those things are necessarily a good idea in a free republic.” Impositions on privacy to reduce crime are a particularly tough sell when crime is dropping sharply: Recently released FBI statistics show that violent crime dropped nearly 10 percent last year, part of a consistent trend since it spiked in 2020 and 2021. Preliminary statistics suggest that 2026 might be even safer. When safety is a less urgent concern, people are less willing to sacrifice privacy for security.
Moreover, the Flock backlash fits into a broader moment of anger—at corporations in general, and at tech companies and artificial intelligence in particular. “Americans feel they have less and less control over their own lives, and they increasingly blame large corporations,” the Financial Times columnist Rana Foroohar recently wrote. Anxiety about AI and surveillance is big and abstract, and the companies and people pushing these anxieties are far away from most Americans. Polls show widespread apprehension about the growth of AI—a Gallup poll this summer found that about half of Americans think AI will do as much harm as it will good; another 39 percent said that it’s mostly bad. But people don’t have a lot of ways to communicate those fears.
Flock cameras, like data centers, provide a physical, local manifestation of this larger complex, against which people can direct their disgust. In other words, Flock protests are reactions to privacy concerns and particular alleged police abuses, but they’re also a way for the public to channel frustrations that it has few avenues to express. You could say that it’s a way of killing two birds with one stone.

If you have ever interacted with the federal government, it’s probably involved a lot of paperwork. According to the federal government’s own estimate, in 2023, 10,503 million hours were spent filling out paperwork across federal agencies. The amount of time that people spend trying to navigate government bureaucracy to get benefits, services, or funding has been coined the “time tax” by journalist Annie Lowrey. This wasted time takes away from time that could otherwise be spent productively on work or leisure and worse, can discourage people from accessing benefits they are entitled to. The government estimates that, each year, about $140 billion in benefits goes unclaimed because of this time tax.
This was the situation before the Trump administration, and it’s likely become much worse. Despite a stated focus on “finding efficiencies,” the administration has significantly increased the bureaucracy Americans — from scientists seeking grants to Medicaid beneficiaries — have to navigate, especially at the Department of Health and Human Services. All of this will have a dramatic effect on America’s health care system and its biomedical research industry.
We’ll start with the scientists. Perhaps no federal agency has been slowed down by administrative burden this past year like the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Before 2025, scientists spent about 40% of their time on administrative-related tasks. That percentage has surely increased. To make sure that grants are in line with new presidential priorities, the agency has been using a computer tool to scan grants for prohibited terms. Grantees are asked to make revisions — sometimes in the middle of the grant lifespan. These changes can be merely language related, but other times they require significant changes to the aims and protocols.
This puts a huge burden on research teams and administrative staff at universities, who not only have to deal with regular grant compliance but now have to contend with surprise requests and additional “DEI”-related screening. All of this also results in delays in grants being awarded — as of the end of June, NIH has spent 25% less on grants compared to 2021-2024. All told, the chances of being awarded a new NIH grant has dropped to 13%.
Now, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has proposed making this process permanent and potentially worse by having a political appointee review all grants before they are awarded, superseding the peer review process. This rule (which would impact all grantees across the federal government, not just academic institutions) was proposed to go into effect Oct. 1, though a Senate bill has prohibited OMB from doing that until at least Dec. 11.
Scientists now are spending an increasing amount of time worrying about keeping the lights on and people employed, which ultimately distracts from time spent doing research. These changes to NIH will certainly discourage young scientists from pursuing a career in research, and push people to look abroad for opportunities.
As a matter of survival, universities will continue to navigate administrative hurdles.
But what about the average person who doesn’t have an army of staff? This is what Medicaid recipients will be facing come Jan. 1.
Thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA), a number of changes coming to Medicaid are poised to kick millions off of their health care. These changes include: increasing renewals to twice a year (rather than annually), introducing “community engagement” requirements (defined as working, volunteering, or going to school at least 80 hours per month) for most people (apart from the elderly, children, people who are “medically frail,” and pregnant women), and kicking off certain groups of immigrants from Medicaid altogether. The vast majority of current recipients (92%) should continue to qualify for Medicaid under these new rules, but many are expected to fall off due to the complex bureaucracy that has to be navigated.
A renewal process happening twice a year instead of yearly automatically increases the administrative load for the state, the individual, and medical providers. Case managers for people who are unhoused will now have to double their workload to ensure their clients stay enrolled in Medicaid.
Then there are the community engagement (i.e., “work”) requirements, which themselves have to be documented. States can use what existing data they have to automate these processes and reduce the burden on the individual. But that requires incredible amounts of investment and government staff time. That’s why implementing work requirements is likely to cost states millions of dollars. When Georgia implemented work requirements in 2023, the state spent $40 million on implementing work requirements, and 80% of that cost was administrative. In 2019, the Government Accountability Office modeled the cost of work requirements for a number of states and found that Kentucky would have to spend an additional $271 million on administrative costs implementing the new policies.
Adding to this burden is the process of getting an exemption from the work requirements, specifically for having a condition that makes you “medically frail” and therefore unable to work. The process now laid out by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services demands that states verify how severe a diagnosis is — this requires an extra visit and paperwork from the doctor. Conditions such as depression, asthma, and chronic pain may not qualify someone from Medicaid automatically, but experts point out that these conditions can be debilitating on some days, even if people can function on others. This process is so burdensome that it is currently subject to litigation from a number of states.
For those not on Medicaid, this process may seem like a slight headache. But in practice, it is a nightmare scenario for millions of Americans. Let’s say you are undergoing cancer treatment, but you don’t have the right paperwork for your renewal. As a result, you’re disenrolled from Medicaid. You desperately try to fix the mistake, but you are faced with long wait times and no answers, so you cease treatment altogether. Across the country, others might be meeting the work requirements but miss the notice to renew in the mail and as a result, experience an interruption in coverage. Paperwork here is not merely an annoyance, it is a matter of life or death for millions with Medicaid coverage.
Then there’s the matter of literacy. Forms can be hard to follow and confusing, and with a third of the country reading at a sixth-grade level, there’s a real risk that people may not be able to understand the forms they are filling out. A 2012 analysis found that most states’ Medicaid renewal applications fail readability tests, and there’s not much indication things have improved. Studies have also investigated a similar concept of “health insurance literacy” and found that clients generally have low literacy especially as changes to forms and text occur.
The OBBA also put into place dramatic changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that similarly increased the burden of paperwork to verify that someone qualifies for the program. In Arizona, this has resulted in more than 440,000 people being dropped from the program even though most still qualify for assistance. People are stuck in procedural limbo waiting for months.
The point of these bureaucratic hurdles is to keep people from accessing federal benefits, whether it’s Medicaid or scientific funding. All of these have impacts beyond the people who directly benefit; every $1 cut to SNAP costs families $14-$20, Medicaid cuts will reduce the GDP by $154 billion in 2029, and cuts to research could cost the country billions if not trillions.
Perhaps more than in any other time in recent history, Americans are severely burdened by paperwork. Time and money are being lost to needless bureaucracy, and people are going hungry and losing health care as a result. Labs are being shuttered and scientific innovation is being interrupted. In its myopic focus to pay for tax cuts, the federal government is ignoring these great costs. But beyond that, government should serve to make your life easier, not harder.
Abdullah Shihipar directs narrative projects and policy impact initiatives at the People, Place, and Health Collective at the Brown University School of Public Health. Brandon Marshall is a professor of epidemiology at the Brown University School of Public Health, and director of the People, Place, and Health Collective at Brown.

Why are there so few African players in the WSL?
- Published
Plenty of talent was on show during the Women's Africa Cup of Nations this month - but why do so few players from the continent play for clubs in England?
The Women's Super League is widely regarded as one of the best leagues in the world and Europe's top talent is flooding in.
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas joined London City Lionesses this summer - the latest figure from Spain's World Cup-winning squad to move to the WSL.
It follows past high-profile moves from foreign players, including Australia captain Sam Kerr who made 158 appearances for Chelsea before joining Gotham.
Some of the United States' biggest stars are in the WSL too, including Chelsea duo Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma, Arsenal's Emily Fox and Manchester City's Sam Coffey.
There has also been an influx of Asian talent in recent seasons, with Japan captain Yui Hasegawa becoming one of the WSL's best players at Manchester City.
BBC Sport explores why the WSL has just four African players - Chiamaka Nnadozie (Brighton and Nigeria), Aisha Masaka (Brighton and Tanzania), Rofiat Imuran (London City Lionesses and Nigeria) and Ines Belloumou (West Ham and Algeria).

Where are Africa's biggest stars?
The small representation in the WSL is not because of a lack of talent in Africa.
National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) clubs in America have shown huge interest, spending big money on some of the continent's best players.
Zambia forward Racheal Kundananji became the most expensive women's footballer at the time in 2024 when she joined Bay FC from Madrid CFF for £685,000.
Her compatriot Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride, was voted the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year in the same year.
Cameroon's Wafcon player of the tournament Monique Ngock is at Washington Spirit, where six African international players currently reside.
Temwa Chawinga won the NWSL Golden Boot and Most Valuable Player awards in her first two seasons with Kansas City Current.
Her sister, Malawi captain Tabitha Chawinga, plays for European giants Lyon and helped her country reach the final of Wafcon last week, where they lost to Cameroon.
Michaely Bihina, who was a standout performer in the tournament for Cameroon, plays for Benfica.
Nnadozie, who notably became the first African goalkeeper to be shortlisted for the Women's Ballon d'Or award, joined Brighton last year. The Seagulls goalkeeper ended her season with an FA Cup final appearance at Wembley against WSL champions Manchester City.
What are some of the barriers?
A major barrier for WSL clubs hoping to sign African talent is the Governing Body Endorsement (GBE) criteria set out in the league's registration rules.
Foreign players must earn a minimum number of points in five categories to be eligible for a GBE visa.
The number of caps they have for their national team, appearances in the Women's Champions League and the ranking of their former clubs play a part.
WSL sides also have to compete with the wages and transfer fees being offered by NWSL clubs, who are targeting the best African footballers.
They have to use resources for scouting which, at the moment, is prioritised across Europe.
Another major issue is the lack of coverage given to the domestic game in Africa, as well as issues around Wafcon.
There was confusion in this edition when the Confederation of African Football (CAF) named Channel 4 as the UK broadcast partner, but no matches were shown live in the opening round as an agreement had not been formally reached.
The tournament had also been postponed just 12 days before it was set to kick off in Morocco, eventually taking place three months later.
