It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Ethiopia submits official bid to host Afcon 2028
- Published
Ethiopia has submitted an official bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
The country's football federation (EFF) says its government-backed proposal affirms "the nation's full readiness to host Africa's biggest footballing event".
Ethiopia has staged Afcon three times, in 1962, 1968 and 1976, but its footballing infrastructure lags well behind others on the continent.
The nation had just one stadium approved for use by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) last season but is in the process of inaugurating a new international stadium and sports complex in Addis Ababa.
That venue in the capital could provide one location for the tournament, but whether Ethiopia has enough compliant venues to host a 24-team Afcon across multiple locations remains a major question.
A number of existing regional facilities are understood not to meet Fifa or Caf standards in terms of infrastructure, facilities and overall match-day requirements.
Ethiopia played its home qualifiers for the 2026 Fifa World Cup at neutral venues in Morocco and Rwanda but did host matches in Dire Dawa earlier this year.
Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe said his organisation had received "exciting bids" for the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Afcons - with the tournament set to move to a four-year cycle after 2028.
Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe announced a joint Southern African bid for the 2028 finals earlier this year.
Despite reports that Morocco - hosts of the 2025 edition - could stage the tournament again in two years' time, BBC Sport Africa understands the kingdom is not in the running and instead is focusing on preparations to co-host the 2030 Fifa World Cup.
Meanwhile, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger - three countries led by military governments - have expressed interest in co-hosting in 2032.
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year, with the competition returning to East Africa for the first time since it was held in Ethiopia in 1976.
Ethiopia won the Afcon title on home soil in 1962 but the Walia Ibex, ranked 143rd in the world and 43rd in Africa, have only qualified for the tournament three times since they last hosted.
Their most recent appearance came at the 2021 edition, when they finished bottom without a win in a group containing Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Cape Verde.
Ethiopia beat Sao Tome and Principe in the preliminary round of qualifiers for next year's Afcon and have been drawn alongside Senegal, Mozambique and Sudan in Group J.
- Is holding Afcon every four years 'totally wrong' or 'good call'? 
  - Published22 January
Infrastructure and security concerns
Analysis by Kaleb Moges, BBC Africa
The EFF's announcement that it wants to host Afcon has generated mixed reactions, with critics questioning whether the country is truly prepared to host a tournament of this scale.
Ethiopia was one of just three nations to play at the first Afcon in 1957, but the 52,000-seat Bahir Dar Stadium in the north of the country is currently the only facility it posseses which is approved by Caf.
Meanwhile, the 62,000-capacity Adey Abeba International Stadium in Addis Ababa is expected to be completed next year.
Three other proposed stadiums are at much earlier stages of development and would need significant work to meet Caf's requirements in time for 2028.
However, hosting Afcon would require more than upgrading or constructing stadiums. The country would also need adequate training facilities, gyms, accommodation and entertainment venues, as well as reliable urban transport and security infrastructure.
Security is a major concern for Ethiopia's bid. Although the capital city is comparatively safe, several parts of the country continue to experience armed conflict, political unrest and other security challenges.
Addressing these concerns, alongside the infrastructure requirements, would be critical if Ethiopia is to successfully host Afcon 2028.

It's taken me a long time to process Olympic experience - Raygun
- Published
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.
Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.
Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.
"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.
She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.
"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.
Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.
Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.
"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.
What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.
There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".
"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.
Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.
"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.
"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."
That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.
"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.
In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.
"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.
"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."
A new Olympic sport and a creative gamble
After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023.
"I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.
Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete.
Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme.
"That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.
In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.
The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games.
"That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.
In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots.
"I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained.
"For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.'
"We never, ever expected the impact it might have."
The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.
That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics.
"I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film.
"I had to not have a face of shock."
'I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me'
It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.
She corrects that notion.
"I don't know where that came from," Gunn said.
"I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."
Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation.
"It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.

In Summary
- The iQOO Z11 is the latest device in iQOO’s mid-segment Z series.
- The phone comes with a curved display, a sleek design, and specs and features that make it a solid mid-segmenter.
- At its starting price of Rs 34,999, the iQOO Z11 is a great option for those who want a phone that is capable of handling most tasks and has flaunt value too.
iQOO’s latest mid-segmenter sports sleek curves of the display sort, packs in decent, entertainment-friendly specs, manages to squeeze a big battery into a slim frame, and tops it all with a generous serving of AI. But will all this be enough for the iQOO Z11 to click with its target audience in a time of rising prices and declining specs? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
iQOO Z11 looks and appearance: Curved display and a Pixel-like camera bar
The iQOO Z11 is a tall, slim phone that will turn heads with its appearance. It sports a curved display in front and also has curved sides, while on the back is a camera bar that reminds us of the Google Pixel. It is a tall phone at 164.4 mm, although it is very slim at just 7.99 mm, and surprisingly light for its size at just 199 grams – that’s taller, and yet lighter and slimmer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. The front is smooth glass while the back and sides are made of polycarbonate, but they can be easily mistaken for metal or glass. The camera bar on the back is made of aluminum, which gives the phone a very premium feel. It comes with IP68/69 dust and water resistance, so it can easily survive a fall in the water, and has a very reassuringly solid feel to it.
The iQOO Z11 comes in Celestial Blue and Aurora Green shades. Both have a subtly shiny look that shimmers and changes shades in the light, and also have matte finishes that do not smudge or stain easily. We got the Aurora Green shade. This phone has flaunt value without being loud – the curved display and the camera bar give it slim and tall Pixel vibes, which is not a bad thing at all.
iQOO Z11 Spec Sheet and Hardware: Solidly upper mid-segment
The iQOO Z11 comes with a 6.83-inch AMOLED display with a resolution of 2800 x 1260 and a refresh rate of 144 Hz, which is rare at this price point. Sound is handled by a pair of stereo speakers. The phone is the first in the Indian market to be powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Ultra processor, which is supposed to be a steady performer with some gaming ability as well. This is paired with RAM and storage variants of 6 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 256 GB, and 12 GB/ 256 GB. The RAM is LPDDR4X, while the storage is UFS 3.1, which are, like the processor, not top of the line, but actually very capable. The camera bar on the back has a 50-megapixel main Sony IMX882 sensor with OIS, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide, while selfie and video call duties are handled by a 32-megapixel front-facing camera. In spite of being very slim, the iQOO Z11 comes with a large 7025 mAh battery with support for 44W charging, and a 44W charger in the box.
The iQOO Z11 runs on OriginOS 6 on top of Android 16 and comes with an assurance of three years of Android upgrades and five years of security patches. Once again, that’s par for the course for the segment. The phone also comes with not only a number of AI tools (apart from Google’s standard Gemini suite), but also with unlimited AI credits for AI captions and AI creations using iQOO’s tools, basically allowing consumers to use them without restrictions, which is rare to see at this price.
iQOO Z11 cameras: Colorfully pleasant mostly
Photography on the iQOO Z11 is largely a single-camera show – something that is beginning to become the rule in this price segment. The 50-megapixel main camera takes very pleasant snaps with ample detail. Purists might feel that the images come with slightly saturated colors, but mainstream users are unlikely to complain. Even low-light and night photography is impressively colorful. We would suggest shooting videos in the daylight, though, as low-light videos are not the best.
The front camera takes good selfies, with plenty of beautification and skin smoothing by default, although these can be toned down. The ultrawide camera is basically good for a different perspective, but its quality is not the greatest. Portraits are impressive, but lossless zoom is limited to 2x, while digital zoom goes up to 10x. There are plenty of shooting and editing options to let one do more with images, but this is a phone for casual point-and-shooters rather than enthusiasts.
iQOO Z11 performance: Doing it all well, instead of doing a few things brilliantly
The iQOO Z11 is one of the rare phones out there that does many things well. The combination of that large display and very good stereo speakers makes it a great phone for viewing content, whether it is viewing shows and films, reels, or just browsing the Web. The 7050 mAh battery comfortably keeps going for a day and a half of normal use, and the 44W charger gets the phone from empty to full in about 70-75 minutes, with half an hour generally being enough to take the phone up to 50 percent (which is enough to see off a day of use).
The Dimensity 7500 Ultra sails through routine tasks effortlessly, and we were able to switch between 6-10 apps quite easily without any lag. While the phone is not a gaming beast, we were able to play titles like Call of Duty and Asphalt after a few minor tweaks, and even Genshin Impact (with graphics toned down) ran well on the phone. The display and speakers again play key roles here. The phone never heated up excessively either, no matter what we burdened it with.
iQOO Z11 Software and UI: Unlimited AI
OriginOS 6 runs smoothly on the iQOO Z11, and there are plenty of AI tools to play around with. AI Creation is a powerful writing tool, and AI Transcript Assist works perfectly for those who love to have written records of meetings, classes, or lectures (do double-check names, though). There are also tools for AI translation, summaries, and more. They all work very smoothly indeed (though you need to log in to an iQOO account and have an Internet connection for most), with many coming with unlimited usage – something college-goers and AI addicts on a tight budget will appreciate. Of course, one also gets Google’s AI tools such as Gemini and Circle to Search.
While there is some bloatware (most of which can be uninstalled), there are a number of handy utilities and features too, including iQOO DocMaster, which lets one work with multiple document formats, the Dynamic Island-like Origin Island, and the ability to easily share information with not just Android but also iOS devices. The software seems to be a little overwhelming, but is extremely useful once one gets the hang of it. And works smoothly most of the time.
iQOO Z11 Review Verdict: Great for those who want a do-it-all, which also looks good
The iQOO Z11 is available in the following RAM and storage configurations at these prices:
6 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 34,999
8 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 39,999
8 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 44,999
12 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 49,999
Given the trend of insanely high prices, these are extremely competitive. In fact, although some might frown at the relatively modest RAM in the base 6 GB/ 128 GB model, the fact that it is priced below Rs 35,000 could tempt many users. Even at its higher price points, its combination of design, specs, and performance makes it very good value for money at a time when prices are increasing dramatically.
It is this unique cocktail of features that lets the iQOO Z11 hold its own against some very tough competition. The Moto Edge 70 Pro has a more powerful processor and cameras with a higher megapixel count but loses out in the looks department and has a smaller battery. The Redmi Turbo 5 brings a quirky design and a powerful chip to the table but has a smaller display. Another contender is the OnePlus Nord CE6, which comes with a huge battery and a good processor, but loses out in the camera and design stakes.
This tick-all-boxes versatility sums up the iQOO Z11. It may not be the very best in any performance category, but there is actually very little that it cannot do. Want a quick gaming session? It will handle it. Want to check or post on social media? It will handle it. Want to binge-watch shows? It has got your back. Want to send images and videos to your iPhone-carrying friends? It can do that too. Want to get notes and summaries? Its AI will chip in, but it does the job.
The iQOO Z11 is very much a generalist, rather than a specialist in any field. It is a masterly jack of all trades. And a very good-looking one too. One of the best all-rounders you can get for under Rs 40,000 right now.
- Eye-catching design with curved display
- Smooth performance
- Very good stereo speakers
- Lots of AI features (some with unlimited usage)
- Good main camera
- IP68/69 rating
- Ordinary ultrawide camera
- Bloatware in OS
- Competition has faster chips and memory

Indonesia doubles down on coal to power its aluminum expansion
The Iran war has dented global supplies of aluminum, raising production costs for the metal used in buildings, cars and airplanes, among other things
BANGKOK -- Resource-rich Indonesia is expanding its production of aluminum as the Iran war disrupts supplies, relying on its abundant coal reserves to power new smelters that run contrary to efforts to curb carbon emissions that cause climate change.
Prices have risen due to fuel shortfalls and attacks on infrastructure that have slowed production in the Middle East of the lightweight, silverish metal used in everything from kitchen foil and power lines to smartphones and cars.
In working to raise its limited manufacturing capacity, Indonesia has a strong ally in China, which makes 60% of the world's aluminum but is keen to reduce pollution and emissions from smelters on its own shores. Chinese companies have invested in about three-quarters of the planned Indonesian projects.
Here's what to know about Indonesia's ambitious aluminum plans:
The Middle East usually makes about 9% of the world’s aluminum, but output from the region is expected to drop 44% this year from 2025, according to Fastmarkets, a commodities information agency.
Energy shortfalls drove Emirates Global Aluminium to back out of deals and Qatar Aluminium Ltd. to slash production, while Iranian strikes damaged Aluminium Bahrain's facilities.
A metric ton of aluminum traded for between $3,150 and $3,250 before the Iran war. But the conflict drove up that price to as high as $3,780 per metric ton in June. It’s now trading near $3,400 a metric ton.
The war has magnified the potential for other regions, like Southeast Asia, to replace Middle East production, said Andy Farida of Fastmarkets.
“When that supply is so unsure, end users look for alternatives,” he said. “The war has really accelerated this transformation and put Indonesia on the map.”
Aluminum is one of the most used metals in the world and its production is highly energy intensive. The process starts with the mining of bauxite ore, which is refined into alumina and then smelted into aluminum.
By the end of the decade, Indonesia wants to quadruple its alumina output to 32.5 million metric tons and ramp up aluminum production from around 1 million metric tons in 2025 to 14.5 million metric tons by 2030, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The Finland-registered nonprofit is tracking 32 prospective off-grid coal plants, built by private companies to exclusively power aluminum smelters. These are known as “captive coal” facilities.
There is limited public data on the emissions from these types of plants, according to Syahdiva Moezbar, with CREA in Jakarta. “This captive coal boom all over Indonesia is essentially not tracked. That is why it’s very concerning,” he said.
Such plans are contrary to Indonesia’s promises to cut its use of coal, the most heavily polluting major fossil fuel and a significant source of planet-warming emissions.
They also threaten to cause more damage at a time when the expansion of Indonesia's globally important nickel industry is sacrificing local environments for industrialization.
The aluminum industry accounts for about 2% of annual global greenhouse gas emissions, equaling about 1.1 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year, according to the World Economic Forum. That’s more than the total annual emissions of most countries.
If all Indonesia’s planned projects begin operating by 2030, CREA estimates that the country's own bauxite reserves will be depleted in less than 12 years.
China has invested between $5.5 billion and $6 billion in Indonesia's aluminum industry, according to CREA, which forecasts this to surge to $30 billion by 2030.
After Beijing set a domestic cap on aluminum production to curb overcapacity in 2017, Chinese companies expanded into other countries that have fewer restrictions, like Indonesia, according to Putra Adhiguna, with the Jakarta-based Energy Shift Institute.
Indonesia categorizes nickel and aluminum as “transition minerals” since they can be used in so-called clean technologies, such as electric vehicle batteries and solar panels.
That's left a loophole for companies to maintain that these nickel and aluminum investments, which are fueled by coal, are in keeping with climate change commitments, despite the fact that Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to stop funding overseas coal plants in 2021.
It is unclear what final products Indonesia-origin metals, like aluminum and nickel, will end up in, said Binbin Mariana with the environmental advocacy group Market Forces.
“It is a huge loophole, an elephant can go through the loophole,” she said. “You say it’s a green product, but it is powered by coal... That’s definitely greenwashing.”
Aluminum smelters could run on cleaner energy like hydropower, but this would take longer and cost more.
Indonesia is prioritizing speed to capitalize on the window of opportunity that the Iran war has created, said Adhiguna, with the Energy Shift Institute. “The speed factor is really what is causing the havoc,” he said.
“This is really running against the grain, against the spirit, of the commitment to the climate movement," he said.
Building more captive coal for aluminum will worsen the toxic haze that often blankets Southeast Asian cities, like Jakarta, according to Muhammad Al Amin, with the Indonesian Forum for Environment.
The environmental advocacy nonprofit, also known as WALHI, has campaigned against increasing the use of coal on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is a nickel production hub.
“If companies want to expand captive coal to aluminum, I think it is very bad news and a very bad development,” he said. “We have seen it, we have felt it — how communities suffer from the captive coal impact.”

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said on Tuesday it authorised Abbott Laboratories' glucose monitor, making it the first device that continuously monitors both ketone levels and blood sugar.
Here are some details:
The device branded as Libre Duo 10 Day is designed for a 10-day wear period for people aged 2 years and older living with diabetes.
The biowearable is designed to alert people of rising ketones that can lead to a diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) emergency, a serious health complication for people with diabetes.
Unlike earlier ketone tests that offered only separate, one-time readings, Abbott's device continuously monitors both ketone and glucose levels, displaying real-time trends.
The device can send automatic alerts, which may help patients and caregivers recognize rising ketones before DKA becomes a medical emergency.
"If glucose is the speedometer, ketones are like the check engine light—providing an alert that something may need attention," said Chris Scoggins, executive vice president of Abbott's diabetes care business.
The device brings both glucose and ketone levels together in a single dashboard, providing a more complete picture to help people with diabetes make more informed decisions, added Scoggins.
Abbott is working with leading pump companies to enable automated insulin delivery systems to connect with the sensors.
The company said the device integrates with the Libre app and expects Libre Duo 10 Day to work with devices from Insulet and Tandem in 2027.

China-Nepal floods: first research shows that no one could have outrun debris flow
First Chinese study of the disaster shows debris reached speeds of 19 metres per second when it struck a border crossing in Tibet
Not even the world’s fastest sprinters could have outrun the devastating floodwaters that struck a border crossing between China and Nepal last week, according to one of the first peer-reviewed assessments of the disaster.
This is almost twice Usain Bolt’s average speed when he set the 100 metres world record of 9.58 seconds in 2009 and 50 per cent higher than his top speed.
“This disaster involved a continuous transition from ice avalanche to debris flow, then to mudslide and finally to flood,” wrote the team from CAS Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.
“The time from the occurrence of the ice avalanche to its impact on the Gyirong Port was extremely short, and the effective response time was limited, which put forward higher requirements for rapid identification, information transmission and emergency decision-making.”

Two sides in Alberta separation debate entrenched, with majority wanting to remain in Canada: poll
Majority of respondents in favour of immigration reforms in October’s referendum, Research Co. poll says
With fewer than 50 days until this October’s referendum, a new poll suggests Albertans remain entrenched in long-held positions tied to the idea of separating from Canada.
The Research Co. poll from August found 74 per cent of respondents would vote for Alberta to remain in Canada, while 22 per cent would vote for the Government of Alberta to start the legal process required to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
Support for the idea of a binding referendum was highest among Albertans aged 35 to 54, at 27 per cent. Twenty per cent of Albertans aged 55 and older voiced support for a further referendum, while 18 per cent of those aged 18 to 34 agreed with the idea.
Public opinion polls, including for CBC News, have consistently shown a majority of Albertans support staying in Canada.
“Even though we still have a few weeks left to go in this campaign, people seem to be very set in their ways,” Mario Canseco, president of the Vancouver-based polling firm, told CBC News.
“This is definitely not a situation that has winning conditions for the side that wants to separate.”
The results come from an online survey of 750 likely voters in Alberta, conducted by Research Co. between Aug. 24 and 26. The survey has a margin of error of +/- 3.6 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
Canseco asks the question around separation about once per year, tracing back to Rachel Notley’s time as Alberta premier. Numbers typically range around 25 to 30 per cent who say they like the idea of secession, he said.
Those numbers track with other polling. In April, a poll directed by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC News found 27 per cent said they’d vote for separation, while 67 per cent said they’d vote against it.
- Support for Alberta separatism flat, struggling high earners more likely supporters: poll
- Majority of Albertans would vote to stay in Canada, find Smith's handling poor: poll
With time ticking toward the Oct. 19 referendum vote, federalist and separatist groups have been ramping up their voter mobilization efforts.
But pollsters like Canseco have found there are few who don’t have their minds made up.
“There’s a tiny level of undecideds when we ask about the separation question — only four per cent,” Canseco said of his latest poll’s findings. “Usually, when you have an election or a referendum, the level of undecideds is higher — maybe 10 to 15 per cent.”
Differences on immigration, constitutional reform
Though Research Co. found the idea of holding a binding vote on separation is “not resonating with the public,” the same can’t uniformly be said when it comes to the other ballots.
In addition to the separation question, October’s referendum includes five questions tied to immigration and four to constitutional reform.
Ranging from 58 to 66 per cent, a majority of likely voters said they would vote “yes” on the five questions related to immigration, according to the poll.
“This is an issue that the government has really connected well on, because you do have people who maybe voted for the NDP in the last election of Alberta, who voted for the Liberals in the last election in Canada, who look at this as an interesting idea,” Canseco said.
The most popular of the proposals is the ballot question asking about requiring proof of citizenship when voting, with 66 per cent support.
On the lower end, 58 per cent said they’d be in favour of a law mandating only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an “Alberta-approved” immigration status would be eligible for provincially-funded programs like health care and education.
- Immigration is on the ballot. Here’s what some of Alberta’s multicultural communities say about the referendum
- AnalysisWhat some immigrants could lose if Alberta votes yes to Danielle Smith's questions
The federalist group Alberta's Voice, run by political strategist Stephen Carter, is behind the “no to the nine” signs, encouraging voters to reject the ballot questions.
Carter said he believes people are starting to ask themselves what the nine other questions actually mean, and that will lead to a decline in support leading up to referendum day.
He doesn’t think most Albertans want the government to implement the kinds of policies he believes the questions will lead to.
“I think that as people become more aware of what these actual questions are asking, we’ll see the numbers start to drop,” he said.
“But for now, it’s fairly easy just to say yes to these questions, even while saying no to leaving Canada.”
The Research Co. poll found that public support was lower on the four questions tied to constitutional reform, ranging from 39 to 46 per cent support.
- Albertans to vote on judicial appointments as premier argues ‘distinct legal traditions’
- Once seeking Senate reform, Alberta now ponders voting to be ‘rid of the darn thing’
Tanya Clemens, co-leader of the Alberta independence group Let Alberta Decide, said the higher support for the questions on constitutional reforms — compared to the separation question — shows a gap in understanding what a vote for independence promises to deliver.
“It was close to a majority wanting constitutional changes. I don’t know if they understand that by voting [to remain], it’s basically voting for status quo and for things to stay the same,” Clemens said.
“It doesn’t give Alberta any more leverage. So to me, it looks like there’s some more education that needs to happen.”
The poll also found that likely voters in Alberta thought the validity of the referendum as a “true representation of the wishes of the public” depends on voter turnout.

'I have fired 40 of my agents for being corrupt', says Nigeria's anti-corruption chief
- Published
Nigeria's anti-corruption agency has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years.
The disclosure was made by Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) chairman Ola Olukoyede at an event assessing the agency's achievements since he took the helm in October 2023.
He said more than five of the dismissed officials were already facing prosecution, while case files are being prepared against others.
The EFCC investigates financial crimes, including fraud, money laundering and corruption - regularly pursuing cases against politicians, public officials, business figures and others accused of misusing public funds.
"In the past two-and-a-half years or three years of my service, I've asked them to dismiss over 40 staff on account of corruption and financial malpractice," Olukoyede told journalists at the briefing in the capital, Abuja.
He went on to explain that as part of the reforms he had overseen at the agency, the EFCC's Department of Internal Affairs had been renamed "the Department of Ethics and Integrity".
To fight against conflicts of interest, a policy on gifts and hospitality had also been introduced.
It requires officers to declare gifts above a certain threshold - which he did not specify - including gifts received from relatives abroad.
"You must be sure that your hands are clean. You can't be fighting corruption when your hands are soiled with corrupt practices," Olukoyede said.
The BBC asked the EFCC for more details about the alleged corruption involving its former staff members, but the agency said this information was not available.
It was keen to point to its other achievements over the last three years - highlighted at Monday's briefing, external.
Olukoyede, 56, said he had overseen a record-breaking time for the EFCC, recovering 1.23 trillion naira ($925m, £683m), with a conviction rate of more than 75%.
"The commission received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions between October 2023 and July 2026," he said.
In the first half of 2026 alone, it had recorded 1,370 convictions from 1,889 filings, the EFCC chairman added.
"These results reflect diligence, resilience and a prosecutorial approach anchored on evidence and courtroom outcomes."
Other figures disclosed at the event show that the EFCC's caseload is increasingly focused on cybercrime and fraud rather than just corruption cases against high-profile officials.

Let’s be frank: Some of Google’s recent Android feature Drops have been duds, offering little more than an expansion of Gemini summaries and chat functions. The new September Drop does have some Gemini flavor, but there are non-AI goodies, too. Your messaging threads are getting prettier and more useful, and those nifty Motion Assist dots that began appearing last week are rolling out widely. And even the Gemini expansion is not without utility.
Since this is an Android Drop rather than a Pixel Drop, these features are coming to a wider range of devices. The OS version does matter, though. If you’re on Android 16 or higher, you can now tell Gemini to log the location of items that don’t have a tracker tag attached. Just tell the AI where you put something, and include a photo if you like.
This information will be logged in Find Hub, which has thus far been used for locating phones, earbuds, and tracker tags. You can ask Gemini to recall that information or simply check Find Hub yourself the next time you forget where you put that item.
Gemini Live is also getting a new feature called Guided Vision that could be a boon for accessibility. Guided Vision can help you locate objects in the camera frame or extract information that you can’t make out, like the text on a menu in a dimly lit restaurant. Gemini interprets the camera feed to help you find things, and it can even tell you how far away your hand is from whatever you’re trying to find.
Guided Vision will be available in the system Accessibility shortcuts and can also be activated from the TalkBack menu. This feature will work on virtually all Android phones, from Android 9 Pie onward.

A devastating flash flood on Wednesday, August 26, near the Nepal-Tibet border, resulted in massive destruction in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, with over 700 dead and over 2,500 people still missing. Reportedly, a glacial landslide of ice and rock caused the flash floods, which destroyed homes roads, bridges and power plants.
In the days following the catastrophe, social media was rife with video clips showing the extent of devastation — from gigantic waves of floodwater gushing through entire villages, to buildings collapsing, and people being swept away under the debris.
However, Alt News found that a large number of these videos circulating on social media were not authentic. Several of these videos were not from Nepal at all, but drawn from various other calamities which occurred across the world in the last few years.
Clip From 2025 Uttarakhand Floods
An X user, Said Ercan (@saidercan), posted a compilation clip on August 27 showing the havoc wreaked by large flood waves. The first clip shows a torrential river flowing through a mountainous area, and eventually sweeping through the houses on the banks, destroying them in an instant. The post has garnered over 5.8 million views and been reshared over 5,000 times at the time of publishing. (Archive)
To verify whether the video is of the Nepal floods, we broke it down into keyframes and ran a reverse image search. This led us to an Instagram post uploaded by The Times of India, on August 5, 2025, featuring the same footage.
View this post on Instagram
The caption states that the footage is of the Uttarakhand cloudburst havoc. “At least four people have died and many are feared missing after a devastating flash flood triggered by a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga river caused large-scale destruction in Dharali village in Uttarkashi district…,” read the caption.
A Dainik Bhaskar report also features the same video to show the scale of damage caused by the cloudburst in Uttarkashi. We ran relevant keyword searches, and found news reports from sources like Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, The Hindu, and others, that corroborated this finding. Thus, the video footage shared by the X user is actually of the 2025 Uttarakhand flash floods, and not of the recent Nepal havoc.
AI-generated Clip
In another instance, X user Ayesha Khan (@Ayesha0Khaan) posted a video clip, of huge waves sweeping away cars, building structures, and people. The clip received over 1 million views. (Archive)
X user Ravi Shankar Singh (@Ravishanka34381) also posted the clip with the same claim. However, we noticed some discrepancies in the video — for instance, around the 0:05 timestamp, a tree log appears out of nowhere in the debris flowing through the floodwater, indicating that the clip could be AI-generated.
We ran the video through Hive’s AI detection tool, which confirmed our suspicion, showing a 99.9% possibility of the video containing AI-generated content.
Clip From 2024 China Incident
News outlet Medya Post (@medya_post) uploaded a clip on X, which showed around 15 people getting swept away by powerful flood waves. The caption stated: “Tourists who wanted to take videos and photos during the flood disaster that occurred in Nepal were swept away by the current and disappeared.” The post had seen massive traction on social media, with over 1.5 million views. (Archive)
Two other X users with the handles (@JMNewsNetwork_) and (@redpillmd) had uploaded the same video, with the former having deleted it after it had been viewed over 45,000 times.
To verify the clip’s authencity, we ran a reverse image search, which led us to an X post, originally uploaded by an user with the handle (@Arab_Storms) on September 8, 2024.
التصوير اصبح اهم من الحياة #شاهد ❗️#الصين جرف المد القوي لنهر تشيانتانج العديد من الزوار الذين كانوا يحاولون التقاط صورة ،،،#Yagi pic.twitter.com/bdiEj7fk9b
— طقس_العالم ⚡️ (@Arab_Storms) September 8, 2024
According to the caption, the video had been taken in China, showing the powerful waves of the Qiantang River overpowering tourists on the shore who were clicking photos. The incident, which occured in the days following Asia’s most powerful storm in 2024, the Super Typhoon Yagi, had also been reported on by The Indian Express, and Newsflare.
Video From West Bengal Landslide
A news outlet TNT Media (@TNT_Media1) posted a clip which showed a mudslide from a vantage point. It also features the narrow escape of some vehicles and people gathered at the spot. The caption, written in Arabic, claims that horrifying scenes correspond to the recent Nepal flash floods. (Archive)
مشاهد مروعة من نيبال.. 😯😯 pic.twitter.com/N7f5jBl4i6
— 𝐓𝐍𝐓 (@TNT_Media1) August 26, 2026
We noticed that the car, visible in parts of the video, bears a number plate whose state code (WB) corresponds with that of West Bengal. Moreover, the recorder of the video, while shooting the clip, speaks in Bengali to warn people to get away from the waves.
A reverse image search on several keyframes of the video led us to this X post, uploaded by The Daily Jagran on August 17.
A biker had a narrow escape after a massive landslide struck the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district. Huge rocks, soil and debris suddenly came crashing onto the road as vehicles passed through.#Kalimpong #Landslide #WestBengal #Biker #ViralVideo #Monsoon pic.twitter.com/HgFLY7Dhjy
— The Daily Jagran (@TheDailyJagran) August 17, 2026
The caption states that the video shows a landslide in the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district, thereby proving that this video clip is not related to the Nepal flash floods.
Compilation Clip From Various Calamities
An X user named “Leonard Sardua $TOR” (@lsardua) posted a compilation of clips showing structures collapsing under the deluge, claiming they showed the devastation caused by the flash flood in Nepal. The clip garnered over 3.3 million views and 3,700 reshares. (Archive)
Two more users, “HadY Azmy” (@HadYAzmy1) and Ahmad Ansari (@Ahmadansari2233), amplified the same clip on August 27. The former video, which has now been deleted, had garnered over than 2.5 million views and over 3,000 reshares.
On running a reverse image search on one keyframe from the viral clip, we were led to an article published by The Times of India on July 21. The report shows the same building structure collapse under the force of floodwater, and states that the video was from the Budgam district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Another segment of the compilation shows a red building being engulfed by the gushing floodwater, sweeping away cars and other structures amid the debris.
Running a reverse image search on this keyframe, we found that the clip could be traced back to a mudslide in Japan’s Atami city from July 2021. An X user with the handle @d_t_dcg_sdh had uploaded several clips showing the mudslide sweeping away houses and vehicles. We also found news reports from Al Jazeera and Spanish news outlet La Nacion, corroborating that the clip was recorded during a mudslide in Japan in 2021.
The same compilation video also included a segment which showed a bridge being torn down by the raging floodwater.
This, we found, was in fact from an incident in Indonesia, showing the collapse of the wooden Molintogupo Bridge, owing to the overflowing of the Bone River. A video uploaded by Newsflare on Dailymotion, notes that the incident occurred on June 11, 2020. It was also reported on by VGTV.
Another segment of the same clip shows two men watching a bridge being dismantled and swept away by floodwater.
We found that this video was from Argentina. A reverse image search on a keyframe led us to this X post by AccuWeather on December 25, 2023, which shows a bridge in Argentina’s Catamarca being blown away by the turbulent floodwater.
A bridge was swept away in Catamarca, Argentina, on Christmas Day, leaving a city completely isolated.  pic.twitter.com/hVdwxmQ7QU
— AccuWeather (@accuweather) December 27, 2023
Another video, showing a white car being dragged along by the torrential flow of mud water, was also part of this compilation.
This, Alt News found, was originally from Islamabad, in Pakistan, dating back to a devastating flood that took place in July 2025.
Similarly, a segment showing a woman overlooking a building structure being swept away by flood water, was also part of this compilation, alleging that it was from Nepal.
A reverse image search proved that the image has existed on X since at least September 2024. On further investigation, we found that it showed the damage caused by Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, United States.
Don’t worry guys, weather modification isn’t real! It’s just a coincidence that Hurricane Helene is one of the most devastating “inland damage storms” in history and that hundreds of pro-Trump counties are being massively impacted during the most important election of our… pic.twitter.com/lyi8YZXB8A
— Matt Wallace (@MattWallace888) September 28, 2024
Another clip showing a submerged bus making its way through the floodwater was also featured in the compilation.
We found that this video was shot during a downpour in Pakistan’s Karachi, which left the city flooded and resulted in at least 16 deaths. Pakistani news media outlet 24 News HD, in their report on the flood dated March 19, used the same clip of the submerged bus.
Thus, the compilation clip uploaded by users “Leonard Sardua $TOR”, “HadY Azmy”, and Ahmad Ansari, with the claim that the footage depicts the havoc in Nepal is fake and misleading. The entire compilation stitches together footage from real calamities, occuring in various other parts of the world in the past few years, to wrongly claim that they are visuals from the Nepal flash floods on August 26.

Man City agree £86m deal for teen midfielder Bouaddi
- Published
Manchester City have agreed a deal in principle worth 100m euros (£85.6m) to sign 18-year-old Lille midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi.
BBC Sport reported earlier this week that the two clubs were in advanced talks over a deal for the Morocco international to join City.
An agreement for the teenager to join Enzo Maresca's side is now in place, with Bouaddi now set to complete his protracted move to England with Lille accepting an initial fee of £81.4m, plus £4.2m in add-ons.
Having sold midfielders Rodri to Barcelona in a £65m deal and Tijjani Reinders to Saudi Arabian side Al-Qadsiah for £52m, City have prioritised central midfield as an area to strengthen.
They remain interested in Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez but it remains to be seen whether a deal can be struck.
They have already added England's Elliot Anderson for £116m from Nottingham Forest.
City host Bournemouth in their Premier League opener on Sunday (14:00 BST), having lost last weekend's Community Shield to Arsenal.

Who is Bouaddi?
Bouaddi impressed at this summer's World Cup - starting five of Morocco's six matches in their run to the quarter-finals - after a starring role in Lille's Champions League victory over Real Madrid in 2024 announced him on the big stage.
He functions as a deep-lying conductor and would complement Anderson, who is comfortable as a box-to-box midfielder as well as the number six role he plays for England.
Bouaddi has played 88 times for Lille since making his debut in October 2023, three days after his 16th birthday, and helped them finish third in Ligue 1 last season.
He became the youngest footballer to ever play for Lille when he made his senior debut against KI just a few days after turning 16 in 2023.
He was serenaded by those inside the Stade Pierre-Mauroy after helping Lille defeat Real Madrid in the Champions League on his 17th birthday.
He then broke a record held by Eden Hazard after making 50 Ligue 1 appearances for Lille at the age of just 18.

The Trump administration is halting vital federal research on the foodborne parasite Cyclospora, despite the record-breaking, nationwide outbreak of the diarrheal pathogen, according to Politico.
Of the three research programs that represent nearly all of the Cyclospora work at the US Department of Agriculture, two have been defunded, and the third is about to lose every scientist working on it. The Trump administration is shuttering the USDA’s Beltsville Agricultural Research Center near Washington, DC, and moving its work to a location in Iowa. That includes relocating the remaining Cyclospora research.
Although the research is still funded, insiders told Politico that not one of the scientists working on the project plans to relocate from Maryland to Iowa. Instead, they are either retiring, being reassigned to a different project, or leaving the USDA’s research services.
“They will have no parasitologists,” one USDA employee told Politico. “There will be a big knowledge gap.”
The US is experiencing the largest Cyclospora outbreak ever recorded. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer. At least 922 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, and two have died. Since 2018, the US has generally reported between 2,000 and 5,000 cases, though the US reported 1,180 cases in 2025.
Lost research opportunities
Cyclospora is difficult to work with in a laboratory compared to other foodborne pathogens, such as E. coli or Salmonella. Cyclospora grow and reproduce only in the human gut, not in lab conditions. Although the parasite can be isolated from feces in labs, it can sometimes be difficult to fish out; it can be shed intermittently or at low levels, requiring repeat fecal samples from an infected person. The parasite is also harder to study using genetic techniques. It has a much larger genome than bacteria, making genomic sequencing costlier and more laborious. It also reproduces sexually, meaning each generation will have new mixes of genes, making it harder to trace back lineages of the parasite to a single contaminated food. That’s in contrast to bacteria, which reproduce asexually, creating clones that are often nearly identical and easy to trace.

From playing Serena Williams on screen to following in her footsteps
- Published
Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.
Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'.
That involved the then 12-year-old working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus.
"Being able to play the role of somebody that I looked up to for my whole life was super special," Frodin told the WTA website., external
"I was honoured. She was one of the players that I looked up to most, just when I was starting to play.
"She's such an inspiration to me."
Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles.
To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion.
"I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin.
"This is a huge opportunity for me to enjoy the moment, have fun and see what I can do.
"The atmosphere, how loud the crowd will be, I feel like I fit well in that environment."
- Venus Williams loses 15th match in row in 2am finish 
  - Published2 hours ago
Frodin, who is ranked 580th in the world, worked on set with Hollywood star Smith for a few days a week over a period of six months.
She has fond memories of her experience working with Oscar-winner Smith, who would always remember to bring hot water to shoots to keep Frodin warm during their cold, rainy days filming out on the courts.
During that time, she became so accustomed to playing like 23-time major singles champion Serena that her coaches had to help her rediscover her natural style.
"After I was done shooting, I got used to her strokes," Frodin told the US Open website.
"My coaches were a bit frustrated because I naturally started to hit like her.
"I picked up Serena's backhand, but I tried as much as possible to go back to my strokes."
- Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit 
  - Published3 hours ago
It has not taken long for Frodin to secure her maiden appearance at the sport's highest level.
The 17-year-old earned a wildcard into this year's US Open women's singles competition - just as Venus Williams has done - by winning the United States Tennis Association' (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championships.
It comes in a year where Frodin reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open girls' singles - her best result as a junior at a major.
She also made her qualifying debut on the WTA Tour as a wildcard in Miami, and pushed former world number 35 Viktorija Golubic in a three-set loss in her first meeting with a player ranked inside the top-100.
But on Tuesday, she will walk out for the biggest match of her life.
"To be standing here right now and actually getting a chance to play in the main draw, it means everything," said Frodin.
"[Rybakina] is number two for a reason, so I'm expecting a battle. Hopefully, I can bring out my best level against her."
And, while she has never met the Williams sisters, Frodin is hoping that can change this fortnight.
"Hopefully, if I get a chance to hit with them or just meet them, anything, I'll take it," Frodin added.
"That would be incredible. That would be a dream."

A change in the manner in which references to Dravida Kazhagam (DK) founder E.V. Ramasamy Naicker (EVR) and an icon of the Scheduled Castes (SC) B.R.Ambedkar have been made in this year’s policy note of the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes and Most Backward Classes Welfare department triggered a political row recently.
Critics have held the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led regime responsible for the omission of the references to EVR and Ambedkar, hailed by their admirers as “Periyar” and “Babasaheb,” in certain portions of the document as compared to the previous year’s policy note.
The Minister for Backward Classes Welfare, V. Sampath Kumar, told journalists late last week that a revised policy note would be issued.
Trio’s coming together
It is not just that the latest controversy has put the two leaders in the same league. But, there were attempts on their part to work together, as, after all, both the DK founder and Ambedkar ran a campaign politically against their common adversary, the Congress. At one stage, the two leaders and former president of the All India Muslim League, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, also called Qaid-i-Azam, had attempted to forge a united front.
On January 8, 1940 in Mumbai, a few months after the Congress governments resigned in several States to protest against the British regime’s announcement of India being at war with Germany, EVR met Ambedkar and Jinnah. At that time, Jinnah had not formally come out with the League’s demand for Pakistan, even though the DK founder began propounding the concept of “Dravida Nadu.” An eminent historian of South Asia and a member of the UC [University of California] Berkeley’s history department (1964-2010) Eugene F. Irschick, in his work Tamil Revivalism in the 1930s (published by Cre-A in April 1986), mentions that EVR was elected president of the Justice Party in December 1938 and “Ramaswami Naicker’s presidential address, read in his absence [due to imprisonment], demanded a separate Dravidian state for the Dravidians.”
The presidential speech in 1938 was the first occasion when the demand for Dravida Nadu was made, according to diplomat-turned-political writer R. Kannan and the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK) general secretary D. Ravi Kumar.
Also read | Tracing the Jinnah connection
Mumbai meet
One of the factors that must have facilitated the January 1940 meeting was that both Ambedkar and EVR had declared support to Jinnah’s call to Muslims to observe December 22, 1939, as a “Day of Deliverance” in the context of the exit of Congress regimes in the States. The extension of support was recorded in an academic paper - “The Historic Meeting of Ambedkar, Jinnah and Periyar,” - presented by an academician K.V. Ramakrishna Rao at the 21st session of the South Indian History Congress in Madurai in January 2001.
On the meeting among EVR, Jinnah and Ambedkar, The Hindu, on January 16, 1940, reported the event and reproduced a statement of the DK founder, who was the then chief of the Justice Party. “Both Janab Jinnah and Dr. Ambedkar hold views about the Congress, identical with my own, and all three of us are agreed that a united effort should be made to counteract the evil influences of the Congress.”
The release, as reproduced by this newspaper, did not refer to the Dravida Nadu demand of the Justice Party. However, on the issue of making Hindi language compulsory in schools, the news report said Jinnah and Ambedkar had supported EVR’s viewpoint. “They considered the scheme to be nothing short of a shrewd scheme for inculcating and strengthening Brahmin religion and culture to the detriment of our own culture. “You will have my fullest support,” said Janab Jinnah when I broached the subject of the renewal of the anti-Hindi agitation in our province, and Ambedkar was one with me in this matter,” The Hindu reported quoting EVR.
However, Dr. Kannan, in his “Anna: The Life and Times of C.N. Annadurai,” (Penguin, 2010), observes that Annadurai (CNA) had “pleaded” with EVR to have a “definite plan and seek Jinnah’s support” for the plan. “Anna said the delegation [led by EVR] returned with ‘bitterness,’” the biographer writes. The delegation included P. Balasubramaniam, T.A.V. Nathan, Thiruvasagamani K.M. Balasubramaniam, T.P.S. Ponnappa, C. Panjatcharam and CNA.
Separate States
Contrary to the impression given by the biographer that EVR did not pursue the subject of Dravida Nadu, the academician’s paper mentions that the demand for separate States for Mahars, Muslims and Dravidians was among the subjects discussed by the three leaders. At the same time, the biographer also records that EVR told a public meeting in Dharavi, Mumbai, on January 7, 1940 that “Tamil Nadu was as populous as England and as large as Germany and that with Jinnah’s and Ambedkar’s help he would establish its freedom.”
Fifteen months after the Mumbai meeting, Jinnah visited Chennai to address the 28th annual session of the Muslim League on the SIAA grounds, behind the Puratchi Thalaivar Dr. MGR Chennai Central Railway Station. Though this newspaper reported extensively the proceedings of the meet on April 13 and 15, 1941 wherein Jinnah had ridiculed stalwarts of the national movement - Mahatma Gandhi, C. Rajagopalachari and Tej Bahadur Sapru, there was not a word about the Muslim League chief speaking in favour of the demand for “Dravida Nadu.” A galaxy of leaders of the Justice Party, including EVR, R. K. Shanmugam Chetti, A P. Patro, K.V. Reddi and M.A. Muthiah Chettiar attended. C.R. Srinivssan, Editor of the Swadesamiitran, was one of the special invitees.
Jinnah’s distancing act
With all the bonhomie, the relationship between Jinnah and EVR did not serve the purpose of the latter. In a reply to EVR in August 1944, the Muslim League leader wrote: “if the people of your province really desire Dravidasthan, it is for them to assert themselves.” At the same time, he mentioned that “you will find me supporting any just and fair claim or demand of any section of the peoples of India, and particularly the non-Brahmins of South India.” Even years after the death of Jinnah in 1948, EVR did refer to him on many occasions. In June 1956, he earned the wrath of the then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, who complained to the then Chief Minister K. Kamaraj about one of his speeches that had a reference to Jinnah. “I think that this is going completely beyond any possible limit and this kind of speech should not be allowed to go without some action being taken. I should like you to consider this matter,” Nehru wrote to Kamaraj on June 18, 1956, according to The Nehru Archives. (https://nehruarchive.in/documents/to-k-kamaraj-18-june-1956-v9lexg)
As for the EVR-Ambedkar ties, the two continued to interact with each other. A month after the split in the Justice Party at the Salem conference in August 1944 which led to the establishment of the DK, EVR called on Ambedkar at the Chettinad House here in Chennai and discussed the political situation, including the deliberations at the conference, reported The Hindu on September 25, 1944. However, Ambedkar, to pursue his agenda of social reforms aimed at uplifting the plight of the SCs, had decided to work with the Congress at the time of Independence and he became Law Minister in the first Cabinet headed by Nehru. It was another matter that he developed differences later with the Prime Minister and quit. But, Ambedkar’s cooperation had brought a pause in the relationship with EVR initially. Many years later, the ties came to an end with the death of Ambedkar in December 1956.

Why the Supreme Court's ballroom ruling could matter beyond the ballroom
The Supreme Court's decision allowing President Trump's White House ballroom construction to continue could have consequences beyond the project, Georgetown Law professor Stephen Vladeck says.
"I think, unfortunately, it sets a bigger precedent," Vladeck told Morning Edition. He said the administration has repeatedly tried to spend money Congress has not appropriated, while the Supreme Court has made it harder to challenge that spending.
Vladeck said that matters because the separation of powers is supposed to be a "two-way street." When presidents spend money Congress has not appropriated, he said, they are not simply expanding executive power but taking away one of Congress' central constitutional powers.
The court majority found that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which was challenging the project, lacked standing — the legal right to sue — because they had not shown a concrete injury.
Vladeck said it was "not necessarily the result" of the case that surprised him, but the court's rationale. He said this ruling will make it harder for plaintiffs to rely on "esthetic injuries," even though the Supreme Court recognized such claims in a 1992 opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia.
The case "comes down to an appropriations dispute that only Congress can litigate," Vladeck said. With the current Congress unwilling to challenge the administration over its spending authority, such disputes could effectively only be litigated during periods of divided government in Washington.
Meanwhile, the administration says crews are working 20 hours a day, seven days a week.
For Vladeck, the flaw is in the Supreme Court's handling of emergency cases. Although the justices describe such rulings as temporary, they can determine what happens on the ground before the underlying legal questions are resolved.
