Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says Tennessee trip isn't sending wrong message amid trade war
Smith was asked Tuesday about upcoming U.S. trip amid trade war
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith denied suggestions Tuesday that her upcoming trip to Tennessee could be sending the wrong message amid a trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.
"I hope no one's surprised to hear that I believe it's my job to continue reaching out at all levels to various influencers in the United States and get our message across that we have an incredible partnership," Smith told reporters at an unrelated news conference in Calgary.
"It's an incredible economic partnership, trade partnership, defence partnership, and we want it to continue."
The premier is set to travel to Nashville later this week on a personal trip, and her office said she'll be taking time out to meet with the head of the city's chamber of commerce, state tourism commissioner Mark Ezell and the chief executive of a Nashville tourism marketing agency.
While Smith positioned the meetings as examples of her diplomacy efforts during the trade dispute, she also said a priority would be learning more about how Calgary can position itself as "Nashville north" and boost investment in the music industry.
"It is a personal trip, but being down there I thought I'd take advantage of some of the expertise that's down there," she said.
Smith said the Tennessee capital made changes 25 years ago to make itself a music industry haven and economic powerhouse and she wants to find out how.
"I want to find out a little bit about what that is and see if we can develop some excellent partnerships with the music industry so that we can do a transfer of talent and transfer of expertise."
Smith also said Alberta wants to expand its tourism economy and that it's a good time to discuss leveraging Calgary's assets.
Nathan Cooper, Alberta's senior representative to the United States, is set to join the meetings.
Smith has said she wants to see Canadian officials double down on diplomacy efforts and get back to the negotiating table with the United States before Ottawa implements retaliatory tariffs next week.
Ottawa's tariffs, set to take effect Sept. 8, are in response to 50 per cent tariffs that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods starting Aug. 22.
Trade talks broke down in the final hours before the U.S. duties kicked in, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the United States was asking for too much and offering too little.

The Fight Between Texas and Minnesota Should Never Have Gotten This Far
A legal battle over one ICE agent’s future is a sign of serious strain between red and blue America.
In the 17 days between the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, another violent incident took place in Minneapolis that received far less attention. An ICE agent allegedly fired a shot into a home, wounding a fleeing man in the leg; the bullet lodged near a child’s playpen inside the house. That shooting is now the subject of a legal dispute between Minnesota and Texas that calls into question one of the most basic premises of the Constitution: that states will engage with one another in good faith for the perpetuation of the union.
In May, officials in Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, filed criminal charges in state court against the ICE agent, Christian Castro. But Castro had left Minnesota for Texas, and Texas Governor Greg Abbott was refusing to return him. Last week, Castro walked free from a Texas jail after a federal judge declined to force the extradition.
“Even though we are separate states, we also function as the United States” because of reliable collaboration between state governments, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty told me. But now, she worries, “somebody can commit a crime in one state and flee to another state, and depending on what the political views or whims are of the governor in that state, that person may not go back to face those charges. How can that be a standard that we can live with?”
Minnesota’s case against Castro was never going to be easy. Immediately after the shooting, Castro claimed that the men he was chasing, Julio Sosa-Celis and Alfredo Aljorna, had attacked him with a shovel and broom in a prolonged struggle before Castro fired and wounded Sosa-Celis. The Justice Department brought charges against Sosa-Celis and Aljorna over the assault—only to drop the case a month later, shortly before ICE and DOJ began investigating whether Castro lied about having been attacked. Castro and his ICE partner were suspended and placed under investigation by ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility, which handles officer misconduct, and by the Justice Department. Moriarty later announced state charges against Castro over the shooting and his alleged lying to law enforcement. (Castro has not made any public statements regarding the case and has not entered a plea.)
The decision to indict Castro queued up a lengthy and potentially risky legal fight over a state’s ability to bring criminal charges against a federal officer. (Hennepin County is currently engaged in a similar skirmish in a different case against an ICE agent who was charged in state court over a road-rage incident.) But Castro’s voyage from Minnesota to Texas complicated matters further: Shortly after the shooting, new court filings reveal, ICE ordered Castro to return from his detail in Minneapolis to his usual posting in the Rio Grande Valley. This meant that Minnesota officials would need the cooperation of Texas authorities in order to ensure Castro’s return to Hennepin County to stand trial—if, that is, Castro refused to return voluntarily to Minnesota. And, it turned out, he did.
Typically, an interstate extradition is not very interesting. “There are tens of thousands of extraditions that are carried out each year without any incident whatsoever,” Ethan Lowens, a fellow at the University of Pennsylvania law school, told me. If a person commits a crime in State A and then travels to State B, Governor B must—by law—respect Governor A’s request to return the defendant to State A for prosecution. This duty traces back to the extradition clause of the Constitution and the Extradition Act of 1793, which helped knit the new states together into a unified whole. Two hundred years later, in the 1987 case Puerto Rico v. Branstad, the Supreme Court sharply limited governors’ ability to refuse extradition requests.
At first, Minnesota, Texas, and the federal government seemed to be working together smoothly. Texas Rangers and federal agents arrested Castro the week after Hennepin County announced the charges against him, and he remained in a South Texas jail while Minnesota waited for Abbott to sign off on the paperwork. When I first spoke with Moriarty, near the end of June, she sounded unconcerned about the process. “It’s not unusual for a request to sit on somebody’s desk for a while” before a governor grants approval for extradition, she said.
But Minnesota’s request for Castro sat on Abbott’s desk for week after week, even as the governor signed off on other extraditions from Texas to Minnesota. What’s more, Castro’s arrest had started a ticking clock, thanks to a quirk of Texas law: A person detained pursuant to another state’s extradition request can be held in jail for only 90 days. Minnesota authorities worried that, if Castro were to hit that limit and be released before Texas allowed extradition, Castro might seek to dodge the charges by fleeing to Mexico. On August 18, with the 90-day limit approaching, Minnesota filed a complaint in federal court asking for a judge’s help in forcing Abbott to turn Castro over—or, alternatively, to extend his stay in jail until Abbott approved the transfer.
Abbott, a staunch ally of President Trump who is up for reelection in a deep-red state, did little to dispel the perception that he had been stalling for ideological reasons. “I don’t trust Tim Walz,” he commented after Minnesota filed its case, nodding to right-wing allegations about fraud in the state. A Texas legal filing responding to Minnesota’s suit included a non sequitur suggesting that Walz “is content to look the other way when the context is sexual violence against children by illegal aliens, but not when the context is immigration enforcement by federal officers.”
In court, Abbott has argued that Castro may not meet the legal criteria for an interstate “fugitive” under extradition law because Castro traveled to Texas under orders by ICE and may not have intentionally fled Minnesota justice. For this reason, Abbott says, the governor’s office simply needs more time to conduct an investigation into whether Castro is legally a fugitive. But, Lowens explained to me, there is little ambiguity under the law that “fled in this context really means left for any reason at all.” In his view, Abbott’s argument looks less like a compelling legal argument and more like “a means to buy them some more time.”
In his ruling last week, Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. likewise seemed skeptical of Abbott’s reasoning. But Rodriguez nevertheless denied Minnesota’s motion, on the grounds that the state had sued too early—because Abbott hadn’t yet rejected Walz’s request. Abbott “managed to manipulate the system to run out the 90-day clock,” Moriarty said.
Meanwhile, according to new reporting from The New York Times, the Justice Department had been planning to bring charges against Castro in federal court. This would have offered Abbott an out: Castro could have been detained on the federal charges without Texas having to yield to Minnesota. But for unclear reasons, the Times reports, the case never materialized. When I reached out to the Justice Department last week to ask about the status of the investigation against Castro, DOJ stated that it “does not comment on the status or existence of pending criminal investigations.”
On Thursday morning, with no federal charges against him and his 90 days in jail expired, Castro walked free from a prison near Brownsville, Texas, just more than 10 miles from the Mexico border. “As far as we understand, he’s free to go wherever he wants to go,” Moriarty said. “There were no conditions of his release.” During an earlier hearing, an attorney for Texas suggested that the federal and Texas governments were “committed to ensuring that he’s not leaving the country,” but Moriarty said that she had not been provided with any information about what that might mean. Asked what that commitment entailed, the Justice Department declined to comment; the Department of Homeland Security also did not answer my question. In response to my query, Abbott’s office sent me a statement declaring that Castro “must understand that the eyes of law enforcement will remain fixed on him” as the governor’s office continues its “investigation.”
Texas’s gambit is both a feat of technical evasiveness and a direct attack on the bonds between states that help cohere the union. Bryna Godar, a staff attorney for the State Democracy Research Initiative, told me that the precedent set by the Castro case “could potentially enable other states to similarly delay on extradition requests if they want to essentially deny them.” Imagine a splintering among the states, where red states reliably aid the law-enforcement efforts only of red states and blue states only of blue.
Romantic visions of American federalism as a force for liberty and democracy do not align neatly with any one political ideology. Some of the earliest interstate extradition fights involved slaveholders seeking the return of Black Americans who fled the South to escape from bondage. A recent round of battles between states began after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, as red states such as Texas criminalized abortion and blue states enacted “shield laws” to protect doctors from prosecution for prescribing medication across state borders. The Castro case is more straightforward—the legal mandate to hand over a defendant applies only when the person flees the prosecuting state—but it is the latest development in what Lowens described as an “arms race” between states over extradition.
The political scientist Donald Kettl has described Trump’s approach to federalism not as a principled stance on the appropriate scope of state or federal power but instead as “yet another arena for political contest.” Already, Trump’s use of presidential power to bully blue states has fractured the structure of “vertical” federalism, meaning the relationship between the federal government and the states. Now the desire to score political points is also weakening “horizontal” federalism, the bonds among the states. Once everything becomes politics, the structures that tie together the nation weaken. “That is not tenable,” Moriarty warned in a press conference after Judge Rodriguez’s decision. “That’s chaos.”
A spokesperson for DHS informed me that Castro remains suspended without pay, and offered a stern statement about the importance of ICE agents upholding their “sacred sworn oath.” Abbott’s stalling will not be able to delay a confrontation forever, at least so long as Castro remains within the United States. Moriarty pointed to language in Rodriguez’s ruling suggesting that, at some point, Abbott must make a decision one way or another. What Abbott chooses could help reinforce the fraying bonds that hold America’s 50 states together—or strain them further.

Quick Answer
PowerShell commands such as Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, Get-Service, Stop-Service, Get-Content, Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Move-Item, Remove-Item, and Set-Location help you manage apps, services, files, folders, and system tasks faster on Windows.
PowerShell is a Windows program that simplifies system administration. You can use it to perform many system tasks efficiently and automate repetitive ones. However, to do either, you must know the right commands, or cmdlets (command-lets), as PowerShell calls them.
A typical PowerShell cmdlet follows the verb-noun structure, where the noun is the object you want to act on, and the verb is the action you want to perform on it. This makes them predictable and easy to remember.
Here’s a quick reference guide covering all the essential Windows PowerShell commands to help you get started with PowerShell.
Table of Contents
Essential PowerShell Commands for Windows
Get-Help
Get-Help is a handy cmdlet you can use any time you want to learn about a PowerShell concept or command. It shows information for everything from cmdlets and functions to aliases and scripts. Plus, it shows the exact syntax along with all the available parameters to eliminate the need for guesswork.
Syntax:
Get-Help
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Help cmdlet:
- Get-Help Get-Process : Find out what the Get-Process command does
- Get-Help Get-Process -Detailed : Get a detailed description for the Get-Process cmdlet
- Get-Help Get-Process -Online : View a detailed explanation of the command with examples on Microsoft’s official documentation online
If Get-Help doesn’t return any result, try updating it by running:
Update-Help
Get-Command
Get-Command lists all executable commands installed on your computer, including cmdlets, aliases (or shortcuts that point to other commands), and functions (snippets or scripts that perform specific actions). It’s useful when you want to make sure the command you’re trying to use is supported by PowerShell and available on your system.
Syntax:
Get-Command
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Command -ListImported : Get a list of all commands in the current session
- Get-Command Get-AppLockerPolicy : View information about the Get-AppLockerPolicy cmdlet
- Get-Command -CommandType Alias : List all alias-type executables
- Get-Command *Service* : Get all the service-related executable elements on your system
Get-Process
Get-Process returns a table of all operating system processes (apps or executables) running on your computer locally. For each item in the table, you see the process name, ID, CPU consumption, and a few other details. This makes it really easy to identify which process is consuming significantly more resources, so you can act on it accordingly and free up system resources.
Syntax:
Get-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Process cmdlet:
- Get-Process -Name notepad : Get details about the Notepad process
- Get-Process explorer | Format-List * : Display detailed information about the explorer processes, including all its properties and their values
Stop-Process
Stop-Process allows you to stop one or more running processes on your computer right from the PowerShell window. To use it, you need the process name or the process ID (or PID), which you can identify by running the Get-Process command.
Syntax:
Stop-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Process cmdlet:
- Stop-Process -Name notepad : Close the Notepad app
- Stop-Process -Name notepad -F : Force close Notepad
- Stop-Process -Id 3380 : Close the app with a PID of 3380
Start-Process
Start-Process is a PowerShell command that lets you launch one or more processes (or apps) on your computer. You can even open an executable file using it. Start-Process also gives you the ability to choose how you want to start a process. For instance, you may start a program as an administrator or open specific files with their default apps.
Syntax:
Start-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Start-Process cmdlet:
- Start-Process notepad.exe : Launch the Notepad app
- Start-Process -FilePath “notepad” -Wait -WindowStyle Maximized : Open Notepad in a maximized window
- Start-Process -FilePath “sort.exe” : Start a process that uses the sort.exe file
- Start-Process -FilePath “powershell” -Verb RunAs : Open PowerShell as an administrator
Get-Service
Get-Service retrieves and gives you the status of all Windows services running on your computer. It’s useful when you want to identify the status of background services.
Syntax:
Get-Service
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Service -Name wuauserv : Check the status of the Windows Update service
- Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running"} : Filter services to only view the ones that are currently running
Stop-Service
The Stop-Service PowerShell cmdlet lets you stop a system service. You’d typically use it after you’ve run the Get-Service command and identified the problematic service running in the background.
Syntax:
Stop-Service -Name
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Service cmdlet:
- Stop-Service -Name wuauserv : Stop the Windows Update service
- Stop-Service -DisplayName “telnet” | Stop-Service : Stop a service using its display name
- Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force : Stop the Spooler service along with other dependent services
Get-Content
Get-Content helps you read the contents of an item within the PowerShell window. You’d mostly use it to get the contents of a file. All you need to do is specify the file and its location. You can even mention the number of lines in the file you want to read, among other things.
Syntax:
Get-Content -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Content cmdlet:
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -TotalCount 10 : Read only the first ten lines of the file
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Wait : Monitor a file and display new lines as they’re added and the file is saved
Get-ChildItem
The Get-ChildItem cmdlet allows you to view all the items (files and folders) at your specified location. Running it without any parameters returns items in your current location, but you can force it to find items at other locations, too.
Syntax:
Get-ChildItem -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-ChildItem cmdlet:
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test : Find files and folders in the Test folder in the D: directory
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Name : Get the names of files and folders at a specified location
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Filter *.txt -Recurse : Scan a directory and its folders for all text files
Copy-Item
Copy-Item lets you copy items (files and folders) from one location to another. You just need to specify the path of the file or folder you want to move along with the path of the location where you want to move it. The copied file continues to live at the original location.
Syntax:
Copy-Item -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Copy-Item cmdlet:
- Copy-Item D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Copy sample.txt file to another location with sample2.txt name
- Copy-Item D:\Test\ -Destination D:\Test2\ -Recurse : Duplicate the Test folder along with all its subfolders and files to Test2
Move-Item
Move-Item is a handy cmdlet for when you want to move an item (file or folder) from one location to another. Unlike the copy command, it doesn’t keep the item at its original location after the operation. Instead, it moves it to the new location.
Syntax:
Move-Item -Path -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Move-Item cmdlet:
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\ : Move the sample.txt file from the Test folder to the Test2 folder
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Move the sample.txt file to the Test2 folder and rename it to sample2.txt
- Move-Item -Path .\*.txt -Destination D:\Test2 : Move all files with the .txt extension in the current directory to Test2
Remove-Item
Remove-Item allows you to remove or delete one or more items (files and folders) from a location. Remember that this cmdlet permanently deletes the item instead of moving it to the Recycle Bin for restoration.
Syntax:
Remove-Item -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Remove-Item cmdlet:
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a dot (.) in their name
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a .doc file extension in the Test folder
Set-Location
Set-Location lets you change the current working location to your specified location. It’s quite handy when you’ve to perform multiple operations on different directories.
Syntax:
Set-Location -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Set-Location cmdlet:
- Set-Location -Path D: : Set the working location to the D: drive
- Set-Location -Path D: -PassThru : Set the working location to the D: drive and display that location
You Should Also Learn Command Prompt
PowerShell is just one of the many powerful tools Microsoft bundles with Windows. You also have Command Prompt (CMD) — a command-line interpreter that lets you perform various system operations using commands. If you haven’t already, be sure to check out our essential Command Prompt commands cheatsheet, as that can help you use your Windows PC more efficiently as well.

Audio that’s easy to enjoy. Huge battery life with ANC on. User-replaceable battery is an important step. Comprehensive codec support. USB-C and 3.5-mm wired listening for hi-res audio. All-day comfort.
TIRED
ANC won’t win awards. Bass-forward tuning might not suit you. Build quality feels a bit more plastic than premium. Not a vast upgrade of the Momentum 4. Feel slightly overpriced.
We’ve waited almost four years for a new pair of Sennheiser Momentum wireless over-ear headphones. That’s eons in a world where Sony, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins have been busy launching stellar Bluetooth headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM6, Apple AirPods Max 2, and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3.
Plenty has happened in the intervening years—not least, Sennheiser’s consumer division being sold to hearing aid company Sonova, which is currently looking to sell it on. Thankfully, the Momentum 5 is a hugely enjoyable pair of premium headphones with some unexpectedly good features, and not the product of a troubled homelife.
Battery Life for Life
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless look good. They strike a middle ground between premium cans (AirPods Max 2, Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3) and more lightweight ones (Bose QuietComfort Headphones, Sony WH-1000XM5). The 10.3-ounce build is mainly plastic, and the ear cups are basic, but the denim trim on the top of the comfortable headband adds fun texture. They are not head turners like the Nothing Headphone (1), but they are still nice to look at, and come in blue denim (pictured), black, and white.
They are, however, very comfortable, with a great level of squish to the earpads. Massive ears (like mine) have room to flap, and the headband doesn’t add any uncomfortable pressure. No over-ear headphone is perfect to wear with glasses, but I happily wore these for hours. When temperatures hit 95 degrees Fahrenheit my ears got sweaty, but so did the rest of me, to be fair.
The Momentum 5 Wireless get up to 57 hours of battery with ANC on, according to Sennheiser. That’s almost double what the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 can do. It’s three hours shy of the older Momentum 4, and 13 hours less than the similarly priced Marshall Monitor III ANC.
I didn’t perform an exact test on the 57-hour battery claim, but it seems fairly accurate in my real-world use thus far. I have been using the Momentum 5 daily for the past month, and they are still at about 50 percent charge.
The more interesting story to me is that the battery can be easily replaced. Remove the left ear pad, unscrew four Phillips-head screws, lift the cover, and the battery can be unplugged and swapped out in seconds.
iFixit has been showing us how to replace batteries in electronics for years, but this is the first time I’ve seen a headphone brand actively encourage consumers to do it themselves. I think Sennheiser embracing our right to repair is worth celebrating, even if, at the time of publication, the replaceable battery isn't available for purchase.
Lively and Warm Sound
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The Momentum 5 Wireless supports SBC, AAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Lossless, and aptX Adaptive codecs, plus multipoint connectivity. Plug in using either the 3.5-millimeter jack or the USB-C port to get digital lossless audio (up to 24-bit/96 kHz).
The Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app is where you can customize ANC levels, transparency, an eight-band EQ, connection preferences, and Dolby Atmos. You can also save sound profiles based on your location, maxing out ANC when you hit the office, for instance.
Controls on the headphones themselves are touch controls on the right ear cup, and they work fine: as in, they didn’t annoy me. A tap pauses music, swipes adjust volume and skip tracks, while a double tap toggles between ANC and transparency modes.
Active Noise Cancellation comes via eight microphones, and it is good, verging on great. It works well on public transport, provides a cocoon in cafés, and gifts solitude in a shared office. If you’ve never used Sony or Bose ANC headphones, you’ll be delighted with the Momentum 5s, but if you’re switching from those two brands, you might find these a bit of a letdown. We’re talking small margins here, but the Momentum 5 just lacks that eerily quiet sealed-off feeling of the WH-1000XM6 or Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen).
Call quality is good too, and the wind-reducing mics kept my voice front and center, but it’s not the reason I’d buy these headphones.
I tested the Momentum 5 Wireless using the best and worst playback resolutions from Spotify—both over Wi-Fi and cellular. I also listened to Qobuz hi-resolution recordings and my own digital music library. And no matter what I played, the headphones offered me a smooth, refined, and expressive performance.
They’re not “high-fidelity” in the sense that the extreme edges of a recording are not exposed, and they happily make poor-quality output sound enjoyable. That said, you’ll get a bit more out of them by listening to higher-fidelity sources. And if you’re still playing the lowest-resolution audio playback on Spotify (or don’t even know what I am talking about), you don’t need to spend $399 on a pair of headphones.
Mixing it up between the pop of Olivia Rodrigo’s excellent new album, the twang of Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band, via Wu-Tang, and more of the Police than I’m comfortable admitting, the Sennheiser made every genre enjoyable to listen to and were totally agreeable. They’re not neutral, with plenty of relaxed warmth to the sound profile.
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Listening to the Sennheisers side by side with the B&W Px7 S3, I noticed a little lack in punch and drive by comparison. The opposite is true when listening to them against the AirPods Max 2, however, with the Sennheiser’s classy midrange cutting through the mix with real authority. This was also the case when comparing them with the now discontinued Momentum 3 Wireless from 2019 (although I wish Sennheiser would bring back the sumptuous leather earpads at least as an add-on).
They are bass-forward, though, and anyone leaning toward acoustic or classical would do well to tweak the EQ via the app. The sound is clean overall, with a tight thump, although not a patch on the taut rumble from the more expensive AirPods Max.
Should You Buy Them?
The Momentum 5 Wireless are long overdue, but at $399, they face stiff competition from more mainstream competitors like Sony, Bose, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins, all of whom have launched serious good over-ear headphones recently. This hasn’t left a lot of room for Sennheiser to compete in, but, sensibly, the brand hasn’t tried to win every battle.
The ANC is very good (but not spookily quiet), and the design is classy (but not indulgent). Sound is warm, expressive, and easy to enjoy for long periods of time, even if the bass might need taming in the EQ. But importantly, Sennheiser has created a headphone with superb battery life, easy wired and hi-res listening, an impressive codec list, and an easily replaceable battery you can swap yourself.
They are not the most exciting headphones in any one area, but they are comfortable, considered, likable, and impressively repairable.

It has raised a total of $516 Mn so far from investors like SoftBank, B Capital, Greycroft, Premji Invest, and others. Most recently, it raised a $50 Mn round last March. As of 2022, its latest valuation is around $5 Bn.

Power failure halts trams running between Hong Kong’s Wan Chai and Admiralty
Disruption comes after westbound line between North Point terminus and Tin Lok Lane halted for several hours on Monday
Tram services between Wan Chai and Admiralty in Hong Kong were suspended Tuesday night due to a power failure, the second such incident in two days.
The Transport Department issued a special traffic bulletin at 9.37pm, saying it had been notified by Hong Kong Tramways that eastbound and westbound services between Admiralty MTR station and Tonnochy Road were suspended because of an electricity fault.
It marked the second consecutive day of tram disruptions.
On Monday night, services on the westbound line between North Point terminus and Tin Lok Lane stopped at about 6pm after a power failure. The suspension lasted until 11.30pm.

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”

They set out to make a film about the Indian freedom movement. A tragic accident blurs the lines between past and present, throwing them into their own conflict against an unjust power structure. The film is funny but also heartbreaking. It celebrates the spirit of the great revolutionaries, and imagines what their modern counterparts might stand for. A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.
Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.
But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.
“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document says.
Financial compensation alone is not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert from Liberia who helped draft the document, said she expected states to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.
“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

Drugmakers are often accused of manipulating the U.S. patent system to crowd out rivals. But an escalating court battle is focusing attention on a nuanced but crucial question: When does acquiring a patent application allow a company to unfairly maintain a monopoly on a medicine?
The litigation — which pits a large health insurer against Amgen, a big biotech company — is being closely watched, because the outcome has the potential to place pharmaceutical patent deals under wider scrutiny at a time when patent maneuvers are sometimes cited as a tool used by drugmakers to maintain high prices.
Adding to the intrigue, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission has unexpectedly weighed in on the side of payers and consumers by arguing the maneuver deserves such attention due to antitrust concerns.

The state government of Haryana has granted full university status to Gurugram-based Masters’ Union (MU), paving the way for the company to operate as Master’s Union University. The Haryana Legislative Assembly passed the Haryana Private Universities (Amendment) Bill, 2026, allowing the six-year old higher education institution to operate as a private university. “Over the next few years, we will be developing departments across Law, Medicine, Agri, Biotech; launch PhD programmes and diplomas, and create entirely new pathways for higher education,” founder Pratham Mittal said in a social media post. MU intends to expand its physical footprint on a 5.14-acre site in Gurugram, including 1.07 Lakh sq ft of already constructed area, its campus will include accelerator hubs, maker labs, and research infrastructure, as well as residences and cultural and sporting facilities. The decision validates MU’s model of entrepreneurship-focused and practitioner-led education, Mittal noted. “In the AI age, access to information is no longer the constraint. The real advantage will come from knowing how to frame problems, make decisions and build solutions. That is why we have always believed in learning by doing – students taking ownership of a real problem, understanding it from the ground up, working with experts, managing resources and making decisions with real-world impact,” he added. Founded in 2020, MU offers programmes in management, technology and engineering, as well as family business and executive learning. Currently, it has over 3,000 students enrolled across multiple disciplines. It touts its faculty, who comprise investors, founders, and industry leaders as a unique selling point. As per its website, former SoftBank India head Manoj Kohli, Swiggy’s food delivery CEO Rohit Kapoor, InfoEdge cofounder Sanjeev Bikhchandani, Zerodha cofounder Nithin Kamath, Lenskart’s Peyush Bansal, and Mamaearth’s Ghazal Alagh, are among its ‘Masters’ or faculty. The university also focuses on student entrepreneurship and has backed more than 80 student startups since inception through various initiatives including its Venture Initiation Programme (VIP). MU claims that 10 VIP-incubated startups have raised over ₹65 Cr and recorded a combined annual revenue of ₹320 Cr in FY25. In its Entrepreneurship Report for 2025, it said that its students have launched over 30 startups in the past five years and more than half have raised over $1 Mn. Besides, MU's sister business and global business school Tetr College of Business also floated a $10 Mn fund to back student entrepreneurs in October 2024. MU also offers a Founder Fellowship through which more than 40 students aspiring to build their own startups have been backed with $50,000 per month in grant funding, mentorship from industry leaders, and fundraising support.

When Tim Cook took over as Apple’s CEO, he did not try to fill the big shoes of its legendary founder and product visionary Steve Jobs. Instead, he took Jobs’ advice: “Never ask what I would do, just do the right thing.”
Fifteen years on, having taken the iPhone maker from a $350 billion company to a more than $4.5 trillion behemoth, Cook will pass the baton to Apple hardware chief John Ternus, who will be steering the company in the AI era.
Cook will become executive chairman on September 1, guiding Apple’s dealings with policymakers amid tense relations between its home market, the U.S., and China, where many of its products are made.
The transition caps one of the most consequential CEO tenures ever.
Unlike Jobs’ product design genius, Cook ascended the Apple ladder by making the company’s supply chain the envy of every manufacturer. As CEO, Cook used this operations-first mindset to take Apple’s cutting-edge products to the masses.
In a perfect example of his business acumen, Cook understood Apple could make money from the customer long after the iPhone sale, turning the 2.5 billion installed iPhone user base into a recurring revenue machine. That business has outpaced growth in the company’s hardware business in recent years.
Apple’s annual sales rose from $108 billion at the start of Cook’s tenure to $416 billion in the last fiscal year, while profit grew more than fourfold to $112 billion.
Its wearables business, home to Cook-era iPhone accessories such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, brought in $35 billion in sales in fiscal 2025.
“Not only did Cook create his own path of operational and supply chain success, but he also created a ‘values-driven’ culture within Apple,” said Christopher Brown, a financial adviser at private wealth management firm Synovus Securities, which holds the iPhone maker’s shares.
“What followed was a consumer brand loyalty and dependency flywheel that generated trillions of dollars in revenue.”
Apple disclosed in a filing on Tuesday that Ternus’ annual salary was increased to $3 million. There will also be an annual equity award with a $55 million target value, starting 2027, a majority of which will be tied to the company’s stock performance.
Cook, meanwhile, will earn $2 million annually, effective September 26, and restricted stock units in 2027 with a target value of $45 million.
Critics have long accused Apple of losing its innovation edge in the Cook era. Cook, they say, has failed to answer what comes after the iPhone, as hardware rivals look to displace the smartphone as the default consumer device.
Cook’s tenure had other misses: a decade-long EV project Apple scrapped in 2024 just as they took off in China. The company also famously botched the launch of Apple Maps in 2012, months after Cook took charge, leading to the departure of close Jobs collaborator and software chief Scott Forstall.
Apple’s bet on the Vision Pro augmented-reality headset, which debuted at a whopping $3,499 in 2023, failed to produce strong sales, and its products have lagged in AI features, including delays in revamping Siri.
“AI is the single biggest challenge for Ternus. Apple needs to demonstrate that AI will be more than an app on the iPhone, more than Siri,” said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which owns Apple stock.
“Beyond AI, the pressure to continue to remove manufacturing from China without pressuring margins is a tall task to undertake but part of that process is already underway,” he said.
Apple’s dependence on China delivered decades of manufacturing efficiency, but rising Sino-U.S. tensions, tariffs and supply-chain disruptions exposed the risks of concentrating production in a single country, prompting the iPhone maker to expand manufacturing in India and other countries.
Those moves, including making most U.S.-bound iPhones in India by the end of 2026 and assembling certain devices such as AirPods and iPads in Vietnam, have helped Apple better navigate the tariff storm that disrupted businesses across the U.S.
Cook elevated a broader leadership team and recast Apple as an institution, giving himself room to focus on strategy and resource allocation while keeping a lower public profile, said Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial.
“This gave Cook space to make unpopular decisions and even be ruthless out of the spotlight.”

How to Raise Resilient Children
Introducing a new newsletter series on parenting with more happiness and less worry
Sign up for Raising Resilient Children, Russell Shaw’s eight-week guide to parenting with more happiness and less worry.
When I was 27, I became dean of students at a school in Northern California. I was responsible for 400 students across grades 6 through 12, immersing myself in the lives of other people’s children and learning so much along the way. But I didn’t have kids of my own.
And then I did. Driving him home from the hospital, I kept twisting around at red lights to check on the tiny person strapped into the car seat behind me. I couldn’t quite believe they were letting me take him home. There was no orientation, no manual, no one checking whether I actually knew what I was doing. Just me, my wife, and this small human we were now responsible for raising into an adult.
That’s the thing no one tells you when you’re 27 and confidently managing other people’s kids or newly a parent yourself: There isn’t a single right way to raise a child. Kids are different, circumstances are different, and anyone pitching a foolproof formula is making a fool’s promise. Still, after 25 years as a parent and more than 30 as a school administrator, I’ve come to believe that some approaches serve kids—and parents—better than others. In my eight-week newsletter series, I want to share some of what I’ve learned. I’m not offering a rulebook. Instead, I’m aiming for an invitation to think a little differently about the job.
Sign up now, and you’ll receive an email from me tomorrow at 6 a.m. ET, and then once a week for seven more weeks. Each week, I’ll discuss a different story I’ve written for The Atlantic. Topics will include motivation, friendship, failure, and AI. I’ll tell you a bit about what inspired the story, why it still feels true to me, and what it might mean for you. I’ll also include an original essay, written just for this course, and I’ll take some of your questions. I don’t have a tidy theory of parenting to sell you, and I won’t pretend that the next eight weeks will resolve the hardest questions that you might be carrying about your own kids. What I can offer is what I’ve noticed along the way: that even on the hardest days, there’s real joy in this work, if you know where to look for it.

As the Centre pushes to widen the role of AYUSH in India’s healthcare system — including through greater coverage, rural outreach and integration with mainstream health services — the country’s AYUSH medical education infrastructure has expanded rapidly.
But the expansion appears to have been driven largely by non-government institutions, according to government data.
India must use the AYUSH opportunity
The number of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) colleges rose from 789 in 2021 to 971 in 2024, an increase of about 23%. Over the same period, total admission capacity grew from 63,477 to 79,593, or nearly 25%, while permitted seats grew from 50,711 to 72,490 — an increase of about 43%.
The 2021 figures cover Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga and Naturopathy, Homoeopathy and Sowa-Rigpa. By April 2024, the Ministry registered 541 Ayurveda, 58 Unani, 17 Siddha, 71 Yoga and Naturopathy, 277 Homoeopathy and seven Sowa-Rigpa colleges.
Of the 541 Ayurveda colleges in April 2024, 467 were non-government — nearly 86% of the total. In Homoeopathy, 236 of 277 colleges, or about 85%, were non-government.
The pattern was similar in other systems. Of the 58 Unani colleges, only 16 were government-run; just three of 17 Siddha colleges and 15 of 71 Yoga and Naturopathy colleges were government institutions. Data clearly indicates that non-government institutions have become an important source of undergraduate medical education in AYUSH.
Additionally, the Ministry’s annual report for 2024-25 shows that 60,890 students were admitted against 63,073 permitted undergraduate seats in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy (ASU&H).
Ayurveda had almost full utilisation, with 39,952 of 40,136 permitted seats filled, Homoeopathy accounted for 1,887 vacancies — more than 86% of the total. The Ministry has also begun collecting admission data from State and Union Territory counselling authorities, improving the availability of national-level vacancy data.
Spending rises from a low base
Central spending under AYURGYAN, the Centre’s scheme supporting AYUSH education, capacity building, continuing medical education, research and innovation, has also increased.
The allocation rose from ₹8.42 crore in 2021-22 to ₹10.5 crore in 2022-23, ₹14.66 crore in 2023-24 and ₹48.5 crore in 2024-25, according to Ministry data placed before Parliament.
This, however, is not an education-only budget as AYURGYAN also supports capacity building and continuing medical education, research, and innovation; from 2023-24, it includes Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research.

There are so many protein products on the market.
What was once relegated to protein powders has transformed into a huge industry, with everything from protein-infused cookies and pancake mix, and now, soda.
Protein soda is essentially a sparkling, sweetened beverage with added protein — but which ones are really worth drinking?
I visited four grocery stores in San Diego County and ultimately found five cherry protein drinks from Summit Popz, Clean Simple Eats, Premier Protein, Proda, and Barebells to review.
For each, the protein source is whey protein isolate, a by-product of cheesemaking that's essentially highly filtered, protein-rich whey with less lactose and fat than typical whey.
In terms of criteria, I was looking for something flavorful and enticing to drink, with a fair amount of carbonation. I also factored in cost and nutritional value, including calories, sugar, and protein.
Here's how they ranked from my least favorite to my top pick.
5. Clean Simple Eats cherry-lime clear protein soda
Cost: $3.49 for one 12-ounce can
Calories: 60 calories
Protein: 10 grams
Added sugar: 0 grams
The cherry-lime clear protein soda by Clean Simple Eats had a milky aroma from the get-go, likely due to the grass-fed whey protein isolate.
There was a touch of cherry-lime flavor, but the milkiness made this taste more like a cherry cream soda to me. Cherry really overpowered the drink.
My main issue with this was that it had a distinct whey-protein taste that made me keenly aware I was indeed drinking something meant to be a protein beverage.
I can appreciate the protein and the no-added-sugar — it uses stevia-leaf extract as a sweetener — but I wouldn't sip this again because of the flavor.
For me, there are other options with similar nutritional content that are more enjoyable.
4. Barebells sweet-cherry protein soda
Cost: $3.49 for one 12-ounce can
Calories: 50 calories
Protein: 10 grams
Added sugar: 0 grams
This Barebells beverage is the outlier of the group because it contains 200 milligrams of caffeine, and the other don't contain any.
This cherry protein soda smelled and tasted like a liquid Jolly Rancher. It's the most candy-like of all the drinks I tried and is sweetened with sucralose (a zero-calorie artificial sweetener) as the sweetener. I didn't really pick up cherry flavoring, mostly a general sweet, fruity candy flavor.
I suppose this would be good if you want something as far removed from a protein soda as possible. To me, it just tasted like an energy drink. In a way, the overt sweetness covered any lingering whey protein isolate flavor.
The result is far too cloying for my taste, but I prefer the candy taste to the distinct whey flavoring of Clean Simple Eats. I wouldn't want to drink this Barebells option again, either, but I could see someone with a sweet tooth (and a caffeine craving) loving it.
3. Summit Popz protein cherry-limeade sparkling beverage
Cost: $1.99 for one 12-ounce can
Calories: 70 calories
Protein: 15 grams
Added sugar: 0 grams
I love Aldi's wide selection of products, so I wasn't surprised to see it offers its own take on protein drinks through its private label, Summit Popz.
It's labeled a "sparkling beverage" rather than a soda, but I included it in this ranking because it met my criteria: It has added protein and is carbonated and sweetened.
It had a clearer cherry-and-lime flavor that made it seem more authentic to its label, and wasn't too sweet despite the use of sucralose.
I appreciate the price, too, as it was the most affordable of the five I tried. However, it can't rank higher because the carbonation felt severely lacking. It's almost like I opened a soda, left it in the fridge for a few hours, and came back to it.
Perhaps I just got a dud of a can, but I felt this needed considerably more effervescence for it to live up to the "sparkling" part of its name.
I would, however, get it again based on price and protein content, which help boost the overall rating.
2. Proda cherry-lime protein soda
Cost: $3.49 for one 12-ounce can
Calories: 40 calories
Protein: 10 grams
Added sugar: 0 grams
Proda's Soda cherry-lime protein soda had the most authentic soda-like feel out of anything so far. It also had a refreshing cherry-lime flavor, so it delivers on both of its names.
It uses stevia and monk fruit to offer sweetness without being cloying, which seems to be a winning combination. There was a touch of whey flavor, but it was somewhat balanced with the cherry lime flavoring.
It has the fewest calories of all beverages, but the real highlight was the flavor and carbonation. This was pleasant to drink, and I enjoyed it well beyond the first couple of sips.
It would be enjoyable as a soda alternative with a meal or just as an afternoon pick-me-up. I did notice this drink had a mild whey aftertaste, but the many pros outweighed this slight con.
It delightfully delivered a mix of soda carbonation, cherry-lime flavors, and protein content.
1. Premier Protein black-cherry sparkling protein soda
Cost: About $2.24 for a 12-ounce can
Calories: 90 calories
Protein: 15 grams
Added sugar: 3 grams
At the time of purchase, I only found the Premier Protein soda available in packs of four for $8.94. The price per can was slightly higher than Aldi's but still considerably cheaper than everything else on this list.
This was the only soda with cane sugar listed as an ingredient, which brings 3 grams of added sugar. I think this helped mellow the flavor without making it ultra-sweet, which I find alternative sweeteners often do. Premier Protein also uses stevia extract, which seemed balanced by the sugar.
This is the highest-calorie option on the list and is tied with Summit Popz for the drink with the most protein, at 15 grams. Impressively, both contain more protein than a ½-cup serving of cottage cheese (14 grams).
It didn't have as obvious a protein taste; instead, the cherry-lime flavor came to the forefront. I could discern both flavors, which gave this drink a fruity, uplifting taste.
Final verdict: Premier Protein's soda was my top pick, but there's a drink here for everyone
Ultimately, Premier Protein's black-cherry sparkling protein soda was the drink I enjoyed most and would be most likely to repurchase.
The tasty flavor, solid carbonation, balanced sweetness, affordable price, and high protein content put it solidly at the top of my ranking.
However, it's the highest-calorie drink I tasted and the only soda on this list with added sugars. If a low-sugar, low-calorie diet is a priority for you and your nutrition goals, you may prefer one of the others on this list.
After all, everyone's taste buds are different — and each drink on this list has its pros and cons.

A makeover for college: No gym, no meal plan and two years of work
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
MONTPELIER, Vt. — The buildings that frame a grassy quad on a hill above Vermont's capital city are all red brick and white trim, dating from as far back as the 1870s.
This quintessential college campus from the 19th century is where a group of business, college and government leaders is working on the task of reinventing higher education for the 21st century.
An entirely new college is being planned here to change not only how higher education is delivered, but at what price. It also proposes to highlight ways the current business model no longer works, as evidenced by the 152 colleges and universities that have closed or merged since 2016, and the 442 others that a new projection says are at risk.
So deeply entrenched are the problems confronting higher education that a growing chorus of innovators says the easiest way to fix them is to begin again from scratch.
The Greenway Institute — "green" as in new — will adopt instructional methods proven to work well, such as real-world training under the supervision of faculty mentors, while stripping away such things as layers of administrators and nonacademic amenities that make college in the United States so expensive.
"It's not fancy. It's a place where you do have a meaningful relationship with your faculty members. But you also take out your own trash," said Mark Somerville, the founding president.
Even more unexpected than the location of this startup is that it comes at a time when so many colleges are closing. In Vermont alone, seven private colleges have shut down in the last 10 years.
But Somerville, the former provost of Olin College of Engineering in Massachusetts, said this "moment of mass extinction" makes it clearer than ever that "we need new models in higher ed."
Enough of these experimental higher education institutions are in the planning stages that they have been organized by Duke University into a Future Universities Alliance. Greenway is a member.
Project Polymath, for instance — founded by Dan Futrell, former CEO of the Pat Tillman Foundation, which gives scholarships to military veterans — proposes to mentor bachelor's degree students beginning in 2028. Each student will take three majors and then be placed in an apprenticeship with an employer for two years.
There is "broad agreement that something has to change and also recognition that changing legacy institutions from within is agonizingly difficult," said Brian Rosenberg, former president of Macalester College in Minnesota. He is also author of the book "Whatever It Is, I'm Against It": Resistance to Change in Higher Education and a member of both the Greenway and Polymath advisory boards.
Greenway bought its campus in 2023 from the Vermont College of Fine Arts, which had mostly gone remote by then and would be acquired a year later by the California Institute of the Arts after enrollment declines and multimillion-dollar deficits.
Many renovations are complete, including the transformation of one building into shop rooms full of tools that students will use to work on real-world projects under faculty supervision.
Inside another building at the center of the campus — four stories of iconic, red-brick, Second Empire-style architecture, with big arched windows and a mansard roof — the Greenway team has arranged on a whiteboard color-coded sticky notes listing the many steps it takes to start a college.
The new school tentatively plans to open in the fall of 2027. It has raised $4.5 million toward a goal of $30 million by 2031, Somerville said — including a grant from the National Science Foundation, which it shares with an existing traditional partner institution, Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. It's also making money by renting out space it doesn't need.
Greenway's founders and advisers include tech executives, CEOs, a onetime Vermont secretary of education, a NASA engineer and current and former administrators from Harvard University, Dartmouth College, Tufts University and other schools. It will teach one subject: engineering.
The project tested its model in the spring semester of 2025 on four college sophomores from other schools, which gave them academic credit for coming to the Greenway campus and doing hands-on work with faculty supervisors in a prototype semester. Instead of sitting in conventional classes and lectures, the students designed wind turbines and solar-powered traffic signals.
"Basically, they learned electrical, mechanical and some controls by doing, versus somebody standing at the front and saying, 'All right, you know, this is Norton's equivalent theorem [of electronic circuits]' that you'll never use in your life," said Troy McBride, co-founder of a Vermont-based solar panel manufacturer and chair of Greenway's board of directors.
New research by scholars at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the Strada Education Foundation shows that work-based learning improves students' likelihood of getting jobs, advancing in their careers and earning more than classmates who studied in other ways. But fewer than half of students at public four-year universities get the experience of paid work-based learning, a separate Strada study shows. (Strada is among the funders of The Hechinger Report, which co-produced this story.)
"We're stuck in the 1950s," McBride said of traditional instruction. "We haven't responded to the internet, let alone AI. We're still memorizing things that don't need to be memorized, and we're not teaching skills and tools. We're teaching facts, which is the least useful thing in these times."
Jazz Gonzalez, who was part of Greenway's prototype semester, said conventional lectures in his previous years at Elizabethtown College left him wanting more.
"I would always say, 'OK, but how do I dig deeper into this? How do I use this, and how do I actually apply it to what I'm going to be doing in the future?'" said Gonzalez, a Pennsylvania native who graduated this past spring.
When Greenway is operating fully, students are expected to live on campus for two years doing projects and then go on to real-world workplaces for an additional two years while continuing to get support from faculty.
That lowers the cost to the college of providing housing. It's also part of the educational strategy: Research from the Association of College and University Housing Officers shows that students who live on campus benefit from a communal setting for the first two years, with lower dropout rates than classmates who live off campus. But "by the time a student is in their junior year at most colleges, they're, like, 'Could I go study abroad now?'" Somerville said.
Greenway students will also shop for their own food and cook it for themselves in communal kitchens with utensils provided, plan their own extracurricular activities and, if they want to go to the gym, sign up for the nearby Planet Fitness or other off-campus options.
"It goes right to the point," said Emmanuel Attah, an engineering major at Elizabethtown who was also part of Greenway's prototype semester.
Not having climbing walls or football games "really didn't matter to us," Gonzalez said.
Those kinds of amenities are part of what's driving up the cost of college. In the 10 years leading up to the COVID-19 pandemic, the consulting firm McKinsey found, spending on noninstructional services grew four times faster than spending on teaching.
"You see tuition going up and up and up and up, and not necessarily for the reasons that a student would want them to go up, like a better educational experience," McBride said. "A lot of it is for amenities, extras and for space sitting empty."
Increasingly, said Somerville, "young people and their parents are looking at [college] and saying, 'Does this actually make sense?'"
There's another reason to make students responsible for cooking their own meals and scheduling their free time, said Annick Dewald, Greenway's first faculty member: so they learn how.
"We assume that they can't balance cooking for themselves and cleaning up for themselves, in addition to being college students, and I'm not totally sure why," said Dewald, who teaches engineering.
"Employers have told me the hardest thing about fresh-from-college undergrads is getting them to show up on time or sleep eight hours at night or to figure out how to feed themselves," she said. "That to me is a product of how we view college or what services we provide."
Hannah Root, Greenway's chief of staff, recounted taking the college's "test" students on their first food-shopping excursion, which she called one of the most challenging moments of the prototype semester. There were "just so many real decisions that they were having to make that it was clear they hadn't really experienced before," such as whether to buy organic produce.
Without the frills, Greenway expects to charge tuition of $25,000 or less per year, offset by what students would be paid during their third and fourth years for their in-person work — generally called "co-op" jobs by other universities and colleges that offer them. The average full-time co-op pays more than $25 an hour for juniors and seniors, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers. That comes to more than $50,000 a year.
The average published total cost of attendance at private, nonprofit four-year universities is $65,470, the College Board reports.
Greenway has to wait until it formally opens to apply for accreditation, a process that then takes at least four years. That's one of the many examples of red tape that makes innovation challenging, its founders say. It also means students won't be eligible for federal grants or loans for a while. Greenway's founders said they expect the money they raise will offset that, and that accreditation would be retroactively applied to graduates' degrees.
The plan is to grow to 500 students in Montpelier, half of them on campus at any given time, and to add other locations nationwide, Somerville said. For now, he said, Greenway needs about 370 students by 2031 to break even.
Greenway may not be for everyone, said Vermont state Rep. Rebecca Holcombe, a former Vermont secretary of education and onetime candidate for governor, and another founder.
It's "for kids who really know what they want to do," she said.
While the particularly large number of closing colleges in Vermont may seem a bad omen for an effort to open a new one, Holcombe said experiencing the problem has made the state that much more focused on it.
"We're ready to start saying, 'OK, if not this, then what?'"
